# ON THE PREFACE TO THE READER
## Author’s Notes.

(1) **To those (five bodies) the number of the heavens, the proportions and the ratio of motions, etc.** *Although all things are coherent with one another, the number of the six primary Orbs is properly derived from the five Bodies of the Sun <note>original: "Corporibus Solis"; Kepler is referring to the spatial arrangement of the planetary spheres around the Sun</note>: the proportion is indeed taken for the most part from the five Geometric Bodies, but it yielded in the smallest details to the motions, as the final cause received into the Idea of the work right from the start. And this must be understood regarding the single slowest and the single fastest motions of each planet—that is, regarding the Motions considered for the sake of their own property. But the periodic Motions: that is, the number of days derived in the circuit of each Planet, have receded further from the 5 bodies, as much from the proportion of the orbs as from the Eccentricities (which were established from the Harmonies).*

(2) **The dispute concerning the primary motion, that it happens by the rotation of the earth.** *You have that discussion fully provided in the first book of the <term>Epitome Astronomiæ|Epitome of Copernican Astronomy, Kepler's influential textbook published between 1617 and 1621</term>.*

(3) **The Solar motion [attributed] to the Earth.** *This dispute was inserted into my Commentaries on the motion of Mars <note>The Astronomia Nova (1609)</note>, especially in the Introduction; it is found accurately in book IV of the Epitome, page 542. Plainly demonstrative arguments, shaped from the restored innermost depths of Astronomy, are gathered there.*

(4) **Which similarity I shall pursue in the Cosmography.** *Indeed, I have published no book under the title of "Cosmography" since that time: but that similarity was related by me in Book I of the Epitome, page 42, where I discuss the outermost figure of the World, and in Book IV of the same, pages 437 and 448, where I dispute concerning the three primary members of the World. Nor is it to be held as an empty similarity; but it should be counted among the causes, as the form and <term>Archetype|The original model or 'blueprint' upon which God designed the universe</term> of the World.*

(5) **Between Jupiter and Mars I interposed a new Planet.** *Not one that would run around Jupiter, like Galileo’s <term>Medicean stars|The four largest moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto), discovered by Galileo in 1610</term>; let you not be deceived, I never thought of those; but one which, like the primary planets themselves, would encircle the Sun placed in the center of the System in its own course.*

(6) **Nor by [the power] of any Number.** *See, even then I rejected "counting numbers," as they call them. I held it among the most important things in that Work to likewise cast them out from Harmonic foundations.*

(7) **Dignity from things posterior to the world.** *The <term>senarius|The number six</term>, however, has something abstract from created things, because it is the first among the <term>perfect numbers|A number equal to the sum of its proper divisors (e.g., 1+2+3=6)</term>: for a thing is held to be perfect if there are as many units in its parts as in the whole. Does this property, therefore, procure some dignity for a "counting number"? Let it be considered both what kind of dignity this is, and how it applies to Number. First, this dignity seems to be nothing. For if there were any dignity, the discipline of Harmony would seem to have provided testimony for all perfect numbers. But that discipline receives none besides the six. For the remaining perfect numbers are multiples of primes, as is clear from the last proposition of Euclid’s Book IX. Therefore (by Axiom III of my Book III of the <term>Harmonices|The Harmonies of the World (1619), where Kepler linked geometry, music, and astronomy</term>, page 11, and by Proposition VIII of Book IV, page 145, which rely on propositions 45, 46, and 47 of Book I), all so-called perfect numbers, except the six, are exiled from the terms that constitute concordances; even the sense of hearing attests to this; and this is because of the Primes, such as the number seven, etc., from which they are derived. For the Harmonic sections in Book III, proposition 19, page 26, are numbered as seven, which is a prime number: but that number seven gives to none of them the quality of being Harmonic; rather, each is Harmonic by itself first, and only afterwards does it happen to them, once all are established, that they are seven in number. But neither does this condition itself, by which perfect numbers are defined, have anything of dignity when considered in itself: namely, that all the numbers which measure one specific number, when fused into one, should equal the thing measured. Equality is indeed something beautiful, but this equality is accidental to the numbers themselves by reason of each individual one; it brings nothing to their constitution, but results by Geometric necessity from things already established; nor does it give this to them, that they be more articulated; even though it is occupied with this very articulation and is in some way defined by it: rather, he who is ordered to affect this so-called perfection is by that very fact restricted from being able to take the most articulated ones. And as we previously reasoned about sections, so now we can also speak about numbers measuring a specific one: namely, that first each of them for its own sake measures the proposed number, not receiving this nature from a pretended equality, but only afterwards does it happen to them individually that as a whole they equal the thing measured. See a similar place in my Book III of the Harmonies, near the end of chapter III, page 31; concerning the occurrence of the number three, for which there is here an occurrence of equality. Therefore, this equality confers no more virtue or skill upon numbers than the discovery of a treasure does to a farmer; as is believable*

JOHN KEPLER’S

*...I do not at all deny that the number six <note>original: "senarius"</note> pleased God the Creator because of this nature. I say secondly, this property does not belong to Numbers as counting units. This is easily proven from Euclid’s Books 7, 8, and 9. For as that author demonstrates, to show that this perfection exists in certain things, he is forced to use <term>figurate numbers|numbers represented by geometric shapes, like a square or triangle</term>—that is, as the schools say, "numbered numbers," or parallelograms divided by equal measure in length and width. Therefore, if this so-called perfection were a mark of the highest excellence, it would belong primarily to Geometric figures. And although the number six has its true and real excellence from the hexagon (by which figure it advances itself in the <term>harmonic discipline|the study of mathematical proportions in music and the cosmos</term>), it is not for that reason suitable for establishing the number of primary bodies in the World. For that figure [the hexagon] divides the circle, as a continuous quantity, into six parts; however, the worldly bodies <note>the planets</note> are not parts of a single continuous quantity. That figure exists among plane surfaces, whereas the bodies of the world must traverse solid spaces, or spaces of three dimensions. I was right, therefore, to reject the gifts of the number six considered by itself, so as not to adopt them among the causes of the six Heavens. I rightly judged that some evident causes ought to have preceded it, from which that "six" of the Heavens would then result of its own accord—just as in the harmonic discipline, once the proper causes of progression are set, the <term>ternary|group of three</term> of consonants results in the same sounds (page 31, later part), and the <term>septenary|group of seven</term> of harmonic divisions (page 27, later part).*

(8) **For quantity [was] in the beginning with the body.** *Indeed, the Ideas of quantities are and were coeternal with God—were God himself. They still exist as patterns in the minds made in the image of God (even in their essence). On this point, the pagan philosophers and the Doctors of the Church agree.*

(9) **The Earth is a Circle.** *I had written those things for myself alone; I understood "the Earth" to mean the Orb on which it is carried, called "the Great Orb" by Copernicus. Thus, for any planet, I meant its orb. And the last clause—"You have the reason," etc.—also pertains to this opinion copied from my notebooks.*

(10) **To suspect wrongly, etc.** *I labored childishly so that no one would accuse me of being a "novelty-seeker" <note>original: "novatorem"</note> who wrote a book only for the sake of showing off my intellect. Against such people, I offered both my prayer and my deepest persuasion of the truth of what the book contained, and finally my eagerness to discuss these discoveries with others. These were, I believe, suitable reasons for driving away a foolish sense of shame.*

## CHAPTER I.

->*By what reasons the hypotheses of Copernicus are made consistent. And an explanation of Copernicus’s hypotheses.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' at the start of the text, containing a woodcut scene of a figure seated at a desk or table in an interior setting.</image-desc>

ALTHOUGH it is a godly act, right at the beginning of this investigation into Nature, to check whether anything is said that contradicts Holy Scripture, I nevertheless think it is premature to stir up that controversy here with too much anxiety. I promise this in general: I will say nothing that would be an insult to Holy Scripture, and if Copernicus is ever convicted of such a thing in my eyes, I will consider his work as nothing. This has always been my mind since I first began to study Copernicus’s books *On the Revolutions* <note>original: "Reuolutionum"</note>.

Since, therefore, no religious objection prevented me from listening to Copernicus if he spoke reasonably, my first faith in him was won by that most beautiful agreement of all things appearing in the heavens with Copernicus’s views. For he not only demonstrated past motions recovered from the furthest reaches of antiquity, but also predicted future ones—not with absolute certainty, perhaps, but far more certainly than Ptolemy, <term>Alphonso|Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored the Alfonsine Tables used in medieval astronomy</term>, and the others. But something far greater is this: that those things which we are taught to marvel at by others, Copernicus alone provides a most beautiful reason for, and he removes the cause of our wonder—which is the ignorance of causes. I could never teach the reader this more easily than if I were to act as an advisor and persuader for him to read the <term>Narratio|The 'First Account' by Rheticus, the first published summary of Copernican theory</term> of <term>Rheticus|Georg Joachim Rheticus, Copernicus's only pupil</term>. For not everyone has the leisure to read Copernicus’s own books, *On the Revolutions*.

(2) And on this point, I could never agree with those who rely on the example of an accidental demonstration <note>original: "accidentariae demonstrationis" — a logical argument where a true conclusion is reached despite starting with false premises</note>—which, by the necessity of a <term>Syllogism|A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>, brings forth something true from false premises. These people, I say, relying on this example, used to argue that it is possible for the hypotheses favored by Copernicus to be false, and yet for true <term>phenomena|the observable appearances of the planets</term> <note>original Greek: "Φαινόμενα"</note> to follow from them just as if from genuine principles.

For that example does not fit. For that sequence of logic following from false premises is a matter of chance; and such is the nature of falsehood that when it is applied to something else related to it, it reveals itself—unless you freely allow that debater to assume infinite other false propositions, never remaining consistent with himself in his steps forward and backward. It is otherwise with the man who places the Sun in the center. For command him to demonstrate anything you please of those things which truly appear in the Heavens, using the hypothesis once it has been established—to go backward, to go forward, to gather one thing from another, and to do whatever truth allows—he will not hesitate in anything, if it be genuine, and even from the most intricate windings of demonstrations, he will return most consistently to that one center. But if you object that the same thing can partly still be said (and could once be said) of the ancient tables and hypotheses—namely, that they satisfy the <term>phenomena|celestial appearances</term> <note>original Greek: "Φαινομένοις"</note>, and yet they are rejected by Copernicus as false—and that the same answer can therefore be given to Copernicus: namely, that although he gives an excellent account of those things which appear, he nevertheless errs in his hypothesis. To this I answer, first, that the ancient hypotheses of several main points give no explanation at all. For instance, they are ignorant of...

IOAN. KEPLERI

...the causes of the numbers, the quantity, and the time of the retrogradations; and why they agree so precisely (3) with the position and the mean motion of the Sun. (4) In all these matters, since a most beautiful order appears in Copernicus's work, it is necessary that a underlying cause also be present. Furthermore, Copernicus denies nothing of those hypotheses which provide a consistent cause for appearances and agree with visual observation; rather, he assumes and explains all of them. For while he seems to have changed many things in the usual hypotheses <note>the traditional Ptolemaic geocentric system</note>, in reality this is not the case. For it can happen that the same result occurs from two different specific assumptions, because those two fall under the same general category, and it is for the sake of that category that the thing in question first occurs.

Thus, Ptolemy demonstrated the rising and setting of stars, not by this most direct and equal middle term: "Because the Earth is immobile in the center." Nor does Copernicus demonstrate this same thing by this means: "Because the Earth, distant from the center, revolves." For it was sufficient for both to say (as both indeed did) that these things happen because there occurs a certain separation of motions between the sky and the Earth, and because no distance of the Earth from the center is perceived among the fixed stars. Therefore, Ptolemy did not demonstrate by a false and accidental means if he demonstrated <term>phenomena|φαινόμενα: observable appearances of the stars and planets</term>. He failed only against the law of <term>by itself|κατ' αὐτὸ: an Aristotelian logical principle (kath' auto) meaning a property belongs to a subject by its very nature</term> because he thought these things happened because of the specific case <note>species</note>, whereas they happen because of the general category <note>genus</note>.

From this it appears that from the fact that Ptolemy demonstrated true things—consistent with the Heavens and our eyes—from a false arrangement of the world, I say there is no reason to suspect something similar about the Copernican hypotheses. Rather, what was said at the beginning remains: the principles of Copernicus cannot be false, since from them such a consistent explanation is given for many <term>phenomena|φαινόμενα</term> unknown to the ancients, (5) insofar as they are rendered from those principles. 

That most fortunate man, <term>Tycho Brahe|A Danish nobleman and astronomer (1546–1601) known for his extremely accurate astronomical observations</term>, an astronomer greater than any praise, saw this. Although he entirely disagreed with Copernicus regarding the location of the Earth, he nevertheless retained from him that for which we have the causes of things previously unknown: namely, that the Sun is the center of the five planets. For even this is a more narrow means for demonstrating the <term>retrogradations|repedationes: the apparent backward motion of planets</term>: "The Sun is immobile in the center." For that general principle is sufficient: "The Sun is at the center of the five planets." 

But why Copernicus took the specific case instead of the general category, and furthermore placed the Sun in the center of the world and made the Earth mobile around it, there were other reasons. For to pass from Astronomy to Physics, or Cosmography: these Copernican hypotheses not only do not offend against the Nature of things, but assist it much more. Nature loves simplicity; she loves unity. Nothing idle or superfluous has ever existed in her; rather, one thing is often destined by her for many effects. Yet while there is no end to the invention of spheres in the usual hypotheses, in Copernicus's system many motions follow from very few spheres. I will not speak for now of the overlapping of the spheres of Venus and Mercury, and other difficulties with which ancient astronomy still struggles in such freedom of inventing spheres. 

And so this man [Copernicus] did not only free Nature from that burdensome and useless equipment of so many immense spheres, but he also opened to us an inexhaustible treasure of most divine reasoning regarding the most beautiful suitability of the whole world and of all bodies. Nor do I hesitate to affirm that whatever Copernicus gathered <term>after the fact|a posteriori: reasoning from observed effects to causes</term> and demonstrated by sight through geometric axioms, all of that—even by the testimony of <term>Aristotle|The Greek philosopher whose physics dominated medieval thought</term> himself if he were alive (as <term>Rheticus|Georg Joachim Rheticus, Copernicus's only pupil</term> frequently hopes)—could be demonstrated <term>from first principles|a priori: reasoning from causes to effects</term> without any ambiguity. But...

Indeed, Rheticus’s account <note>referring to Georg Joachim Rheticus, who published the *Narratio Prima* in 1540, the first printed introduction to Copernican theory</note> and Copernicus himself have previously dealt with all these matters more extensively and with the dignity they deserve. If anything can be explained more fully, (6) there will be another time and place for it; for now, it is enough to have touched upon it, so that by this mention, the reader might recognize the second reason that drew me to the side of Copernicus.

Nor did I embrace this sect <note>referring to the "school" of Copernican thought</note> rashly or without the most serious authority of my teacher, the most famous mathematician Michael Maestlin. For although he was my first guide and instructor, both in other matters and especially in these philosophical reflections—and therefore ought to have been mentioned in the first place—he nevertheless provided me with a (7) third reason for holding this view through another specific observation. He discovered that the Comet of the year 1577 <note>this comet was a pivotal event in astronomy; Maestlin and Tycho Brahe used it to prove that comets were farther away than the Moon, challenging the ancient idea that the heavens were made of solid, impenetrable spheres</note> moved most consistently according to the motion of Venus as presented by Copernicus. By concluding from its <term>supralunar|above the moon</term> height, he found that it completed its course within the Copernican sphere of Venus itself. If anyone considers how easily a falsehood contradicts itself, and conversely, how constantly truth harmonizes with truth, they might, by this alone, rightly take it as the strongest argument for the Copernican arrangement of the spheres.

->*However, so that you may find all those things I have said about both hypotheses to be most true: receive this brief explanation of the Copernican hypotheses, and the two tables created for this purpose.*<-

To understand the order of the Spheres of the World according to the opinion of Copernicus, look at the first Table at the end of this chapter and the notes written upon it. (8) Four motions are attributed to the Earth by Copernicus according to various respects (Copernicus, aiming for brevity, says three, which are in reality four), all of which create a certain apparent variety in the motions of the remaining planets.

The first is the motion of the sphere or Orbit itself, which carries the Earth like a star <note>Kepler uses "star" here in the general sense of a celestial body, including the planets</note> around the Sun annually. And since that orbit is <term>eccentric|off-center; a circle where the Sun is not at the exact geometric center</term>, with (9) an eccentricity that is moreover changeable, (10) it must be considered by us in three ways. (11) Initially, by setting aside the eccentricity: this Orbit, and the motion of the Earth, provides these advantages: we do not need the three eccentrics used in the common hypotheses—namely, those of the Sun, Venus, and Mercury. For because the Earth is carried around these three planets, the inhabitants of the Earth think those three are carried around themselves while immobile. Thus, from one motion, they make three. If there were more stars within the orbit of the Earth, they would ascribe this motion to even more of them. With this orbit established, three great <term>epicycles|small circles whose centers move along the circumference of a larger circle; used in the old system to explain why planets seem to move backward</term> of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars also vanish, along with their motions. How that happens can be seen in the attached parallel diagrams. For again, because the Earth travels in its orbit in the sight of Saturn (which is as if it were at rest because it is slower), moving away from and toward Saturn, the inhabitants think that Saturn is traveling in its own epicycle, approaching and receding, while they themselves rest in the center of its orbit. Therefore, they think the circle A B is the epicycles g, i, l. Likewise, because of this same approach and recession of the Earth in its orbit relative to the Planets, the very <term>latitudes|the north-south position of a planet relative to the ecliptic</term> of the five planets seem to us to take on a certain variety; to save this <term>libration|an oscillating or swaying motion</term>, it was necessary for Ptolemy to establish five other motions. All of these vanish once a single motion of the Earth is established.

And although all these motions, eleven in number, are banished from the world

# JOHANNES KEPLER

...they were born <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the motions of the planets.</note>, by substituting this single motion of the Earth: nevertheless, causes are still provided for many other things which Ptolemy could not explain from so many distinct motions.

For first, one might ask of Ptolemy: how does it happen that the three <term>eccentrics|off-center circular paths</term> of the Sun, Venus, and Mercury have equal periods of revolution? The answer is that they do not truly revolve themselves, but rather the single Earth revolves in their place. 2. Why do the five planets become <term>retrograde|appearing to move backward in the sky</term>, but the <term>Luminaries|the Sun and Moon</term> do not? Regarding the Sun, the answer is first that it is at rest; thus it happens that the motion of the Earth, which is always direct, appears to belong purely and undisturbed to the Sun itself, though seen from the opposite part of the heavens. Regarding the Moon, it is because the annual motion of the Earth is truly shared between the Moon's heaven and the Earth.
<margin>(12)</margin>
Now, two things that possess the same motion in every respect seem to be at rest relative to one another. Hence, the motion of the Earth is not felt in the Moon as it is in the other planets. Regarding the "superior" planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—the answer is: because they are slower than the Earth, and because that circle and motion of the Earth is mistakenly thought to belong to them. Therefore, just as to those who might look out from the globe of Saturn, the Earth would sometimes seem to move forward (while it traveled through the half-circle PBN above the Sun) and sometimes seem to move backward (while it traveled through NAP) and stand still at points N and P; so it must be that to us looking out from the Earth, Saturn appears to be rolled in the opposite direction. Thus, while the Earth is at B, N, or A, Saturn is seen at b, n, or a of the other diagram. The "inferior" planets, Venus and Mercury, appear to move backward because they are faster than the Earth; thus, just as if the Earth stood motionless, Venus—running in the more distant part of its circle—describes a path plainly contrary to the one it completes in the part of the circle near the Earth.

3. Likewise, one could ask (though Ptolemy provides no answer): why are there such tiny <term>epicycles|small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger ones</term> in the large orbits, and why such immense ones in the small orbits? That is, why is the <term>prosthaphaeresis|the geometric correction or "equation" used to calculate a planet's true position</term> <note>original: "προσθαφαιρεσις"</note> of Mars greater than that of Jupiter, and Jupiter's greater than Saturn's? And why does Mercury not have a larger one than Venus, since it is lower <note>closer to the Sun</note> than Venus—given that among the other four, the lower one always has a larger one? Here the answer is easy. For the ancients thought the true orbits of Mercury and Venus were epicycles. Moreover, Mercury, being the swiftest, also has the smallest orbit. Regarding the superior planets, as each one is closer to the orbit of the Earth, it has a larger proportion to it and appears larger. Therefore, Mars, being the closest, has the greatest equation, while Saturn, being the highest, has the smallest. For if the eye were placed at G, the orbit PN would be seen under the angle TAV. But if it were at L, the same orbit would be seen under the angle RLS.

4. Similarly, the ancients wondered, not without reason, why the three superior planets are always at their lowest point in their epicycle when in opposition to the Sun, and at their highest in conjunction; as if, when the Earth, Sun, and Mars are in the same line, why Mars could not then be in any other place on its epicycle than at point γ. In Copernicus, the cause is easily rendered: for it is not Mars in an epicycle, but the Earth in its own orbit that causes this variation. Hence, if the Earth moves from A to B, the Sun will be between Mars (G) and the Earth (B). And then Mars will seem to have ascended from δ to γ in its "epicycle." But with the Earth existing at A, which is the point closest to G, Mars and the Sun will appear from A to be opposite each other. And these are the things that can be demonstrated to the eye from the diagram.

Now, next, let us also consider the eccentricity of this orbit.
<margin>(13)</margin>

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY

...turning, not by means of <term>deferents|the large circular paths that carry a planet</term>, but by an <term>epicycle|a smaller circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one</term> returning to its starting point a little more slowly than its own orbit. This motion of the <term>Apogee|the point in an orbit furthest from the center</term> also introduces something into the motions of the other planets. For Ptolemy calculates the <term>eccentricities|the distance by which an orbit's center is offset from the Earth</term> of the other planets from the center of the Earth; but if the center of the Earth's eccentricity and its Apogee should move into another part of the Zodiac according to the sequence of the signs, leaving behind the slower Apogees of the others, some change in the eccentricities of the other planets will occur. 

Ptolemaic astronomy will be greatly astonished by this once again and will flee to the invention of new spheres to demonstrate how these things can happen, even though they will follow from the single motion of the Earth. And indeed, this will barely happen after many centuries, but thirdly <margin>(15)</margin> the change in the Earth’s eccentricity—by which the center of the eccentricity approaches the Sun and recedes from it—has, from Ptolemy’s time even to our own, introduced a great effect in Mars and Venus. Since their eccentricities appear to have changed, what do you think Ptolemy would say? Would he again adopt new circles into that infinite crowd of others? None of these are necessary in the system of Copernicus. Copernicus achieved all these many great things through the position and motion of a single circle, AB; for which reason he deservedly gave it the name **GREAT**, even though it was relatively small. This first motion of the heaven of the Moon was shared with the Earth.

Now let us see further what the remaining motions of the Earth achieve, which occur within that small circle of the Moon at A.

Therefore, the second motion is not of the whole orbit, but <margin>(16)</margin> of the celestial small-sphere, which encloses the globe of the Earth closely like a kernel. It tends in the opposite direction from East to West, just like the epicycles of the "superior" planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note>, by which their eccentricity is preserved by Copernicus. By its annual arrangement, it ensures that the <term>equinoctial|the Earth's equator projected onto the sky</term> always tilts toward the same part of the universe. For the poles of the Equinoctial (or of the body) are distant from the poles of this sphere by 23 and a half degrees. Since this motion is slightly faster than the annual motion of the "Great Circle," it causes the intersections of the circles—that is, the locations of the <term>equinoxes|the two times a year when day and night are of equal length</term>—to move gradually forward. 

Because of this tiny globe, that monstrous, huge, <term>starless|original: ἄναστρος (anastros)</term> Ninth Sphere of the <term>Alfonsine Tables|a 13th-century set of astronomical tables</term> collapses, as its function has been transferred to that previously necessary small sphere. The motion of the deferents of the Apogee of Venus also collapses, as it does not move unless the fixed stars are stated to move.

<margin>(18)</margin> The third motion is that of the Poles of the terrestrial globe, consisting of two <term>librations|slow, swinging oscillations</term>, one of which is twice as fast as the other and at right angles to it. This is managed through four circles, such that pairs of circles create each libration, and the combined librations themselves provide the appearance of a twisted garland, in this manner: One libration occurs in the <term>solstitial Colure|the great circle passing through the celestial poles and the solstices</term>, and it accounts for the variation in the declination of the Zodiac, which was noticed long after Ptolemy's time. Ptolemy would have also needed to invent something similar, and some modern thinkers have attempted to provide it by inventing an eleventh celestial sphere.

<image-desc>A small woodcut diagram showing two overlapping elongated ovals or figure-eights, representing the geometry of the third motion of the Earth's poles (the "librations").</image-desc>

The other libration, which occurs in the <term>equinoctial Colure|the great circle passing through the celestial poles and the equinoxes</term>, accounts for the unequal <term>precession of the equinoxes|the slow change in the orientation of Earth's axis</term>, and it eliminates the motion of <term>trepidation|a hypothesized oscillation of the equinoxes</term> from the eighth sphere of the fixed stars (which is the last sphere in Copernicus's system), restoring that sphere to its own rest. # JOHANNES KEPLER’S

...of all seven planets, as well as the motions of the <term>Apogees|the points in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun (or Earth in older models)</term>, which they would have had to possess (not without the assistance of several new circles) because it has been discovered that all motions proceed uniformly through the fixed stars.

Finally, the fourth motion is proper to the terrestrial globe itself and the surrounding air; its period is 24 hours, moving in the same direction as the others—namely, from West to East. Because of this, the rest of the world is thought to be carried from East to West, with its secondary motions undisturbed—a great miracle. Thus, that incredibly high and swift tenth "starless" <note>original Greek: ἄναστρος (anastros)</note> Sphere falls away; otherwise, its speed would have to cover millions of miles. And I ask you, look at the table and consider that our Earth, whose motion is being debated, barely equals a seventieth part of the diameter of the tiny lunar circle at A. From this little circle, then, turn your eyes to the vastness of Saturn, and from there to the inestimable height of the fixed stars. Finally, conclude whether it is easier to believe and to do: that the tiny point within circle A, the Earth, rotates in one direction; or rather that the whole world, with ten distinct motions (since there are ten spheres independent of one another), travels with unspeakable rapidity in the other direction, regarding nothing except that tiny point—that little image of Earth—and it alone remains immobile because there is nothing outside it.

(1) **[Untimely.]** Copernicus himself addresses this concern in his preface to Pope Paul III, the <term>Supreme Pontiff|the Pope</term>, but perhaps a bit too rigidly. He eventually paid the price for his speech more than 70 years after the publication of his book and his death; for he was "suspended," says the Censor, "until corrected." I believe this also implies: "until explained." For I have attempted to show, through reasons and examples in my *Introduction to the Commentaries on the Motions of Mars* <note>Known today as the Astronomia Nova (1609)</note>, how he is not contrary to Scripture, as he was dealing with a very different purpose. I also explained Copernicus's own words more clearly at the end of Book I of the *Epitome of Astronomy*. In these places, I hope the devout will be satisfied, provided they bring such talent and knowledge of astronomy to this judgment that the glory of God's visible works can be safely entrusted to their protection. To be sure, there is a "language of God," but is it not the common language of men? Therefore, in the most evident matters, every devout person will be extremely careful not to twist God's language so that it refutes the "finger of God" <note>Kepler uses "finger of God" to refer to the physical evidence of the natural world</note> in nature. Let him who cares for the praises of our Creator and Lord read, I say, my fifth book of *Harmonics* <note>The Harmonice Mundi (1619)</note>. Once the most exquisitely harmonic governing of motions is perceived, let him reflect whether there were just and significant reasons for the reconciliation I sought between the language and the finger of God. Or would it be better, by rejecting that reconciliation, to suppress the fame of this immense beauty of God's works through censorship? Such fame can never be achieved by any command, so that it might reach the knowledge of the common people, or even the lightly educated. Ignorance refuses to look at authority; it leaps into battle of its own accord, relying on the crowd and the shield of custom, which is impenetrable to the arrows of truth.

Indeed, the edge of an ax struck against iron is no longer useful even for wood. Let him whom it concerns take note of this.

I showed for what reason and to what extent a false hypothesis can sometimes reveal the truth.

(3) **[With the position and mean motion of the Sun.]** I did not yet know what I later wrote in the *Commentaries*...

### THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

...of Mars I have demonstrated; the Anomaly of the Great Circle <note>original: *orbis Magni*; referring to the Earth's orbit</note> or of Commutation, which causes the Retrogradations <note>the appearance of planets moving backward in the sky</note>, I have restored to the true motion and position of the Sun itself. Indeed, those who retain the old form of Astronomy are forced to marvel at this even more. From this very fact, demonstrative arguments arise: retrogradations do not arise from any real motion, either of the planets or of the entire celestial system, but are transferred to all the planets from the motion of the Earth alone through the imagination.

(4) Further, the following sentence, *With all which, etc.* <note>original: *Quibus omnib. &c.*</note> was carelessly conceived; for this is what I wished to say: since in Copernicus there appears a most beautiful order, such as exists between a cause and its effects, it is necessary that this itself be the true cause of retrogradations which Copernicus describes; namely, so that this Hypothesis is not merely a fiction.

(5) *Insofar as it is rendered from them.* <note>original: *Quatenus ex illis redditur.*</note>] Because, as follows now, the cause of certain things is rendered not from their special arrangement, but from the general one which Copernicus shares with Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used</note>; yet the cause of some is rendered from them as if from a special arrangement. Likewise, if we look at the most particular conditions and dimensions of the Copernican Hypotheses, the cause of some small details in the Observations could not be rendered: for that reason, the Copernican Hypotheses concerning particulars, both as to form and dimensions, had to be corrected by me according to the rule of Observations. Even if what I said needed amending in form, those things are such that they look toward the perfection of Copernicus’s hypotheses—that is, toward a further deduction of them from the usual path—rather than toward any new arrangement: because, as I said somewhere in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>his 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova*</note>, Copernicus himself was unaware of his own riches.

(6) *Another will be the place and time for that.* <note>original: *Alius id loci & temporis erit.*</note>] The greatest weight of this labor, as far as Astronomy is concerned, lay in the *Commentaries on Mars*; but in collecting physical or metaphysical arguments, I am more expansive in the *Epitome of Astronomy, Book IV*, which book contains the "actual task" <note>original: *τὸ ἔργον*</note> that I promised in this place. See the whole thing.

(7) *The third cause for me thinking so.* <note>original: *Tertiam mihi causam ita sentiendi.*</note>] Yet the same thing voluntarily reminded me later that this collection is not necessary. For since a Comet does not continue its motion for many days, and since we have the freedom of increasing or decreasing its motion in the adopted Hypothesis when observations (which are mostly coarse) seem to require it, it follows that different particular Hypotheses represent the same observations of a Comet. And Brahe, in his book on Comets on page 282, examines Maestlin's <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler’s university professor</note> Hypothesis, compares it with his own, and refutes it. He himself on page 206 proposes such a Hypothesis in which the Comet's own circular motion is shown as slow at the beginning, soon more intense, and slow again at the end. Therefore, I believe in this kind of argument, so shaped that from what the craftsmen were able to provide, by simple belief and that general conjecture, what truth harmonizes with truth, something may be presumed about the truth of the suppositions. 

But in turn, I occupy the same citadel by another way. For if the motion of the earth is useful for this—so that the straight-line motions of Comets, and their perpetual uniformity, or increase, or contrary perpetual decrease, satisfy the observations—then surely, as much likelihood as there is in the uniform straight-line motion <note>rectilinear motion</note> of vanishing bodies, so much faith will be added to the motion of the Earth, especially if it is established that the irregular curves of the apparent paths occurred by occasion of the Earth's motion, and the reason for other things which appear in Comets is rendered. For example, that very Comet of the year 1577, rising from the last parts of Sagittarius, showed there the greatest daily motion, a head of 7 minutes, and a tail 22 degrees long; all these were diminished toward the end, so that in the sign of Pisces, which is a quarter-circle away from Sagittarius, it seemed about to come to a standstill, had it not vanished. 

The question is: what is the cause why Comets, around the square of the place in which they appeared greatest and fastest, approach a standstill; why, near the standstill, some are hidden under the Sun, like that one; while others even gradually vanish opposite the sun, as that of the year 1618 did? For most do these things. But if you take the liberty of attributing circular motion to a Comet, you will not be able to state the same cause for all Comets. But if you reduce yourself to the narrow constraints of a straight-line trajectory, the necessity of the phenomenon immediately appears. Thus, I would have arranged the plane of the trajectory of the Comet of 1577 in that line through which, a few days after its disappearance, it would have been seen because of its length, if it had survived: I would have made the trajectory itself fast at first, and slower in the following days, and that in proportion to the proximity of the parts of the trajectory line to the Sun, because the Comet was fleeing from the Sun by an oblique path, and the Earth simultaneously from the Comet. By which reasoning it was brought about that at the beginning the Comet had half the altitude of the sun; from there it crossed the spheres of Venus, the Earth, and Mars, and in the end turned out more than three times higher than the Sun: therefore it is no wonder that no parallax <note>the apparent displacement of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</note> could be detected in it. But enough of this matter: if the reader seeks more in this place, let him go to my booklet on Comets, which I sent out at the Autumn fair of the year 1619.

# JOHANNES KEPLER

(8) **Four motions are attributed to the Earth.**] At the time I was writing this, I was still learning; do not be disturbed, therefore, by that multitude of motions. Properly speaking, there are only two: one depending on an internal principle, the *daily rotation around its own center*, and the other brought upon the Earth from the outside by the Sun, the *annual motion around the Sun*. Although the magnetic force, inherent in the fibers of the Earth, regulates and shapes that motion, what was considered the third motion here is rather the rest of the Earth's axis in a parallel position while the center is carried around the Sun. And what is frequently cited as the fourth here is a slight disturbance of this rest, arising from the deviation of the first two proper motions. But more on these matters below.

(9) **Moreover, with a changeable eccentricity.**] The authors were forced to establish this—others regarding the Sun, Copernicus regarding the Earth—because they gave too much weight to the observations of Hipparchus and Ptolemy. <note>Hipparchus (c. 190–120 BCE) and Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE) were the foundational astronomers of antiquity whose data Kepler eventually realized was less precise than Tycho Brahe's.</note> But these observations are not of such great subtlety that a dogma of such importance could be built upon them. Therefore, in my *Commentaries on the motions of Mars* <note>original: "Commentariis Martialium speculationum," referring to his 1609 work *Astronomia Nova*.</note> and in Book VI, Part I of the *Epitome*, I confidently rejected that opinion as being quite hostile to celestial physics, and I do not yet yield to that sentiment; I will demonstrate the evident weakness of this opinion elsewhere.

(10) **To be considered by us in a threefold way.**] Not because the motion itself is triple, but because while being one and the same, it has three distinct aspects, each of which has its own multiple uses and duties in reformed astronomy.

(11) **In the beginning, with eccentricity set aside.**] That is, putting aside the consideration of eccentricity. For that eccentric circle is superior not because of its eccentricity itself, but solely because it revolves around the Sun.

(12) **However, two.**] Namely, the heaven of the Moon (not the Moon by itself) and the Earth, have the same motion of translation from place to place through the Great Orb <note>The "Great Orb" is the term used by Copernicans for the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun.</note>. Therefore, since the Earth is always in the same place where the heaven of the Moon is found, this heaven of the Moon—and through it the Moon itself—receives no such appearance of its own motion from the motion of the Earth as the Sun receives from that translation, since the Sun is truly at rest. It would be otherwise if, when the Earth moved forward, the heaven of the Moon remained at rest or moved from place to place with another distinct motion; for then the motion of the center of the Earth would be transcribed by a certain imagination onto the heaven of the Moon, and thus, if the heaven of the Moon could appear retrograde by the shifting of its position, it would do so no less than the rest of the planets.

(13) **Copernicus makes the Apogee of the Sun.**] Two things are hinted at here: one pertains to the Sun itself, the other overflows from the Sun onto the planets. Ptolemy places the Sun in an eccentric, and includes the eccentric within two "deferents" <note>In Ptolemaic astronomy, a deferent is the main circular path around which a planet or epicycle moves.</note>; Copernicus attaches the planet to an epicycle, and the epicycle to a concentric circle. Ptolemy, therefore, in order to move the Apogee forward, attributed a specific, very slow motion to his deferents; Copernicus provides the same thing through slight deviations in the restoration of the epicycle from the rest of the concentric circle, since both are nearly annual. However, it is more likely that those slow motions result from deviation rather than from positive motion. Especially since the annual motion is inherent in the epicycle only with respect to the eccentric, by which the epicycle is rotated in the opposite direction; but with respect to the fixed stars, it presents the appearance of rest, because in this unfolding it happens that the same parts of the epicycle are always turned toward the same regions of the fixed stars, except for how much the deviation disturbs it. But in the *Commentaries on Mars* and in Book IV of the *Epitome of Astronomy*, I provide a physical cause both for the changed eccentricity and for the transposition of the apogees—a cause which is inherent in the fibers of the planetary body and needs neither deferents nor epicycles. But understand this part, pertaining to the Sun itself (or the Earth), as being touched upon at least in passing, so that from it may now be shown what overflows from the transposition of the Sun's apogee onto the other planets.

(14) **He computes eccentricities from the center of the Earth.**] These things become clearer through an inspection of Table V. It is indeed a matter of prophesying to say what will happen after many centuries, since this technical difficulty does not yet press upon the old astronomy in the present. But it is so arranged with the adaptation of Ptolemy’s particular decrees into the Copernican hypothesis that this mention could not be omitted by me. For even Copernicus computed the eccentricities of the five planets as if from the center of the Great Orb—as if that (rather than the center very close to the Sun itself) were the genuine basis of the planetary system. However, during these 25 years since I published this small book, astronomy has been so established by me that all eccentricities (of the primary planets) are referred to the very center of the Sun, or the true basis of the world. Therefore, the eccentricities of all the planets can remain the same, wherever the apogee of the Sun may betake itself. See the first part of the *Martial Commentaries* on the equivalence of hypotheses, especially Chapter VI.

(15) **The change of terrestrial eccentricity.**] These things were transcribed from the warning of Copernicus himself. And it is true that whoever moves the center of the Sun's orbit even slightly away from the Earth (or the Earth's from the Sun), as I contend Ptolemy and Hipparchus did—if he refers the eccentricities of the planets to this point,

### THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

...otherwise it is necessary to grant those planets different quantities than the observer who today holds a corrected value for the Sun's eccentricity. But if the eccentricities <note>In astronomy, eccentricity measures how much a planetary orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> are computed from the center of the Sun itself—as I do—then this change in the eccentricity of the Sun or the Earth does not affect them, whether that change be true (as Copernicus believed) or false and based on mere persuasion (as I believe). Look into this matter in Table V and the narrative of Rheticus, as well as the final chapter of my *Commentaries on Mars* <note>original: "Martialium," referring to Kepler’s landmark 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova*.</note>.

(16) **The celestial small circle, the Earth's globe or nucleus.**] Copernicus gave the occasion for this imaginary concept; either he wished to make it easier to understand, or he himself was truly stuck in the complexity of a matter that cannot be clarified with flat diagrams, though it could be with three-dimensional models—but those are very difficult to prepare. However the matter stands, *that motion is not really a motion*, but should rather be called rest. It cannot be better represented by anything than by that very physical cause, which is found in my *Commentaries on Mars* and Books I, II, III, and VI of the *Epitome of Astronomy*. It is this: while the Earth's globe is carried around the Sun in its annual motion, it meanwhile keeps the axis of its revolution always parallel to itself in different positions. This is due to the natural and magnetic inclination of its "fibers" toward remaining at rest, or perhaps due to the continuity of the daily rotation around this axis, which keeps it upright, much like a spinning top that is driven and moving about. Therefore, just as this motion is not truly a motion but rather rest, so also there is no need for a made-up small circle. Tycho Brahe rightly accused me here of being guilty of the ancient and erroneous belief in the solidity of the celestial Spheres; after reading my booklet, he sent me letters for this very reason.

(17) **The locations of the Equinoxes moving gradually into the preceding ones.**] The entire doctrine of the precession of the equinoxes <note>Precession is the slow "wobble" of Earth's axis that changes the positions of stars over thousands of years.</note> is fully explained by contemplating the axis and poles of the Earth. Thus, there is no need for a "New Sphere" or that small circle around the Earth. See Part V of the *Commentaries on Mars* and the *Epitome of Astronomy*, Books I, II, III, and VII.

(18) **The third motion is that of the Poles.**] We have reduced the "second motion" to the mere rest of the axis; now the third must be reduced to the second and fused with it into one. For if, by the meeting of physical causes, the Earth's axis is found to be tilted back from its original position by some insensible amount after one annual revolution; and if it nevertheless maintains a constant inclination toward the sides of the world (or the poles of the "royal way" <note>original: "via regia," referring to the Ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path.</note>); and if thirdly the Ecliptic itself—which is the Earth's orbit—has its own latitudes relative to the royal way just like the other planets, and these shift from place to place under the fixed stars through a similar anticipation: from these facts it follows spontaneously, without any "libration" <note>A slow oscillation or swaying motion.</note> of the poles, that both the declination of the Ecliptic changes and the equinoxes are sometimes accelerated and sometimes retarded. Indeed, something even greater follows from this, which went unnoticed by Copernicus but was discovered by Tycho Brahe and the Landgrave of Hesse: that the latitudes of the fixed stars change. Even if the oscillation of the equinoxes is not as great or as fast as Copernicus's calculations suggested, that quantity is not yet clear; moreover, the constant regularity detected before and after the time of Ptolemy calls the whole business into doubt, along with Ptolemy's observations. For only the era of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the most influential astronomer of antiquity.</note> is off track; the observations of all other eras agree with a uniform rule. Copernicus, who labored to explain this oscillation by including his own era's data, is refuted by the most trustworthy observers of the following age. See my *Commentaries on Mars* in the final chapters, and the *Epitome of Astronomy*, Book VII.

JOHANNES KEPLER

## CHAPTER II.

### *Outline of the primary demonstration.*

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a figure holding celestial or geometric objects, surrounded by scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

**H**aving established these premises, I now come to my main purpose: to prove Copernicus's newly reviewed hypotheses about the "new world" through a new argument. I shall recount the matter from the very beginning—"from the egg," as the saying goes—with as much brevity as possible.

The first thing God created in the beginning was body <note>By "body," Kepler refers to physical, three-dimensional matter or substance.</note>. If we understand its definition, I believe it will become reasonably clear why God chose to create body first and nothing else. I contend that the concept of **quantity** <note>Kepler uses "quantity" to mean geometric extension or the property of taking up space.</note> was the goal before God’s mind. To achieve this, everything pertaining to the essence of a body was required, so that the quantity of a body, insofar as it is a body, is a kind of "form" and the origin of its definition. God willed quantity to exist before all else so that there might be a comparison between the **curved** and the **straight**. In this one matter, the divine Nicholas of Cusa <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464) was a philosopher and mathematician whose work on the "coincidence of opposites" and the nature of the circle deeply influenced Kepler.</note> and others seem significant to me: they placed such high value on the relationship between the straight and the curved, even daring to compare the **curved** to God and the **straight** to created things. Those who have tried to compare the Creator to His creatures—God to man, divine judgments to human ones—have performed no more useful a service than those who try to equate the curved with the straight, or a circle with a square.

Even if the suitability of quantities and the nobility of the curved had been established by God for this reason alone, there was another, far greater reason: the image of the Triune God is found in the **spherical surface**. Specifically, the Father is represented in the center, the Son in the surface, and the Holy Spirit in the equality of the <term>relationship <note>original Greek: *σχέσεως* (schesis), referring here to the proportional connection or disposition between the center and the circumference.</note></term> between the central point and the circumference. For while Cusanus might attribute these things to the circle, and others perhaps to the globe, I claim them for the **spherical surface** alone. I cannot be persuaded that anything among curved things is nobler or more perfect than the spherical surface itself. A globe is more than a spherical surface, as it is mixed with straightness, which alone fills its interior. A circle, truly, cannot exist unless it is on a flat plane—that is, unless a spherical surface or a globe is cut by a flat plane. Thus one can see that many properties flow here from the cube to the globe, or there from the square to the circle, secondarily, because of the straightness of the diameter.

But why, finally, were the distinctions between the **Curved** and the **Straight**, and the nobility of the curved, set before God in the adornment of the world? Why indeed? Except that it was absolutely necessary for a most perfect Creator to establish a most beautiful work. For it is not right, nor was it ever right (as Cicero says in his book *On the Universe* <note>original: *de vniuersitate*, Cicero’s partial translation of Plato’s *Timaeus*.</note>, following Plato's *Timaeus*), for Him who is best to make anything except that which is most beautiful. Therefore, when the Creator preconceived the **Idea of the world** in His mind (we speak in human terms so that humans may understand), and since an "Idea" is of a prior thing—indeed, as was just said, of the best thing, so that the form of the future work itself becomes the best—it is clear that by these laws which God in His goodness prescribes for Himself, He could have chosen no other Idea for the construction of the world than His own essence. How excellent and divine that essence is can be considered in two ways: first in itself, insofar as it is one in essence and three in persons, and then by a comparison made with created things.

THE COSMIC MYSTERY
23

God wanted to imprint this image, this Idea, upon the world, so that it might become the best and most beautiful, and so that the world might be able to receive it. The most wise Creator devised as much as he founded, and he conceived of quantities whose entire essence, so to speak, would fall into these two categories: the **Straight** and the **Curved**. Of these, the Curved represents God to us in those two ways just mentioned <note>Kepler refers back to the idea that the curve represents the infinite and the divine nature</note>. For it should not be thought that such suitable distinctions for foreshadowing God existed by chance, as if God did not think of these very things but merely founded physical body for other reasons and by another plan, and then afterwards the comparison of the Straight and the Curved, and this similarity with God, arose of its own accord, as if by accident.

Rather, it is likely that at the beginning of all things, the Curved and the Straight were chosen by God through a deliberate plan to foreshadow the divinity of the Creator in the world. So that these might exist, there were quantities; and so that quantity might be had, **Body** <note>Physical matter or three-dimensional substance</note> was created first of all.

Let us now see how the Best Creator employed these quantities in the fabric of the world, and what—according to our reasoning—is likely to have been done by the Creator. We shall then look for that very thing in both the Ancient and the new hypotheses <note>Kepler refers to the Copernican "new" system versus the Ptolemaic "ancient" system</note>, and we shall award the prize to whichever system it is found in.

Aristotle argued quite extensively that the whole world is enclosed in a spherical shape, drawing arguments (among others) from the nobility of the spherical surface. Even now, Copernicus’s outermost sphere of the fixed stars, although it lacks motion, maintains this same figure and receives the Sun into its innermost heart like a center. Indeed, the circular motion of the stars proves that the other orbs are round. Therefore, that the **Curved** was employed for the decoration of the world needs no further proof. 

However, since we see three kinds of quantities in the world—the figure, the number, and the size of bodies—we have so far found the Curved only in the figure. For size provides no specific ratio when one thing is inscribed in another similar thing (a sphere within a sphere, or a circle within a circle) from the same center: it either touches everywhere or nowhere. Furthermore, the Spherical itself, since it is unique and one-of-a-kind in its type of quantity, cannot be subject to any number other than the <term>triad<gloss>The number three, which Kepler links to the Holy Trinity</gloss></term>. 

If, therefore, God had only looked to the **Curved** during creation, then nothing would exist in this worldly structure except for: the Sun in the center (representing the Father); the sphere of the fixed stars, or the <term>Mosaic waters<gloss>A reference to the 'waters above the firmament' in Genesis 1:7</gloss></term>, at the boundary (representing the Son); and the celestial air filling all things, or that expansion and firmament (which would be the image of the Holy Spirit). If this were the case, I say, nothing else would exist in this worldly building. 

But in reality, the fixed stars are innumerable, the catalog of moving bodies is fixed and certain, and the sizes of the heavens are unequal to one another. It is therefore necessary that we seek the causes for all these things from **straightness**. Unless, perhaps, we think God did anything in the world at random while better reasons were available—a thing which no one will persuade me to believe, even regarding the fixed stars. Although their placement seems most confused to us, like a random scattering of seeds, it is not so.

Let us come, therefore, to **Straight** quantities. Just as the spherical surface was previously assumed because it was the most perfect quantity, so now let us cross over in one leap to <term>solid bodies<gloss>Three-dimensional geometric shapes</gloss></term>, as they are the perfect quantities derived from Straight lines and consist of three dimensions; for it is fitting that the Idea of the world be perfect. (1) But straight lines and surfaces are infinite, and therefore...

JOAN. KEPLERI

...[those shapes] least capable of order, let us cast them out from a world that is finite, most orderly, and most beautiful. Again, from among the bodies—of which there are infinitely infinite kinds—let us select some by taking a census based on certain characteristics: namely, those that have their sides, or angles, or faces—whether single, alternating, or mixed in any constant manner—equal to each other; so that in this way, with good reason, we may arrive at something finite. 

If a certain genus of bodies, described by fixed conditions, consists of species that are finite in number, yet is multiplied into a massive quantity of numbers: let us use the angles and centers of the planes of those bodies (2) <note>Kepler suggests using the vertices and faces of geometric shapes to explain the placement of stars</note> to demonstrate the multitude, magnitude, and position of the fixed stars, if we can. But if that labor is not for man, then let us for a while postpone seeking the reason for their number and position until someone describes to us every single one of them—how many and how large they are. Therefore, letting go of the fixed stars and leaving them to Him—the most wise Architect, who alone "counts the multitude of the stars and calls each by name" (Psalm 147)—let us turn our eyes to those that are near, few, and moving <note>Kepler refers here to the planets</note>.

Finally, if we have a selection of bodies and have cast out the whole crowd of mixed ones, and keep only those whose planes are all equilateral, equiangular, and equal to each other, there will remain for us these five **Regular Bodies** <term>Platonic solids: geometric shapes where every face is the same regular polygon</term>, to which the Greeks gave these names: the **Cube** or **Hexahedron**, the **Pyramid** or **Tetrahedron**, the **Dodecahedron**, the **Icosahedron**, and the **Octahedron**. <margin>☞</margin> And that there cannot be more than these five, see the scholion <note>an explanatory note</note> after proposition 18 in Book 13 of Euclid.

Therefore, just as the number of these is definite and very small, while the species of others are either innumerable or infinite, so it was fitting that in the world there should be two kinds of stars, distinguished from each other by an evident difference (of the sort that motion and rest are): one kind similar to the infinite, like the fixed stars; the other narrow in number, like the Planets. This is not the place to argue about the causes why these move and those do not. But assuming that the Planets required motion, it follows (3) that to obtain this, they ought to have received round orbits.

We have the sphere <note>or orbit</note> on account of motion (4), and the [regular] bodies on account of their number and magnitudes; what remains further but to say with Plato, *God always geometrizes* <note>original: "θεὸν ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖν"</note>; and that in this workshop of moving things, He inscribed bodies in spheres and spheres in bodies, until no body remained that was not clothed both inside and outside by moving spheres. For one can see from [propositions] 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17 of Book 13 of Euclid how these bodies are by their nature suited for this inscription and circumscription. Therefore, if five bodies are inserted into one another, with spheres mediating and enclosing them, we will have the number of six spheres <note>Kepler’s famous "nesting" theory: 6 planetary spheres are required to enclose 5 regular solids</note>.

<margin>Proposition</margin> If any age of the world debated the arrangement of the world in this way—so as to place six moving spheres around an immobile Sun—it certainly handed down the true Astronomy. Now Copernicus has six such spheres, and these are in such a proportion to one another in pairs that all five of these bodies can be most aptly placed between them; this will be the sum of what follows. Therefore, he [Copernicus] must be listened to until someone either offers better hypotheses for these philosophical reflections or teaches that what has been deduced with the best reason from the very principles of nature could creep into numbers and into the mind of man by chance. For what is more wonderful, what more suited for persuasion...

can be said or imagined; for those things which Copernicus established from the **phenomena** <note>original: Φαινομένοις; the observable appearances of the stars</note>, from the effects, and from the consequences—"like a blind man steadying his step with a stick," as he himself used to say to Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus was Copernicus’s only pupil and the first to publish an account of the heliocentric system</note> (relying on a lucky rather than a confident conjecture, and believing it to be so)—all those things, I say, are now found to be most correctly established by reasoning **from first principles** <note>original: à priori</note>, from causes, and from the very Idea of Creation.

For if anyone wishes to object to these philosophical reasons without providing their own, or to elude them by mere practice—on the grounds that I, a newcomer at the end of the ages, am bringing forth these philosophical matters while those ancient lights of philosophy are silent—I shall bring forth for them a leader, author, and guide from the most ancient age: **Pythagoras**. He is mentioned much in the schools because, when he saw the excellence of the five Solids, he judged it—for exactly the same reason two thousand years ago as I do now—not unworthy of the Creator’s care to look upon them. He accommodated non-mathematical things to mathematical ones, judging them physically and by their respective accidental properties. (5) For he equated the **Earth** to the **Cube**, because both are stable—though this is not strictly said of the cube. To the **Heaven** he gave the **Icosahedron**, because both are rotatable. To **Fire** he gave the **Pyramid** <note>Also known as the Tetrahedron</note>, because this is the shape of a flickering flame. The remaining two bodies <note>The Octahedron and Dodecahedron</note> he distributed between air and water, because of a similar kinship on both sides with their neighbors. But Copernicus was missing for that man, to tell him first what was actually in the world. Without him, there is no doubt that Pythagoras would have found *why* it was so, and this proportion of the heavens would be as well known now as the five solids themselves; it would be as widely accepted as that opinion about the Sun’s motion and the Earth’s rest has grown strong over the course of time.

But come, let us finally test whether these proportions of the bodies exist between the spheres of Copernicus. At first, let us consider the matter roughly. The greatest difference between distances in Copernicus is between **Jupiter** and **Mars**. As you see in the explanation of the hypotheses in Table 1 and below in chapters 14 and 15, the distance of Mars from the Sun does not equal even a third part of Jupiter’s. Let us therefore seek the body that creates the greatest difference between its circumscribed and inscribed sphere (6) (allow us this **according to its origin** <note>original: κατὰ γένεσιν</note>, to consider the hollow as a solid), which is the **Tetrahedron** or **Pyramid**. There is, therefore, a Pyramid between Jupiter and Mars. After these, the distances of **Jupiter** and **Saturn** make the next greatest difference; for the former equals a little more than half of the latter. A similar difference appears in the innermost and outermost sphere of the **Cube**. Therefore, Saturn surrounds the Cube, and the Cube surrounds Jupiter.

There is an almost equal proportion between **Venus** and **Mercury**, not unlike the spheres of the **Octahedron**. Venus, therefore, surrounds this body, and Mercury is contained within it.

The remaining two proportions, between Venus and the Earth, and between the Earth and Mars, are the smallest and nearly equal—namely, the inner is a **three-quarters** <term>dodrans: a Roman fraction for 3/4</term> or **two-thirds** <term>bes: a Roman fraction for 2/3</term> of the outer. In the **Icosahedron** and **Dodecahedron**, the distances of the two spheres are also equal, and they utilize the smallest proportion among the remaining regular bodies. Therefore, it is likely that Mars surrounds the Earth by means of one of these two bodies, and the Earth is separated from Venus by means of the other. Thus, if anyone asks me why there are only six moving spheres <note>The six known planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, I will reply: because there ought not to be more than five proportions, just as many...

### An old annotation on the second chapter.

<margin>preceding leaf</margin>
And because of these five) The nobility of these Solids arises from their simplicity, and from the equality of the distance of their planes from the center of the figure. For just as God is the norm and rule for all creatures, so the **Sphere** is the norm for all solid bodies. And indeed, it possesses these specific properties: 1. It is the simplest, because it is enclosed by a single boundary—namely, itself. 2. All its points are most equally distant from the center. Therefore, among all bodies, the regular solids approach most closely to the perfection of the Sphere. Their definition is this: they must have 1. all sides, 2. all planes, and 3. all angles equal to one another in both kind and size, which is a mark of simplicity. From this definition, the following points follow naturally: 4. that the centers of all their planes are equally distant from the middle; 5. that when inscribed in a globe, all their angles touch the surface; 6. that they remain fixed within it; 7. that they touch an inscribed globe with the centers of all their planes; 8. that consequently the inscribed globe remains unmoved; 9. and that the solid shares the same center with that globe. By these things, a second likeness to the Sphere is achieved, which arises from the equality of the distance of the planes.

<margin>* Above, in the same place</margin>
(7) Moreover, that **Scholion** <note>original: Scholion; a marginal or explanatory note in a mathematical text</note> reads as follows: I say that besides the five mentioned figures, no other solid figure can be constructed that is contained by planes that are equilateral, equiangular, and equal to one another. For a <term>solid angle</term> <note>the corner or vertex where three or more faces of a shape meet</note> cannot be formed from only two triangles, nor indeed from any two other figures.

But from three triangles, the angle of a **Pyramid** <note>original: Pyramis; the regular tetrahedron</note> is formed.
From four, the angle of an **Octahedron**.
From five, the angle of an **Icosahedron**.

However, a solid angle cannot be formed from six equilateral and equiangular triangles meeting at the same point. Since the angle of an equilateral triangle contains two-thirds of a right angle <note>original: recti vnius bessem; 60 degrees</note>, six such angles would be equal to four right angles <note>360 degrees</note>. This is impossible, for every solid angle must be contained by angles that sum to less than four right angles, according to **Euclid** <note>original: 21. 11.; referring to Book 11, Proposition 21 of Euclid’s Elements</note>.

For these same reasons, a solid cannot consist of more than six such plane angles.

Furthermore, the angle of a **Cube** is contained by three squares.
From four squares, none can be formed, for again they would equal four right angles.

The angle of a **Dodecahedron** is contained by three equilateral and equiangular pentagons. But from four, none can be formed. Since the angle of an equilateral pentagon is one right angle plus a fifth part of a right angle <note>108 degrees</note>, four such angles would be greater than four right angles. This cannot happen. Nor indeed can a solid angle be contained by any other polygonal figures, as an absurdity would follow from that as well. Therefore, it is clear that besides the five mentioned figures, no other solid figure can be constructed which is contained by equilateral and equiangular planes.

->REGARDING CHAPTER TWO<-
->Author’s Notes.<-

(1) **L**ineas verò & superficies <note>original: "Lines and surfaces indeed."</note>.] *Oh, how poorly that was done! Should we cast them out from the world? On the contrary, I have reclaimed them by right of return in my <term>Harmonics</term> <note>Referring to his later work, *Harmonices Mundi* (The Harmony of the World, 1619).</note>. But why should we cast them out? Is it because they are infinite, and therefore least capable of order? Yet it was not the things themselves, but my own ignorance at that time—shared with most people—that was least capable of understanding their order. And so, in Book I of the Harmonics, I taught a certain selection among the infinites, and brought to light the most beautiful order within them. For why should we eliminate lines from the blueprint of the world, when God himself expressed lines in his very work—namely, the motions of the Planets? Therefore, the language must be corrected, but the intention held firm. In establishing the number of bodies and the magnitude of the spheres at the outset, let lines certainly be eliminated; but in adorning the motions, which are completed in lines, let us not despise lines and surfaces, which alone are the origin of Harmonic proportions.*

(2) Pro fixarum multitudine <note>original: "For the multitude of fixed stars."</note>.] *There is a huge distinction, by argument of their names, between the fixed and the moving; why should there not also be some distinction in the adornment of each kind? Who would understand the beauty of Order, if he did not see nearby the army of fixed stars, which is devoid of such order? Who would distrust Astronomy, if the similarity of configurations or constellations were perpetual? There is an adornment proper to forms, and one proper to Matter. Let there be, therefore, a proper and beautiful adornment of matter, which is made through an infinite mass, multitude, and variety, as much in position as in magnitude and brightness.*

(3) Vt hunc, motum, obtinerent, rotundos orbes accipere debuisse <note>original: "To obtain this motion, they must have taken up round orbits."</note>.] *Not those solid ones <note>Kepler is clarifying that he does not believe in physical, crystalline spheres holding the planets, but rather empty paths in space.</note>; I was misunderstood here by <term>Tycho Brahe</term> <note>The famous Danish astronomer (1546–1601) whose precise observations Kepler used.</note>. Rather, I mean spaces that are entirely circular, so that the revolutions of the stars could return into themselves and be perpetual; and toward the poles likewise circular—that is, spherical surfaces—because of the motions of latitude; not because they had need of poles to which they might be attached, like a physical material sphere.*

(4) Et corpora propter numerum <note>original: "And the bodies because of the number."</note>.] *Understand "bodies" as the five regular geometric solids; these are the blueprint, while the Orbs are the work to be constructed.*

(5) Terram enim Cubo æquiparauit <note>original: "For he compared the Earth to the Cube."</note>.] *See Book I of the Harmonics in the preface, page 4; and Book II, proposition 25; and Book V, chapter 1. And the Epitome of Astronomy, Book IV, page 456.*

(6) Concedatur nobis hæc <note>original: "Let this be granted to us."</note>.] *Indeed, must either the spherical also be counted among the solids—which we call a globe—or do these solid bodies not deserve to be called such? Nor should arguments have been woven from "solidity" (that is, from the perfection of three dimensions) for the adornment of the Orbs through them. For the orbs themselves (or spaces) are hollow, and these figures are noble for this reason: because they most closely emulate the perfection of the sphere by the all-encompassing enclosure of the space they have embraced. Solidity, however, both in the globe and in these figures, is the genuine idea of matter, just as the surface is the idea of form.*

(7) Scholion autem illud <note>original: "However, that scholium (explanatory note)."</note>.] *This is half of my second book of Harmonics, concerning the Congruence of planes in a solid.*
