### ON THE SECOND CHAPTER
->Author’s Notes.<-

(1) **Lines and surfaces indeed.**] *Oh, poorly done! <note>Kepler is critiquing his own earlier writing here.</note> Shall we cast them out of the world? On the contrary, I have reclaimed them by right of return <note>original: "postliminio reuocaui," a legal term for restoring rights</note> in my **Harmonics**. <note>Referring to his later work, *Harmonices Mundi* (1619).</note> But why should we cast them out? Is it because they are infinite, and therefore least capable of order? Yet it was not they themselves, but my own ignorance at that time—shared with most people—that was least capable of understanding their order. And so, in Book I of the **Harmonics**, I taught a certain selection among the infinites, and I brought to light a most beautiful order within them. For why should we eliminate lines from the archetype of the world, when God himself expressed lines in the work itself—namely, the motions of the Planets? Therefore, the language must be corrected, but the meaning held. In the number of bodies and the amplitude of the spheres to be established at first, let lines indeed be eliminated; but in the adorning of motions, which are perfected by lines, let us not despise lines and surfaces, which alone are the origin of Harmonic proportions.*

(2) **For the multitude of the fixed stars.**] *There is a huge difference, by the argument of their names, between the fixed and the moving; why should there not also be some difference in the adornment of each kind? Who would understand the beauty of Order, if he did not see nearby the army of the fixed stars, which seems devoid of order? Who would learn Astronomy, if there were a perpetual similarity of patterns or constellations? There is an ornament proper to forms, and one proper to Matter. Let there be, therefore, a proper, material, and beautiful adornment, which is made through an infinite mass, multitude, and variety, as much in position as in the clarity of magnitude.*

(3) **That they ought to receive round orbs to obtain this motion.**] *Not solid orbs; I was misunderstood here by Tycho Brahe. <note>Tycho Brahe was the leading observational astronomer of the era; he famously proved that solid "crystalline" spheres could not exist because comets passed through them.</note> Rather, I meant spaces that are indeed circular, so that the revolutions of the stars could return into themselves and be perpetual; and likewise circular toward the poles, that is, spherical surfaces, on account of the motions of latitudes. It is not that they had need of poles to which they might be attached, like a material sphere made of wood or metal.*

(4) **And bodies on account of number.**] *Understand "bodies" as the five regular solid Geometric bodies; <note>These are the Platonic solids: the Cube, Tetrahedron, etc.</note> these are the archetype, while the Orbs are the work to be constructed.*

(5) **For he likened the Earth to the Cube.**] *See Book I of the **Harmonics** in the preface, page 4, and Book II, proposition 25, and Book V, chapter 1. Also the **Epitome of Astronomy**, Book IV, page 456.*

(6) **Let this be granted to us.**] *Should the spherical also be counted among the solids—what we call a globe—or do these solid bodies not deserve to be called such? Arguments for the adornment of the Orbs through them were not to be woven from "solidity"—that is, from the perfection of three dimensions. For the orbs themselves (or spaces) are hollow, and these figures are noble for this reason: they most closely emulate the perfection of the spherical by the all-encompassing closure of the space they embrace. Truly, solidity in both the globe and in these figures is the innate idea of matter, just as the surface is the idea of form.*

(7) **That Scholion, however.**] *This is half of my second book of the **Harmonics**, concerning the "Congruence of planes in a solid."*

## C H A P T E R III.

### *That these five bodies are distinguished into two orders; and that the Earth is correctly located.*

Furthermore, it might seem accidental and flowing from no cause that the six Copernican spheres <note>The "six spheres" refer to the orbits of the six known planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> receive these five bodies within the distances between one another—unless that very order existed among them which I have used to interpose each one. For if Saturn were as close to Jupiter as Venus is to Earth, or conversely, if these two were separated from each other in the Copernican system by as great an interval as Jupiter and Mars are separated, then a different order would have to be used in inserting the bodies. In that case, there would be a Dodecahedron <note>A 12-sided solid with pentagonal faces.</note> or Icosahedron <note>A 20-sided solid with triangular faces.</note> in the first place between the two outermost spheres, and a Tetrahedron <note>A 4-sided solid with triangular faces; Kepler often calls this a "Pyramid."</note> in the fourth place. Since such an order cannot be admitted by mathematical reasoning, it would be easy to reveal the futility of the theorem I have conceived. 

But now let us see by what reasons it is proven that the bodies ought to have been arranged in this very order between the spheres. To begin with, these bodies are distinguished into three primary ones—the Cube, the Tetrahedron, and the Dodecahedron—and two secondary ones—the Octahedron <note>An 8-sided solid with triangular faces.</note> and the Icosahedron. And that this distinction is most true, note the properties of each class:

1. The primary bodies differ from each other in the shape of their faces <note>original: "plano," meaning the flat surface or face of the solid</note>; the secondary ones both use the same triangular face.
2. Each of the primary bodies has its own unique face: the Cube has the square, the Pyramid has the triangle, and the Dodecahedron has the pentagon. The secondary ones borrow their triangular face from the Pyramid.
3. All the primary bodies use a simple vertex <note>original: "angulo," meaning the solid angle or corner where faces meet</note>, namely one enclosed by only three faces; the secondary ones join four or five faces into a single solid vertex.
4. The primary bodies owe their origin and properties to no one else; the secondary ones have acquired most of theirs from the primary ones by a process of exchange <note>This refers to geometric duality, where the centers of the faces of one solid form the vertices of another.</note>, being as it were born from them.
5. The primary bodies cannot be moved harmoniously unless the axis <note>original: "diametro"</note> is driven through the centers of one face or its opposite; whereas the secondary ones are moved through an axis driven through opposite vertices.
6. It is characteristic of the primary bodies to stand; of the secondary ones to hang. For whether you roll the former onto a base or set the latter upright on a vertex, the eye will shrink from the deformity of the sight on both sides.
7. Finally, add that the primary bodies are three in number—a perfect number—while the secondary are two—an imperfect number. Also, the primary ones possess every species of angle: the Cube has the right angle, the Pyramid the acute, and the Dodecahedron the obtuse. The secondary ones, however, both belong to the obtuse-angled class. Even the angle of the Octahedron wanders through all three species: it is obtuse at the joining of the edges, right between two opposite edges, and the solid vertex itself is acute. 

Since, therefore, the distinction between the bodies was manifest, nothing more appropriate could be done than that our Earth—the sum and compendium of the whole world, and thus the most worthy of the moving stars—should be distinguished by its sphere between the said orders, and should fall into that place which we 

->assigned to it above.<-

THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

## CHAPTER IV.

### Why do three bodies surround the Earth, and the remaining two are clothed within?

Permit me now, fair-minded reader, to play for a little while in a serious matter and indulge in some Allegories. For I believe that from the love of God toward mankind, many causes of things in the world can be deduced. Certainly, no one will deny that in decorating the dwelling-place of the world, God repeatedly looked toward the future inhabitant. For the end of both the world and of all creation is man. Therefore, I believe the Earth—which was destined to provide and nourish the genuine image of the Creator—was deemed worthy by God to circle among the middle planets, such that it would have just as many within the embrace of its orbit as it would have outside of it. To achieve this, God reckoned the Sun among the other five Stars <note>In the 16th century, "stars" (stellis) often referred to the planets or "wandering stars."</note>, even though the Sun differs entirely in its nature. This seems all the more consistent because, since the Sun was previously established as the image of God the Father, it is believable that by this association with the other Stars, he intended to provide proofs to the future inhabitant of his love for mankind <note>original: "$\phi\iota\lambda\alpha\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi\iota\alpha\varsigma$" (philanthropias)</note> and his human-like feelings <note>original: "$\alpha\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi o\pi\alpha\theta\epsilon\iota\alpha\varsigma$" (anthropopatheias)</note>, which God was to employ toward men, humbling himself even to domestic familiarity. For in the Old Testament, he frequently joined the number of men and wished to be called the friend of Abraham; just as we see the Sun join the number of the moving things. Since, however, the Sun was surrounded by the Earth <note>Kepler is describing the Sun's position relative to the Earth's orbit in the Copernican system.</note>: according to what has been said, that order of bodies had to be included within the Earth which embraces at least two: namely, so that two moving things <note>Venus and Mercury.</note> along with the immobile Sun would produce the same number three which is found in those excluded from the Earth's orbit. Thus, with the Moon especially surrounding the Earth, the best Creator placed our dwelling in the midst of seven Planets. For if the order of the three remaining solids had approached the Sun, there would have been four Stars <note>Planets</note> within the Earth along with the Sun, but only two outside. This disorder <note>original: "$\alpha\tau\alpha\xi\iota\alpha$" (ataxia)</note> of number, since it lacks reason, was omitted by the Creator. Furthermore, since containing is a sign of perfection (like an action), and being contained is a sign of imperfection (like a passion); and since the primary things are more perfect than the rest; it is fitting that the order of the three primary solids should contain the Earth, while the rest should be contained within the circuit of the Earth's orbit. And so we have, in passing, the reason why three Planets are moved outside the Earth and two within. If this is less than convincing to the reader, let him consider this an honorary point, not the principal one. For even if we did not know the cause for which three Stars <note>Planets</note> go above the Earth (or above the Sun, for Ptolemy), nevertheless the following facts would stand with the preceding ones, because the FACT itself is certain to us. Nor has anyone ever doubted that ♄ <note>Saturn</note>, ♃ <note>Jupiter</note>, and ♂ <note>Mars</note> are superior planets. Let us only hold to this: since in Copernicus there are three Planets above the Earth, we ought to place the order of the three primary bodies—the Cube, the Pyramid <note>The Tetrahedron.</note>, and the Dodecahedron—outside the orbit of the Earth, and the Octahedron and Icosahedron within; if we wish to win the prize in this business.

# CHAPTER V.

->*That the cube is the first of the bodies, and is placed between the highest planets.*<-

---

<image-desc>Decorative initial V set against a landscape background featuring a tree and a classical building.</image-desc>Let us now come to the primary three solids, and assign to each its own space. And indeed the Cube ought to approach the fixed stars <note>In the Copernican system, the "fixed stars" refers to the outermost sphere of the universe, which remains stationary.</note> and establish the first proportion—which is between Saturn and Jupiter—because the fixed stars are the most noble part of the world outside the Earth, just as the circumference is to a circle (after the center). The Cube is truly the first body in its own order for several reasons: 1. For it alone is generated from its own base, whereas the remaining four are not generated by their own faces, but are either cut from the Cube—like the Pyramid <note>Kepler refers to the Tetrahedron here as the "Pyramid."</note>, once four rectangular pyramids are discarded—or enlarged, like the Dodecahedron, by adding six "pentahedrons" <note>Kepler describes the Dodecahedron as being built up by adding wedge-like shapes to the faces of a cube.</note>. 2. It alone can be resolved into homogeneous cubes without a prism. 3. It alone extends in every direction and reaches into three straight dimensions. For the faces of the others are inclined, and in some places, while they offer themselves to two direct sections, they fail the divider in the rest. 4. Hence it is that it alone has as many faces as a three-fold dimension has boundaries, namely six, and double the number of sides, namely twelve. 5. It alone everywhere has an equal angle, namely a right angle. But in a regular Pyramid, the rule which is applied to the middle planes differs if you twist it toward an angle; nor do the solid angles square to that norm which measures the long lateral angle placed between. 6. Hence also it alone possesses what Simplicius cites from the <term>single book</term> <note>original Greek: "$\mu o \nu o \beta \iota \beta \lambda \omega$" (monobiblō), referring to a lost work by Ptolemy on dimensions.</note> of Ptolemy in his commentary on Aristotle's *On the Heavens*, Book 1, Chapter 1, as the cause of perfection in the number three; namely, that no more than three straight lines perpendicular to a solid place can meet to divide it into right solids. 7. It is the simplest body of all rectilinear solids. Even if this is debated in the case of the Pyramid, it is easily proved by the fact that the measure of a pyramid is the Cube, and it is fitting that the measure be prior to the thing measured. Truly, measurement is not only by human institution—whereby whatever solids men measure, they conceive its quantity in their minds in small cubes—but much more so by nature. For a right angle is equal to any other right angle when it is extended onto a plane. It is therefore perpetually equal to itself, and thus unique, while of the other angles there are infinite varieties on either side. It is fitting for a measure to be one and the same, and also finite. 8. Hence so fruitful is the inscription of a right angle in a circle, without the mediation of which neither the triangle, nor the pentagon, nor those derived from them can be inscribed. 9. But neither should we overlook that skillful nature has most perfectly attributed those same six <term>extensions</term> <note>original Greek: "$\delta \iota \alpha \sigma \tau \alpha \sigma \epsilon \iota \varsigma$" (diastaseis), meaning dimensions or directions of growth.</note> to the most perfect animal: a clear argument of how much this body is valued by her.

THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *That the Pyramid is between Jupiter and Mars.*

Now, no one will be very surprised that the Pyramid <note>Kepler uses the term "Pyramid" to refer to the Tetrahedron, the four-sided Platonic solid where every face is an equilateral triangle.</note> follows the Cube, since: 1. It almost dares to contend with the cube for the position of leadership. 2. Furthermore, either the pyramid itself or its irregular <term>homologous <note>original Greek: "homologa." In geometry, these are parts that correspond in relative position or proportion.</note></term> parts contribute to the construction of the other solids. For twenty pyramids, slightly shorter than the tetrahedral ones, compose an Icosahedron; eight even shorter ones compose an Octahedron. Although the Dodecahedron consists of a hidden square, it must still be resolved into pyramids. 3. Nor should we overlook the fact that a Tetrahedron can be resolved into four perfect pyramids and one Octahedron whose sides are half as large. 4. Just as in plane geometry all polygons are resolved into triangles, so for the sake of measurement, all other solids are resolved into pyramids—which we then measure by cubes, just as triangles are measured by squares. Therefore, the pyramid is the measure of the others, and of all shapes, it is most easily measured by the cube. 5. Hence, most of its lines, like those of the cube, so easily derive their quantity from the ratio of the diagonal, yet only through square numbers. 6. The regularity of the pyramid depends solely on its sides, whereas the cube depends also on its angles. Thus, among equilateral shapes, there is only one pyramid <note>The regular Tetrahedron.</note>, but among <term>hexahedrons <note>original Greek: "hexaedra," or six-sided figures.</note></term>, even with equal sides, there is an infinite variety of angles. For this reason, if there were no other arguments, I would leave it in doubt whether it should be preferred over the cube or placed after it. 7. Human beings, imitating this cleverness of nature, first erect their building materials perpendicularly and join them at right angles, then reinforce and stabilize them with triangles. 8. Furthermore, since the pyramid has an acute angle, it is prior to those with obtuse angles. For that which has a "just" or exact quantity is always first in order; that which is "less than just" <note>Kepler is comparing the acute angle (less than 90 degrees) to the "just" right angle of the cube.</note> seems to follow it, both because it seems further from infinity than that which is "more than just," and because it is simpler. For an obtuse angle seems in a way to be a multiple of a right and an acute angle. Therefore, it is less surprising why the small number of angles in the base, and even of the bases themselves of the tetrahedron, does not take precedence over the cube. For the number of angles and bases necessarily follows the specific type of angle adopted. Hence, if the right angle is prior to the acute, then the <term>hexahedron <note>The cube.</note></term> is also prior to the Tetrahedron, and the four-angled face prior to the three-angled face. 9. And this can also be gathered from the fact that the "perfect" is always first everywhere; next, that which is "deficient"; and finally, that which is "excessive." Since, therefore, the number six <note>The number of faces on a cube.</note> is a perfect number <note>In classical mathematics, a "perfect number" (like 6) is equal to the sum of its proper divisors: 1+2+3=6.</note>, it follows that the pyramid, which is "deficient" <note>The tetrahedron has only 4 faces, fewer than the perfect 6.</note>, should not precede the cube, but should follow immediately after it.

We now have the reason why the pyramid is in the second place, between Jupiter and Mars. Previously, it was left undecided which body belongs in the third place, between Mars and the Earth. That is easily decided here. For since the Dodecahedron is the remaining one of the primary solids, it will be third in order, between Mars and the Earth. What should be thought of its properties will be easily seen by comparing it with the previous ones.

### CHAPTER VII.

*On the order and properties of the secondary [solids].*

As far as the **secondary solids** <note>Kepler divides the five Platonic solids into two groups: the "primary" (Cube, Tetrahedron, Dodecahedron) and the "secondary" (Octahedron, Icosahedron) based on their geometric properties and how they are "born" from one another.</note> are concerned, since the **Octahedron** is prior to the **Icosahedron**, it might seem strange to some why that which is later in the order of Nature should come first in the world? For because **Mars** was assigned the **Dodecahedron** along with **Earth**, it follows from what we have said that the **Icosahedron** lies between **Earth** and **Venus**.

And many things prove that the **Octahedron** is prior to the **Icosahedron**. 1. First, the Octahedron is born (not truly, but as if it were born) from the **Cube** and the **pyramid** <note>The Tetrahedron.</note>, which are the first in their order; it borrows the number of sides <note>Kepler likely refers to the number of vertices here, as the Octahedron has 6 vertices, matching the Cube's 6 faces.</note> from the former and its triangular base from the latter. The **Icosahedron**, however, is born from the pyramid and the **Dodecahedron**, which are the last in their order. For it again borrows its base from the former, and its number of sides from the latter. 2. If you look at the angles, the Octahedron displays the square base of the cube, while the Icosahedron displays the five-angled <note>Pentagonal.</note> base of the Dodecahedron. 3. The Octahedron is equated to the cube, as we shall see, and the Icosahedron to the Dodecahedron. 4. The Octahedron with the cube, and the Icosahedron with the Dodecahedron, exchange their number of faces and angles. For the faces of the Cube and the angles of the Octahedron are six, while the angles of the Cube and the faces of the Octahedron are eight. Likewise, the faces of the Dodecahedron and the angles of the Icosahedron are twelve on each side; conversely, the angles of the former and the faces of the latter are twenty. 5. The Octahedron imitates the right angle of the Cube; the Icosahedron imitates the obtuse angle of the Dodecahedron. From these points, it is clear that the Octahedron is the head of its order, just as the cube is the prince of the first solids.

---

### CHAPTER VIII.

*That the Octahedron is between Venus and Mercury.*

However, it does not follow that the Octahedron must immediately follow the Dodecahedron in the world for that reason. 1. For because there are truly two different orders, they can also look toward different regions of the world with their "heads" <note>Their primary or leading shapes.</note>. 2. And furthermore, because the **Cube** approaches the most noble region of the world outside the Earth—namely, the circumference or the fixed stars—it was fitting that the head of the other order <note>The Octahedron.</note> should approach a more noble place in the world within the orbit of the Earth. Nothing, however, is more noble than the center and the **Sun**. 3. Even if we were to consider the placement of both orders as one, what could be more elegant than for that order to be enclosed on both sides by similar and primary bodies? 4. It is also more beautiful for multifaceted bodies to follow one another in the middle, and for one to descend gradually from a plurality of faces toward a few on both sides (if nothing else prevents it), rather than if a body with few faces followed one with many, only to be followed again by another with far more faces than either of them. 5. And since the Dodecahedron was the last in its order, it was fitting that it should be succeed—

Since it turned out that it was closely surrounded on the outside by a many-faced solid <note>original: "multifacium"; here referring to the Dodecahedron</note>, it was fair that it should also be closely embraced on the inside by a many-faced solid <note>The Icosahedron</note>. These two orders of these five bodies were thus reduced to one by the wisest Creator, so that they might be turned with their "heels" <note>Kepler uses anatomical metaphors to describe how the nested shapes touch one another</note> toward the Earth, which is their dividing wall, and their "heads" might depart into different regions of the world.

### On Chapter V. Author’s Notes.

(1) **Hence the inscription of the right angle into the circle is so fruitful.**] From the aptitude of the right angle, namely, and because every angle in a semicircle is a right angle <note>A fundamental theorem of Euclidean geometry: any triangle drawn from the diameter of a circle to any point on its circumference will have a 90-degree angle</note>.

## CHAPTER IX.

->The solids distributed among the Planets, their properties adapted, and the mutual kinship of the planets demonstrated from the solids.<-

I cannot pass by without tasting here some things from that part of Physics which concerns the qualities of the Planets; so that it may appear that even their natural powers observe this order, and retain that proportion toward one another. For if you count those planets that go around the Earth with those solids that they contain inscribed within them, and if you assign to the planets enclosed by the Earth's orbit those solids by which each is circumscribed—which I think can be done for the best reason—**Saturn** will have the **Cube**, **Jupiter** the **Pyramid** <note>The Tetrahedron</note>, **Mars** the **Dodecahedron**, **Venus** the **Icosahedron**, and **Mercury** the **Octahedron**. The **Earth**, indeed, since it is nothing but a boundary <note>The "maceries" or dividing wall between the inner and outer planets</note>, is counted toward neither. Astrologers also distinguish the **Sun** and **Moon** by the greatest interval from the other five, so there is no need to mention them here, and the number of solids beautifully matches with the five Planets.

**Jupiter**, therefore, (1) being beneficial himself in the middle of the malicious ones <note>original: "maleficarum"; in astrology, Saturn and Mars were considered "malefic" or harmful, while Jupiter was "benefic" or helpful</note>, has drawn many into admiration, and even stimulated Ptolemy to an investigation of the causes. We see something similar in the pyramid, which, between two bodies partly related and partly abhorrent to each other, differs so much from both that it is almost in danger of its place in the previous reasonings. Each of the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note> exercises (2) hostile hatreds with the others. Also, in the case of their three solids, nothing whatever of those things which appear is consistent. Yet **Mars** nevertheless conspires with **Saturn** in malice alone. To this I compare...

-># JOHANNES KEPLER<-
<meta>catchword: Mercury’s</meta>

the instability of the angles, which is characteristic of them and common to both <note>Kepler is likely referring to Venus and Mercury here, whose orbits and astrological "tempers" were considered more variable</note>. Therefore, an argument for their goodness will be the opposite: namely, the stability of the angles in the sides alone. This is the argument for why Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are "benefics" <note>In astrology, "benefic" planets—Jupiter and Venus, and sometimes Mercury—are thought to have a positive, helpful influence on human affairs</note>. The Cube, which is Saturn’s body, measures all other things by its own "rightness" <note>The 90-degree right angle of the cube symbolizes moral and physical rectitude</note>. The planet itself makes men into "measurers"; in character, he is rigid, a guardian of the right, not yielding a hair’s breadth <note>original: "ne latum vnguem cedens"; literally "not yielding a fingernail’s width"</note>, inexorable, and inflexible. This is what the rightness of the angle brings about.

A very clear kinship exists in the "bases" <note>In geometry, the "base" or face of the solid. Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are linked here because their associated solids share triangular faces</note>; because Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury (I mean the planet in place of its solid body) use the same bases, we have the cause of their friendship, as mentioned above. For stability is found first in the triangle.

The second degree [of kinship] is the apparent plane with the angle as a sort of "navel." Let us therefore no longer wonder what delights might lie hidden within the hard and fiery Mars, for whose sake the delicate Venus, frustrated with her husband’s bed, conspired with Mars <note>A reference to the mythological affair between Venus and Mars</note>. For Mars’s pentagon <note>The five-sided face of the Dodecahedron</note> is found in Venus. Likewise, Saturn’s quadrangle <note>The square face of the Cube</note> in Mercury reconciles the same habits in both. The third degree is when the same property of one thing exists or appears in two others; then, in those causes, a common friend agrees. Therefore, in matters of Jupiter, Venus agrees with Mercury because they use Jupiter’s common base. In matters of Saturn, Mercury agrees with Mars for a short while, because in the former is Saturn’s square, and in the latter is the "hidden cube." It is also clear from this why there is no kinship between Venus and Saturn, and which [kinships] are strongest, and why Mercury’s versatile nature applies itself to all four, yet least of all to Mars.

Saturn is also solitary and a lover of solitude, clearly because the rightness of his angle cannot bear any inequality, even the smallest, for the sake of which it might become manifold. On the other hand, Jupiter, having obtained one angle from the class of infinite acute angles, was thereby made "popular" <note>In the sense of being social or public-facing</note>, yet in a moderate and temperate way. For he is the author of more honorable friendships. Likewise, Mars and Venus are popular themselves, but too much so. For their obtuse and "prodigal" angle denotes intemperance. Mercury is of the nature of Saturn and Jupiter by reason of his angle. Indeed, men of letters love solitude, but they are not inhumane. They love those who delight in the same studies; they set a limit on their conversations, more so than Jupiter, whose every action is in gatherings of men and among the "purple-clad" <note>original: "purpuratos"; referring to high-ranking officials or royalty who wore purple robes</note>.

Jupiter and Venus are fertile. This is surely because Jupiter contributes to the composition of most things; Venus, however, is like the offspring of Jupiter, since one Venus <note>The Icosahedron, associated here with Venus, contains twenty triangular faces</note> contains twenty "short" Jupiters <note>The Tetrahedron, associated with Jupiter, is a triangular pyramid</note> within herself. Jupiter, moreover, is more favorable toward males, and Venus toward females; hence he is called male and she female. For the Pyramid <note>The Tetrahedron</note> is the active "effector," and the Icosahedron is the "effect" and the offspring. From these same principles, a somewhat clearer reason is given for why Mercury is of "mixed sex" <note>In traditional astrology, Mercury is considered androgynous or "common," taking on the gender of the planets it is near</note> and why he is of middling fertility.

The tranquility and constancy of character in Jupiter first, then Saturn, and finally Mercury, comes from the small number of faces; the turbulence and lightness of Venus and Mars come from their many faces. "A woman is always a fickle and changeable thing" <note>original: "Varium et mutabile semper femina"; a famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*</note>. And the figure of Venus is the most varied and volatile of all. And these are the degrees: whence Mercury is in the middle, with middle-level reliability.

-># THE MYSTERY OF THE COSMOS<-

The versatile and swift character of Mercury is reflected in the mobility of the **Octahedron**. For if you roll it upon two of its opposite corners, four continuous edges pass through the middle of the figure in a straight path. In all other figures, no matter how you roll them, you will see the edges move across the middle in a crooked and hindered way.

**Mars** produces fewer planes [faces] from many edges; **Venus** produces more planes from the same number of edges. <note>Kepler is comparing the Icosahedron (Venus) and the Dodecahedron (Mars). Both have 30 edges, but the Icosahedron has 20 faces while the Dodecahedron has 12. Note that Kepler's mapping of planets to solids shifted throughout his career; here he explores their numerical properties.</note> Furthermore, many of Mars's attempts are in vain; Venus is equal to him in her attempts, yet she enjoys a more prosperous fortune. Nor should this be a wonder. For dances are more easily established than wars, and it was only fitting that loves should reach their end more quickly than rages; because the latter destroy men, while the former produce them. By the same logic, Mercury is more fortunate than Saturn.

# ON CHAPTER NINE
## Notes by the Author.

Although this chapter is nothing but an <term>astrological game</term><note>original: "lusus astrologicus"; Kepler often distinguished between "serious" physical astronomy and the more symbolic or popular astrology of his day, though he sought a physical basis for both.</note>, and should not be considered a core part of this work but rather an excursion: nevertheless, let the reader compare it with the reasoning of **Ptolemy**, both in his *Tetrabiblos* and his *Harmonics*. He will see that our arguments are not inferior to Ptolemy’s, and perhaps even better.

(1) **In the midst of the malefics.**] I am speaking here in the language of the astrologers. For if I were to state my own opinion, I consider no planet in the heavens to be a "malefic" <note>In traditional astrology, Saturn and Mars were called "malefics" because they were thought to cause harm; Jupiter and Venus were "benefics."</note>. I hold this view for many reasons, but especially because of this: it is the Nature of the human being himself, dwelling here on Earth, which mediates the effect within itself from the radiations of the Planets. This is just as the sense of hearing, being equipped with the faculty of distinguishing the harmonies of voices, grants to Music the power to incite the listener to dance. I have discussed this matter at length in my *Response to the Objections of Doctor Roslin* regarding my book on the *New Star*, and elsewhere throughout my writings, especially in Book IV of the *Harmonics*, particularly in Chapter 7.

(2) **It carries out hostile hatreds.**] This can be defended by physical reasoning if understood allegorically: for instance, if by the word "hatred" we understand any kind of difference in position, motion, light, or color. Let the reader see the final chapter of Ptolemy’s *Harmonics* when it is published, and what I have noted therein—especially my latest speculation regarding the mutual excesses or defects of **Saturn** and **Mars**, and the moderation of **Jupiter**.

# CHAPTER X.
## (1) On the origin of the noble numbers.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut capital letter "I" showing a figure amidst swirling vines and leaves.</image-desc>

It would be an endless task to pursue every single detail; nor would an Astrologer think further on these things without profit. Let us now look at the Arithmetic of the Astronomers and their sacred numbers: 6, 12, and 60. Therefore, with the exception of the <term>quadrant</term> and the <term>sextant</term> (namely, 15 and 10), all the divisor parts of sixty are found in these five bodies. (2) Conversely, with the exception of the plane angles of the Octahedron and the Cube (each of which has 24), all other things that are counted are a multiple part of sixty. Thus, I suspect that hardly any number could be assigned to any natural thing—not even by **Pythagoras**—that is more proper to it than this number 60 is to the five mentioned bodies.

There is one **Cube**, one **Pyramid** <note>The Tetrahedron</note>, one **Dodecahedron**, one **Icosahedron**, and one **Octahedron**—each one solitary, without anything like it.

### ON CHAPTER TEN
->Author’s Notes.<-

(1) **CONCERNING** the origin of the noble Numbers.] As has already been said above, all the nobility of Numbers (which <term>Pythagorean Theology</term><note>The ancient philosophical tradition that viewed numbers as the fundamental building blocks of reality and divinity.</note> especially admires and compares to divine things) originates primarily from Geometry. While there are indeed many parts to geometry, these five solid figures are not the first nor the only cause of this nobility; rather, it happens that many elements conspire toward the same number. For the first origin of the suitability of numbers comes from regular plane figures that can be inscribed in a circle, and their congruence; from these, the solids later arise. See books I and II of my *Harmonics*. Lest you be confused when you read that the proofs for the sides used by the figures are summoned from the numbers of the angles—as if the Number, as the "counting agent," were therefore prior and more worthy. Not at all; for the angles of a figure do not become countable because the concept of that number preceded them, but rather the concept of the number follows because geometric things have that multiplicity in themselves, existing as the <term>numbered Number</term><note>original: "Numerus numeratus"; a Scholastic term referring to the quantity inherent in things themselves, rather than the abstract "counting number" (numerus numerans) in the mind.</note> itself.

(2) In turn excepted, etc. and below, Eight bases.] Behold a manifest hallucination <note>Kepler here uses "hallucinatio" to mean a clear oversight or error in his previous thinking or in the text he is commenting upon.</note>: Eight is not a part of sixty, but it is certainly a part of the number 120, which is twice 60.

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

### CHAPTER XI.

->(1) *On the placement of the bodies, and the origin of the Zodiac.*<-

I will have the physicists as my enemies in these chapters, for the reason that I have derived the natural properties of the planets from immaterial things and mathematical figures; and furthermore, that I even dare to investigate the origins of the circles from the mere imagination of certain sections. To these few I wish to respond: that (2) God the Creator, since He is Mind and does what He wills, is not prohibited from looking toward things that exist either without matter or in the imagination when fitting the forces and designating the circles. And since He wills nothing except with the highest reason, and nothing exists outside of His will: let my adversaries say, then, what other reasons God had for fitting the forces, etc., when there was nothing besides quantities? But if, while they find nothing, they flee to the "unsearchable powers of Creating Wisdom," let them indeed keep this restraint in inquiry, and let them enjoy that alongside their reputation for piety; but let them suffer us to offer probable causes derived from quantities, provided we say nothing unworthy of so great a Maker. Bound, therefore, by no such religious scruple <note>original: "nulla igitur vinctus religione" — here meaning a constraint or hesitation rather than a lack of faith</note>, I proceed to the investigation of the Zodiac.

At the beginning, I think a more probable placement of the bodies cannot be devised than when the Cube, the largest of the figures, is inserted into the sphere in any way (for in a circle there is no beginning. (3) However, it is necessary to establish principles without a reason, (4) lest there be an infinite regress; (5) and so that we may eventually have a transition from infinite potentiality to finite act.) Now, therefore, let one of the faces be considered the base. The <term>Pyramid <note>Kepler uses "Pyramis" to refer to the four-sided Tetrahedron</note></term>, therefore, to be inserted into the Cube by means of the Jovian sphere <note>the sphere of Jupiter</note>, (6) must hold its base <term>parallel <note>original: παράλληλον (parallēlon)</note></term> to the base of the Cube: and (7) the Dodecahedron to the base of the pyramid. Otherwise, the properties of the secondary solids dictate, as we have seen. The Icosahedron must then be erected within the Dodecahedron, so that its diagonal becomes perpendicular to the centers of both opposite bases of the Dodecahedron. In the same way, (8) the Octahedron, the smallest of the figures, must be suspended within the Icosahedron, so that a straight line passes:
1. through the center of the base in the Cube,
2. through the center of the Tetrahedral base,
3. through the center of the Dodecahedral pentagon,
4. through the vertex <note>angle</note> of the Icosahedron,
5. through the vertex of the Octahedron,
6. through the center of the world and the solar body,
and further through similar intervals through the opposite points:
7. the Octahedron's vertices,
8. the Icosahedron's vertices,
9. the center of the Dodecahedral plane,
10. the Tetrahedral vertex,
11. the center of the Cubic plane.
For the sake of greater clarity, I refer you to the small plate in the second chapter, where all the bodies are expressed in this manner. With these things thus established, not only does the square appearing in the Octahedron—equally distant from the two said vertices—divide all the figures and indeed the whole world into two equal parts if it is extended all around; but also the mutual sections of all the sides (9) which one can consider middle points between the said vertices and centers—I say, if all of these (10) are placed regularly—which to one looking from the center...

# ON CHAPTER ELEVEN
## Notes by the Author.

(1) **On the placement of the bodies, and the origin of the Zodiac.** *This whole chapter, as far as its goal is concerned, could have been omitted, for it is of no importance. For this is neither the genuine placement, nor the fitting together of the five Geometric bodies among themselves, as will be clear below; nor, if it were, would the Zodiac come from it.*

(2) **The Creator, since He is Mind.** *Behold how this principle, in which I was already most firmly persuaded back then, has paid me interest over these twenty-five years: namely, that mathematical things are the causes of natural things <note>This is Kepler's "Platonic" view: that the physical world is shaped by mathematical laws</note> (a dogma which Aristotle attacked in so many places). This is because God the Creator had mathematical things with Him from eternity as <term>Archetypes</term> <note>Archetypes: original patterns or blueprints from which all things are modeled</note> in the simplest and most divine abstraction, even from the quantities themselves, considered materially. Aristotle denied the Creator and established the world as eternal; it is no wonder, then, if he rejected archetypes. For I confess that they would have had no future power if God Himself had not looked upon them in creating. Therefore, the causes of the <term>Eccentricities</term> <note>Eccentricity: the amount by which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note> were also finally discovered from this principle. Anyone who seriously thinks about them must greatly wonder at their inequality—anyone who, with Aristotle, asks about celestial things thus: **"Why is it that the lower any Planet is, it is not carried by more orbs?"** <note>original: "Quare non quo quilibet Planeta humilior, eo pluribus orbibus vehitur?"</note> For he who thought he should inquire into this in the Astronomy of his time, and in that false persuasion of solid orbs: if that same man were alive today, and knew our pure and genuine doctrine of the heavens, he would think he should ask much more: **"Why is it that the more interior any Planet is, it does not also have a smaller eccentricity?"** And so, having exhausted all the reasons which his own principles might suggest, with that perpetual voice, "Why not?"; if Aristotle were finally taught that the most beautiful and clearly necessary causes of this matter can be rendered from Harmonies as if from an Archetype; I think that with the fullest assent he would have accepted both the Archetypes and—because these have no efficacy by themselves—God as the architect of the world. These things, then, regarding the thesis itself: which nevertheless was not successfully applied to the hypothesis in this chapter, as I began to say.*

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s mathematical and philosophical defense of his geometric model of the universe. In the previous pages, he discussed the "unfolding" of the Platonic solids to represent planetary paths. Here, he responds to potential philosophical objections—specifically from Aristotelian logic—regarding why the world is structured the way it is and how these geometric shapes must be positioned (or "inscribed") within one other to maintain perfect symmetry.</meta>

-># THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.<-

<meta>catchword: are</meta>

(3) *“However, one must establish principles without a reason.”*] This was said concerning those things which, in the category of quantities, have the nature of **matter**. For example, the **spherical** itself is, by its own nature, one whole and everywhere similar to itself in its **form** <note>original: "formaliter," referring to the essential shape or idea</note>; but in its **matter** <note>original: "materialiter," referring to physical or divisible substance</note>, as a surface, it consists of part after part. Since the infinity of division dominates the sphere by way of its parts, the sphere is therefore not considered according to its form when it is divisible into parts, but according to its matter. Or, what is the same: the sphere has no "formal" parts. The parts that are considered within it are "material" parts, insofar as the shape of the sphere uses quantitative matter and can be divided. Now, when a **Cube** is actually inscribed in a sphere, if the sphere is considered "formally" as a shape, there is no room for the question of at which points the corners of the cube should be placed. But if you consider it "materially," as a surface of infinite points, then there is indeed room for the question: at which points? But it cannot be answered, since there is no reason why it should be in these points rather than in others; indeed, it could be in infinite different points.

*Questions of this kind are also of this nature: When an infinite **space beyond the world** <note>original: "spatium vltramundanum"</note> is imagined, and it is asked of it, why the world is placed in this part of space rather than another; likewise, when **eternal time** (a contradiction in terms <note>original: "oppositum in adiecto"</note>) is imagined, and it is asked: Why was the world finally founded six thousand years ago, while God abstained from creating from all eternity? For both space and time, in the category of quantities, have the nature of matter, at least in respect to the shapes of quantities. Matter, of itself, supplies no reasons; in itself it has one and only one property: the infinity of parts—actual infinity if the whole is actually infinite in number or quantity; but potential infinity of number if the whole is actually finite. This latter is the only possibility when quantity exists in physical or celestial bodily matter. See the first book of the **Epitome of Astronomy**, page 40, where the shape of the heavens is discussed.*

(4) *“Lest there be an infinite regress”*] This reasoning, familiar to **Aristotle**, is applied here irrelevantly; indeed, not even a starting point is given for any "regress" in assigning reasons where there is plainly no reason at all.

(5) *“And so that we may at last make a transition.”*] If, I say, the beginning of a work must not be made without a reason, then no beginning could ever be made; for the reasons for choosing this or that beginning, where infinite options are given, are plainly non-existent. Therefore, when something that could equally happen in infinite points happens in one of them, it is beyond all reason why it should be in that one specifically, with the others passed over.

(6) *“It ought to have a base parallel to the base of the cube.”*] And yet **Geometry** teaches a far more elegant <note>original: "concinniorem"</note> and perfect placement of the **Pyramid** <note>the four-sided tetrahedron</note> within the **Cube**: more elegant, because the same reason that governs the geometric inscription of the former in the latter will also be elegant in the world; but geometrically, the Pyramid is inscribed in the Cube such that any side of the Pyramid becomes the **diagonal** of one of the Cube's faces. It is a "more perfect" placement because, if one base of the Pyramid were made parallel to one base of the Cube, the placement of the three triangular sides of the base would still be uncertain in relation to the four sides of the square base. For any of those could be set parallel to any of these; or it could be stretched toward one of the corners so that the perpendicular of the triangular plane matches the side of the Cube in the same plane. Finally, a placement is not "perfect" where similar positions do not occur for all planes; but when one plane of the Pyramid is parallel to a plane of the cube, its remaining planes will be parallel to none of the cube's planes. The same should be said of the edges and the angles.

(7) *“Dodecahedron to the base of the Pyramid.”*] Here the placement is inconsistent with both shapes, both the Pyramid and the Cube. For geometric inscription teaches that the four angles of the Pyramid ought rather to be joined to (or placed upon) four of the twenty angles of the **Dodecahedron**. Likewise, the geometric inscription of the Cube into the Dodecahedron teaches that eight of the twelve diagonals of the Dodecahedron become the eight edges of the Cube. Therefore, if the Dodecahedron were conversely inside the Cube, six of the thirty edges of the Dodecahedron must be placed subordinate to the six planes of the Cube in a parallel position.

(8) *“The Octahedron will have to be suspended.”*] In this way, the position of the innermost **Octahedron** within the outermost Cube will correspond to its geometric inscription in the Cube. But it will not be lawfully adapted to the Pyramid, Dodecahedron, or **Icosahedron** unless their positions in the Cube are corrected according to the laws already prescribed. For then there will coincide, in one straight line drawn from the common center of all the figures: 1. an angle of the Octahedron, 2. the midpoints of the edges of the Icosahedron, 3. of the Dodecahedron, 4. and of the Pyramid, and 5. the center of the cubic plane. There will be six such lines, and the placement will be everywhere similar to itself.

(9) *“Which one can judge as midpoints between the said angles and centers.”*] Because in the Pyramid, through this faulty placement, we are hindered from being able to judge the midpoints of the sides.

(10) *“If they are placed regularly.”*] Then indeed, even in the Pyramid, four midpoints of the sides will be found; then also the placement of the figures within one another will respect the laws of geometric inscriptions.

(11) *“For the said sides of the others cannot be placed together in a fitting way.”*] Not pos—

<summary>Kepler critiques the placement of Platonic solids within one another, arguing that they must follow strict geometric "laws of inscription" rather than arbitrary positioning. He also addresses Aristotelian philosophy, arguing that while "matter" (like space and time) provides no inherent reason for specific placement, "form" (geometry) reflects the purposeful design of the Creator.</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Kepler, Platonic solids, geometry, Aristotle, matter vs form, cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron, cosmic harmony, inscription of solids</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s commentary on the spatial arrangement of the five Platonic solids and their relationship to the celestial spheres. In the preceding text, he began addressing the problem of "indifference"—the idea that if space is uniform, there is no inherent reason why a shape or a planet should be placed in one specific spot rather than another. Here, he moves into a direct critique of Aristotelian physics and explains how God’s creative "thought" establishes order where there was once only a "negation" of space.</meta>

# JOHANNES KEPLER

<meta>catchword: CA-</meta>

I say, all the sides of one coincide with the sides of the other—least of all in the case of the **Pyramid** <note>original: "Pyramidis," referring to the tetrahedron</note>. Certainly, they cannot be placed coincidently for the reason that the starting point of their positioning was not made regular.

(12) [*But if the angle of one is at the midpoint of the side of the other.*] This is indeed the legitimate positioning of these two bodies relative to one another; but the positioning of the **Octahedron** adopted here is illegitimate.

(13) [*What remains, then, but for us to say.*] Certainly, many things remain that prevent us from saying this. For the positioning that marks the poles here is illegitimate. Indeed, insofar as the positioning is legitimate in two cases—the **Dodecahedron** and the **Icosahedron**—there could be as many poles as there are angles of the former or faces of the latter: namely, twelve. Consequently, there would be six intermediate zones. The **Planets** would therefore be uncertain as to which way they should go. In general, this is hindered by the fact that those figures are not expressed in the world by the actual physical positioning of their parts relative to one another; rather, only the proportion of the figurative orbits taken from them was transferred into the celestial spheres, and the number of spheres was established by the figures. Therefore, we more rightly reject as absurd *this question: why do the planets run along this path rather than another?* For since the circle was in the intention of God—being necessary for the motions of the planets—God surrounded that circle, established by His intention, with a material and starry spherical shell. 

Nor did any doubt hold God back from His work, as if He could not make a beginning of it without a specific reason. For at that time, no body pre-existed in respect to whose parts He might have doubted. Indeed, space without a body is a pure negation. There is enough reason for making a beginning in the infinite "Nothing" simply to think, however lightly, of something. For such a thought is immediately infinitely more excellent than the remaining infinity which is neither actual, nor existent, nor thought of; and thus, it is prior to that infinity and fit for a beginning. 

Nor am I the first who has exhausted myself with this useless question: *Namely, why was the Zodiac drawn here, when it could have been in infinite other places?* You can find a similar question in **Aristotle**: *Why do the Planets go into this region rather than into its opposite?* For even here, there is no reason for one over the other, since every line, by the condition of its length, possesses two directions <note>original: "plagas," meaning regions or directions of space</note> which are in a straight line toward its two ends. Aristotle indeed confesses there that, in general, the reasons for all things cannot be sought in the same way; yet he attempts this question. *He says that Nature always chooses the best among possibilities; but it is better that the stars be carried into a more noble region;* and yet, *the region "forward" is more noble than "backward."* 

This is ridiculous. For before there was motion, neither region was called "forward" or "backward"; the premise is being assumed <note>term: "principium petitur" (begging the question) — a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise</note>. He argues indeed from the similarity of the world to animals, establishing the *idea of the world* as **Animals with their six regions** <note>Aristotle's six directions: up/down, front/back, left/right</note>. But again, the premise is assumed. For let us grant that *the world was made according to the likeness of an animal;* let him then say first concerning the animal itself, why this is "forward" for it and that is "backward," and not vice versa. That is, why are the eyes, ears, nostrils, tongue, and mouth directed toward the image in a mirror, the joints of the arms, hands, and fingers bent toward them, and the palms of the feet extended toward them; and not rather, like the limbs of the image in the mirror, backward away from the man? For it could have been done that way too. That is: the heart, which is now on the left, could have been placed in the seat which we now consider the right. And since the reason for this world is established, what then? Could its application to the sides of the world not have been made just as easily in reverse? What prevented it from stretching the left toward the South and the right toward the North when it was commanded to mark out the regions of the world? For in that case, it would have turned its face toward the region which is now called the West; thus the stars would have had the opposite region as "forward," toward which they would tend in their motions. 

Aristotle would have done better, therefore, to have refrained from a solution to this foolish question, obeying his own warning. For among those things which could all happen equally, Nature finds no choice between **Better and Worse**; for this involves a contradiction. Rather, let us argue thus: Since **Being** <note>original: "Ens"</note> is superior to **Non-Being**, and the World did not yet exist, whatever region of it was conceived as "forward" in the beginning now has better reasons on its part why it should be "forward" than its opposite does—by this very fact: because its opposite is conceived to be in **Non-Being**. Even if that opposite had been made "forward," the World would still have been made similar to this present one. A comparison of Worlds has no place where there is only one. 

Farewell, then, to material questions of this kind, and with them also the marking out of the **Zodiac**, or rather (since it moves from its places in succession), the **Royal Road** <note>original: "via Regia," refers to the Ecliptic, the sun's apparent path</note> shown by the circle of the Solar body midway between its poles. For if the poles and axis of the solar body had been turned toward other regions of the world, the Royal Road would also have been drawn elsewhere. The same must also be said of the figures of the **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron**. For let us grant that it is their office to mark out the Zodiac by the mutual intersections of their sides, and indeed of a certain order from the six which we said were possible; certainly, if the positioning of the figures in the sensible World were transferred, another seat would also fall to the Zodiac.

<summary>Kepler critiques Aristotle’s teleological explanations for the direction of planetary motion, arguing that spatial directions like "forward" only exist once God initiates motion. He asserts that the geometric structure of the universe arises from divine thought, which transforms "Non-Being" into a singular, ordered reality.</summary>

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY

### CHAPTER XII.
#### *The division of the Zodiac, and the aspects.*

Many have held the division of the Zodiac into twelve precise signs to be a human invention, a thing, namely, which has no natural reality beneath it. For they do not believe that these portions <note>original: "μόρια" (moria)</note> differ in their natural powers or properties, but were adopted because of the suitability of that number for calculations. (1) Although I do not entirely disagree with them, nevertheless, lest anything be rejected rashly, I shall propose the cause of this division based on the same principles <note>referring to the five Platonic solids</note>, to which it is not unlikely that the Creator accommodated the properties of the signs (if indeed they have distinct ones).

We have seen above what the subject of numbers is. And (2) certainly, besides quantity, or something similar to quantity endowed with some power, there is nothing in the whole universe that can be numbered, except for God, who is the very same venerable Trinity <note>original: "ipsissima veneranda Trinitas"</note>. Now, therefore, (3) we have dissected all the bodies <note>the five Platonic solids</note> through the Zodiac. Let us see (4) what the Zodiac itself has gained or undergone through this sectioning. When the bodies are cut in the stated manner, the face of the **Cube** resulting from the section will be square, as will that of the **Octahedron**; the **Pyramid** <note>the tetrahedron</note> will be triangular; and the remaining two <note>the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron</note> will be decagonal <note>ten-sided</note>. Four times three times ten makes a sum of one hundred and twenty. Therefore, when the square, the triangle, and the decagon are inscribed in a circle at the same point, they mark out various arcs on the circumference, all of which are measured by a portion no larger than a one-hundred-and-twentieth <image-desc>A circular diagram containing an inscribed square and an equilateral triangle, both sharing a vertex at the top point of the circle.</image-desc> part of the whole circle. Thus, the natural division of the Zodiac into 120 parts arises from the regular positioning of the bodies between the spheres. Since three times this is 360, we see that this division is not based on no reason at all. Now, if we again describe the square and the triangle separately from the same point, the smallest portion of the circle will be the twelfth part of the circuit, namely a **Sign** <note>a "Sign" of the Zodiac equals 30 degrees, or 1/12th of the circle</note>. It is wonderful (5) how both the monthly motion of the Sun and Moon, and (6) the **Great Conjunctions** <note>the rare meetings of Jupiter and Saturn</note> of the outer planets, so aptly square with the portions that are distinguished by these same bodies through the triangle and the square.

(7) And indeed, to see how much this twelve-fold division is valued by nature, take an example from outside this field; so that although the cause does not entirely compel it to be so, an opportunity may nonetheless open up for thinking more excellently about these five figures.

Let there be a certain string <note>a monochord</note> proposed, and its sound be **Gamma ut** <note>the lowest note in the medieval musical system, equivalent to a low G</note>. Therefore, as many times as consonant notes occur from **Gamma** up to the octave (8), just so many times, and no more, can you rationally divide the string, so that the parts of the divided string harmonize both with each other and with the whole. Furthermore, the ears indicate how many notes of that kind occur. I shall state it with a diagram and numbers.

(9) And these sounds alone seem natural to me, for the reason that they possess an indubitable number. Other sounds cannot be expressed by a certain proportion to those already established. (10) For you will draw out the sound **F fa ut** <note>F in the Guidonian system</note> one way from **C sol fa ut** from above, and another way from **B-flat** from below, even though these two may seem to be perfect fifths. But to the matter at hand: the first and second concordances <note>musical harmonies</note> are in a way companions; so too are the fifth and sixth. (11) Since all of these are imperfect <note>in Renaissance music theory, thirds and sixths were "imperfect" consonances, while octaves and fifths were "perfect"</note>: they always breathe together in pairs, one "hard" <note>major</note> and the other "soft" <note>minor</note>, so that they are in some way made equal to the individual perfect concordances. Nor do they have very different divisions. For 4/5 and 5/6 relate to each other as 24/30 and 25/30, which differ by only one thirtieth. Likewise, 3/5 and 5/8 relate to each other as 24/40 and 25/40. They differ, therefore, by only one fortieth part. And so, properly speaking, we have only five concordances in Music, corresponding to the number of the five bodies <note>the Platonic solids</note>. (12) Indeed, if you seek the least common multiple of the seven divisions into 6, 5, 4, 3, 8, 5, and 2, you will again find 120—just as above, when we were discussing the division of the Zodiac. However, the least common multiple of the perfect concordances is again 12. (13) It is quite as if the perfect concordances proceed from the square and triangle of the **Cube**, **Tetrahedron**, and **Octahedron**, while the imperfect ones proceed from the decagon <note>ten-sided figure</note> of the remaining two bodies <note>the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron</note>. And this is the second kinship of the bodies with Musical concordances. (14) But because we are ignorant of the causes of this kinship, it is difficult to match individual harmonies to individual bodies.

(15) We do indeed see two orders of harmonies: three simple perfect ones, and two double imperfect ones; just as there are three primary bodies and two secondary ones. However, since the rest do not agree, this reconciliation must be deferred, and another attempted. Namely, just as the **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron**, by their decagon, increased the number twelve up to 120, so here the imperfect harmonies do the same.

Therefore, the perfect harmonies will have to be matched to the **Cube**, the **Pyramid** <note>Tetrahedron</note>, and the **Octahedron**, and the imperfect ones to the **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron**. To this is added another point, and by heaven, (16) it points an index finger toward the most hidden cause of these things, which we shall have in the next chapter: (17) namely, that there are two treasures of Geometry: one, the ratio of the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle to its sides <note>the Pythagorean theorem</note>; the other, a line cut in extreme and mean ratio <note>the Golden Ratio</note>. From the former flows the construction of the **Cube**, **Pyramid**, and **Octahedron**; from the latter, the construction of the **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron**. This is why the inscription of the **Pyramid** into the **Cube**, and the **Octahedron** into both, is as easy and regular as that of the **Dodecahedron** into the **Icosahedron**. (18) However, how the individual Harmonies are to be matched to the individual bodies is not so obvious. (19) Only this is clear: that to the **Pyramid** is owed the harmony they call the **fifth** <note>diapente</note>, which is fourth in order, because in it the smaller portion is a whole 1/3 part, just as the side of the triangle (which the **Pyramid** uses) subtends 1/3 of a circle. More on this below.

<summary>Kepler argues that the five musical concordances correspond to the five Platonic solids, noting that the mathematical logic (least common multiples) linking them also governs the 120-fold division of the Zodiac. He identifies the Pythagorean theorem and the Golden Ratio as the two geometric "treasures" that define the shapes and harmonies of the cosmos.</summary>

For as we have seen, (28) Nature recognizes no such concord in musical voices. Since in all other things the ratio of astrological influence and musical harmonies is the same, it is credible that it is the same here as well. (29) The cause on both sides is undoubtedly the same, and stems from the five solids—a matter I leave for others to seek. (30) Since, therefore, all four harmonies resonate with their aspects, and yet there remain three more harmonies in music; I once suspected that it should not be ignored in the judgment of births <note>horoscopes</note> if planets are distant by 72, 144, or 135 degrees, especially since I see that one of the imperfect harmonies has its own aspect. # ON CHAPTER TWELVE
## Author's Notes.

(1) **Although I do not entirely oppose these things.**] *I have treated this theme in detail in my book on the New Star <note>"De Stella Nova" (1606), concerning the supernova of 1604</note>, and in my response to the objections of Röslin: namely, that the four quadrants of the Zodiac circle are shown by the conditions of the two motions, the daily and the annual motion of the Sun, which the limits of Light and Heating also follow. But as for the subdivision of the individual quadrants, the internal signs precisely have nothing of the sort from either motion or power whose effect could be judged—except those parts which no necessity demands to be equal, nor even parts at all: for it is enough that the whole line of the quadrant be considered the middle, and for the beginning and the end, the two boundaries or points of the line, which are not a part of the line.*

(2) **Nothing in the whole universe is numerable except quantity, or something similar to quantity, endowed with any power whatsoever.**] *A ridiculous opinion escaped me—truly not an opinion. For what is "Nothing besides Everything"? Numbering, an action of the Mind, is added to all things, divine and human: there is no distinction, not even the slightest, whether real or intentional (be it first or se-*

of the second, or third, or any level of intention; <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "first intention" is a concept of a thing itself; a "second intention" is a concept of that concept—a level of mental abstraction.</note>) which does not have some similarity with the division of a straight line into parts. See what I have discussed concerning numbers in Book IV of my *Harmonics*, Chapter I, page 117. This, however, was in my mind when I conceived this opinion: that whatever is numbered by us (except for the Divine Persons in the Most Holy Trinity) has some quantitative aspect, at least in the intention of the one doing the counting.

(3) [**We have dissected the solids through the Zodiac.**] By imagining a plane drawn through those sections of the sides and through the center of all the figures, and extended all the way to the fixed stars; the intersection of this plane with the sphere of the fixed stars produced the Ecliptic <note>The path the Sun appears to follow across the sky.</note> in that conception.

(4) [**What the Zodiac itself gained by this section.**] Namely, if from the common center of the figures, straight lines are projected through the sections of the said plane with the sides of the figures, all the way to the fixed stars. It must be added: if all five figures are also fitted together in such an irregular position that the individual sides of each stand in one such straight line by their sections; for then the Zodiac will be divided into such parts as are measured only by a one-hundred-and-twentieth of the whole <note>This would divide the 360-degree circle into 3-degree segments.</note>. However, since that position is irregular—while the regular position through the eight angles of the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron falling on both sides into the said plane divides the Zodiac into irrational parts—it is clear that this division is not proper to the five figures. Therefore, in the *Epitome of Astronomy*, Book II, page 181, I demonstrated that this belongs properly to the plane figures, the demonstrable Regular figures, if they are inscribed in a circle from one of its points.

(5) [**The monthly motion of the Sun and Moon.**] For the Sun, understand "annual." For while the Sun completes its annual circuit, the Moon completes nearly twelve months. And so I establish this distribution of the year, and the accommodation of the motions of the Sun and Moon, at least in the first concept of their proportion, as archetypal <note>meaning part of God's original blueprint for the universe</note>. From this ordering, and from the concurrence of natural moving causes, I derive the causes of certain inequalities in the Moon, as I advised in the *Prolegomena to the Ephemerides*, and teach fully in the *Epitome of Astronomy*, Book IV. You may find something similar there also concerning the proportion of the year to the 360 daily revolutions (in the first intention), to which are then added, due to the concurrence of causes, 5 and a quarter revolutions—from which a new equation of time is elicited. Although I am still deliberating and weighing observations.

(6) [**The great conjunctions of the superior planets.**] <note>The "Great Conjunction" refers to the meeting of Saturn and Jupiter in the sky, which happens roughly every 20 years.</note> This indeed is accidental, not archetypal. For as I teach in Book V of the *Harmonics*, the periodic times of the planets arise from the harmonic tempering of the extreme motions. For at Aphelion <note>the point in orbit furthest from the Sun</note> the proportion of the motions ought to be almost 2 to 5; at Perihelion <note>the point closest to the Sun</note>, however, it is 5 to 12. This is so that between the Aphelion of Saturn and the Perihelion of Jupiter there could be a **Twelfth** <note>original: "Diapente Epi Diapason"; a musical interval of an octave plus a fifth</note>, but between the Perihelion of Saturn and the Aphelion of Jupiter, a perfect **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, because these two harmonies are related to the **Cube**. This is the first and archetypal cause in the motions. If, therefore, as with the motions at Aphelion, the proportion of the whole periods were 2 to 5, then in 60 years exactly two revolutions of Saturn and five of Jupiter would occur; in 12 years, one of Jupiter. And Saturn and Jupiter, joined for example at the beginning of Aries, would meet again exactly after 20 years at the very beginning of *Sagittarius*. For Jupiter, having overtaken Saturn, while it traverses the *Zodiac* chasing the fleeing Saturn, the latter has meanwhile moved from Aries only so far that Jupiter catches it in only five revolutions, because Saturn escaped through two out of the five; thus three conjunctions remain distributed in a perfect triangle across five Jovian periods. Behold how this triangular position of conjunctions is a necessary consequence of the archetypal cause taken from the Harmonies; it would happen by the trisection of the *Zodiac*, whether by a pyramid or by a triangle, if anyone contended that it was archetypal, as I was proposing in this chapter. Conversely, if the proportion of the whole periods of Saturn and Jupiter were that which, because of harmonic temperings, the motions of the *Perihelions* ought to be (namely 5 to 12), then in 150 years Jupiter would return twelve times, once every 12 and a half years. Therefore, taking 5 from 12, 7 would remain; that is how many times Jupiter would overtake Saturn. Thus the Zodiac would be divided by these conjunctions into 7 parts, by five of which (that is, 257 degrees) two conjunctions would be removed from each other; for example, after one in the beginning of Aries, another would happen at 17 degrees of Scorpio. <insert>¶</insert> The third at 4 degrees of Virgo. But because the periodic times are composed of motions both at Aphelion and Perihelion, and all those in between, from this also arises the intermediate proportion of the periods and the distribution of conjunctions through the Zodiac. Thus, with the first placed at the beginning of Aries, the second does not come exactly to the beginning of Sagittarius, nor does it run as far as 17 degrees of Scorpio, but by a middle and uniform rate progresses three degrees beyond the triangular location. If the division of the Zodiac into three thirds by geometric figures had been the genuine and archetypal cause of this arrangement of conjunctions, it would certainly have expressed a perfect triangle; for the divine work does not wander from its archetype. Therefore, it should no longer be a wonder why the meetings of Saturn and Jupiter allude to a triangle; for the allusion is neither perfect nor plainly accidental.
