# JOHANNES KEPLER

(7) [**And even how much these.**] *These are the very principles of my work on Harmony <note>original: "Harmonici"</note>, and they are not merely opinions that had to be corrected in later times, but are the absolute truths of the matter itself. For every philosophical speculation must take its beginning from the experiences of the senses. Here, indeed, you have a most refined and full expression of what the sense of hearing testifies concerning the number of voices in a single consonance, and what the sense of sight testifies concerning the length of consonant strings.*

(8) [**So many times, and no more.**] *It is indeed a marvel that, although so many writers on Harmony have existed since ancient times, this observation—which is entirely fundamental to the number of harmonic sections and leads directly to the causes—is nowhere to be found among them. This is despite how obvious it is for anyone to experiment on any stretched string (the space beneath which can be divided by a compass <note>A tool for measuring and drawing circles</note>) by the simple application of a hard object, like a knife or a key, to the string with one hand, and striking the distinct parts with a plectrum <note>A pick used to pluck strings</note> in the other. Therefore, it was a stroke of great luck at the beginning of my speculation as I moved toward writing a work on Harmony, even though I had not yet destined it for my mind at that time. The reason why there are seven voices in order, up to the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> including the lowest note, is this: a string can be divided harmonically seven times. In each of those acts, individual sounds are established that are consonant with the sound of the whole string. See Book III of my *Harmonics*, Chapter II.*

(9) [**And these alone.**] *This is true if you call "Natural" that which is drawn out at the very first fitting of the sections, in the very footprint of the proceeding causes; so that it may be distinguished from that which is established by a secondary reason, as if artificially and by the imitation of Nature. But if you look not at the order of origin but at the proportion itself, those intervals must also be called natural which adopt those previously established proportions by imitating Nature. As in the sequence of voices Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, the interval Fa-Sol is a "Natural" interval, called a major tone, because it is formed first when the interval Re-Fa is not yet divided. If now between Re and Fa the voice Mi is designated by such a proportion of the string Mi to the string Re as Sol is to Fa, then the voice Mi itself must also be considered Natural. However, as for the reason I gave here for the distinction—as if Fa and Sol had unquestionable numbers, while Mi did not—this must be forgiven as the work of my apprenticeship <note>original: "tyrocinio"</note>. For in Book III of my *Harmonics*, Chapters V and VII, I have provided the best reasons by which even the sound Mi and similar notes are assigned their own unquestionable numbers.*

(10) [**For the voice F-fa-ut, another from.**] *This is true if you wished to establish a perfect Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> on both sides. And yet, what I did not know then is that a significant part of the discipline concerns "adulterine" <note>False or dissonant</note> consonances, which I discussed in Book III of my *Harmonics*, Chapter XII.*

(11) [**For since they are all imperfect.**] *This is what they are usually called; the ancients did not even consider them consonances. In my work on Harmony, on page 83 of the latter part, and no less in Chapters I and IV of Book III, and throughout, I also called them "imperfect," but that word does not have the same weight as "adulterine." For an adulterine consonance lacks some tiny thing that keeps it from being a full consonance; whereas nothing is lacking in a legitimate third or sixth to prevent them from being counted among the consonances. Therefore, for the sake of distinction, it is better to call thirds and sixths "minor consonances," and this not only in respect to quantity, but also in species.*

(12) [**But if of the seven divisions.**] *I established this as the heart of my argument at that time: the Zodiac is divided into 12 and 120 parts, and a string is divided harmonically into just as many; therefore, these numbers are held in high value by nature. But since the division of the Zodiac comes from the five solids (as I believed then), it seemed to follow that the division of the string was from the same source, and thus those five figures were the Ideas of the Harmonies. But now, let the reader seek the genuine causes of harmonies from my work *Harmonices Mundi*; for they are not those five geometric solids, but rather the plane figures inscribed in a circle, etc.*

(13) [**Clearly as if perfect concords from the Square and Triangle.**] *It is pleasant to look back at the first efforts of discovery, even the wandering ones. Behold the genuine and archetypal causes of concords, which I was groping for <note>original: "cæcutiens," literally "blinking" or "going blind"</note> as if they were absent, searching for them anxiously while they were right in my hands. Plane figures are the causes of concords in themselves, not insofar as they become the surfaces of solid figures. In vain did I look to the solids in establishing the harmonic proportions of the motions.*

(14) [**But because we are ignorant of the causes of this kinship.**] *And yet you now see the causes named: the plane figures. And yet it is not kinship <note>original: "cognatio"</note> nor common blood <note>original: "consanguinitas"</note>, but a naked affinity. For the plane figures, on one hand, divide the circle harmonically, and on the other hand, they fit together into the five solid figures. Therefore, both the harmonic division of the circle and the five figures meet in a third thing: namely, in the plane figures.*

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY

(15) [***We see indeed two orders of Harmonies.***] Note this diligently, and recognize from this one example the power of other accidental coincidences. The seven forms of concords, or the seven harmonic sections, were reduced in the previous pages to a group of five <term>Quinarius; a grouping of five things</term> in whatever way possible, so that two imperfect ones were always counted as one. This group of five departs into two members, so that three stand on one side and two on the other. And yet, the group of five [Platonic] solids also has three on one side and two on the other; however, those three have no kinship with these three, nor do those two correspond to these two. For two double forms of imperfect concords share the <term>decagon; a ten-sided polygon</term>, which is here related to one of the three primary solids and one of the two secondary solids. It happens, therefore, with respect to one thing or the other, that it uses the same division. Many such accidental things occur in mathematical and natural matters; against their coincidence, our weakness of judgment must be strengthened as something <note>original: "ἀνάξιον" (anaxion); meaning unworthy or beneath consideration</note>, lest it be immediately carried away by any sort of credulity without the guidance of reason. See what I have disputed above regarding those things which are three, or six, or seven in number.

(16) [***He points his index finger at the most hidden cause of these things.***] Behold again the author making progress while writing! For this very cause was discovered, as can be seen in the axioms of Book III, Chapter I [of *The Harmony of the World*]. For the figures that have perfect demonstrations and are <term>effable; expressible in rational numbers</term> (the Triangle, the Square, and the Hexagon) also give birth to the perfect major consonances. However, those which have a meaner demonstration and <term>ineffable; irrational</term> sides (such as the Octagon, the Pentagon, and the Decagon) gave birth to the meaner major concords, commonly called "imperfect." This perfection, or contrary meanness, is present in the consonances because of the plane figures themselves, and it is present in the solid figures as well. Thus, once again, it is not kinship but only a certain affinity that comes between those double and more imperfect harmonic sections and the primary Dodecahedron and the secondary Icosahedron.

(17) [***Namely, the two treasures of Geometry.***] Two theorems of infinite utility, and therefore most precious, but there is a great difference between the two. For the first—that the square of the sides of a right angle equals the square of the side opposite the right angle <note>The Pythagorean Theorem</note>—this, I say, you might rightly compare to a mass of gold. The other—concerning the proportional section <note>The Golden Ratio, or "Extreme and Mean Ratio"</note>—you might call a Gem. For it is indeed beautiful by itself, but without the first, it is worth nothing. Yet it advances science further at the point where the first treasure, having led us some distance, now leaves us: namely, for the demonstration and discovery of the side of the Decagon and its related quantities.

(18) [***Just as individual Harmonies...***] It is no wonder that the fitting of Harmonies to the solid bodies is not immediately obvious; for what is not in the heart of Nature cannot be drawn out. These things, described by this number and this quantity, are incompatible. Although I do associate Harmonies with the solids in *Harmonies of the World*, Book V, Chapter IX, this is not done for the sake of one arising from the other, but for the sake of their use in the adornment of the World. There are indeed many arguments for this association in Chapter II from formal reasons, both of the solids and of the Harmonies. But those arguments are always common to many Harmonies among themselves; individual Harmonies are not claimed for individual solids through them. Therefore, external arguments of a different kind are added, or arguments deduced from a comparison of the figured proportions with the harmonic ones. By these, finally, not these harmonies but many larger than these are associated with the solids. Yet even this association is not immediate: rather, the Harmonies are attributed to the motions of those Planets whose Orbs have obtained the individual Regular solids between them. Thus the Harmonies do indeed migrate into the neighborhood of the five solids, separated by their own boundaries, and are not received under the same roof.

(19) [***Only this is clear, that the Fifth is owed to the Pyramid.***] Indeed, not even this is absolutely true. None of those intervals which are smaller than the <term>Diapason; the Octave</term> is more closely related to the Pyramid <note>the Tetrahedron</note> because of the Triangle, which provides the base for the Pyramid and the origin for the <term>Diapente; the musical Fifth</term>. Yet there cannot be a place for the Fifth where the Pyramid is placed between the orbits. This aptitude of Harmonies for figures must be judged by other signs, concerning which see *Harmonies of the World*, Book V, Chapter II. Furthermore, the Fifth is not even the closest offspring of the Triangle alone, but the Octave-plus-a-Fifth <note>original: "Diapason epi diapente"</note> precedes it; see *Harmonies*, Book IV, Chapter VI, page 154. Here in the text itself, though I was then ignorant of it, I placed the truest cause of this assertion: namely, the third part of a circle.

(20) [***The secondary solids receive those which describe lines.***] That is, those concords are to be associated with the secondary solids which are represented by the section of a string in such a way that, if a circle is made from the string marked with its perfection, the straight line connecting the marks does not become the side of any perfect figure. Instead, it remains either a single solitary line or becomes the side of an "abundant" figure, which I chose to call "stars" in Books I and II of the *Harmonies* because of their appearance. It was a beautiful fiction <note>original: "pulchrum commentum"</note> for the cause, and a beautiful distribution of Harmonies among the five solids according to it, if you look at the numerical correspondence. But in itself, this has neither the appearance of a cause, nor does the <term>major sixth; a sixth above the octave</term> have any commerce with the Icosahedron.

(21) [***They only make lines.***] As if stars were not also figures? Surely something...

...was to be devised, by which the Eight-Pointed Star <note>original: "stella Octangularis"; likely referring to the stellated octahedron or "stella octangula," a shape Kepler discovered</note> might be associated with the Diameter, under the same, as it were, genus, while Nature reclaimed it. It was therefore rightly done that I did not rest content with this distribution.

(22) [***Or whether we prefer the fourth for the Octahedron.***] I clearly followed this in Book V of the *Harmonies* <note>original: *Harmonices Mundi*</note>, but with a different purpose. For here [in the earlier edition] I was seeking the origin of individual harmonies; but in Book V of the *Harmonies*, a choice was made among those already originated—specifically, which harmony should be associated with which planets, and by means of which solid figure. Therefore, although the origin of the <term>Diapason; the musical octave (a 2:1 ratio)</term> itself is not correctly ascribed to the Cube here; yet in the said Book V of the *Harmonies*, the Diapason is correctly associated with it. This is not because it causes the origin of the interval, but because of their "cohabitation" among the same planets. It is also correctly associated with the Octahedron (which is the "spouse" or dual of the Cube) and the <term>Disdiapason; a double octave (a 4:1 ratio)</term>, to which the <term>Diatessaron; a musical fourth (a 4:3 ratio)</term> is attached in the harmonic section. See Book V, chapter IX, Propositions VIII and XII.

(23) [***To leave the first imperfect one to the Icosahedron.***] Here again, by chance (since I was not then in my proper field of speculation), I stumbled somewhat onto the truth. For in Propositions XV and XXVII of the said chapter IX, the <term>Diapente; a musical fifth (a 3:2 ratio)</term> is assigned to the Dodecahedron, but to the Icosahedron both of the <term>Sixths; musical intervals of a major or minor sixth</term> are assigned. It is proved in Proposition VI that there is no place for the Thirds.

(24) [***Let us now come to the Aspects.***] My fourth book of the *Harmonies* is on this subject. <note>In astrology, "aspects" are specific angular distances between planets that Kepler believed influenced the soul and weather through harmonic resonance.</note>

(25) [***How three perfect harmonies with three...***] A small amount in this comparison needs to be corrected; see Book IV of the *Harmonies*, chapter VI, page 154.

(26) [***Which they say is the weakest of all.***] Experience testifies that it is by no means weak, but often stronger than the <term>Trine; an astrological aspect of 120 degrees</term> itself; I give the cause from my principles in Book IV of the *Harmonies*.

(27) [***Such as Ptolemy indeed did not give.***] Think of this as referring to the *Tetrabiblos* <note>Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century work on astrology</note>. But in his *Harmonics*, which I had not yet seen then, he touches on this cause, but poorly, as will be clear from my notes on Ptolemy. For altogether, both one and five signs constitute effective aspects, which I call the <term>Semisextile; an aspect of 30 degrees</term> and the <term>Quincunx; an aspect of 150 degrees</term>.

(28) [***Nature recognizes no such concord in voices.***] This is literally false. For between strings in a ratio of 1 to 12 there is a <term>Triple Octave plus a Fifth; a complex musical interval</term>; likewise, between strings 5 and 12 there is a minor Third above the Octave. I therefore had something else in mind when I wrote these words: namely, that there is no three-fold harmonic section that corresponds to these divisions of the circle. Because even if 1:12 and 5:12 are consonant, the remainders 11 and 7 are discordant with both terms. But I teach throughout the whole of Book IV of the *Harmonies*, especially in chapter VI, that the reasoning for Aspects is not the same as that for <term>Consonances; musical harmonies</term>.

(29) [***Causes on both sides, etc., from the five solids.***] Not at all from these [the Platonic solids], but rather from plane figures, of which the <term>Dodecagon; a twelve-sided polygon</term> is not the least noble.

(30) [***Since therefore all...***] With this beginning, I started to increase the number of aspects: although I poorly handled the <term>Sesquadrate; an aspect of 135 degrees</term>, and I poorly omitted the Semisextile (30 degrees). See the often-cited chapter VI of Book IV of the *Harmonies*.

(31) [***Causes which [I cited] probably...***] In vain: for experience confirms the <term>Quintile; a 72-degree aspect</term> and the <term>Biquintile; a 144-degree aspect</term>. Regarding the Sesquadrate, why it is less effective than all the others, far different causes are handed down in Book IV of the *Harmonies*, chapter V. Indeed, those five causes reviewed here must be refuted by us again, lest they hinder the Quintile and Biquintile.

For as far as the first cause is concerned; just as the Sextile with the Trine fills the circle, and one Square with another, so also the <term>Tridecile; an aspect of 108 degrees</term> with the Quintile, the <term>Decile; an aspect of 36 degrees</term> with the Biquintile, and the <term>Sesquiquadrate; 135 degrees</term> with the Sesquadrate fill the semicircle, and Music does not reject these. Therefore, efficacy does not come from this equalization of the semicircle.

The second cause is relevant: but it does not completely reject the Quintile, it only makes it more imperfect than the Trine and Sextile—as far as its own power goes, since it is not alone. Now I call "irrational" <note>original: "irrationale"</note> according to common usage what in the *Harmonies* I call "Ineffable" <note>original: "Ineffabile"; Kepler used this for geometric ratios involving the Golden Ratio that cannot be expressed as simple integers</note>.

The third cause coincides with the first; for every angle in a semicircle is a right angle. And if this cause is formulated differently—that two aspects always produce the sum of two right angles—now the semicircle is again their measure.

The fourth cause is futile. For if the <term>Minor Third; a musical interval</term> <note>original: "Tertia mollis"</note> is in some way perfect because it uses the same division as the perfect ones, namely the duodecimal [division by 12]; then surely the vigesimal [division by 20] is also established with the help of the quaternary [division by 4], and the sexagesimal [division by 60] with the help of the ternary [division by 3]. If the <term>Major Third; a musical interval</term> <note>original: "Tertia dura"</note> does not fit the duodecimal because of its larger term 5; surely the minor third does not fit the vigesimal because of its larger term 6. Again, if the minor third is held to be perfect because it is half of the Fifth, much more will the major third be held for perfect, because it is also half of the Fifth, exceeding it as much as the minor third falls short of the half. Therefore, caution...

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

I distance myself here from that accidental collusion, namely that the <term>Sextile; an astrological aspect of 60° (1/6 of a circle)</term> is also exactly half of a <term>Trine; an astrological aspect of 120° (1/3 of a circle)</term>, and that the Sextile corresponds to the <term>Minor Third; a musical interval with a 6:5 ratio</term>. For I have taught in Book IV, Chapter VI of my *Harmonics* <note>original: *Harmonicorum*; referring to his book *Harmonices Mundi* (1619)</note> that it is not the Minor Third that corresponds to the Sextile, but rather the <term>Fifth over a double octave; a musical interval with a 3:1 (or 12:1) ratio</term>. The Minor Third itself is the common offspring of both the pentagon and the hexagon, because it is encompassed by these numbers, 5 and 6. The reason that divides the Trine into two perfect Sextiles is very different from the reason that divides a <term>Fifth; the Diapente, a 3:2 ratio</term> into two Thirds, the <term>Major; a 5:4 ratio</term> and the <term>Minor; a 6:5 ratio</term>. This is apparent from the fact that in the first case the parts are equal, while in the second they are unequal. Therefore, nothing is taken away from the nobility of the Major Third, nor added to the Minor Third, simply because the Sextile is half of a Trine while the <term>Quintile; an astrological aspect of 72° (1/5 of a circle)</term> is not half of its corresponding larger aspect. One might just as easily value the Quintile because it is half of a <term>Biquintile; an astrological aspect of 144°</term>, and so on. Indeed, no small part of skill consists in being wary of such accidental coincidences. Like the Sicilian Siren <note>A reference to the mythological Sirens who lured sailors to their doom; here, Kepler means intellectual distractions</note> who once detained sailors with her song, these coincidences detain those philosophizing with the pleasure of apparent beauty and apt responses (provided they stick here, captured by admiration where there is no cause of one thing in the other), so that they cannot reach the predetermined goal of true science.

The fifth cause is an effect of the second, and it ensures that just as the Quintile is a less perfect aspect, the Major Third is a less perfect (or rather, a different kind of) consonance. It does not mean that the aspect has no efficacy at all, or that the consonance has no sweetness. For this should have been said long ago regarding all five objections: if they were valid, they would be just as valid in *Music* as they are in the business of aspects; yet no reason is given why these causes should be valid in the former but not in the latter.

**(32) [***Why not even the Octangular.***]** The matter of the Eight-pointed star <note>original: *Octangula stella*; a geometric figure formed by two intersecting squares</note> is different. For why should it be eliminated from the aspects—or rather, postponed—along with the <term>Sesquiquadrate; an aspect of 135°</term>, while the <term>Minor Sixth; a musical interval with an 8:5 ratio</term> (born from the Octagon) is not likewise eliminated from Music? I have explained the reasons for this in Book IV, Chapter VI of the *Harmonics*. Clearly, the situation was equal in both Music and the aspects regarding the proportions 3 and 5 to 8, for they are lowly on both sides. But because of the coincidence in one section of three proportions—3:5, 5:8, and 3:8—of which no account is taken among the aspects, this Octagonal division is more noble in Music.

**(33) [***Nor the Twelve-angled ray.***]** Nay, indeed, this one also operates, as experience testifies, yet it experiences the opposite fortune of the Octangular. In Music, it establishes no peculiar division. See the frequently cited Chapter VI of Book IV of the *Harmonics*. You see, therefore, that the fifth cause is based on nothing—as if those figures that do not <term>fill the plane; a geometric property where shapes can tile a flat surface without gaps, like hexagons or squares</term> cannot become aspects. For even if they do not fill the plane as individual species, they do so when joined together.

**(34) [***And here I almost separate.***]** Some separation was necessary, but for reasons far different from those mentioned here in the fifth place.

**(35) [***For certainly, that which comes from the angles is genuine to the rays.***]** Excellent: for this very point remains valid even in the true cause. See *Harmonics*, Book IV.

**(36) [***But not because of the figure.***]** This is too much, and contrary to what was sent before. If it is because of the angle, then surely it is also because of the figure; for a figure is established by its angles, and the choice of angles is made through the figures. But see the difficulty concerning the central and circumferential figures, discussed in Book IV, Chapter V of the *Harmonics*.

**(37) [***They can, however.***]** This paragraph embraces almost the entire arrangement of my *Harmonics*. For I placed that common Geometry at the beginning as the archetypal cause in Books I and II; then I explained what it causes in Music in Book III, and what it causes in the aspects in Book IV.

**(38) [***Ptolemy's Music.***]** The reader will say for himself that I waited in vain for these causes from <term>Ptolemy's Harmonics; a 2nd-century treatise on music theory by the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy</term>, if ever these authors are published with my notes, should God prolong my life. For Ptolemy remains stuck in numbers as the cause, without regard for figures—treating them as "numbered numbers" <note>original: *numeri numerati*; abstract numbers without geometric context</note>. Thus, he unjustly proscribes some harmonies along with the ancients, and admits certain intervals among the melodic ones through no merit of their own. See my *Harmonics*, Book III, page 27.

**(39) [***What from Euclid's Music.***]** Regarding these, I have seen nothing beyond the propositions transcribed by <term>Dasypodius; Conrad Dasypodius (1532–1600), a mathematician who edited Euclid</term>. However, there is no hope that things will be found in Euclid which <term>Ptolemy</term> or <term>Porphyry</term>, who lived later, did not possess.

JOHANNES KEPLER'S

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *On calculating the spheres which are inscribed in, and circumscribed around, the [regular] bodies.*

---

Until now, nothing has been said except for certain consistent signs and likelihoods <note>original Greek: εἰκότα (*eikota*), meaning probabilities or reasonable expectations</note> of the adopted Theorem. Let us now pass to the distances <note>original Greek: ἀποστήματα (*apostēmata*)</note> of the astronomical spheres and Geometric demonstrations; which, unless they agree, we will undoubtedly have wasted all our preceding effort. First of all, let us see in what proportion the spheres inscribed in each of these five regular bodies stand to those circumscribed around them.

And indeed the radii, or semidiameters, of the circumscribed spheres equal the semi-diagonals of the bodies. For unless all the corners of the figure touch the same surface, the body will not be regular. Moreover, two mutually opposite corners and the center of the figure are always on the same line or axis of the sphere. The one exception is the Tetrahedron, which has its individual corners opposite to the centers of the individual faces.

Now, the straight line connecting the centers of the figure and its base is the radius, or semidiameter, of the inscribed sphere, according to the final book (Book 15) of Campanus's edition of Euclid <note>Campanus of Novara was a 13th-century mathematician whose commentary on Euclid was the standard text in Kepler's time</note>. For the inscribed sphere must touch all the centers of the [faces of the] figure; and the inscribed figures possess the same center as the circumscribed ones.

Since this is the case, it is easy to see that the <term>power; the square of a length, used here in the context of the Pythagorean theorem</term> of the radius with which a circle is circumscribed around the base must be subtracted from the power of the radius of the circumscribed sphere, so that the remainder is the power of the sought-after line, namely the radius of the inscribed sphere. In the attached diagram, HOM is the axis of the circumscribed sphere, the center of which (O) is common to the inscribed figure. Let OHGL be one plane of the figure, which here serves as the base; I is the center of the base, and HI is the radius of the circle circumscribing that base. And the straight line dropped from the center of the sphere O to I (the center of the smaller circle) will be perpendicular to that circle and to the line HI. Therefore, in triangle HIO, the angle at I is a right angle. Consequently, the power of HO equals the powers of HI and IO combined. And the power of HI, subtracted from the power of HO, leaves the sought-after power of IO, according to the 47th proposition of the first book [of Euclid]. <note>This is the Pythagorean theorem: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. Here, $HO^2 = HI^2 + IO^2$</note>

-> [Image: A geometric diagram showing a sphere with center O. A vertical axis runs from M to L. A horizontal radius OH is shown. Below the center, a horizontal plane is represented by a dashed ellipse, with point I at its center. A right-angled triangle is formed by O, I, and H.] <-

From this it appears that in order to obtain IO in all figures, the radius of the base HI must first be sought. Moreover, the radius HI is obtained if the side of the figure (around which the circle is circumscribed) is known. Hence again, to obtain the radius of the base, the side of any given figure must first be sought.

Assuming, therefore, the radius of any circumscribed sphere to be the quantity of the <term>total sine; the maximum value of a sine in a table, here acting as a radius of 1000 units for ease of calculation</term> of 1000 parts (this magnitude of the radius is sufficient for our purpose), the power of the side of a cube—according to the 15th proposition of Book 13 of Euclid's *Elements*—is a third part of the power of the axis. Thus, if the axis has 2000 units, the side of the cube has 1155. The power of the side of an Octahedron, by the 14th proposition of the same book, is half the power of the axis. The power of the side of a Tetrahedron is, by the 13th proposition of the same book, one-and-a-half times <note>original Latin: *sesquialtera*</note> the power of the axis. And thus far, that golden theorem of Pythagoras concerning the powers of the sides in a right-angled triangle (Book 1, Proposition 47) has been of use. In the other two bodies...

times we have need of that other treasure of Geometry, concerning a line cut according to the extreme and mean ratio <note>original Latin: "linea secundum extremam & mediam rationem secta." This is what we now call the Golden Ratio. Kepler famously called it one of the "two jewels" of geometry, the other being the Pythagorean theorem.</note>, which is Proposition 30 of the sixth book [of Euclid]. For the side of a Dodecahedron is the larger part of the side of a cube when that side is cut according to the extreme and mean ratio, according to the 17th corollary of the thirteenth book. Likewise, to find the side of the Icosahedron, one first seeks the radius of that circle which touches the five angles of the Icosahedron, which is AC in circle AB. Its square <note>original: "potentia," literally "power," used in geometry to mean the square of a line's length</note> is one-fifth the square of the axis, according to the 16th corollary of the thirteenth book. Therefore, according to the 5th and 9th [propositions] of the same book, if that radius AC is cut according to the extreme and mean ratio, the larger segment AD is the side of the decagon <note>A ten-sided polygon</note> which can be inscribed in that same circle AB. Therefore, the combined squares of the whole radius AC and this larger segment AD make the square of the side EF of a pentagon in that circle, by the 10th [proposition] of the thirteenth book. Since this side lies between two angles of the Icosahedron, it will indeed be the side of the Icosahedron, by the 11th and 16th [propositions] of the same book.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a circle with an inscribed pentagon. The center of the circle is marked 'C'. The vertices are labeled 'A', 'D', 'B', and 'E'. A line connects 'A' and 'C', and another 'A' and 'D'. The label 'F' appears to the right of vertex 'B'.</image-desc>

We now have the sides of all the figures in proportion to the axis of the circumscribed sphere. It follows that we should investigate the radii of the circles which are inscribed in the faces <note>original: "basibus," referring to the flat faces of the 3D shapes</note> from the sides we already know; anyone can achieve this very easily with the aid of sines <note>Kepler suggests using trigonometry (tables of sines) as a faster alternative to geometric proofs</note>, if they consider that highly precise numbers are not required here. However, if anyone prefers to work more artfully, I will set down for them the foundations of the matter from Euclid. Since there are only three shapes for the faces—triangles, squares, and pentagons: in the case of triangles, the square of the side GH is three times the square of the sought radius HI, according to the 12th [proposition] of the book often cited; in a square, the square of side GH is twice the square of the sought radius; finally, in a pentagon, the combined squares of the side GH and the chord KH (from the given lines) are five times the square of the sought radius HI, according to the 4th [proposition] of the fourteenth book according to Campanus <note>Johannes Campanus of Novara, whose 13th-century edition of Euclid was the standard for Kepler’s generation</note>. We now have the radii of the circles in the faces in the same proportion as the sides.

<image-desc>A vertical series of three circular diagrams illustrating inscribed polygons. The top circle contains an equilateral triangle with side 'GH' and radius 'HI', marked with a triangle symbol. The middle circle contains a square with side 'GH' and radius 'HI', marked with a square symbol. The bottom circle contains a pentagon with side 'GH', radius 'HI', and a chord 'KH' subtending two sides, marked with a pentagon symbol. The center of each circle is labeled 'I'.</image-desc>

Therefore, by subtracting the squares of these radii from the square of the total sine <note>The "total sine" refers to the radius of the outer, circumscribed sphere</note>, which is the quantity of the semidiameter or radius in the circumscribed sphere, there will remain (as proved above) the squares of the radii of the inscribed spheres <note>The inner spheres that fit perfectly inside the solid bodies</note> that we are seeking. However, as I said, you will find it more convenient and easier to use sines.

But we must not overlook certain other shortcuts here, lest we labor too industriously. First, the spheres inscribed in the Dodecahedron and the Icosahedron are of the same size, provided the figures are inscribed in the same outer sphere. For the faces of both figures have the same radius [of their inscribed circles] by the 2nd [proposition] of the fourteenth book. Let the same judgment be made concerning the cube and the octahedron. For the square of the axis is three times the square of the cube's side, and this is twice the square of the radius in the face; therefore the square of the axis is six times the square of the radius in the face. In the octahedron, conversely, the square of the axis is twice the square of the side, and this is three times the square of the radius in the face. Therefore, here too, the square of the axis is six times the square of the [radius of the] face. Therefore, since by hypothesis the radius of the circumscribed spheres (or HM in the first diagram of this chapter) is the same, and since the radius of the faces HI is also the same, and the angle IOH is always a right angle: therefore the radius of the inscribed spheres (namely the third side OI) will also be the same by the converse of the 26th [proposition] of the first book. Thus, having found the inscribed radii for the cube and the Icosahedron, there is no need to inquire further regarding the Octahedron and Dodecahedron.

(1) Thirdly, an octahedron and a pyramid <note>In the geometry of this era, "pyramid" usually refers specifically to the four-sided tetrahedron.</note> with equal sides have the same height. Therefore, the larger the side of the pyramid, the higher the figure itself. An octahedron and a pyramid with sides twice as large have the same inscribed sphere <note>original: "orbem inscriptum"</note>. For if a pyramid is cut at the midpoints of its sides, it falls into four smaller pyramids and one octahedron with sides half as large. And since the pyramid has four faces, the small pyramid cut away does not remove the center from any of them, as the center is far below the cut; thus, the inscribed sphere remains in the octahedron from the cut, touching the four old centers and—by the definition of a regular body—also touching the four new centers appearing from the section. Therefore, whether the inscribed radius of the pyramid, the octahedron, or the cube is obtained first, the quantity of the other inscribed radius will be very easily obtained through the proportion of the sides.

Briefly, the squares are related to each other as follows: OI: 1. IP: 2. HP: 6. HI: 8. NO: 9. NI: 16. NP: 18. NH: 24. NM: 36.

### ON CHAPTER THIRTEEN
->Author’s Notes.<-

(1) Thirdly, an octahedron and a pyramid with equal sides have the same height.] *The height of a pyramid is indeed measured from the center of the base up to the opposite vertex <note>original: "angulum," literally angle or corner.</note>; however, the height of the octahedron considered here is that which exists between two parallel bases. The demonstration is easy: for if the sides of a pyramid are bisected and the four smaller pyramids are removed, there remains an octahedron with sides half as large as the sides of the large pyramid. Its four planes—one below and three around it—are parts of the four bases of the large pyramid. Therefore, the three surrounding planes have the same inclination as the three rising from the base of the pyramid to the summit <note>original: "fastigium"</note> of the vertex, even though they have their right angles turned downward. Therefore, the proportion of the perpendicular line in such a plane to the perpendicular of the body is the same as the proportion of its perpendiculars to this one in the tetrahedron.*

# THE SECRET OF THE UNIVERSE.

### CHAPTER XIV.

*The primary goal of this small book, and the astronomical proof that these five regular solids are situated between the planetary spheres.*

<margin>
Copernicus, Book 5, chapters 21, 22. And below in the Table.
</margin>
THEREFORE, to come to our main proposal: it is well known that the paths of the planets are eccentric <note>original: "eccentricas"; meaning their orbits are not perfect circles centered exactly on the Sun</note>. Consequently, the accepted opinion among "physicists" <note>In Kepler’s time, "Physicists" referred to natural philosophers who studied the physical reality of the world, often following Aristotle.</note> is that the celestial spheres possess a thickness as great as is required to account for these observed variations in movement. Up to this point, Copernicus actually agrees with our philosophers. However, from here on, a significant difference in opinion is seen. For the Physicists believe that from the lowest surface of the lunar sky all the way to the tenth sphere, there is no vacuum between the celestial spheres; instead, one sphere is always touched by another, and the bottom surface of a higher sphere is perfectly joined with the top surface of the lower one. Thus, if one were to ask what the physical "place" of the sphere of Mars is, they would answer: the inner surface of Jupiter's sphere. This reasoning can perhaps be maintained in the system of Ptolemy <note>The ancient Greek astronomer whose Earth-centered model dominated for 1,400 years.</note> and the traditional description of astronomy, because in those systems there is no opportunity or means for investigating the proportions of the spheres. Just as no one easily contradicts those who have written about the "New Indies" <note>The Americas.</note> if they have not traveled to those places themselves, so the astronomer cannot reject the petty arguments of the physicists concerning the contact of spheres if his own experience with observations and the requirements of his hypotheses have not lifted him into the heavens themselves, between the spheres.

But now, from the hypotheses of Copernicus and from the motion of the Earth, it follows that there is no difference between neighboring spheres that does not exceed the eccentricity of both spheres by many parts. Take an example of this from the spheres of the Earth and Venus, which are the ones least distant from each other. On a scale where the average distance of the Earth from the center of the world is 60, the average distance of Venus from the same center is 43 1/3. The difference is 16 5/6 minutes <note>original: "scrupula"; here used as units of measurement based on a radius of 60.</note>. Now, the Earth at its perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center.</note> approaches Venus by 2 1/4 minutes; likewise, Venus moves toward the Earth at its apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the center.</note> by 2 1/2 minutes; the sum is 5 minutes. Therefore, these two bodies remain separated by twelve remaining minutes even when they are at their closest to each other.

If someone should assert that this intermediate space is filled by the "nodes" <note>Points where an orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> that carry the planets or by circles of latitudes, let them consider this: those functions can be performed by spheres far thinner than those needed to fill such a massive gap. Nature should not be burdened with the immense mass of such giant spheres. Indeed, by Hercules, all of Copernicus's hypotheses are so arranged, so fit together, and so serve one another, that we do not seem to need any sphere that wanders beyond the path of a planet to account for its motions.

But let us suppose that in the nearby planets these spaces are filled by spheres; I ask you, let us see what that would look like. Since the distance from the perigee of Jupiter to the apogee of Mars is calculated to be a space twice as long as the distance from Mars itself to the center of the world (for Jupiter's distance is triple that of Mars), is it really true that to vary the tiny movements of a little planet—hardly even perceptible—in length and width, this entire space, twice as thick as the whole of Mars's orbit, must be filled with such monstrous spheres? What luxury is this of Nature's? How in-

From this, it can be seen that in Copernicus’s model, no sphere is touched by another, but instead vast intervals are left between the systems—certainly filled with the celestial ether, yet belonging to neither of the neighboring systems. (In this table, I present to your eyes <margin>Table four belongs here.</margin> the sizes of the spheres and the intervals according to their true proportions, just as they were expressed in numbers by Copernicus.) Since I declared at the beginning that I would provide the reasons for these spaces from the five bodies <note>Kepler is referring to the five Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>—why the Best and Greatest Creator left such specific gaps between pairs of planets—namely, because each specific shape produces a specific interval: let us now see how successfully that has been attempted, and let us debate this cause before Astronomy as the judge and Copernicus as the interpreter. I assign to the spheres themselves a thickness as great as the ascent and descent <note>original: "ascensus descensusque"; this refers to the planet moving further from and closer to the sun because its orbit is not a perfect circle centered on the sun.</note> of the planet requires; however, whether that is sufficient, you will see below in Chapter 22. But if the figures are placed in between, as I have said: it is necessary that the bottom surface of the higher sphere be equal to the circumscribed shape <note>The "outer" shape that touches the corners of the sphere.</note>, and the top of the lower sphere be equal to the inscribed shape <note>The "inner" shape that fits inside the sphere.</note>; the figures, moreover, are to be considered in that order which I confirmed by reasoning above. Wherefore:

Look at the numbers (2) parallel and close to each other, and those of Mars and Venus are indeed the same. Those of the Earth and (3) Mercury are not very different; only those of Jupiter are excessively discrepant, but that is something no one should wonder at in such a great distance. And in Mars and Venus, neighbors to the Earth’s sphere, you see how much difference the little sphere of the Moon makes when added to the thickness of the Earth’s sphere: (4) which little sphere, however, barely equals 3 minutes <note>original: "scrupula"; small units of measurement.</note>, of which the Earth's sphere has 60.

From this you can gather how easily it would have been noticed, and how great an inequality of numbers would have appeared, if these things were attempted against the nature of the heavens—that is, if God himself had not looked to these proportions in the Creation. For certainly this cannot be accidental, that the proportions of the bodies are so close to these intervals: both because of other reasons and, most importantly, because the order of the intervals is the same as the one I assigned to the bodies by the best reasoning above; see Chapter 3. THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY. 55

## ON THE FOURTEENTH CHAPTER
->Author’s Notes.<-

(1) **Copernicus agrees with our Philosophers.**] *Understand this regarding the geometric space of the Spheres: for concerning matter—that is, the adamantine <note>Likened to diamond; incredibly hard and unbreakable.</note> solidity of the spheres—not even Ptolemy philosophized so crudely.*
(2) **Behold the parallel Numbers.**] *Those situated in the same region, such as 577 and 635; or 333 and 333.*
(3) **Of Mercury, not very different.**] *If for Mercury <note>original: "☿"</note> you do not take 577 as the radius of the inscribed Octahedron, but 707 as the radius of the Octahedron inscribed in a square, then that value does not differ much from 703.*
(4) **Which small circle, however.**] *Here the proportion of the Spheres of the Sun and the Moon is assumed to be 20 to 1, as ancient Astronomy generally handed down. But I teach in Book 4 of my Epitome <note>Referencing his later work, the "Epitome of Copernican Astronomy."</note> that it is almost three times larger; although in the Ephemerides <note>Astronomical tables predicting the positions of celestial bodies.</note>, using a certain modesty, I employed a value one and a half times larger, namely 30 to 1, until I could conclude the matter clearly.*

## CHAPTER XV.

### The correction of distances and the diversity of prosthaphaereses <note>A term for the adjustments or "add-subtractions" used to calculate the difference between the mean and true positions of a planet.</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial N featuring a figure amidst foliage.</image-desc>Lest I give you, dear reader, any reason to reject this entire enterprise on account of some trivial disagreement, you must be warned here—and I wish for you to remember this well—that Copernicus’s intent was not focused on Cosmography <note>The physical description of the universe's structure.</note>, but on Astronomy. That is, it was of little concern to him if he erred slightly regarding the true proportion of the spheres, provided he established numbers from observations that were as suitable as possible for demonstrating motions and computing the positions of the Planets. But if anyone should attempt to provide more suitable numbers, and correct these Copernican figures in such a way that it disturbs the "prosthaphaereses" little or not at all, they may easily do so by the leave of Copernicus.

So that I may finally put the finishing touches on this business, and so that it may appear what and how much is changed in the parallaxes of the terrestrial sphere for each individual Planet, I shall construct a new world-model. Since the proportion of the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>original: "ἐκκεντρότης"; the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> to the semi-diameter of the sphere has already been investigated by skilled craftsmen, if anything is changed in the farthest or nearest distance of a sphere from the center of the world through the interposition of the [Platonic] solids, it must be noted proportionally in the <term>eccentricity</term>. The starting point will be from the greatest distance of the Earth upward, and the smallest distance downward toward the center.

Before all else, however, Copernicus's numbers must be unraveled and specially adapted to the present purpose. For although he undoubtedly placed the center of the whole universe in the solar body, nevertheless, to aid the calculation with a shortcut—and lest he disturb the diligent reader by receding too far from Ptolemy—(1) he computed the greatest and smallest distances of all the Planets, as well as their positions in the Zodiac (which have retained the names of Apogees and Perigees <note>The points in an orbit farthest from and closest to the center.</note>), not from the center of the Sun, but from the cen-

...of the Great Orb <note>The *Orbis Magnus*, or the orbit of the Earth around the Sun.</note>, as if that were the center of the Universe; although it always differs from the Sun by as great an interval as is at any time the maximum eccentricity <note>original: "ἐκκεντρότης", the distance by which the center of an orbit deviates from the Sun.</note> of the Earth (or Sun). If I were to keep these numbers in the present task, this inconvenience would follow: either an error would be committed in the inscription <note>The geometrical fitting of one shape inside another.</note>, while the orb of the Earth were considered a solid body when it is at least a surface (as can be seen in the preceding Table IV), or I would leave no thickness for the terrestrial orb, as I do for the others. Therefore, the centers of the Dodecahedral planes and the Icosahedral angles would be on the same spherical surface; and thus the whole world would sit more tightly and become far narrower than the experience of motions and observations allow.

And when I revealed this doubt to Michael Maestlin, my most distinguished teacher, to find out if he would approve of this newly proposed Theorem: with an unexpected zeal for helping me, he took this labor upon himself. Not only did he re-calculate the distances of the Planets anew from the Prutenic Tables <note>Astronomical tables published in 1551, based on Copernicus's work, named after the Duke of Prussia.</note>, but he also prepared the present Table for me; and thus he relieved me—who was then occupied with many other tasks—of a great, difficult, and troublesome labor.

<margin>The fifth table belongs here.</margin>Which table I share with you, Reader, by the author's [Maestlin's] permission: and I commend it to you as something that will not only benefit you in the present task but will also solve a most intricate knot before your eyes, and even lead you by the hand into the inner sanctum of the Prutenic and Copernican systems. For it is pleasant to learn from it how the different apsides <note>The points of greatest or least distance in an orbit.</note> of the Planets fall into different places of the Zodiac; which, in Venus, produces a difference of more than a full third. For its Apogee <note>The point furthest from the Earth.</note> is in Taurus <note>original: "♉"</note> and Gemini <note>original: "♊"</note>, while its aphelion <note>original: "ἀφήλιον", the point furthest from the Sun.</note> is in Sagittarius <note>original: "♐"</note> and Capricorn <note>original: "♑"</note>. One may also see that the lines of distances from the Sun are far different from those from the center of the Earth's orb. This difference is greatest in Saturn <note>original: "♄"</note>, because the entire eccentricity <note>original: "ἐκκεντρότης"</note> of the Earth is added to its distance. In Jupiter, however, it changes little, because it does not become highest in the region of the Sun as Saturn does, but in Libra <note>original: "♎"</note>, where it is almost equally distant from both the center of the Sun <note>original: "☉"</note> and the Great Orb.

And from this, the demonstration of what Copernicus hints at in very few words in Book 5 of *On the Revolutions*, chapters 4, 16, and 22 near the end, concerning the mutable eccentricity of Mars and Venus in relation to the change of the Earth's, is clear to the eye; Rheticus, however, pursues this more copiously in his *Narrative* <note>The "Narratio Prima," the first published account of the Copernican system by Georg Joachim Rheticus.</note>. There is also something else of which this table reminds us, which, because it can be more conveniently said in another place, I will now defer.

Now to the matter. I shall set forth a fourfold order of numbers. In the **first** will be the departures of the Planets from the center of the Great Orb; just as those departures and numbers are elicited from Copernicus and the Prutenic tables simply and without change. In the **second** will be the departures of the orbs from the center of the Sun, which come from Copernicus after that resolution of numbers of which you have just seen the table. In the **third and fourth** will come again the departures of the planets from the Sun, insofar as they have been changed by the interposition of the [Platonic] bodies. And the third order indeed will be from that structure of the world which will have for its foundation the simple thickness of the terrestrial orb, without including the Lunar system. Finally, the fourth will provide a thickness of the terrestrial orb great enough to cover above and below the radius of the Lunar orb.

Kepler uses the Latinized Arabic term "Auges."</note> of the planets fall in different locations of the Zodiac; in Venus, this creates a difference of more than a third of the circle. One can also see that the lines of distance from the Sun are far different than those from the center of the Earth's orbit. This difference is greatest in Saturn ♄, because the entire eccentricity of the Earth is added to its distance. In Jupiter, however, it changes little, because Jupiter does not reach its highest point opposite the Sun like Saturn does, but in Libra ♎︎, where it is almost equally distant from both centers—the Sun ☉ and the Great Circle. From this, the demonstration of what Copernicus briefly hints at in Book 5 of *On the Revolutions*, chapters 4, 16, and 22 regarding the mutable eccentricity of Mars and Venus due to the Earth's motion becomes visible to the eye; Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus, the disciple of Copernicus who published the *Narratio Prima*, the first printed summary of Copernican theory.</note> pursues this more fully in his *Narratio*. 

There is something else this table reminds us of, which I will delay for now as it is better discussed elsewhere. Now to the matter at hand. I will present a fourfold order of numbers. In the first will be the departures of the planets from the center of the Great Circle, as those departures and numbers are drawn from Copernicus and the Prutenic tables simply and without change. In the second will be the departures of the orbits from the center of the Sun, which come from Copernicus after that rotation of numbers which you just saw in the table. In the third and fourth will come again the departures of the planets from the Sun ☉, as they have been changed through the placement of the [Platonic] bodies. The third order will be from the structure of the world based on the simple thickness of the Earth's orbit, without including the Lunar system. Finally, the fourth will show the thickness of the Earth's orbit large enough to cover the radius of the Moon's orbit above and below.

Now I shall further subjoin a table of arcs which are due to those limits produced by the highest departures <note>original: abscessus; essentially the furthest points from the Sun</note> of Venus and Mercury, if the mean distance of the Earth is taken as the <term>whole sine</term> <note>the radius of a circle in trigonometric calculations</note>. For the superior planets, the arcs are those produced if the mean distance of the Earth is the radius when their furthest departures are the whole sine. -> ### Author’s Notes on Chapter 15. <-

> (1) **T**he distances of all the Planets.] *In my Commentary on the motions of that planet [Mars] <note>Kepler refers here to his Astronomia Nova, 1609</note>, I have carefully explained, specifically in the first part concerning the equivalence of hypotheses, what error is committed by this sort of dislocation of the planetary system, and how this error is refuted by the Brahean <note>from Tycho Brahe</note> observations of Mars. And because it was necessary to place the foundation of the world, as it were, in the very center of the sun to avoid these errors, it followed that the places in the Zodiac where the planets become highest and lowest could no longer retain the names "Apogees" and "Perigees," as they did in Copernicus's work (by improper use), but should be properly and significantly designated by me as **Aphelia** and **Perihelia**.*

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*A special note on the Moon, and on the matter of the bodies and the spheres.*<-

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'N' featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc>
Therefore, the sphere of the Moon, however small it may be, raises no small difficulty <note>original: "scrupulum," literally a small sharp stone that causes discomfort in a shoe; a doubt or difficulty</note>. Therefore, it is now time that I say something further about the Moon. And I begin indeed without beating around the bush, dear Reader, to sincerely set forth my mind: namely, that I will follow in this cause wherever the proximity of the numbers leads. If the interposition of the Moon makes the numbers and arcs of Copernicus more true, I shall say that this system must be added to the thickness of the "Great Orb" <note>The "Great Orb" (Orbis Magnus) is the term used by Copernicus for the Earth's orbital path around the Sun.</note>. If, however, by casting out the Moon we can better agree with Copernicus, I shall also say that the Great Orb is not so thick all around that it covers the lunar heaven; but rather that it stands out sometimes upward, sometimes downward—the entire hemisphere of the Moon being above or below the margins of the Great Orb—and sometimes (and indeed mostly) less than a hemisphere stands out: entirely according as the body of the Earth itself, which is the center of the Moon’s sphere, has either ascended or descended through the thickness of its own orb. (1) And by Hercules, I do not know toward which side the Cosmographical or even Metaphysical reasons more strongly incline. (2) It seems indeed to be a neat arrangement that there should not be any sphere in the heavens that carries such a "knot"—like a ring carrying a gemstone—whose protrusion would prevent the most absolute roundness of the sphere from being maintained. And conversely, in judging the figure of the sphere, what is the point of taking the Moon into account, since it does not properly belong to the Earth’s sphere in the same way that the wanderings of the other planets upward and downward belong to theirs (which are most conveniently demonstrated physically through epicycles <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in pre-Keplerian astronomy to explain retrograde motion.</note>)? For it is to the Earth that the Third Orb from the Sun is owed; she herself, by her own rowing, travels around the Sun among the other planets; she accomplishes her variations through herself and through her own epicycles, with no service from the Moon for this purpose, as the teachings of Copernicus show. The Moon, however, occupies this tiny little home around the Earth as if by prayer or on lease; the Moon follows, or is rather dragged, wherever the Earth walks and with whatever variation. Imagine the Earth standing still: the Moon would never find a path around the Sun, let alone travel around it. For she runs about here and there, enclosed in narrow spaces around the Earth, serving as a provider of light and moisture to the Earth, just like a hall-steward <note>original: "Atriensis," a servant who managed the atrium or entrance of a Roman house.</note> around a master, or like those who walk about on a ship, yet do not advance in their journey by their own tiring efforts, unless the great force of the waters moves them forward, even if they were standing still. And just as the Moon has obtained its space and motion from the Earth’s sphere, so too Mästlin <note>Michael Mästlin, Kepler's university professor and mentor.</note> proves by many conjectures that it has acquired many conditions of the terrestrial globe—namely, continents, seas, mountains, air, or things corresponding to these in some way—and I myself hold several such views. Thus, for this reason alone, Copernicus is more likely to be correct, as he grants the same sharing of place and motion to these two bodies. And certainly, the philanthropic <note>original Greek: "φιλανθρωπος" (philanthrōpos); Kepler refers to God as the lover of humanity.</note> Creator seems finally to have clothed the Earth with this Lunar sphere because He wished to attribute to it a position similar to the position of the Sun; so that if she herself were also the center of some sphere (as the Sun is the center of all things), she might, in the likeness of the Sun...

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY. 59

...could be held as a certain reason on account of which the Earth itself was commonly regarded as the common center of the entire universe.

It is entirely—to play again with an **Allegory**—that man is a kind of God in the world, and his dwelling is the Earth; just as for God (if he has any bodily dwelling) it is surely the Sun, that inaccessible light. <note>original: "lux inaccessa," a reference to 1 Timothy 6:16. Kepler frequently blends astronomical physics with light theology.</note> Therefore, just as man responds to God, so the Earth ought to respond to the Sun. Proof of this thing is <margin>(3)</margin> almost the same proportion of the Earth’s globe to the Moon’s orbit as the Sun’s globe to the median elongation of Mercury from the Sun.

Nor indeed is it to be feared that the lunar orbits might be crushed or squeezed out by the proximity of the proportions of the [Platonic] bodies, if they are not hidden and enclosed within the orb itself. For it is absurd and monstrous to place in heaven these bodies clothed in some kind of matter which does not allow passage to another body. Certainly, many do not fear to doubt whether there are such **Adamantine** <note>original: "Adamantini," referring to the classical belief in crystalline spheres as hard as diamond/steel.</note> orbs in heaven at all; or whether the stars are transported through the fields and ethereal air, free from those shackles of orbits, by a certain divine power, <margin>(4)</margin> with the intellect of Geometric proportions governing their courses. Indeed, no weight will make the mover’s steps hesitant or staggering, so that it might ever wander out of its circle.

<margin>(5)</margin> For no point, no center is heavy. Indeed, all things follow a center of the same nature as the body. Nor does a center acquire weight from the fact that it attracts other things to itself, or is sought by them: <margin>(6)</margin> no more than a **Magnet** becomes heavier while it actively pulls iron. Or this Earth, which we have determined with Copernicus is moved—by what levers, by what chains, by what celestial Diamond is it inserted into its orbit? Namely, by that air which all of us humans all around on the surface of the Earth breathe (fermented and mixed with vapors); which we penetrate with our hands and bodies, yet we do not part or remove it, since it is the vehicle of <margin>(7)</margin> celestial influences into the middle bodies. For this is the heaven in "which we live, move, and are," <note>Kepler quotes Acts 17:28, traditionally applied to God, here applied to the physical heavens/atmosphere.</note> both we and all worldly bodies. Though why is there a need for so many words? For even if the little orb of the Moon stands out above the Earth’s orb: what is there about the **Dodecahedron** or **Icosahedron** that would prohibit it from passing through? You saw above in chapter XI where the plane of the Zodiac cuts these two bodies, that no angle, no center of a face is encountered, but there exists from the section a decagon <term>decangulum|a ten-sided polygon</term> on both sides, of which the line falling perpendicular from the center to the side is far greater in the Dodecahedron than the radius of the inscribed sphere, and far shorter in the Icosahedron than the radius of the circumscribed sphere: and indeed so long that not only that heaven of the Moon, but something much larger extending above the orb, could pass through that middle path and between those decagons. But although all these things are left in their place, the matter stands no worse.

<meta>This page contains Kepler’s self-commentary on Chapter 16 of the Mysterium Cosmographicum. Written years after the first edition, these notes reflect his more mature astronomical views following his discovery of the laws of planetary motion and the publication of his works *Harmonies of the World* and *The New Astronomy* (Commentary on Mars). He acknowledges how his views on "celestial intelligences" shifted toward physical, magnetic forces.</meta>

JOHANNES KEPLER
# ON CHAPTER SIXTEEN
## Author’s Notes.

(1) **Nor, by Hercules, do I know which way the arguments more incline.**] *But now that my "Harmonic contemplations" have been brought to light, this controversy has been settled in Book 5 of The Harmonies of the World. First, the proportions of the Orbs were partially taken away from the five [Platonic] solids themselves: that is, the final and most absolute proportion of the Orbs was made common to both the solids and the Harmonies (Propositions 48 and 49, Chapter 9). For this reason, nothing can be disputed regarding the Moon in one direction or another based solely on the solids. Second, even if the proportions of the orbs were formed primarily from the five solids of the Sun, the method of this formation is different—established in Propositions 46 and 47—whereby the physical inscription of the orbs would emulate the degrees of perfection of Geometric proportions. Third, it is established from all the axioms and propositions of that book that a final limitation of the proportion of the intervals <term>diastematum; the distances between planetary spheres</term> is made necessary because of the motions of the Planets; namely, so that certain harmonies could exist between the extreme motions. If this is so, then no account can be held for the Moon, which runs around the Earth, since she contributes nothing to the speeding up or slowing down of any Planet's motion, nor does she perform her circuit around the Sun, nor does her motion appear regular from the Sun. For if viewed from the Sun, the Moon’s motion would appear to proceed by leaps. Thus, the orb of the Earth must be discussed as if the heaven of the Moon added no thickness to it.*

(2) **It is indeed elegant that there should be no such orb with a Node.**] *These words can be taken in a double sense. The first, fitting the text, is this: that there is indeed an Orb with a node <note>The "node" here refers to the lunar sphere or the intersection of orbits; Kepler is debating whether the lunar orbit occupies a "thick" physical shell.</note>, but the orbit of the Planet is included within such a thickness that this node, or the heaven of the Moon, lies entirely hidden inside, in no way hindering the absolute roundness of the outermost and innermost surfaces. The other sense of these words could be grasped as this: that it is generally absurd for the Moon to go around the Earth while the Earth, in the meantime, moves around the Sun. Therefore, to dissolve even this objection, I say: this could have seemed "elegant" back when the Jovian Planets <note>The four large moons of Jupiter discovered by Galileo in 1610.</note> and other new things in the heavens had not yet been detected. But since we have known of those, it should by no means seem elegant any longer that something which definitely exists should not be; namely, a fourfold "Node" around Jupiter—if by "Node" you understand the spaces of the circuits arranged around Jupiter just as the Moon's circuit is arranged around the Earth. For concerning the bodily solidity of the Orbs, enough was cautioned above, and is also cautioned in the following text.*

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram showing the orbital relationship between the Sun (labeled SOL at the center), the Earth (labeled T), and the Moon. The Earth is positioned on a circular path and is surrounded by its own smaller lunar orbit. Various points on the Earth's larger orbit are labeled with letters A through H, illustrating the geometric path of the Earth-Moon system around the Sun.</image-desc>

`*` **[The Moon] has acquired many conditions of the terrestrial globe.**] *On this point there is a consensus of many philosophers through all ages who dared to be wiser than the common crowd. Diogenes Laertius attributes this to Anaxagoras; and in my own book titled "Appendix to Witelo" <note>referring to his work *Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena* (1604) on optics</note>, in the chapter on the light of the stars, I cited Plutarch's "On the Face in the Moon." Aristotle is also cited by Averroes. But most recently, Galileo, with the Belgian telescope <note>original: "Telescopio Belgico." The telescope was invented in the Netherlands (the "Belgic" regions) shortly before Galileo used it.</note>, has rendered this doctrine most firmly confirmed. See also my "Dissertation with the Starry Messenger" <note>Kepler's *Conversatio cum Nuncio Sidereo*, written in response to Galileo's discoveries.</note> of Galileo.*

(3) **Almost the same proportion of the Earth’s globe to the Moon’s orbit.**] *That proportion is indeed certain, namely about 1 to 59. But the proportion of the Sun's body to the orbit of Mercury is a little different; namely, not the median orbit of Mercury, but the innermost and narrowest must be assumed. In the table of Chapter 15, 14 degrees are attributed to this, while the Sun's semi-diameter, viewed from that same Earth, contains 15 minutes; therefore the proportion is almost 1 to 56.*

(4) **With the understanding of proportions governing the courses.**] *I certainly thought so at that time; but afterward, in the "Commentary on Mars" <note>His 1609 book *Astronomia Nova*.</note>, I demonstrated that there is no need for such an "intellect" in a mover. For although certain proportions are prescribed for all motions—and that by the supreme and unique Intelligence itself, that is, by God the Creator—those proportions of motions are preserved invariably from the creation until now, not by some intellect created into the Mover, but through two other things. The first is the most uniform and perennial rotation of the solar body, with its immaterial emanation <note>original: "specie sui immateriata." Kepler's theory that the Sun's rotation pushes the planets via a light-like force.</note> spreading out into the whole world, which emanation takes the place of a mover. The other cause is the unchangeable and perennial balances and magnetic alignments of the moving bodies themselves. Thus, there is no more need for an "intellect" in these creatures to maintain the proportions of their motions than there is a need for a "mind" in a balance scale with its pans and weights to produce the proportion of the weights. Nevertheless, there are other arguments by which it is proven that there is in the bodies of the Planets—at least the Earth and the Sun—some kind of soul, not indeed a reasoning one as in man, but rather an instinct...*

<summary>Kepler updates his earlier theories on the Moon's orbit and planetary motion, incorporating Galileo's telescopic discoveries and his own shift from "celestial intelligences" to physical, magnetic forces emanating from the Sun.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s retrospective notes on Chapter 16 of the Mysterium Cosmographicum. In these annotations, added for the 1621 edition, Kepler updates his early theories with the revolutionary physical principles he developed in the intervening 25 years, particularly the concepts of "inertia" and the Sun as a physical motor.</meta>

...distinct as in a plant, by which the species of the flower and the number of leaves are preserved. Concerning this, see the Epilogues of books 4 and 5 of our *Harmonies*. <note>original: "Harmonices nostræ." Referring to Kepler's 1619 work, *Harmonice Mundi*.</note>

(5) **For no point is heavy** ] This argument was conceived in such a way that I would like to hear what natural philosophers <term>physicos; those who study the physical laws of nature</term> might say against it. For in these twenty-five years, no one, to my knowledge, has emerged to examine it. But honesty alone moves me to examine it myself. You see then, Reader, what I intended: *That the center alone is what is first driven into a circle around the Sun.* I thought this could happen by a mere nod of will, since a center is not "heavy," as it has no parts. A natural philosopher cannot take this proposition away from me if he contends—as follows here—that all things follow the center. And because the common physical doctrine holds this regarding the center of the world—that all heavy things seek that center—I therefore thought that heavy things could, by the same logic, seek the center of their own body. 

But in Book 1 of the *Epitome of Astronomy*, I demonstrated that *this axiom of the physicists is false: that heavy things seek any center as such; and it is most false that they seek the center of the whole world. It is true, though only by happenstance, that they seek the center of the Earth—not because of what that point is, but because they seek the body of the Earth. Because the Earth is round, it follows that this seeking is directed toward the middle, and thus toward the center.* Indeed, if the Earth had a sensibly distorted shape, heavy things would not tend toward a single point from every side. Therefore, as this foundation collapses, the structure built upon it is also overturned. Specifically, the bodies of the Planets in their motion, or their translation around the Sun, are not to be considered as mathematical points, but clearly as material bodies, and as having a certain "weight" (as I wrote in the book on the New Star). By this, I mean they are endowed with a power of resisting motion applied from the outside, according to the bulk of the body and the density of its matter. 

For because all matter inclines toward rest in the place where it is (unless a neighboring body attracts it by a magnetic force), it follows that the moving power of the Sun fights with this **inertia** of matter. Just as two weights fight on a scale, the speed or slowness of a Planet finally arises from the proportion of both forces. See the introduction to the *Commentary on Mars* <note>The *Astronomia Nova* (1609)</note>, and the *Commentaries* throughout; but especially Book 4 of the *Epitome of Astronomy*.

> *Yet it does not follow from this—as I was trying to suggest here through a false reasoning—that the steps of the "mover" <note>the Sun's driving force</note> are made wavering or stumbling if it labors under the weight and wins in the struggle. For the proportion of the forces between each other is certain and constant, and the victory is shared according to the measure of the forces; so that the Planet neither stays stuck in the same place, nor does it keep up with the speed of the Solar rotation.*

(6) **No more than a magnet, while it actually holds iron, becomes heavier.** ] This is found to be false by clear experiments. Weigh the iron separately, and the Magnet separately; add the weights into one sum. Then, let the iron be hung from the Magnet by 그 invisible force; let the Magnet be tied to the scale, or placed in it (since the force passes through the scale-pan, if it is not iron). You will see that the Magnet, while it actually holds the attracted iron, will weigh the same as both did when they were previously separated from each other.

(7) **The vehicle of celestial influences in intermediate bodies.** ] Not indeed that celestial influences need some matter by which they are carried to us; for that idea of Aristotle’s is false—that air is needed to transport the sensation of the Solar body to the eye, as I demonstrated in my *Optics*. Rather, the less matter encountered in the middle of the journey, the less light is hindered in its passage. Therefore, these words mean: just as bodies do not hinder celestial influences from penetrating into the innermost parts, so too the Moving powers do not need any intermediate bodies, like chains or levers, to grip the bodies of the Planets that are to be moved. 

I chose to play with the word "air" a bit boldly. What is an Orb or a heaven? What is it but air? And what is air? What is it but the immaterial species <note>an "image" or "form" projected through space</note> of the body that brings motion to the Planets, while turning in a rotation? But putting play aside, let us concede that our air is a material body, permeable by magnetic, moving, heating, illuminating powers, and the like; so that it is a vapor not entirely different in kind from the air, but at least distinguished by degrees of thickness from the surrounding fields of air.
