# CHAPTER XVII.

->Another observation concerning Mercury.<-

You will wonder even more at this: although I promised that I intended to inscribe the planets within the geometric bodies themselves, why did I not inscribe Mercury within the Octahedron <term>Octahedron; a solid shape with eight triangular faces</term>? Instead, I allowed it to wander within a certain circle beyond the inscribed sphere, expanding to the size of the Octahedron’s square. For above, in chapters 13 and 14, instead of the number 577 for the inscribed sphere, I used the number 707 for the circle inscribed in a square. <note>Kepler is referring to the ratio between a square’s side and its diagonal, roughly 1 to 1.414. The number 707 represents a larger path than the 577 originally calculated for the sphere tucked inside the octahedron.</note> I will give the reason. First, because Mercury’s divergence from the Sun is so long that it could not possibly be contained in such narrow cages. Second, because both the Octahedron among the solid bodies and the motion of Mercury among the planets have something unique in common. For only in an Octahedron standing on its point does it happen that a square, with its sides aligned, shows a path for a larger circle to pass through the middle than the inscribed sphere allows. This happens in no other solid body, no matter how it is turned. In all others, the sides will always get in the way, crossing through the middle and blocking the path.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an octahedron in projection. The shape consists of two square-based pyramids joined at the base. It is oriented vertically with the top point labeled X and the bottom point H. A circle is drawn through the center. Points R, I, T, and V mark the centers of the triangular faces, which define the size of a sphere that could fit inside. Points Q and S mark a wider horizontal path through the middle of the shape.</image-desc>

In this diagram, the four outermost lines are the four perpendicular heights of as many planes in the Octahedron. **R, I, T, V** are the centers of those planes, which determine the size of the inscribed sphere, the "Great Circle" of which you see here. If that sphere is understood to be rotated on the points **X** and **H** (the two corners of the figure), it will find at the **P** Quadrant <note>a quarter-circle or 90-degree position</note> from the poles a certain width larger than the radius of the sphere **O I** or **O P**—namely **O Q**. The difference between them is **P Q**. And such is the width of the circle which, running out beyond the sphere like a "Horizon" <term>Horizon; here meaning a boundary ring like those on a brass armillary sphere</term>, can pass through the middle of the Octahedron. For **Q** and **S** are the midpoints of two edges, and therefore the points closest to the sphere.

Now, if a certain "animated" <note>Kepler often played with the idea that planets might be guided by a soul or mind</note> planet were ordered to run through the middle of the Octahedron, and to observe the two corners as its poles and the width of the inscribed sphere as its racetrack; by heaven, it is no wonder if, enticed by that extra space where no boundaries blocked it around the whole circuit, it should occasionally stray out of bounds—just like that famous Phaethon <note>In Greek myth, Phaethon was the son of the Sun god who lost control of his father’s chariot and veered off course</note>—at least until it was repelled by an oncoming side of the shape. What I have said in jest, the Astronomers <term>Artifices; literally 'the practitioners of the art'</term> say seriously happens to Mercury. For while all the other planets describe circles of the same width in each revolution (for as much as they move away from the Sun on one side, they approach it by the same amount on the other), (1) Mercury alone has obtained from the Astronomers the reputation of being said to describe sometimes a larger and sometimes a smaller circle.

<image-desc>A simple diagram showing a horizontal line segment YZ with a center point O. An arc of a circle is visible above it. A small vertical segment 'r' indicates a distance or radius.</image-desc>

And they say he holds this as a pure privilege. For they say that he approaches and recedes from the Center of his orbit **O** along a straight line **Y Z**, where the radius **O Y** describes a much smaller circle than **O Z**. As for all the other inequalities, he shares them equally with the others...

it is established; and it has not changed this wandering. (2) And while the <term>eccentricities; the degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term> of all the others decrease—if not proportionally, then at least in a sequence where the smaller orbit always has a smaller eccentricity—Mercury alone possesses an enormous one, namely ten times that of Venus, even though less should be owed to it as an inferior planet. Therefore, even if I have not yet fully reconciled that private inequality with this difference between the circle and the sphere, nor perhaps can it be reconciled perfectly as it has been handed down by the <term>experts; refers here to professional astronomers like Ptolemy or Copernicus</term>: nevertheless, I do not doubt that the Creator looked to the prescription of this geometric figure in assigning motions to Mercury. Because of this, Astronomy, the teachings of Copernicus, and these five bodies themselves seem more and more divine to me.

(3) Let others who wish to do so seek the causes of the remaining eccentricities, each from its own solid body. For since these wanderings were not granted to the individual planets by God at random and without cause, the investigation of these causes must not be despaired of.

Furthermore, regarding how the variety of Mercury might be accommodated to the Octahedron, it could be handled as follows. The proportion of Mercury’s eccentricity to its mean distance from the Sun would be taken as certain; since in Copernicus the distance (as you see in Table V, Chapter 15) is 488 at its furthest, 231 at its nearest, the mean will therefore be 360, and the total thickness 257. This thickness would then be corrected proportionally; since the circle of the Octahedron allows no more than 474 for Copernicus’s number of 488, the thickness will be 250 in this proportion, and the corrected mean distance 349. Now see what the <term>orb; the three-dimensional celestial sphere carrying the planet</term> allows in the Octahedron: specifically 387. Therefore, the difference between 387 (the highest point of the orb) and 349 (the mean) is 38, and double that is 76 for the thickness of the orb in the manner of the others—greater indeed than that of Venus, but not so monstrous. The remaining difference between the highest point of the orb (387) and the highest point of the circle (474), which is 87, is owed to the peculiar wandering of Mercury. Whether this <note>original: "ἐπιχείρημα" (epicheirēma)</note> <gloss>attempted argument</gloss> is to be rejected, or reconciled with a <note>original: "ὀρθοτέρᾳ" (orthotera)</note> <gloss>more correct</gloss> form of the motions in Mercury, or whether a new account of the motions must be established, let the experts consider. For the errors regarding this star have not been so well explored that its orb does not require correction.

### Author’s Notes on Chapter XVII.

> **(1) Mercury alone** obtained.] *What sort of thing that is, which the experts specifically ascribe to Mercury, you will better seek from Ptolemy himself, and from the Theories of <term>Peuerbach; Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), an astronomer who modernized Ptolemaic theory</term> and <term>Maestlin; Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), Kepler’s university professor</term>. Finally, how Copernicus transferred that into the form of his own hypotheses in two ways (because he did not satisfy himself), yet contradicted himself, achieving something more (through his motions that mimic a sort of triangulation) than he had intended to express from Ptolemy: all of that is not so necessary to explain in this place, since it concerns the opinions of men, not the truth of things; and if anything useful can be said, it is better referred elsewhere. For in reality, the fact is that Mercury creates an enormous eccentricity of its circle from the Sun—which circle Ptolemy calls an Epicycle, and I call an eccentric—and that it moves unequally in that eccentric according to the proportion of the eccentricity. From these principles, and from the eccentricity of the Earth, how that fantasy of a double <term>perigee; the point in an orbit closest to the center</term> in Mercury was forged, and thus a motion that is almost triangular: that will be explained in the demonstration of the motions of Mercury; nor do I entirely pass over the heart of the matter in Book 6 of the Epitome of Astronomy. It is enough to warn in this place that there is no Archetypal cause of this Mercurial singularity derived from the Octahedron, and therefore the Hypothesis of this chapter is false. Yet the memory of this <note>original: "Epichirematis"</note> <gloss>attempted argument</gloss> is most pleasant, so that it may appear by what steps of ignorance I ascended to the science and construction of Astronomy.*

### CHAPTER XVIII.

->On the discrepancy in the **prosthaphaereses** <note>The "equation of the center," a technical term for the difference between a planet's actual position and its mean position</note> derived from the bodies compared to the Copernican figures in general, and on the precision of Astronomy.<-

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'S' decorated with winding floral vines and a seated figure within the letter's curves.</image-desc>

**S**ince in Chapters XIV and XV I seemed to be held under some suspicion of falsehood regarding the distances—which Copernicus reported differently from these geometric figures—I appealed to the **apogeal prosthaphaereses**; <note>Greek: προσθαφαιρέσεις ἀπογείως; the adjustments made when a planet is at its furthest point from the Sun</note> nor did I beg for mercy if my figures receded somewhat from those of the Copernicans. And yet, after I presented the similar arcs of the equations of the center <note>Greek: προσθαφαιρέσεων</note> from the elongations from the Sun at the end of Chapter XV as witnesses before this court, they seemed to testify against me. For there was no planet that retained the arc assigned to it by Copernicus. I took away 4' 1" from Saturn; 6' from Jupiter; I added 3' 0" to Mars; but for Venus, I removed a massive 2 degrees 1' 8", and for Mercury 6' 1". Therefore, those who wish to examine everything more exactly will think that because the calculation of the bodies does not agree perfectly <note>Latin: "ad vnguem," literally "to the fingernail"</note> with the decrees of Copernicus and his numbers, all my effort has been in vain. Unless I raise a defense, I shall lose my case by my own admission.

Now, to the Physicists or Cosmographers—the role I sustain in this little book—I owe no explanation for this difference. For even if they borrow the arguments for their beliefs from Astronomers, they do not reduce them to calculations with such precision as Astronomers do; nor are they so sharp-sighted or grumpy <note>Latin: "morosi"</note> as to be moved by this trivial difference. Therefore, I have won my case before the Cosmographers.

Although I rightly fear the common crowd of Astronomers, nevertheless, since it is fitting for skilled artists to preside with judgment, I do not despair of victory against them either. First, I bid them to hope for the best regarding the calculation. For even if the difference is occasionally somewhat large, let them remember that the numbers were excerpted from the most obvious points of the entire circle, and from the meeting of all inequalities. For the discord between the positions assigned to the planets from the solid bodies and those from Copernicus is not so great throughout the entire circle, nor is it equal in every revolution. And this is what I believe: even if the **Prussian Tables** <note>The *Tabulae Prutenicae*, astronomical tables based on Copernicus's work</note> were absolutely certain and true, these errors would still be committed by the placement of these bodies; nevertheless, such a beautiful **argument** <note>Greek: ἐπιχείρημα</note> could not be rightly cast aside simply because the error was in the smallest details. ## THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

...be involved: so much so that there would have been a strong suspicion against me if I had agreed entirely with the numbers of *Copernicus*.

Of those arguments, let this be the first: that the *Prutenic* <note>The *Prutenic Tables* (1551) were astronomical tables calculated by Erasmus Reinhold based on the Copernican model; they were the standard for the time but still contained errors.</note> calculation is not infrequently mistaken in gathering the locations of the Planets. Indeed, *Copernicus* restored much for us in the collapsed science of motions; and our *Astronomy* is much purer than that within the memory of our fathers. Nevertheless, if we look into the matter deeply, we will certainly be forced to admit that we are not much closer to that blessed and desirable perfection than the ancient *Astronomy* is from that of today. The road is long, and there are various twists and turns toward this truth. The ancients showed it to us; our predecessors entered upon it; we have overtaken them and stand at a closer step, but we have not yet reached the goal. I do not say these things in contempt of *Astronomy*: *It is something to advance thus far, even if it is not granted to go further* <note>original: "Est aliqua prodire tenus, si non datur ultra"; a quote from Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.32</note>; but I say it so that no one may rashly decide something too grave regarding this discord, and while attacking me and these five bodies, insult the very foundations of *Astronomy*. I appeal to the observations of all Craftsmen: from which it can be seen how great a difference there often is between the true location and that which the calculation indicates—a difference which sometimes (2) in certain cases increases to the length of two entire degrees. Since this is so, it is advantageous for me to depart somewhat from the numbers of *Copernicus*; and now it is left to the judgment of diligent observers to see which arcs agree more closely with the heavens: mine, or the *Copernican* ones.

The second argument, by which I transfer the blame for this difference onto the *Prutenic* values themselves, is provided to me by the suspect *Eccentricities* <term>eccentricity: the distance between the center of a planet's orbit and the central point of the system (the Sun), which causes the planet's path to appear non-circular</term> of the Planets; this tends toward the fact that, although my arcs are not entirely perfect and certain (as I am forced to admit), they have nonetheless contracted a flaw from the "contagion" of the *Eccentricities*. If the bodies were constructed upon the spherical surfaces of the planets' mean distances—so that the same surface touched the centers of the circumscribed body and the angles of the inscribed body—then I would have no concern with the thickness of the spheres, which the *Eccentric* paths of the Planets require.

(3) However, since that could not be done, and the cause of the *Eccentricities*, as well as of the differences, has not yet been similarly explored; I had to borrow the thicknesses of the spheres from *Copernicus* as if they were certain; though it is well known that they are not perfectly certain. For although the entire history of celestial motions is a slippery path, requiring very long and difficult observations, this appears especially in establishing the *Eccentricities* and the locations of the *Apogees* <term>apogee: the point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Sun (or Earth, in older models)</term>. The *Solar (or terrestrial) Eccentricity* ought to be the most accurate of all; for the *Earth* <note>original: "Tellus"</note> is the nearest of the stars to us inhabitants, (4) and is carried by fewer motions than the rest. But in constructing the world through the interposition of bodies (as we saw above in Chapter XV), how much momentum the addition or removal of the small lunar <note>original: "σεληνίου" (selēniou); refers to the sphere of the Moon</note> sphere alone contributes to tightening or loosening all the spheres—which exceeds the thickness of the terrestrial sphere by only a very tiny portion! (5) Here, therefore, is the sphere which ought to have been measured most certainly, and which seemed possible to measure; here, I say, see in what great difficulty *Copernicus* himself is involved, who in Book 3 of the *Revolutions*, Chapter 20, complains (6) that we are forced to reason about great things through certain very small and scarcely perceptible details, because sometimes they pass by under a single minute of difference <note>original: "scrupulus"; used here as a minute of arc</note> across 5 or 6 degrees, and a moderate error propagates itself immensely. How much worse, therefore, will they [fare]...

## CHAPTER XVIII.

### On the discord of the <term>equations</term> <note>original: "προσθαφαιρέσεων" (prosthaphaereses); these are the mathematical corrections added or subtracted to a planet's mean motion to determine its true position.</note> resulting from the [Platonic] bodies compared to the Copernican data in general, and on the precision of Astronomy.

ABOVE, in chapters 14 and 15, when I seemed to be held by some evidence of falsehood regarding the distances—which *Copernicus* reported differently from these figure-based ones—I appealed to the apogeal equations; nor did I plead against condemnation if my own figures receded somewhat from the Copernicans. And yet, after I stood those similar arcs of the equations from the elongations from the Sun as witnesses before this judgment toward the end of Chapter 15, they seemed to testify against me. For there was no Planet that retained the arc assigned to it by *Copernicus*. From Saturn I took away 41 minutes; from Jupiter, 6 minutes; to Mars I added 30 minutes; but from Venus I took away a massive amount—2 degrees and 18 minutes; and from Mercury, 61 minutes. Therefore, those who wish to examine everything more exactly will judge that all my labor has been wasted, because the calculation of the bodies does not agree to a hair's breadth with the decrees of *Copernicus* and his numbers. 

And indeed, to the Physicists or Cosmographers—whose persona I sustain in this booklet—I owe no account for this difference. For even if they borrow the arguments for their decrees from the Astronomers, they do not reduce them to calculations as subtly as Astronomers do; nor are they so perceptive or fussy as to be moved by this slight difference. Therefore, I have won my case before the Cosmographers.

However, although I rightly fear the common sort of Astronomers, yet since it is proper for Craftsmen to preside with judgment, I do not despair, nor do I despair of victory against them. And first, I bid them to hope well of the calculation. For even if the difference is sometimes rather large, let them remember that the numbers were excerpted from the most evident places of the entire circle, and from the concurrence of all inequalities. For the discord of the positions assigned to the Planets by the bodies and by *Copernicus* is not so great throughout the entire circle, nor is it equal in all revolutions. And I think thus: even if the *Prutenic Tables* <note>Erasmus Reinhold's 1551 astronomical tables based on Copernicus's work.</note> were most certain and most true, and these errors were committed through this interposition of the bodies, such a harmonious <term>enterprise</term> <note>original: "ἐπιχείρημα" (epicheirema); a logical venture or argument.</note> could not rightly be cast aside simply because that error was in the smallest details. ...turned out: so much so that there would have been a great suspicion against me if I had agreed entirely with the numbers of Copernicus.

Of those arguments, let this be the first: that the **Prutenic calculation** <note>The *Prutenic Tables* (1551) were astronomical tables based on Copernicus’s work; they were the standard for the era but often contained significant errors.</note> is not rarely mistaken in determining the positions of the planets. Copernicus indeed restored much for us in the collapsed science of motions, and our **Astronomy** is much purer than that within the memory of our fathers. Nevertheless, if we look deeply into the matter itself, we will certainly be compelled to confess that we are not much closer to that blessed and desirable perfection than the ancient astronomy is from that of today. The road is long, and there are various windings toward this truth. The ancients showed it to us, our ancestors entered upon it, and we have outstripped them and stand at a closer step, but we have not yet reached the finish line. I do not say these things out of contempt for Astronomy: *It is something to advance this far, if it is not granted to go further* <note>Kepler is quoting the Roman poet Horace (*Epistles* 1.1.32), suggesting that even partial progress is valuable.</note>; but I say it so that no one may rashly pass a heavier judgment on this discord, and while attacking me and these **five bodies**, insult the very foundations of Astronomy. I appeal to the observations of all craftsmen: from which it can be seen how great a difference there often is between the true position and that which the calculation indicates, which sometimes (2) in certain cases increases to the length of two entire degrees of longitude. Since this is the case, it is advantageous for me to depart somewhat from the numbers of Copernicus; and now it is left to the judgment of diligent observers to see which arcs agree more closely with the heavens, mine or the Copernican ones.

The second argument, by which I transfer the blame for this difference to the Prutenic tables themselves, is offered to me by the suspected **Eccentricities of the Planets**; this leads to the point that, although my arcs are not entirely perfect and certain (as I am compelled to confess), they have nevertheless contracted a fault from the "contagion" of the Eccentricities. If the bodies were constructed upon the spherical surfaces of the planets' mean distances, so that the same surface touched the centers of the circumscribed body and the angles of the inscribed one, then I would have nothing to do with the "thickness" of the spheres, which the **eccentric paths** of the planets require.

(3) But since that could not be done, and the cause of the **eccentricities**—as well as the differences—has not yet been similarly explored, it was necessary for me to borrow the thicknesses of the spheres from Copernicus as if they were certain; yet it is well known that they are not the most certain. For although the entire history of celestial motions is accessible through long and difficult observations, this appears especially in establishing the **eccentricities** and the positions of the **apogees** <note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Sun (or, in older models, the Earth).</note>. The solar (or terrestrial) eccentricity ought to be held the most correctly of all; for the Earth is the closest of the stars to us inhabitants, (4) and is carried by fewer motions than the others. Indeed, in constructing the world through the intervening bodies, we saw above in Chapter XV how much weight the addition or removal of the lone lunar **outpouring** <note>original: "ἐκχυσις" (ekchysis). Kepler uses this term to describe the "overflowing" or thickness of the Earth's orbital sphere required to encompass the Moon's path.</note> brings to the tightening or loosening of all the spheres, which exceeds the thickness of the terrestrial sphere by only a very tiny portion. (5) Here, then, is the sphere which ought to have had the most certain measurement, and it was likely that it could; here, I say, see in how much difficulty it is involved according to Copernicus, who himself in Book 3 of the *Revolutions*, Chapter 20, complains (6) *that we are compelled to reason through certain very small and barely graspable things, which sometimes pass by under a single minute of difference or 6 degrees, and a modest error propagates itself immensely.* How much worse, therefore, will they [have]...

### JOHANNES KEPLER

...will have the thicknesses of the orbs, both for those more remote from us and for those subject to more varieties of motion. But if either those thicknesses <note>original: "πάχη" (pachē), referring to the depth or thickness of the planetary spheres.</note> were most certainly explored, or at least the probable causes were revealed why such great dimensions were attributed to each by the **Creator** (7): then I promise that I would produce from these bodies arcs that are consistent with the motions in every way. For I believe that whatever still hinders this discovered proportion of the heavens from reaching an exact knowledge of motions (8) is all to be blamed on the faults of the **eccentricities** <note>In early astronomy, an "eccentricity" describes how far a planet's circular orbit is centered away from the Sun or Earth.</note>; once these are removed (9), I think **these five solids** <note>The five Platonic solids (Cube, Tetrahedron, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron, Octahedron) which Kepler nested between the planetary spheres.</note> will be a great help to Craftsmen for the correction of motions, which many here and there are contemplating.

To promise them this regarding the eccentricities, I was also moved by this: (10) that everywhere there is controversy over a smaller particle than the whole thickness <note>original: "πάχος" (pachos)</note> of the entire orb. For take away from all six orbs their known thicknesses, or attribute double to each; you will see the world and all the **circumferences** <note>original: "περιφερειας" (peripherias)</note> collapse and increase immensely in one case, and in the other be pulled apart and diminished. Thus the truth stands somewhere between nothing and double, and it should not be feared that the Craftsman [the astronomer] has too much license to change eccentricities if someone tries to fit them to these figures. And so this is the second reason that can excuse me for the discord between my numbers and those of **Copernicus**.

The third reason is provided to me by the numbers of the **Prutenic Tables** <note>The *Prutenic Tables* (1551) were calculated by Erasmus Reinhold based on Copernican theory; they were the standard of the time but still contained errors.</note> themselves, which are still coarse, and not so precisely expressed that one cannot occasionally depart from them by half a degree with good leave. **Reinhold** <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), a leading astronomer and mathematician who promoted Copernican calculations.</note> indeed arranged everything most diligently in the Prutenic Tables. But I would not want anyone, enticed by this appearance of scrupulousness, to despise the somewhat coarse numbers in **Astronomy**, or to judge the matter more exactly than it is. That minute and scrupulous care of that greatest of men was either for the sake of the certainty of the calculation, or it was unnecessary in the fractional parts of the numbers; but the whole numbers themselves, which he divided so scrupulously, he took from Copernicus, just as he found them.

And indeed, how lenient **Copernicus** himself is in accepting whatever numbers happen to come somewhat near his wish and suit his purpose: the diligent reader of Copernicus will experience this. He does not reject numbers that, through various operations and the force of demonstration, should have agreed perfectly, even though they differ by several minutes [scruples]. He reads observations in **Walther** <note>Bernhard Walther (1430–1504), a Nuremberg astronomer whose precise observations were used by Copernicus.</note>, in **Ptolemy**, and elsewhere in such a way that he uses them more conveniently to build his calculation; hence he has no religious scruple about neglecting or changing hours in time, or quarters of degrees and sometimes more in arcs. In some places, as in the changed eccentricity of **Mars** and **Venus**, he even accepts sines <note>A trigonometric function used to calculate positions in an orbit.</note> differing from the truth, only because they point a finger slightly toward those he desires. Many things that, by his own confession, should have been amended, he takes whole and sincere from Ptolemy, while changing other similar things; and upon these he later builds the foundations of the new Astronomy. Of all these things, **Maestlin** <note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), Kepler’s professor and mentor at Tübingen.</note> gave me many proofs, which I omit for the sake of brevity. And so he might rightly seem to incur blame, unless he had done it deliberately, because it was better to have an Astronomy that was in some way imperfect than none at all. For difficulties of this kind will occur while the stars run; to overcome these, and to aspire to the constitution of science with the least loss without being hindered, as Copernicus dared, is the mark of a brave man; for the cowardly to shrink back...

### THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY. 67

...to flee, the timid to despair, and to cast away all this care. Just as Copernicus himself neither hides nor shamefully confesses these remedies <note>original: φάρμακα (pharmaka), used here to mean "corrective measures" or "astronomical fixes" for errors.</note> I have just recounted regarding himself. He protects himself by the example of Ptolemy and the ancients, excuses himself by the difficulty of observing, and everywhere leads the way for others by example in despising these tiny defects during the confirmation of noble discoveries. For if this had not been done before, Ptolemy would never have published that *Great Composition* <note>original: μεγάλην σύνταξιν (megalēn syntaxin), the Greek title of the *Almagest*.</note>, nor Copernicus his books *On the Revolutions* <note>original: τῶν ἀνελιττοσῶν (tōn anelittosōn), likely a Greek rendering of the title *De Revolutionibus*.</note>, nor Reinhold the *Prussian Tables*.

Nor does that table of Mästlin <note>Michael Mästlin was Kepler’s university professor and a supporter of the Copernican system.</note> inserted in Chapter 15 provide me with no excuse in the fourth place. Since Copernicus borrowed the **eccentricities** <note>In early astronomy, an "eccentricity" describes how far a planet's circular orbit is centered away from the Sun or Earth.</note> of the planets from Ptolemy, he suspected nothing less than this divine proportion of the heavens; so that one might quite rightly marvel that he came so close to it. Nor did he think it would ever happen that necessity would force an inquiry into the distances from the Sun and the locations of the **aphelia** <note>The point in an orbit where a planet is furthest from the Sun.</note>. What wonder is it then, if in this restoration to life and analysis <note>original: ἀνάλυσιν (analysin)</note> of the world many rough spots are found, when the craftsman did not look at the smallest details? Just as in a small painting, which hardly expresses a whole face to the senses, if one seeks the true proportion of the eye or the pupil, he must necessarily be deceived. For the painter neglected this because of the smallness, content if he represented in some way what is more evident.

Thus, although I have approached this analysis with the best reasoning, driven by the force of demonstration and the condition of the matter proposed, I would not want anyone to persuade himself that he has brought back absolutely certain numbers from it. For it could be that this very restoration was the cause of further error. Behold, these are not slight indications. Copernicus attributes the cause of why the eccentricities of Mars and Venus change to the change of the Earth's orbit. Therefore, their true eccentricity from the Sun does not change; you have a visual demonstration of this in the table. But if this is so, it would be necessary to derive the eccentricities from the Earth—those that existed in Ptolemy's century and those in ours—to the same point, and to conclude from both the same eccentricity from the Sun. And yet, consult the calculation, and you will see this does not happen as it should. For the eccentricities of the aphelia <note>original: ἀφηλίων (aphēliōn)</note> will also turn out to be discrepant with each other. Let the same be said of the locations of the aphelia, because these are mutually connected; and this is one point.

Next, it is easily gathered from a look at the table that since both the **aphelia** and the **apogees** <note>The point in an orbit where a planet is furthest from the Earth.</note> proceed unequally, a great diversity of **eccentricities** <note>original: ἐκκεντροτήτων (ekkentrotētōn)</note> will arise from this over the course of centuries. Today the **apsides** <note>The points in an orbit where the planet is closest or farthest from its center of motion.</note> of Saturn and the Earth are nearly joined, which is why the distance of Saturn from the center of the Earth's orbit is smaller by the whole eccentricity of the Earth than its distance from the Sun <note>Kepler uses the symbol ☉ to represent the Sun.</note>. When they stand at a right angle, each will be equal both from the Sun and from the Earth; for Copernicus, his Saturnian eccentricity will grow until the apsides of Saturn and the Earth are opposite each other. Even though the world will not last until that event, if astronomy were perfect, it ought to use such hypotheses that would suffice for a world that is, as it were, eternal. And yet neither Copernicus nor Reinhold warns of any of these things. Therefore, their numbers are not most perfect, nor do they explain to us the complete spheres of the planets, through which we might understand that those wild motions can happen. Since these and similar matters disturbed me not a little, and I was stuck, lacking a plan, like someone trying to put the scattered gears of a clock back into order—

...knows not how to reduce it to order; Mästlin comforted me, and indeed discouraged me from these over-subtleties. He used to say that we cannot exhaust all the treasures of nature; that a "well-settled evil" <note>A Latin idiom meaning a problem that is currently manageable should not be stirred up if the cure is worse than the disease.</note> should not be disturbed; and that we should rather tolerate and support this "rupture" in the human body of science with certain soothing remedies, rather than subject the patient to such an exquisite anatomy <note>dissection or rigorous analysis</note> that the sufferer is cast into the most immediate danger of life. He presented to me the example of Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus, the sole pupil of Copernicus who helped publish his work.</note>, and a concern of his that was similarly curious to my own, and how Copernicus rebuked him for it. There is a letter by Rheticus prefixed to the *Ephemeris* of 1551, which, because it is not commonly available and wonderfully assists this whole chapter in many places, I shall subjoin here as a concluding flourish to this chapter. Thus Rheticus wrote to the reader among other things:

*Copernicus, however, wished his inquiries to be moderate, not excessive. Therefore, by design—not through laziness or the weariness of fatigue—he avoided those minute divisions which some have even affected, and which there are those who demand, such as the subtlety of Peurbach <note>Georg von Peurbach (1423–1461), an influential astronomer whose tables sought high precision.</note> in his tables of eclipses. For you see some people putting all their care into these things, so that they scrutinize the positions of the stars quite scrupulously; yet while they gape at seconds, thirds, fourths, and fifths of minutes <note>These refer to increasingly small fractions of a degree: 1/60th, 1/3600th, and so on.</note>, they meanwhile pass over whole degrees and pay no regard to them, and in the moments of the* phenomena <note>original: $\tau\tilde{\omega}\nu \: \varphi\alpha\iota\nu o\mu\acute{\varepsilon}\nu\omega\nu$ (tōn phainomenōn)</note> *they often err by hours, and not infrequently by whole days. This is surely what happens in Aesop’s fables to the man who, commanded to lead back a lost ox, is so intent on catching certain small birds that he neither catches them nor keeps the ox itself. I remember when I too was driven by youthful curiosity and desired to reach, as it were, the inner sanctum of the stars. And so I even quarreled occasionally regarding this inquiry with that greatest and best of men, Copernicus. But he, while indeed delighted by the honorable desire of my mind, used to rebuke me with a "gentle arm" and urge me to learn to "take my hand off the painting" <note>A classical expression (manum de tabula) meaning to know when a work is "good enough" and stop over-refining it.</note>. "I," he said, "if I can bring the truth to within a sextant—which is ten minutes of a degree—I shall exult in my mind no less than we hear Pythagoras did when he discovered the rule of the triangle." While I marveled and said we must strive for greater certainty, he demonstrated that this could only be reached with difficulty, for many reasons, but especially for three. The first of these, he said, was that he noticed most observations of the ancients were not "Lyncean" <note>named after Lynceus the Argonaut, famous for his keen eyesight; meaning "perfectly sharp."</note> but were adjusted to fit whatever doctrine of motion each observer had specifically established for himself. Therefore, it required singular attention and industry to separate the corrupt data from those to which the observer’s opinion had added little or nothing. The second reason, he said, was that the positions of the inerrant stars* <term>inerrant stars|the "fixed" stars that do not change position relative to one another, used as a reference for planetary motion</term> *were not investigated by the ancients beyond ten minutes of a degree; and yet the positions of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> must be taken chiefly according to these. He made a few exceptions where the recorded declination of a star from the equator helped the matter, because from this the position of the star could be more certainly established. The third reason he mentioned was this: we do not have such authors as Ptolemy had after the Babylonians and Chaldeans—those lights of the art, Hipparchus, Timocharis, Menelaus, and the rest—upon whose observations and precepts we can lean and trust. He said he would much rather rest content with those things whose truth he could vouch for, than to show off the sharpness of his intellect in the doubtful subtlety of ambiguous data. Certainly his indications would not be further, or perhaps even closer, than a sextant or a quadrant of one degree from the truth; far from repenting of this defect, he rejoiced greatly that he had been able to proceed this far through a long time, with immense labor, the greatest exertion, and singular study and industry. Mercury indeed, as if according to the Greek proverb, he left in the middle as common property; because he said it had not been observed by his own study, nor had he received anything from others which could greatly assist him or which he could entirely prove. Warning, suggesting, and instructing me in many things, he especially urged that...*

...to give attention to the observation of the fixed stars, especially those appearing in the zodiac <term>signifero: literally 'the sign-bearer,' the zodiac</term>, because the conjunctions of the wandering stars <term>planets</term> with these could be noted, etc. Thus far from the letter of Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus, the disciple of Copernicus who first published an account of his system.</note> are those things which were relevant to the matter. ## ON CHAPTER EIGHTEEN
->Author’s Notes.<-

(1) *Yet it is not only uncertain by whose fault.* Although it is true that the Prutenic Tables <note>original: "Prutenicas"; these were astronomical tables published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551 based on Copernican theory</note> are in error, both elsewhere and especially in the *prosthaphareses* <term>prosthapharesis: a technical term for the 'equation' or correction added to or subtracted from a planet's mean motion to find its true position</term> of the annual sphere; yet the most powerful cause is not only this matter—that the intervals of the spheres do not exactly fit the proportions of the five geometric solids—but also another greater matter: namely, that the planetary spheres each have such great and such different eccentricities. The cause of both things, I say, lies in the archetype <note>the original divine blueprint</note> of the decoration of motions, according to Harmonic ratios. Since the exact figured proportions <note>the Platonic solids</note> could not stand alongside the Harmonic proportions, it was necessary for the former—as they incline more toward the physical proportions of matter—to be slightly diminished, so that the Harmonic proportions might hold their place: the former in the spaces of the world, the latter between the motions through those spaces. See this most ornate arrangement in Book V of *The Harmony of the World* <note>original: "Harmon: lib. V"; Kepler's 1619 masterpiece</note>, chapter 9, propositions 46 to 49, at length.

(2) *In some cases up to 2 whole degrees.* Indeed, in Mars three degrees, in Venus five degrees across, in Mercury 10 or 11 degrees (if it is permitted to affirm anything based on the hypothesis of the theory of Mercury established by me, even regarding those places where this planet cannot be seen) are in error at certain locations of the spheres, according to the Prutenic Tables.

(3) *Since, however, that could not be done.* The centers of the planes of the circumscribed figure and the angles of the inscribed figure could not be joined in this archetype of the world. The cause has been stated above. For the spheres would settle too much: the corrections of the great sphere for each planet would become larger than what we observe. Therefore, one had to look to the distances of the planets from the Sun, which are not average, but the aphelion <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Sun</note> of the two inner ones and the perihelion <note>the point closest to the Sun</note> of the outer one; that is, to the eccentricities of the planets, which form the distances of aphelion and perihelion. Yet in this I was looking at uncertainties: for the cause of the eccentricities was not yet known—why there was such great eccentricity for individual planets; why such a difference; why Saturn and Jupiter had average ones, Mars and Mercury the greatest, and Earth and Venus the smallest. The cause being unknown, it was necessary that the quantity be unknown from the start <note>original: "à priori"</note>; I was sent back to naked observations.

(4) *And with fewer motions than the rest.* So indeed Ptolemy holds, and Copernicus from him. For the Sun (or the Earth) not only lacks an epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle moving on a larger one, used to explain planetary loops</term>, but even an Equant <term>equant: a point from which a planet's motion appears uniform</term>, as they thought. But according to the truth of the matter, in that motion of translation around the Sun, the Earth is similar to every one of the remaining planets in all things; as has been demonstrated by me in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>original: "Comment. Martis"; referring to his 1609 *Astronomia Nova*</note>, part three; and *Epitome of Astronomy*, book 7.

(5) *This therefore is the sphere, which most certainly.* This sphere is called the Sun's by Ptolemy, the Earth's by Copernicus, and the "Annual" by the Prutenic Tables.

(6) *Because through certain very small things.* This complaint of Copernicus specifically touches the locations of the apogees <note>the point where a planet is furthest from the Earth (or Sun)</note> (which have nothing to do with this business of the proportion of the spheres); it is not the same regarding eccentricities. Therefore, the thickness of the spheres themselves is not worse, but better.

(7) *Then I promise I will bring forward.* Behold the audacity of the promise, supported by the difficulty of the condition proposed here! Yet see also the success: the quantities of the eccentricities have been explored by me from the observations of Tycho Brahe <note>the Danish astronomer whose precise data Kepler used to discover the laws of planetary motion</note>; the causes of the individual eccentricities have been revealed in my *Harmonics*; and behold, I have brought forward arcs consistent with the motions in all respects, not indeed from the geometric figures alone, but most powerfully from the causes of the eccentricities (the Harmonies).

(8) All this is due to faults in the Eccentricities.] *You will, I think, praise even a three-year-old boy who imagines in his mind a battle with giants. But once the Eccentricities have first been found through the Observations of Brahe as <term>the fact of the matter <note>original Greek: τὸ ὅτι</note></term>, then finally there is a place for the investigation of the causes, or <term>the reason why <note>original Greek: τὸ διότι</note></term>, based on these five figures and the joined Harmonic proportions.*

### CHAPTER XIX.

#### On the remaining discrepancy of the individual Planets in particular.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' featuring elaborate scrollwork, foliage, and two figures amidst the vines.</image-desc>
These, therefore, were the general matters which can relieve my case. Now let us see in particular whether anything further can be excused. Let us take our start from Saturn. And indeed, a great addition has been made to its <term>distance <note>original Greek: ἀπόχημα</note></term>; but this nevertheless caused a difference in the <term>prosthaphæresis <note>The correction added or subtracted to a planet's mean motion to find its true position.</note></term> of no more than 41 minutes. For just as its vast distance provides the easiest cause for error in observation, so an error in distance, however clear, produces a small and smaller-than-expected difference in the calculation of the position. And yet, one could see that even the motions of this star were not measured with total certainty by astronomers, as was evident this past winter alone. For on the 22nd and a half day of November in the year 1594, Saturn was seen exactly between the Neck and the Heart of Leo <note>The star Regulus</note>, where it ought to have been according to the calculation on the 21st or 31st day of October past. This is a difference in longitude of about 37 minutes, more or less. If its discrepancy from Copernicus's <term>prosthaphæresis</term> does not exceed this amount, once the distance is corrected, astronomers should consider themselves abundantly satisfied.

In Jupiter, nothing can be rightly found wanting. For it has a small difference, and less than a sixth of a degree.

However, the fact that in Mars half a degree is in excess is no surprise, nor does it move me; what moves me rather is that the difference is not greater. For Mästlin testifies in the preface of his Ephemeris <note>An astronomical almanac giving the positions of celestial bodies.</note> for the year 1577 that the errors of this star cannot be forced within the narrow limits of two degrees of calculation.

Now as far as the lower planets, Venus and Mercury, are concerned, although they seem to have some advantage over the higher planets—because it is easier to measure their orbs from their maximum elongation <note>The greatest angular distance from the Sun as seen from Earth.</note> than from <term>acronychal observation <note>original Greek: ἀκρονυχίᾳ; observing a planet when it is opposite the Sun, rising at sunset.</note></term>—the very method of observing them is suspect to me. However, I leave this to be judged more correctly by astronomers: namely, whether in these planets they are not sometimes deceived by (1) the density of vapors and physical parallax <note>Refraction caused by the Earth's atmosphere.</note>, which neither the Sun nor the Moon escapes. Certainly Mästlin, in his *Disputation on Eclipses*, thesis 58, affirms regarding Venus that not rarely its distance from the Sun seen near the horizon was notably smaller than the true distance. How much more so...

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

The same can be said of Mercury, which is almost always hidden under the rays of the sun; and although it occasionally emerges, it never presents itself to our sight except near the horizon through an intervening abundance of vapors <note>Kepler is referring to atmospheric refraction and "exhalations" near the horizon that distort observations.</note>. And although Venus is aided by the fixed stars appearing simultaneously and nearby, Mercury more frequently remains at fault, for the planet itself is rarely seen, and the fixed stars near it even more rarely. Since these difficulties occur today, it is credible that they could have happened even to the ancient masters <note>original: "Artificibus"</note>, however great they were. For the fact that they do not warn the reader about this increases the suspicion regarding the faulty dimensions of these planets. This serves as evidence that any error arising from it was neither noticed nor corrected by them. Therefore, in reading the ancients, I think we must primarily consider whether the instruments and methods of the individual observations alleged could have been subject to this error.

Next, I fear—and not without reason—that many things in the reasoning of the hypotheses for these two planets remain uncertain. Copernicus (as is gathered from what was just quoted from Rheticus, and below from Maestlin's letter) followed the views of Ptolemy more than the necessity of observations in correcting his theories. Rheticus, in his *Narration* <note>The *Narratio Prima*, the first published account of the Copernican system</note>, ensured that Copernicus would be less blamed in this matter; there he warns that one must adhere most scrupulously to the footsteps of the ancients, and nothing should be easily changed until the extreme necessity of observations demands it. Because such exquisite observations could not be obtained, that was perhaps a sufficiently great reason for that most prudent Master [Copernicus] to attempt nothing further regarding these planets beyond accommodation to his own views.

Therefore, as for the great diversity of arcs you see in Venus, attribute the blame for this matter—among the other things I previously stated in general (which I wish you to remember well)—also to these obstacles just mentioned; and you will easily overcome the magnitude of the disagreement with your composure, if you have weighed each point well. In this matter, it will be a great comfort to you that the Copernican number is a mean between the arcs resulting from the inclusion of the Moon and those from its omission. For if you stuff the great orb <note>The "Great Orb" refers to the sphere of the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> with the system of the Moon: the **Icosahedron** <note>One of the five Platonic solids, which Kepler placed between the orbits of Earth and Venus.</note> moves Venus further away from the Earth than Copernicus reported; but if, by removing the Moon, you make the great orb thinner: the figure allows Venus to come too close and permits it to be larger than it is in Copernicus. Therefore, something less than the [full] Moon could help the matter if Copernicus is to be maintained.

Concerning Mercury, so much has already been said, and more could be said, that I think you, fair reader, would digest and excuse it even if something more were lacking. (2) Nor does the diversity of its motion seem worthy of me raising a great dispute over it. Certainly, this is the one that most prostitutes the reputation of astrologers and disturbs the whole logic of weather phenomena <note>original: "meteororum"; referring to atmospheric events and weather prediction.</note>.

<margin>These numbers are in Table V, which is in Chapter 15 for Mercury <note>The symbol ☿ denotes Mercury.</note>.</margin>
> Mercury is so marvelous that it almost deceived even me. And no wonder, for I notice it was also quite troublesome for Copernicus and Reinhold <note>Erasmus Reinhold, whose *Prutenic Tables* were the standard astronomical tables of the era.</note>. Copernicus admits this of himself: "This star," he says (Book 5, Chapter 30), "has tortured us with many twists and labors so that we might investigate its motion." Consequently, besides the fact that he records no observations of his own made on Mercury, but borrows them from Bernhard Walther of Nuremberg, he is also inconsistent in establishing the location of its apogee <note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>. For the apogee which he found (Chapter 26) in the first years of Antoninus, around 140 AD, according to Ptolemy's observations, to be at 10 degrees of Aries <note>♈</note>, and under the starry sphere at 183 degrees and 20 minutes from the first star of Aries: he places the same 183 degrees and 20 minutes (Chapter 29) at the 21st year of Ptolemy Philadelphus, just as if this apogee of Mercury had remained unmoved under the sphere of fixed stars for the intervening 400 years; even though it seemed to him (at the end of Chapter 30) to have moved one degree every 63 years—adding, however: "if only the motion were uniform." The calculation of the Prutenic Tables reveals that Reinhold was stuck in the same difficulties; it is argued from this that Reinhold assumed the same location for this apogee for that time of Philadelphus as Copernicus did, namely 183° 20' from the first star of Aries. But at that time of Ptolemy, it falls into a place far removed from Ptolemy's manifest observations and Copernicus's assumptions. For there its location is computed not as 183° 20', nor 10° of Aries, but 188° 50' under the starry sphere, and 15° 30' of Aries. Therefore, those numbers of mine were indeed adapted to Ptolemy's age, but they do not agree in all respects with the calculation of the Prutenic Tables, but rather with Ptolemy's observations; for Copernicus also both retained and followed those, and produced the same numbers from them. However, I did not want to compute these numbers for our age, or that of Copernicus, because they would become quite different due to the diminished eccentricity <note>The "eccentricity" refers to how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of the Great Orbit <note>The "Great Orbit" refers to the Earth's path around the Sun.</note>; and because in Copernicus they were not investigated and confirmed by any more recent observations. I would wish (as you may remember me saying in person) that Copernicus had taken new observations rather than ancient ones as the foundations for these dimensions. For it is a great and monstrous postulate (Book 5, Chapter 30) when he says: "we think it must be granted that the proportions of the circles have remained from Ptolemy even until now." (4) For the diminished eccentricity of the Earth itself requires different numbers. Nor is it true, as Rheticus says in his *Narration*, that no change in eccentricity is felt in Mercury—just as in Jupiter—for similarly, the side of the Apogee alone closes with its own Apogee. To this is added that the Ptolemaic observations are quite coarse and partial, which certainly ought to have been corrected by more precise ones. But one may now complain of these things in vain. ### ON CHAPTER NINETEEN
#### *Author’s Notes.*

(1) [By the density of vapors and physical parallax.] *Tycho Brahe* <note>The great Danish astronomer whose precise observations Kepler used to derive his laws of planetary motion.</note> calls these "refractions of the stars." He is the one who established and refined this part of astronomical doctrine in his book *Introductory Exercises* <note>original: *Progymnasmatum*</note>, which was published around that time. I also treated this part of astronomy in my *Optical Part of Astronomy* <note>Kepler's *Astronomiae Pars Optica* (1604), a foundational text in optics.</note> published 15 years ago, and expanded upon it in the *Epitome of Astronomy, Book 1, from page 52.*

(2) [Nor does the diversity of its motion seem worthy to me.] This was believed about Mercury until now; nor do I deny that there is a great diversity of errors even in its motions. However, this diversity is a matter of quantity, not of form or principles, as we were taught until now. In these principles, Mercury differs in no way from the rest of the planets.

(3) [And indeed in predicting the winds.] At that time, I followed the common opinion that Mercury specifically excited the winds more than the other planets. But many years of experience have taught me that the forms of weather changes are not distributed among specific planets. Instead, "sublunary Nature" <note>The Earth’s atmosphere and environment, which Aristotelian physics placed "under the moon."</note> is generally stimulated by the aspects <note>term: aspects; the geometric angles between planets, such as 90 or 180 degrees, thought to influence Earthly events.</note> of two planets, or by the "stations" <note>When a planet appears to stand still in the sky before changing direction.</note> of individual ones. This causes Nature to "sweat out" vapors or fumes from the mountains and subterranean workshops. These vapors and fumes then turn into rain, snow, chasms <note>A term used for atmospheric phenomena like auroras or openings in the clouds.</note>, lightning, hail, or winds, depending on the circumstances of place and time. 

Certainly, great winds are never—or very rarely—solitary: all rain drives winds before it when it first attacks with force; and when winds rage most fiercely, it is a sign of the year's humid constitution. For either it is raining in the mountains from which the winds blow, or snow is melting there, or a humid vapor carried upward by force is condensed into drops in one place, while elsewhere it seethes, strikes the cold of the upper air, and recoils. This is indeed the origin of even a gentle breeze: when vapor boils out of some mountain, it is reflected and flows down into all the surrounding regions. There are times when all the air, stretched across entire continents, is set into a flow once the beginning of motion is given in the highest of all mountains. Thus, every wind can be stirred up by all causes or investigations of nature indiscriminately; the origin of the winds cannot be blamed on Mercury alone.

(4) [For the terrestrial eccentricity itself was diminished.] As said above, this is not probable, nor were the observations of the ancients required to be so accurate as to make such a demonstration necessary. Therefore, I embrace the axiom of Copernicus placed here: **Namely, it must be granted that the proportions of the circles have remained constant.** For the nature of the heavens and the evidence from the other planets suggests this.

(5) [Relying on the most certain hope that it will be soon.] In those days, he <note>Kepler is referring to his younger self in the third person.</note> used to animate these cares with such words and hope. Although he was frustrated in his hope regarding the timing—for that which follows twenty-four years later is not "soon"—he eventually became master of his hope through my *Harmony of the World* <note>original: *Opus Harmonicum*; Kepler's 1619 masterpiece where he finally resolved the proportions of the solar system.</note>.

# JOHANNES KEPLER

## CHAPTER XX.

->(1) *What the proportion of the motions to the spheres may be.*<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' featuring floral scrollwork and architectural elements.</image-desc>

And up to this point, that argument has been resolved which I believe brings the greatest strength to the new hypotheses <note>The "new hypotheses" refers to the heliocentric (Sun-centered) system of Copernicus.</note>: and it has been demonstrated that the <term>apostemata [distances]</term> of the spheres in the Copernican hypotheses utilize the proportions of the five regular solids. Let us now see whether, by another argument deduced from the motions, both the new hypotheses and these very Copernican dimensions of the spheres can be confirmed, and whether a more certain ratio of the motions to the <term>apostemata [distances]</term> can be obtained from Copernicus than from the common hypotheses. In which matter, *while I build up the sizes of the spheres closest to those of Copernicus from the well-known* <term>periodic [orbital]</term> *times of the motions*, favor this most beautiful endeavor, gentle Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy</note>; it is your honor that is now at stake.

First, everyone desires that the further any sphere is from the center, the more slowly it should proceed. For nothing is more consistent with reason—as Aristotle testifies in Book 2 of *On the Heavens*, chapter 10—than "that the motions of each occur in proportion to the distances" <note>original Greek: κατὰ λόγον γίγνεσθαι τὰς ἑκάστου κινήσεις τοῖς ἀποστήμασι</note>. In which passage, even if the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> brings forward another reason foreign to our purpose—namely, the hindrance from the encounter with the very swift <term>primi mobilis [first mover]</term> <note>In the old geocentric system, the "First Mover" was the outermost sphere that rotated the entire universe once every 24 hours.</note>—nevertheless, by this other reason he still fights for me, and in his entire opinion he militates against Ptolemy, and even against himself. For it pleases him that an equality of motion comes from the movers into all the spheres; but the inequality of the return <note>The time taken to complete one orbit.</note> is caused by the spheres themselves: so that, for instance, any particle of Saturn would be just as swift as the lowest sphere of the Moon by the force of equal motion; but it happens to the former that, having obtained a wider space, since it is no swifter than the others, it returns more slowly. 

And yet the Philosopher could not obtain this cheaper "equality" in the tradition of the ancients; because it was necessary that they assign equal returns to the three planets of unequal spheres—the Sun, Venus, and Mercury <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the Sun, Venus, and Mercury were all thought to orbit the Earth in exactly one year.</note>—and thus they always made the higher planet in its sphere swifter than the lower one. In Copernicus, such a proportion offers itself at first glance. For of the six moving spheres, the one that is narrower always returns more quickly. For the course of Mercury is three months, of Venus seven and a half months <note>original: *sesquiocto mensium*</note>, of the Earth one year, of Mars two years, of Jupiter twelve, and of Saturn thirty years. But if you recall this to calculations, so that just as the proportion of Saturn’s motion is to the circuit of its sphere, or to its distance (for the proportion of the circles is the same as that of the semi-diameters), you make the proportion of each of the others to its own sphere the same; you will find that a simple proportion of this kind does not hold place. Take this table as an index of this matter.

Just as the source of Light is in the Sun, and the beginning of the circle is in the place of the Sun (that is, in the center), so now life, motion, and the <term>soul of the world</term> <note>anima mundi</note> fall back into that same Sun. Thus, the fixed stars are at rest, the planets perform secondary acts of motion, and the Sun performs the primary act—which is incomparably more noble than the secondary acts in all things, not unlike the Sun itself in the beauty of its appearance, the efficacy of its power, and the [splendor] of its light.

# JOHANNES KEPLER

[The Sun] far surpasses all others in splendor. Here now, those noble titles apply far more correctly to the Sun: the Heart of the World, the King, the Emperor of the Stars, the Visible God, and so on. (4) But the nobility of this subject requires a far different time and place, and it has already appeared clearly enough from the *Narratio* of Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus was the first disciple of Copernicus; his *Narratio Prima* was the first published account of Copernican theory.</note>.

Now, however, we must consider the method of establishing this sought-after proportion. It was seen above that if the size of the orbit alone contributed to the increase in the periodic time <note>original: "$\pi\epsilon\rho\iota o\delta\iota\kappa\grave{o}\nu$"</note>, then the difference between the motions and the mean distances would have been the same. That is to say, the proportion of the 88 periodic days of Mercury to the 225 days of Venus would be the same as the proportion of the semidiameter of Mercury's orbit to that of Venus. But now, the weakness of the motive soul <note>original: "motricis animæ"; Kepler initially conceived of a "moving spirit" or force emanating from the Sun that pushed the planets, a precursor to his later concept of gravity.</note> at a greater distance mixes itself into this proportion of motions. We must therefore see how it is compared with this weakness. Let us assume, therefore—which is very likely (5)—that motion is dispensed by the Sun in the same proportion as light. Experts in optics <note>original: "Optici"</note> teach the proportion by which the weakening of light spreading from a center occurs. For there is as much light in a small circle as there is light (or solar rays) in a large one. Since it is more densely packed in the small circle and thinner in the large one, the measure of this thinning must be sought from the proportion of the circles themselves; and this applies as much to light as to the motive power. Therefore, as much as Venus's orbit is larger than Mercury's, so much is the motion of the latter stronger, faster, swifter, or more vigorous than the former—or by whatever word you please to express the matter. But as much as one orbit is larger than another, it also requires more time for a circuit, even if the force of motion were equal on both sides. Therefore, it follows from this that a single greater distance of a planet from the Sun contributes twice toward increasing the period: (6) and conversely, the increase of the period is double the difference of the distances <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\pi o\sigma\eta\mu\alpha\tau\omega\nu$"</note>.

Therefore, half of the increase added to the smaller period ought to show the true proportion of the distances, so that the sum represents the distance of the superior planet, and the simple smaller period represents the distance of the inferior planet in the same quantity. For example, the periodic motion of <term>Mercury</term> <note>☿</note> is almost 88 days; that of Venus is almost 224 and <term>two-thirds</term> <note>original: "besse"; a Roman term for 2/3 of a unit.</note>; the difference is 136 and two-thirds; half of that is 68 and a third. This, joined with 88, makes 156 and <term>one-third</term> <note>original: "trientem"; a Roman term for 1/3 of a unit.</note>. Therefore, as 88 is to 156 and a third, so is the semidiameter of Mercury’s mean circle to the mean circle of Venus. If you work in this way for each case, and explain the resulting pairs of distances by the numbers of sines <note>mathematical values used for calculating distances</note>, so that the semidiameter of the superior planet is always the "total sine" <note>the base unit of 1000 in Kepler's calculations</note>:

->the semidiameter of the orbit will result as:<-
$\left. \begin{matrix} \text{Jupiter} & 574 \\ \text{Mars} & 274 \\ \text{Earth} & 694 \\ \text{Venus} & 762 \\ \text{Mercury} & 563 \end{matrix} \right\}$ 
->But in Copernicus it is:<-
$\left\{ \begin{matrix} 572 \\ 290 \\ 658 \\ 719 \\ 500 \end{matrix} \right.$

(7) As you see, we have come closer to the truth. Although I doubt whether that practice of dividing the difference has followed the theorem he had established by a demonstrative method in all respects, another method of calculation—which brings me back to the same numbers—commands me to believe that something is not entirely hidden in these figures. For because it is probable that the strength...

<meta>This page continues Kepler's mathematical attempt to link planetary distances to their orbital speeds. He is using a hypothetical calculation to show that the Sun's "motive force" weakens with distance, a key step toward his later discovery of the laws of planetary motion.</meta>

...that motion is in proportion with distances; it will also be probable that however much any planet exceeds the one above it in the strength of its motion, it is exceeded by that same amount in distance. Let, for example, the distance and the power of Mars be one unit. Therefore, by whatever fraction of Martian power the Earth is stronger than Mars, it will lose that same fraction of the Martian distance. This is easily done through the **Rule of False Position** <note>The "Regula Falsi" is an ancient mathematical method for solving linear equations by making a trial guess and then correcting it based on the result.</note>: for I posit that the radius of the Earth's orbit is to that of Mars as 694 is to 1000. Therefore, I say, if the circumference of a circle marked by 1000 is traversed by the Martian motive force in 687 days, then a smaller circle, marked by 694, will be traversed by that same Martian force in 477 days. Now, because it is certain that the Earth’s circuit is not 477 days, but 365, I proceed by the **inverse rule** <note>original: "regulam inversam"</note> thus: 477 days would be consumed by the simple Martian force; how much of the Martian force is consumed by a circuit of 365 and a quarter days over the same path that Mars would complete in 477 days? For there is no doubt that a stronger power than the Martian one is required. There results, therefore, beyond the whole Martian force, an additional <gloss>306/1000</gloss> part of that same power. And the Earth is that much stronger than Mars: it ought, therefore, to be that much closer to the Sun. Specifically, if Mars is removed from the Sun by 1000 units (for the distance of the higher planet is always taken as a whole unit), the Earth will be closer by 306 of those parts. And by subtracting the 306 from the 1000, the number 694—which was posited at the beginning—ought to result, if that position was true. If it were false, you would operate according to the instructions of the rule and elicit the true position.

You see that from this second theorem nothing other than the previous numbers result; from which it is certain that these two theorems differ in form but in fact coincide and rest upon the same foundation. However, how that happens, I have never been able to investigate until now.

->Author’s Notes.<-

(1) **What the proportion of the motions to the Orbs may be.]** *This is the proper subject of Book IV of the Epitome; transferred from there into Book V of the Harmonics. For in Chapter III of that book, this very question is unraveled and taken among the foundations by which it is demonstrated that the extreme motions of the Planets are contained by **Harmonic proportions**. Although in this chapter I had not yet attained what I was seeking, I have nonetheless found most of the principles employed—which even then seemed to me agreeable to the nature of things—to be most certain and useful throughout these last 25 years: especially in the **Commentaries on the motions of Mars**, part IV.*

(2) **Motive souls.]** <note>original: "Motrices animas"</note> *I proved that none of these exist in the Commentaries on Mars.*

(3) **That there is one motive Soul.]** *If you substitute the word **Force** <note>original: "Vim"</note> for the word **Soul** <note>original: "Anima"</note>, you have the very same principle upon which the **Celestial Physics** <note>original: "Physica cælestis"</note> in the Commentaries on Mars is established, and further developed in Book IV of the Epitome of Astronomy. For formerly, I believed that the cause moving the Planets was absolutely a Soul, being thoroughly imbued with the dogmas of J. C. Scaliger regarding **Motive Intelligences** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger was a 16th-century scholar; "Intelligences" were thought to be spiritual beings that guided the planets.</note>. But when I weighed the fact that this motive cause weakens with distance, just as the light of the Sun is attenuated with distance from the Sun, I concluded from this that this Force must be something corporeal—if not properly so, then at least equivocally; just as we say light is something corporeal, that is, an **emanation** <note>original: "speciem"</note> dropped from a body, but immaterial.*

(4) **But the nobility of this subject requires a far different time and place.]** *Naturally, it found its place in the **Commentaries on Mars** published in the year 1609: from there the sum of the matter was taken and repeated in the Epitome of Astronomy, Book IV.*

(5) **By the same reasoning, motion from the Sun.]** *All these things remain valid without any change even in the Commentaries on Mars.*

(7) Nearer, as you see, to the truth.] Truly nearer through such an arithmetic mediation than through a geometric one, although the geometric one was legitimately concluded from the assumed principles: because since in reality the proportion of the proportion is not double, but only sesquialterate (1.5): it happened here that the arithmetic mean approached the mean of the sesquialterate proportion more than the geometric mean, or that of the double proportion: because the arithmetic mean is always closer to the larger term than the geometric mean: as in the example 6, 9, 12 and 6, 8, 12. The second was thus. Given the distance of the Earth is 694. Two steps thus: The distance of Mars 1000 gives a period of 687. What does the distance of the Earth 694 give? It follows as an Earth period of 477. I proceed therefore by the inverse proportion.

The true period 365 1/4 gives a false one of 477, as if from Mars; what does 1000, the force of Mars, give? It follows as 1306, the force of the Earth. Therefore, the excess of power 306 above the Martian 1000 is the same as the excess of the Martian distance 1000 above the assumed Earth distance 694. This happens for this reason: because I apply to Mars the number 1000 as the index of the period, as well as the power, and also the distance. And yet this is not a matter of being revolved by the necessity of the <term>Rule of False Position<note>A method of solving equations by making a trial guess and then adjusting it proportionally based on the error produced.</note></term> to the same numbers that were in the first process; but it is to find again what you had placed at the beginning. For since in the first process an arithmetic mediation is made between 687 and 365 1/4 through 526 1/8; two different proportions are therefore established, as in every such mediation: the higher and smaller 687 to 526 1/8, and the lower and larger 526 1/8 to 365 1/4, which was transferred by the <term>Rule of Three<note>original: "regulam Detri." The basic mathematical rule for finding a fourth value from three known values based on proportions.</note></term> into the distances 1000 and 694.

In the second process, while the distance of Mars is set at 1000 and Earth at 694, there is placed between the distances of Mars and Earth the lower part of the arithmetically bisected proportion of the periods, namely 526 1/8 to 365 1/4. That is truly transferred into other numbers, namely 687 to 477, by the Rule of Three. If therefore you take away from the proportion 687 to 365 1/4 the lower part of the arithmetically divided part, applied however to the higher term 687, it is necessary that the higher part of the same be left with the lower term, namely 477 to 365 1/4. Which sort of transposition, if I may mention in passing, I also used in the political digression at the end of Book 3 of the *Harmonics*. And yet by the Rule of Three this proportion was transferred into other numbers, 1306 to 1000. Wherefore since the same number 1000 is in both parts of the proportion, it follows therefore that between its two associated terms, namely 694 (assumed first) and 1306 (established last), an arithmetic mediation was made through 1000. Because what was previously the lower part between 687 and 365 1/4, namely 526 1/8 to 365 1/4, was here again assumed as the lower part 1000 to 694. But what was the higher part there, namely 687 to 526 1/8 (for it is the same as 477 to 365 1/4), was here again established as the higher part, namely 1306 to 1000. If the arithmetic mean 1000 was established between 1306 and 694, it is necessary that equal differences come forth, namely 306 on both sides. It was sufficient, therefore, to have proposed to make it so that as 526 1/8 is to 687 and 365 1/4, so is 1000 to two others: whether that was done through the simple Rule of Three or through the Rule of False Position, it was the same. For it was certain that the smallest term to be produced was 694, because even in the first process it was made so that as 526 1/8 is to 365 1/4, so 1000 is to 694.
