# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY

<note>original: "nescius in tenebris contingit & horrescit"</note> unaware, I stumbled in the dark and shuddered) I had wandered from my purpose, wishing to prove that the proportion of the <term>virtues<note>In this context, Kepler uses "virtue" to mean the moving power or physical influence emanating from the Sun that drives the planets.</note></term> was the same as that of the distances. However, I now establish a smaller proportion for the virtues: namely, 1000 for Mars to 1306 for the Earth; while for the distances, it is larger: 1000 for Mars to 694 for the Earth. Indeed, the proportion would have been the same on both sides if I had used a geometric mean rather than an arithmetic one.

Too much has been said of this process; for it ought to be buried, not only because it is erroneous, but even if it proceeded quite legitimately. This is because the proportion of the periods is not double the proportion of the mean distances, but is most perfectly and absolutely <term>sesquialterate<note>A sesquialterate ratio is 3:2. This is the foundation of Kepler's Third Law: the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun.</note></term> to it. That is: if one seeks the cube roots of the planets' periodic times, such as 687 <note>for Mars</note> and 365 1/4 <note>for Earth</note>, and these roots are then squared, then in these squared numbers resides the most certain proportion of the semi-diameters of the Orbits. These operations can be performed easily, either by the Table of Cubes by <term>Clavius<note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer.</note></term>, which is added to his *Practical Geometry*, or far more easily by the <term>Logarithms of Napier<note>John Napier (1550–1617), the Scottish mathematician who invented logarithms, which revolutionized astronomical calculations.</note></term>, the Baron of Scotland, as follows: Let our numbers be extended for necessity and convenience, so that they are 68700 and 36525—we shall not seek the highest precision for now. Their logarithms, from Napier’s canon, are approximately 37543 and 100715.

The third parts of these are 12514 and 33572.
And the doubles of these (their two-thirds) are 25029 and 67144. These show, among the sines, these numbers: 77858 and 51097. Between these lies the proportion of the orbits of Mars and the Earth. For if the proportion is transposed into other numbers, and it is made so that 51097 is to 100000, then 77858 is to 152373, which is clearly the quantity of the mean distance of Mars, in units where the Earth is 100000 distant from the Sun.

The reason why the proportion of the periods is not double the proportion of the Orbits, but rather sesquialterate, you will find explained in the *Epitome of Astronomy*, Book 4, page 530.

Therefore, let this second and indeed most excellent secret now be added as a supplement to these Cosmographic Mysteries. Having proclaimed this to the public, I now wish to summon everyone—theologians as well as philosophers—with a loud voice to judge the <term>Aristarchian dogma<note>Kepler refers to the heliocentric (sun-centered) theory by the name of Aristarchus of Samos, the ancient Greek who first proposed it, though it was revived in Kepler's time by Copernicus.</note></term>. **Pay attention, you most religious, most profound, and most learned men:**

> If <term>Ptolemy<note>The 2nd-century astronomer whose Earth-centered model dominated for 1,400 years.</note></term> speaks the truth about the motion of the mundane bodies and the arrangement of the Orbits: then there is no constant and identical proportion across all planets of the Motions, or periodic times, to the Orbits.
>
> If <term>Tycho Brahe<note>A Danish astronomer who proposed a hybrid system where the planets orbit the Sun, but the Sun and Moon orbit a stationary Earth.</note></term> speaks the truth—that the Sun is indeed the center of five planets, like five epicycles, but the Earth is the center of the Sun's orbit, so that while the Earth remains still, the Sun goes around it, carrying and twisting the entire planetary system—then there is indeed the same proportion of periodic times to the orbits across all planets; namely, the proportion of the periods (for example, of the Sun and Mars) is sesquialterate to the proportion of their orbits, but the motion is not dispensed from the same center. For the motion of the five planets around the Sun is dispensed by the Sun, but the motion of the Sun around the Earth is dispensed by the Earth; thus the Sun is established as the mover of the planets, but the Earth as the mover of the Sun.
>
> If, finally, <term>Aristarchus</term> speaks the truth—that the Sun is the center of both the five planetary Orbits and also of the sixth, which carries the Earth, so that while the Sun remains still, the Earth is carried among the other planets around the Sun—then the orbits of any two planets have such a proportion to each other that encompasses two-thirds of the proportion of the periods; or, the proportion of the periods is most perfectly sesquialterate to the proportion of the orbits; and the motion of both the Earth and the other five is dispensed from a single source, the Solar body.
>
> Here there is plainly no exception; the proportion is most strongly fortified on both sides. On the side of the senses, the daily observations of astronomers attest to it with all their precision; on the side of reason, Aristarchus supports us in generalities, and in particular, most evident causes are available (positing the immaterial species of the Solar body) as to why the proportion ought to be neither simple nor double, but clearly sesquialterate. Causes are also available as to why the Sun can be the mover of the other planets and the Earth, rather than the Earth being the mover of the Sun. Finally, the natural light of reason dictates that the appearance of the works of God is more worthy and more archetypal...

[of the works] of God, if all motions flow from one source, rather than if many flow from one source, while that source itself flows from another more ignoble source. <note>Kepler is arguing that a universe with one center of power (the Sun) is more divine and simpler than one where motions are divided between the Sun and the Earth.</note>
,,        Add to this the very formation of the proportion of the spheres, established separately before motion, through the five figures and through Harmonies. For if Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used, but whose Earth-centered system Kepler rejected.</note> speaks the truth, these things have no place, unless one admits some circle of the Earth through the imagination, led between the spheres of Mars and Venus: and God would have had care not for the thing itself, but rather for the imagination, distorting the Worldly work itself so that the imagination of the work might be beautiful: whereas infinite other similar imaginary appearances (such as stations and retrogradations) lack such ornament. But if Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BCE), an ancient Greek astronomer who proposed a heliocentric (Sun-centered) universe long before Copernicus.</note> speaks the truth, then that ornament is found in reality; whereas all imaginary appearances, without exception, are permitted by the necessity of the laws of optics.

Having weighed these things, I hope you will be fair judges of these dogmas; nor will you show yourselves as enemies to the most exquisite ornament of the divine Works. Farewell.

### CHAPTER XXI.

-> (I) What is to be inferred from the discrepancy. <-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'S' featuring scrolling floral patterns.</image-desc>
So, therefore, this other argument holds: by which it is proved by the authority of Aristotle that the new hypotheses are preferable, because through them the motions—on a double account, both of the intensity of the power and the speed of the return—become proportional to the Copernican <term>distances<note>original: "ἀποστήμασι" (apostēmasi), a Greek term for distances or intervals between celestial bodies.</note></term>, which could in no way happen in the ancients' tradition concerning the world. And indeed, this alone ought to have been the intention of this treatise on motion. Truly, it is not difficult for me to guess that there will be those who wish I had omitted this last part of the booklet. For (they will say) if you had established the true proportion of the heavens through the bodies: certainly the motions would confirm it. For Truth does not disagree with itself. And yet you yourself see, **KEPLER**, how much the motions and the bodies—that is, the distances constructed on both sides—disagree with each other. Therefore, you expose your naked side to the enemy; indeed, you strike yourself, nor is there any need to be slaughtered by another's sword. <note>Kepler is anticipating critics who will point out that his mathematical model (the five Platonic solids) doesn't perfectly match the observed orbital data.</note>

To respond to these things, first I invert the reasoning, and appeal to the judgment and conscience of those people, indeed of everyone; whether they think the one argument about the bodies, or this one about motion, is more likely. Nor does it seem probable to me that anyone would say otherwise than that this accommodation of motions to the spheres is quite elegant, and a marvelous <term>handiwork<note>original: "χειρόεργημα" (cheiroergēma), a Greek term referring to a work produced by hand or skilled craftsmanship.</note></term> of God the Creator. Hence, if faith must be placed in either argument, they will side with this one over the bodies, as if with a more evident thing; even though the numbers still somewhat disagree with the Copernican ones. If I have obtained this confession from the Reader, I will use it for the confirmation of the bodies, and as an excuse for that discord, as being many times smaller than this dissonance in motion. For if the Reader here, on account of the elegance of the discovery, willingly overlooks a large error, he will far more easily tolerate a small error there. For that diversity regarding the bodies...

# THE COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY. 81

...the Astronomical circle <note>original: "calculum Astronomicum"</note> disturbs nothing at all; but this indeed brings in something a bit greater regarding the motions. And this is the first point; namely, the **region** <note>original: (1) "plaga"</note> set back. Next (2), since the **solids** <note>Platonic solids</note> differ from the motions, as is truly objected against me; I am certainly compelled to confess that one or the other is in error. Nevertheless, I believe it can be demonstrated (3) that it is not necessary to completely abandon either discovery (neither that of the proportion of the motions, nor that of the spheres). Which of the discoveries is at fault is easy to conjecture from the previous points. First, the motorial distances <term>motoriae distantiae; Kepler’s theoretical distances calculated from orbital speeds</term> recede further from the Copernican ones than the figural ones <note>distances based on the geometry of the five solids</note>. Next, if you compare the motorial with the Copernican values, one by one, and note the deficiencies, you will see a certain relationship of the deficiencies with the numbers themselves, and thus with the solids, except in the case of Mercury. Behold:

| | | Copern. | Motorial | Differences | |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| Saturn | Jupiter | 572 | 574 | ± 2 | Cube. |
| Jupiter | Mars | 290 | 274 | — 16 | Tetrahedron. |
| Mars | Earth | 658 | 690 | ± 26 | Dodecahedron. |
| Earth | Venus | 719 | 762 | ± 43 | Icosahedron. |
| Venus | Mercury | 500 | 563 | ± 63 | Octahedron. |
| | or | 559 | | ± 4 | |

Specifically, there is a relationship in four cases, and less so in the fifth. For out of the four, the solids are always similar in pairs, while the fifth is solitary. Next, arrange Mercury—as it is so varied—into order, and consider that something deeper than the average thickness of the sphere should be judged for the average distance (4), namely, as much as the sphere of the Octahedron (which you heard above is greater than the average thickness), and it will obtain 559 for the average distance, not 500. Therefore, the order of its numbers will be: Mercury 559, 563, difference ± 4. Behold: in Saturn-Jupiter and Mercury, the differences are smaller, namely 2 and 4; in Mars-Earth and Earth-Venus they are larger, namely 26 and 43. This is just as the solids placed between them—there the Cube and Octahedron, here the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron—are similar. And note this: where there is a great difference between the inscribed and circumscribed [spheres], there is a small difference in the distances; conversely, where the ascribed [spheres] are almost equal, the motorial distances differ from the Copernican ones by a large interval.

Since, therefore, there is a certain equality in this deficiency, and indeed nothing ordered happens by chance: we must therefore think that these numbers allude to the truth; yet they have not yet fully attained it. (5) Certainly, something can still be polished in the theorem itself; or the theorem is indeed correct, (6) but neither operation <note>method of calculation</note> has attained its sense. Although I could have suspected this right from the start, I did not want the Reader to lack this opportunity, and as it were, a stimulus for trying more things. (7) For what if one day we see that day where both these discoveries are reconciled? (8) What if from here the ratio of eccentricities <term>eccentricitas; the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term> can be elicited? For among other things, the reason why I more stubbornly retain even this theorem about the motions is that the proportion of one motorial distance to another never wanders from the whole Copernican sphere, but always points a finger at something pertaining to the thickness of the spheres. And there is in this, which you might wonder at, also a certain equality. So that you may see it, I explain to you the order of the motorial distances in parts where the average distance of the Earth is 1000, and I set the Copernican distances alongside them:

This equality is such that in the regions far from Earth <note>the outer planets: Saturn and Jupiter</note>, the values come very close to the mean distances. In the nearby regions of Mars and Venus, the motorial distance <term>motoria distantia; the theoretical distance calculated from the Sun's driving force</term> is closer to Earth on both sides than the Copernican mean distance.

You see also that nowhere is a body <note>one of the Platonic solids</note> excluded from its place, nor is the order disturbed; rather, at the very least, a gap opens up between the mean distances that is large enough to receive the solid body. So, if anyone wishes to accept these motorial distances as being perfectly demonstrated (though this is still doubted), he (10) might perhaps remove the *manner* in which the bodies are interposed, but he does not remove the interposition itself. For the motorial values indicate, as it were, (11) that two outer families [of solids] sit similarly between the mean distances, and two inner ones similarly between the mean and the extreme. Specifically: the **Dodecahedron** <note>the 12-faced solid</note> from the lowest point of Mars to the mean of Earth; and the **Icosahedron** <note>the 20-faced solid</note> from the mean of Earth to the highest point of Venus. Let the **Tetrahedron** <note>the 4-faced pyramid</note> truly enjoy its own privileges and sit between both extremes. But let all these things be judged in their proper place; they are certainly built from the uncertain numbers of the motorial theory, and for no other purpose than to stimulate others toward a reconciliation—a path upon which I have led the way.

# CHAPTER XXII.

->Why a planet moves uniformly about the center of an equant.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' at the beginning of the chapter, featuring a floral or scrollwork design within a square frame.</image-desc>

You have just learned, Reader, to recognize even imperfect things; therefore I fear less that you will reject this final and cold catastrophe <note>original: "catastrophen"; used here in the classical sense of a final resolution or conclusion to a story</note>. But I wanted to report it last, both because I hold it in the last place, and because it is connected with motions and cannot be explained without Chapter 20, although it properly belongs to Chapter 14, as you were warned there.

When I had submitted this figurative proportion of the heavens to the judgment of Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler's university professor and mentor</note>: he warned me about the epicycles of the superior planets, which Copernicus introduced in place of equants <term>equant; a mathematical concept used to account for the observed speed changes of planets</term>, and which make the thickness of the sphere twice as large as the planet's ascent and descent requires. And in the inferior planets indeed there are other motions, by which the planet is raised to every height of that epicycle and descends to all its depths, whence in those, instead of the eccentrepicycle <note>a combination of an eccentric circle and an epicycle</note>, an eccentric of an eccentric <note>original: "eccentrus eccentri"</note> was assumed by Copernicus: but in Mercury a certain peculiar diameter, through which it approaches and recedes from the Sun, is likewise sometimes extended much further from the Sun than the star itself ever is. He thought, therefore, that such thickness should be left to the spheres as would be sufficient for demonstrating the motions. To which...

This equality <note>or agreement</note> consists in the fact that for the planets distant from the Earth, there is a very close approach to the mean distances; for the neighboring planets Mars and Venus, the motive distance on both sides is closer to the Earth than the Copernican mean.

You see also that nowhere is a body <note>planet</note> excluded from its place, nor is the order disturbed; rather, at the very least, a gap opens up between the mean distances large enough to receive the [geometric] body. So if anyone wishes to accept these motive distances as perfectly demonstrated (though this is still doubted), he (10) perhaps removes the *manner* of the interposition of the bodies, but he does not remove the interposition itself. For the motive distances indicate, as it were, (11) that two outer [solids] of a similar kind are placed between the mean distances, and two inner similar ones between the mean and the extreme; namely, the **dodecahedron** <term>dodecahedron: a 12-sided solid that Kepler placed between Mars and Earth</term> from the lowest part of Mars to the mean of the Earth, and the **icosahedron** <term>icosahedron: a 20-sided solid placed between Earth and Venus</term> from the mean of the Earth to the greatest of Venus. Indeed, let the **tetrahedron** <term>tetrahedron: a 4-sided pyramid placed between Mars and Jupiter</term> also enjoy its own privileges and lie between both extremes. But let all these things be judged in their proper place, for they are built upon the uncertain numbers of the motive distances, and for no other purpose than to stimulate others toward a reconciliation—toward which path I have led the way.

# CHAPTER XXII.

## Why a planet moves uniformly around the center of its equant.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'D'. Inside the letter's frame are two figures amidst swirling foliage and vines.</image-desc>

You have just learned, Reader, to recognize even imperfect things; for that reason, I am less afraid that you will reject this last and cold conclusion <note>original: *catastrophen*</note>. I wanted to relate this last point, both because I hold it in the last place, and because it is connected with motions and cannot be explained without Chapter 20, although it properly belongs to Chapter 14, as you were warned there.

<margin>See Table IV, Chapter XIV.</margin>
When I had submitted this figurative proportion of the heavens to Maestlin's judgment, he warned me about the epicycles <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic and Copernican systems, a small circle that rolls around the circumference of a larger one to explain planetary retrograde motion.</note> of the superior planets, which Copernicus introduced in place of equants <term>equant</term> <note>A mathematical point used to explain the varying speeds of planets; Kepler eventually replaced these with his law of elliptical orbits.</note>, and which make the thickness of the sphere twice as great as the planet’s ascent and descent require. And in the inferior planets indeed, there are other motions by which the planet is raised to every height of that epicycle and descends to its every depth, which is why for those, instead of an eccentric epicycle <term>eccentrepicyclo</term>, an eccentric of an eccentric was assumed by Copernicus. But in Mercury, there is a certain peculiar diameter through which it approaches and recedes from the Sun; likewise, it is sometimes extended much further from the Sun than the star ever is. He thought, therefore, that such thickness should be left to the spheres as would suffice for demonstrating the motions. To which

<meta>catchword: I replied,</meta>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s retrospective defense and refinement of his model. # JOHANNES KEPLER

I responded, first, that the whole matter would have to be set aside if the spheres were made twice as thick; for too much of the *prosthaphairesis* <term>prosthaphairesis</term> <note>original: προσθαφαιρέσεως. A technical term in ancient astronomy meaning "addition or subtraction." It refers to the "equation of center," the correction required to account for a planet's varying speed as it moves in an elliptical or eccentric orbit.</note> would be taken away. Second, I argued that nothing of the miraculous nobility of this arrangement is lost, provided that the paths of the planets themselves, described by their small spheres, retain this proportion—regardless of whether they are driven by large or small spheres. And I added what you find in Chapter 16 regarding the "matter" of the geometric figures: that there is none. Therefore, it is not absurd to include the physical bodies of the planets in the same place as the spheres. Indeed, this inequality of the path can be defended even without spheres at all. I see that the noble and most excellent mathematician Tycho Brahe, the Dane, is occupied with this same opinion. However, our findings indicate the cause and the method more clearly.

(1) Namely, if the cause of the slowness and speed in the spheres of individual planets is the same as it was for the whole world in Chapter 20, it works like this: the eccentric path of a planet is slow at its highest point <note>Aphelion, the point furthest from the Sun.</note> and fast at its lowest <note>Perihelion, the point closest to the Sun.</note>. To demonstrate this, Copernicus assumed (2) epicycles, and Ptolemy assumed equants <note>The "equant" was an imaginary point used by Ptolemy to explain why planets seemed to speed up or slow down; Kepler eventually replaced these geometric fictions with his Law of Areas.</note>. Let a concentric circle be described that is equal to the eccentric path of the planet; its motion will be equal in every part because it is at an equal distance from the origin of motion. Therefore, in the half of the eccentric path that rises above the concentric circle, the planet will be slower, because it recedes further from the Sun and is moved by a weaker power; in the remaining part, it is faster, because it is closer to the Sun and is in a stronger power. And anyone can easily gather that this variation of motion is demonstrated by a small circle just as if the planet truly moved with a uniform motion in that circle. You have the cause of this slowness; now let us look at the measurement.

-> [IMAGE: A diagram showing nested circles with centers A, B, C, and D. A represents the Sun at the bottom. Various paths are labeled EFGH, NOPQ, and IKLM, illustrating how a planet's speed changes based on its distance from the central "moving soul" at A.] <-

Let **A** be the source of the moving soul <term>moving soul</term> <note>original: *anima motrix*. This was Kepler’s early term for the force emanating from the Sun that pushes the planets; he later moved toward a more physical, magnetic-like force.</note>, namely, the **Sun**. Let **B** be the center of the path **EFGH**, along which the planet travels, but with an unequal pace. Let **BD** be equal to **BA**, and **CB** be half of that. Since **EF** is further from **A** than the standard distance by the amount **AB**, it was appropriate that the planet in **EF** should be as slow as if it had receded twice as far from **A**—that is, by the amount **AD**—and was running around the center **D**. Conversely, since **GH** is closer to **A** than **PQ** by that same amount **AB**, it was appropriate that the planet in **GH** should be as fast as if it had approached twice as close to **A**, namely by that same amount **AD**. In both cases, therefore, it is the same as if it proceeded around center **D**. (3) For above, in Chapter 20, such was the proportion of the motions to the spheres.

Therefore, consider how the two causes that converged there throughout the whole circle are here inverted and mixed together. In that case, the entire larger and more distant circuit of the same sphere increased the period, and the smaller and closer one decreased it. Here, however, the circles **NOPQ** and **EFGH** are equal, but one part of this circle is more distant and the other is closer to the center **A**, the Sun. Because of this, the moving power in **A** acts on **EF** and **GH** as if the planet were at **IK** in the first case and at **LM** in the second. Moreover, the common measure of both that slowness and this speed is found in **D**. Thus, a planet progressing along the path **EFGH**, becoming slow, fast, and medium around **R** and **S**, acts just as if it were moving uniformly around the center **D** on the path **IKLM**. Now see the craftsmen who established essentially the same thing: Ptolemy made **D** the center of the equant and **B** the center of the planetary path. Copernicus, however, lead an "eccentric of an eccentric" or an "eccentric-epicycle" around center **C**, the midpoint between **D** and **B**. The result for him is that the path of the planet is as close as possible to **EFGH**, but the equality of motion is regulated around **D**, just as the motion of the intermediate sphere between **EFGH** and **IKLM** is regulated around **C**.

<sig>L 3</sig>

(4) You have here the reason why the center of the equant <term>equant</term> <note>The "equant" was a mathematical point used by ancient astronomers to explain why planets seem to speed up and slow down. Kepler was trying to find a physical reason—magnetic or solar force—for why this happens.</note> is distant from the center of the eccentric <term>eccentric</term> <note>An "eccentric" is a circular orbit where the Sun is not exactly in the center.</note> by a third part of the total eccentricity. (5) Suppose, then, that the whole world is full of soul, which sweeps along whatever stars or comets it reaches, and does so with that speed required by the distance from the Sun and the strength of the power at that location. Next, suppose there is a specific soul in each planet, by whose steering the star ascends in its own circuit; the same will follow for the distant spheres.

Regarding these matters on the Equant, I know that when some people read them, they will be thrilled. For if astronomers admire Ptolemy for having assumed this same measurement of the center of the Equant without proof, they will now wonder much more that there was a physical cause for this thing—and yet Ptolemy did not suspect it, even though he took the matter exactly as it is; it was as if he reached the proper place while blind, led by a divine nod.

But I would wish them to be warned that nothing is blessed in every part. (6) For in Venus and Mercury, this slowness and speed is adjusted not to the planet’s distance from the Sun, but to the motion of the Earth alone. And if anyone should use the different condition of their motion compared to the superior planets <note>The "superior" planets are Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which orbit further from the Sun than Earth.</note> as a pretext for this: what cause, finally, will he bring for the (7) Earth’s annual motion? For that motion required an Equant neither in Ptolemy’s work nor in Copernicus’s. Therefore, let this uncertain dispute hang under the judgment of the astronomer.

### In Chapter XXII. Notes of the Author.

(1) **Namely, if the cause were the same.** *If any cause brings it about that Saturn, being high, is slower than Jupiter, who is lower and closer to the Sun, let that same cause bring it about that Saturn, when high and at its furthest point <note>Apogee/Aphelion</note>, is slower than itself when at its lowest and closest point. The cause of both things is the rectilinear distance of the planet from the Sun, greater or lesser, because when it is far distant from the Sun, it is moved by a Solar power that is thinner and weaker.*

(2) **Epicycles for Copernicus, equants for Ptolemy.** *I have taught the equivalence of these hypotheses in my "Commentaries on Mars" <note>Usually titled Astronomia Nova (1609)</note>, Part 1.*

(3) **For above in Chapter XX, those of the motions to the Orbs.** *I have indeed corrected this in the annotations. The ratio was not double the periods, thus comparing slowness to the proportion of the orbs, but at least one-and-a-half times <note>Kepler is alluding to his Third Law: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the distance.</note>. But in the motions of a single planet, as seen from the sun at the furthest and nearest points, a precisely double proportion of the distances reigns; in the daily motions themselves, as they are arcs of the eccentrics, it is the exact simple proportion of the distances. See "Commentaries on Mars," parts 3 and 4. The most evident cause of this diversity is found in Book 4 of the "Epitome of Astronomy," page 533.*

(4) **You have the reason why the center of the equant is at the third part.** *This is true of Copernicus, for whom C is the center of the equant (or rather the eccentric-eccentric), B is the center of the planet's path, and B-C is a third part of A-C. But in Ptolemy, the ratio is different. For him, D is the center of the equant, B of the Eccentric, and therefore B-D is half of A-D.*

(5) **Namely, the whole world is full of soul.** *Again, for "soul," understand the immaterial species <term>species</term> <note>Kepler uses "species" to mean an emanation or force, like light or magnetism, that transmits power through space without being material.</note> of the Sun, extended like light: and you will have here in a few words the sum of my celestial physics, handed down in the "Commentaries on Mars," parts 3 and 4, and repeated in Book 4 of the "Epitome of Astronomy."*

(6) **For in Venus and Mercury.** *There is no need for an exception: it is truer than truth even for Venus and Mercury. For the fact that Copernicus ties some of these planets' inequalities to the motion of the annual orb is an error.*

(7) **The Earth’s annual motion did not need an equant.** *In Ptolemy and Copernicus, indeed. But in my "Commentaries on Mars," the most important of my books, I did this one thing and placed it like a cornerstone in the foundation—indeed, I have rightly called it the "key to astronomy": I clearly demonstrated from the motions of Mars itself that the annual motion, whether of the Sun or the Earth, is regulated around a separate center of an equant, and that its eccentricity of the orbit is only half of the eccentricity believed by previous authors.*

You see therefore, studious Reader, that the seeds of each and every thing were scattered in this little book, which since that time...

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### On the Astronomical Beginning and End of the World, and the Platonic Year.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'P' featuring intricate floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

After the banquet, after the weariness that comes from being full, let us turn to the desserts. I propose two noble problems. The first concerns the beginning of motion; the second, its end. (1) Certainly, God did not establish the motions at random, but from a certain specific beginning and a brilliant conjunction of the stars, and at the start of the Zodiac, which the Creator fashioned through the tilt of the Earth, our dwelling—for all things exist for the sake of man. (2) Therefore, if the year of Christ 1595 is related to the year 5572 of the world (which is commonly and by the most approved authors judged to be 5557), the Creation will coincide with a brilliant constellation at the beginning of Aries <term>Aries</term> <note>The first sign of the Zodiac, traditionally associated with the spring equinox and beginnings.</note>. For in the first year of the assumed number, on the 27th day of April, calculated backward on the Julian calendar, on Sunday—which is the day of the Creation of all things—at the eleventh hour of noon in Prussia (which is six in the evening in India), such an appearance of the heavens is shown by the Prutenic calculations <term>Prutenic calculations</term> <note>These were astronomical tables based on the Copernican system, published by Reinhold in 1551.</note>.

| Planet | Degree | Sign |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sun | 3 | Aries |
| Moon | 3 | Libra |
| Saturn | 15 | Aries |
| Jupiter | 10 | Aries |
| Mars | 24 | Gemini |
| Venus | 10 | Taurus |
| Mercury | 3 | Aries |
| Lunar Node | 18 | Virgo |

If you delay or advance the motions of Mars, Venus, and the Lunar Node <term>Lunar Node</term> <note>The points where the Moon's orbit crosses the path of the Sun.</note> by a small amount, they will come into related positions, and perhaps the Node will be in Libra with the Moon. Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous contemporary scholar and chronologist.</note> wrongly insists on a New Moon. For the Moon, established in the power of the night, surely shone on that first night. The calculations do not provide a more likely beginning for many years past or future. (3) But if we follow reason, we ought to seek this beginning with the Sun positioned in Libra <term>Libra</term> <note>The sign associated with the Autumnal equinox.</note>, namely with this appearance of the heavens:

| Planet | Degree | Sign |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Saturn | 0 | Aries |
| Jupiter | 0 | Aries |
| Mars | 0 | Aries |
| Moon | 0 | Libra |
| Lunar Node | 0 | Libra |
| Venus | 0 | Libra |
| Mercury | 0 | Libra |
| Sun | 0 | Libra |

The authority of the ancients wishes this—that the World was created in Autumn—and reason itself, following Copernicus, suggests that the Earth should stand at the same beginning as the others. Therefore, the superior planets <term>superior planets</term> <note>The planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> will appear in Aries, and the inferior planets <term>inferior planets</term> <note>The planets closer to the Sun than Earth: Venus and Mercury.</note> and the Sun in Libra. The Moon, since it is around the Earth, fits in neither Aries nor Libra, lest it disturb the number...

...the triad of superior and inferior planets. And with the sun setting (for thus the world was founded), the night is nowhere more rightly dominated than from the middle of the heavens, which is the Sun <note>original: "☉"</note>. Saturn <note>original: "♄"</note> could thus consist in the highest apsis <term>apsis</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from or nearest to the center of motion.</note> of its epicycle. And because its orbit is adventitious <note>meaning "added from the outside" or external</note>, let it also obtain an adventitious and peculiar position of its beginning. Its nobility and fame among men also comes from its lunations, and the most powerful quadrant of those lunations. Moreover, I refer the Head <note>The North Node of the Moon, where it crosses the ecliptic going north.</note> to Libra and the Tail <note>The South Node, where it crosses the ecliptic going south.</note> to Aries, so that it might be in a rational position with the Moon, yet without an Eclipse; and so that the Moon may be at its maximum northern limit. Therefore, the Earth will be in the middle even by visual position among the stars; just as its orbit obtained a middle place among the orbits by the certain counsel of God; because all things exist for the sake of man. But if you also place the Sun here in Aries <note>original: "♈"</note>: Saturn <note>original: "♄"</note> will be in Libra <note>original: "♎"</note> and the Moon <note>original: "☽"</note> in Cancer <note>original: "♋"</note>, and the rest similarly. (4) Furthermore, the mean motions must be taken, for it is fitting that these be "true" at the beginning of their course, namely from the apsides. This prize <note>original: "palma," referring to a victor's palm branch</note> is placed in the middle; if anyone can achieve this or something similar, either from calculation or from the restoration of Astronomy, he alone "shall have Phyllis" <note>A reference to Virgil’s Eclogues, meaning he will win the ultimate prize or the beloved.</note>. So much for the beginning.

(5) I have established by reason no end to motion, and I shall prove by a single postulate that there will be no Platonic Year <term>Platonic Year</term> <note>The theoretical period in which all planets return to the exact same relative positions they held at the moment of creation.</note>. For let it be granted that the eccentricity is in a rational proportion with the orbit: the radii of the orbits will therefore be irrational to one another, because they relate to each other as bodies inscribed in and circumscribed around the [Platonic] solids. These are irrational because they result from the ratio of the diagonal in a square, and from the division according to the extreme and mean ratio <term>extreme and mean ratio</term> <note>Now known as the Golden Ratio. Kepler argues that because planetary distances are based on these geometric ratios, they cannot be expressed as simple whole numbers.</note>; which are two examples of irrationals in Geometry. Now, since the motions are in proportion with the radii, the motions are therefore irrational to one another; and thus they will never return to the same beginning, even if they were to endure for infinite ages. This is because never, not even in an infinite division of time, would a common measure occur which, being repeated often enough, could constitute a single terminus for all motions and the goal of a Platonic Year. And now, at last, it is pleasing to exclaim with the divine Copernicus: *So great indeed is this divine fabric of the Best and Greatest [God]*; and with Pliny: *The world is sacred, immense, all in all, indeed it is itself the whole, finite and yet resembling the infinite.*

---

### Author’s Notes on Chapter XXIII.

<margin>(1)</margin> Certainly God did not establish the motions at random.] *Yet we cannot immediately conclude that all the planets were conjoined under the same degree of the Zodiac; it is enough if at least in general there was some Harmonic arrangement, and a division of the Zodiac by the planets, if not from the center of the Earth, then at least from the center of the Sun. See the Harmonies, book 4, chapters 2 and 3.*

<margin>(2)</margin> *Therefore, if the year 1595 is related.*] *Astronomy does not tolerate, even assuming the uniformity of periods, that this constellation be perfected and reduced to a purely Harmonic arrangement.*

<margin>(3)</margin> *But if we follow reason, it is necessary.*] *Neither is this necessary; nor is the authority of the ancients regarding Creation to be rigidly urged: for the harvest of crops (not the memory of creation) could have provided the reason why autumn was considered the end of the year.*

<margin>(4)</margin> *Mean motions must be taken.*] *What if not even this is the case? What if the planets were not created in their apsides, as if at the extremes where there is no equation <term>equation</term> <note>In historical astronomy, the "equation" is the difference between the mean position and the true position.</note>, but in the middle interval, where the equation is greatest? Therefore, this exercise remains proposed to all astronomical calculators, and it is indeed full of pious persuasion concerning the origin of time. Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler's teacher.</note> attempted some things. Accept also another from me, where all things from the center of the Sun are in opposite and squared places, and indeed at the Cardinal points.*

*In the year 3993 before our common era, according to the Julian calendar extended backward, on the evening of July 24, beginning the second day of the week in Chaldea, the Sun and Moon were at the beginning of Cancer near the Heart of the Lion <note>The star Regulus.</note>; all motions of the Moon were in quadrants, as were all the rest: Saturn and Mercury were toward the beginning of Libra,*

# JOHANNES KEPLER’S COSMOGRAPHIC MYSTERY.

<columns>
Jupiter and the Earth are towards Capricorn; the Moon, Mars, and Venus are towards Cancer. In Mercury, a few degrees are in excess, but these can be accounted for by its maximum "ablative equation" <note>In historical astronomy, an "equation" is a mathematical correction applied to a planet's mean (average) position to find its true position.</note>, provided its mean motion is well enough known so that they are not lost through a correction of it. In Venus there is also something in excess that cannot be removed by an equation. The Second Day <note>of Creation in Genesis</note> belongs to the Firmament, or the expansion between the waters and the waters; it is as if the Orbs or Planets, commanded to travel through this expansion, began to move immediately at the very birth of the expansion. But on the Fourth Day, the outermost heaven was finally adorned with the fixed stars, the Sun, the Moon, and so on, as the final hand was applied to the work.

(5) I have established no "end" to motion <note>i.e., no final state where the planets stop or restart</note> through reason. That dogma <note>the idea of a perfect "Platonic Year" where all planets return to a starting point</note> rested on this as its primary foundation: that among the celestial Orbs there exists a proportion, specifically the one belonging to the five Geometric figures <note>the five Platonic solids</note>. For the proportions of four of those figures are "ineffable" or, as I have called them here following the common term, "irrational." But now we have refuted this foundation, because the proportion of the celestial orbs is not derived from the five figures alone. 

One asks: what then should be held regarding this dogma, and is there any perfect *Apocatastasis* <term>Apocatastasis</term> <note>A Greek term for a "restoration" or "great return," referring to a hypothetical moment when all celestial bodies return to their original starting alignment.</note> of all motions? I say that although this foundation has been undermined, no such *Apocatastasis* is given. I prove it thus: It is certain that if the proportions of the periodic times are "effable" <note>rational numbers that can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers</note>, then "consonant" and "dissonant" <note>original Greek: συνητὰ and ἀσύνθετα</note> alignments are possible; if they are ineffable, they are not. Now, whether they are effable or ineffable must be judged in this way: All proportions of the motions at the Apogees and Perigees <note>the points furthest from and closest to the Earth/Sun</note> are effable, for they are taken from the Harmonies <note>Kepler’s theory that planetary speeds correspond to musical intervals</note>, and those are all effable, as are all the "concinnous" <note>musically pleasing</note> intervals and the smaller intervals that serve them. 

Thus, in Book V of my *Harmonics* <note>*Harmonice Mundi* (The Harmony of the World), published in 1619</note>, chapter IX, proposition XLVIII: All these motions are expressed and spoken in their own numbers, for those precise numbers are to be understood. Now, the proportion of periodic times among themselves is of the same quantity as that of the mean motions. However, the mean motions participate in a middle choice between the extremes (the aphelion and perihelion); this middle point between these effable terms is itself effable. They also participate in the Geometric mean between them. But between two effable terms, there is not always an effable Geometric mean. Therefore, the mean motions of the planets are ineffable and incommensurable with the extreme motions of all the planets. (See *Harmon. lib. V. Cap. IX. Prop. XLVIII*). Since there is no *a priori* reason that forms the mean motions, but rather they each result from their own extreme motions, the mean motions will not be commensurable even with one another; for nothing ordered, such as "effability," is likely to exist by chance. Therefore, the periods of time will not be commensurable with each other either. Thus, no perfect *Apocatastasis* of motions is given which could be held as a formal or rational goal for the motions.

You have here, Reader, the examination of my little book titled *The Cosmographic Mystery*, which I promised ten years ago in Part III of my *Commentaries on Mars* <note>Kepler’s *Astronomia Nova* (1609)</note>. Truly, there was no place for this examination before the publication of the *Harmonics*. Therefore, having brought this commentary to a close, let us turn to the hymn which ends the book.

---

->CONCLUSION OF THE BOOK.<-

Now you, friend Reader, do not forget the end of all these things, which is: the knowledge, admiration, and veneration of the Most Wise Creator <note>original: "Opificis," the Divine Craftsman</note>. For it is nothing to have proceeded from the eyes to the mind, from sight to contemplation, and from the visible course of the stars to the deepest counsel of the Creator, if you wish to rest here and not, with a single impulse and the total devotion of your soul, be carried upward into the knowledge, love, and worship of the Creator. Therefore, with a chaste mind and a grateful heart, sing with me the following Hymn to the architect of this most perfect work.

JEHOVAH, Sower of the World, and our eternal power,
How great is your fame through all the circle of the earth?
How great is your glory? Which, spread above the walls
Of heaven, flies admirable on shaken wings.
The child acknowledges you; the infant, sated by the rejected breast,
Builds strong arguments from stammering lips at your dictation:
Arguments by which the prideful enemy is confounded,
The scorner of you, and the scorner of law and equity.
But I—so that I may believe in the Divinity in this spacious world—
Will look up astonished at the massive works of the vast heaven:
The work of the Great Artist, the mighty miracles of his right hand,
How you have distinguished the five starry orbs by rules,
Within which, in the middle, the Minister of Light and soul <note>the Sun</note>
Governs the reins of the eternal course by law;
What changes the Moon takes, what labors she suffers,
How you have scattered so many stars in the immense field.

<column-break/>

Greatest Maker of the world, by what reason did 
The small, helpless, humble inhabitant of so tiny a clod of earth,
The son of Adam, compel you to take up the cares of his affairs?
You look upon the undeserving, you carry him to the heights;
His race is nearly that of the Gods, you bestow such great honors,
And you circle his magnificent head with a diadem;
You establish him as King over the monuments of your hands.
What is above his head—the great orbs and their motions—
You subject to his intellect: and whatever is created on Earth,
The cattle born for work, and those fit for smoking altars,
The generations of other wild beasts that inhabit the forests,
And that race of birds who beat the air with light wings,
And whatever fish swim the tracts of the sea and the rivers;
All these you command him to suppress with his empire and powerful right hand.

JEHOVAH, Sower of the World, and our eternal power,
How great is your fame through all the circle of the earth?

# JOHANNES KEPLER’S MYSTERY OF THE COSMOS

Jupiter and Earth are toward Capricorn; the Moon, Mars, and Venus are toward Cancer. In Mercury, there is an excess of several degrees, but these can be accounted for by its maximum subtractive equation <note>In astronomy, an "equation" is a correction applied to an average (mean) motion to find the actual position of a planet.</note>, provided its mean motion is sufficiently known so that they are not merely consumed through a correction of it. In Venus, there is also some excess that cannot be removed by the equation. The second day <note>original: "Feria secunda." Kepler is mapping the days of the biblical Creation to astronomical events.</note> belongs to the Firmament, or the expansion between the waters and the waters; it is as if the Orbs or Planets, commanded to travel through this expansion, began to move immediately at their very origin; but on the fourth day, the outermost heaven was finally adorned with the fixed stars, and the Sun, and the Moon, etc., as the final hand was laid upon the work.

(5) **That no end to the motion was established by reason.** ] This dogma relied on this as its primary foundation: that there is a proportion between the celestial Orbs, specifically that of the Orbs of the five geometric figures <note>The "five figures" are the Platonic solids (cube, tetrahedron, etc.), which Kepler famously proposed were the spacers between the planetary spheres.</note>. For the proportions of four of those are "ineffable," or as I have called them here in the common manner, irrational. Now, we have indeed refuted this foundation: because the proportion of the celestial orbs is not derived from the five figures alone. It is asked, then, what must now be held regarding this dogma, and whether any perfect <term>Apocatastasis</term> <note>Apocatastasis: The hypothetical moment when all planets return to the exact same relative positions they held at the beginning of time.</note> of all motions is granted? I say that although this foundation has been overturned, no *Apocatastasis* is granted nonetheless. I will prove it. It is certain that if at least the proportions of the periodic times are "effable" <note>Kepler uses "effable" (expressible) to mean numbers that can be written as simple ratios of whole numbers (rational numbers).</note>, an *apocatastasis* is granted; if they are "ineffable" (irrational), it is not. Now, whether they are given as effable or ineffable must be judged as follows: All mutual proportions of the Apogees and Perigees <note>The furthest and closest points of an orbit.</note>, both of pairs and of individuals, are effable; for they are drawn from the Harmonies, and those are all effable, as are all the Concinnous <note>Musically pleasing or well-proportioned.</note> intervals and those serving them. Thus, in Book V of the *Harmonics*, chapter IX, proposition XLVIII: All these motions are expressed and spoken in their own numbers: for those numbers are to be understood as precise. Yet now, the proportion of the periodic times to one another is of the same quantity as that of the mean motions. Indeed, the mean motions participate in the arithmetic mean between the extremes, the aphelion and perihelion; which mean, being between these effable terms, is itself effable: they also participate in the geometric mean between the same. But between effable terms, the geometric mean is not always effable. Therefore, the mean motions of the planets are ineffable and incommensurable with the extreme motions of all the planets. See *Harmonics*, Book V, Chapter IX, Proposition XLVIII. Since, moreover, there is no *a priori* reason that forms the mean motions, but rather they spring back individually from their own extreme motions: the mean motions will not be commensurable even among themselves; for nothing ordered, such as "effability," is accustomed to exist by chance. Therefore, the periods of time will not be commensurable with one another. Thus, no perfect *Apocatastasis* of motions is given which could be held as a formal or rational "end" to the motions.

You have therefore, Reader, the examination of my little book, titled *The Secret of the Universe*, promised ten years ago in the third part of the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>Referring to his 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova* (The New Astronomy).</note>. Truly, before the edition of the *Harmonics* <note>*Harmonice Mundi* (The Harmony of the World), published in 1619.</note>, there was no place for this examination. Therefore, having placed an end to the commentary, let us turn to the hymn which closes the book.

# MASTER MICHAEL MAESTLIN
## OF GÖPPINGEN, TO THE
### Kind Reader, Greetings.

Plato rightly called Geometry and Arithmetic the "Wings of Astronomy." Geometry—dealing with the celestial body, which is a measurable, spherical entity moving regularly in circular motion—uses observations taken at different times to not only find the paths of the stars but also to explain the reasons for their apparent irregularities based on regular motions, revealing their certain measurements and demonstrating the sizes and heights of those sublime bodies. Arithmetic, meanwhile, by casting the parts of this measurable body into numbers, measures those sizes and heights and constructs tables. From these tables, the positions of all the stars and the entire face of the heavens can be shown for any given time. However, although these matters are admirable and difficult, our distinguished mathematician, **MASTER JOHANNES KEPLER**, teaches us to soar to far higher things by the rowing of these wings. Truly, the things that skilled astronomers have found up to this point are great; yet, until now, all have approached Astronomy only "from behind," <note>original: "à tergo." Maestlin means they looked at effects (observations) rather than starting from the underlying causes.</note> and have taught how to investigate the motions, sizes, and distances from observations alone. Whether any entrance to measuring these things "from the front," <note>original: "à fronte," or *a priori*—reasoning from causes/principles rather than just effects.</note> or whether any other geometric rule besides observation could be held for examining the numbers found for motions and quantities, has not entered the mind of even the most skilled artist until now, even in a dream.

But now, our Kepler, by a most skillful discovery from Geometry, provides a certain and finite number and order of the celestial orbits or spheres, and—what is greatest of all—a certain proportion of their sizes and motions to one another. Taking his starting point from a slightly higher level, he shows that God, the Creator, the Best and Greatest, in the creation of the world, fashioned, extended, arranged, adorned, and ordered the mobile celestial spheres according to the proportion of the five regular geometric solids—otherwise well known to all geometers. <note>The "five regular geometric solids" (or Platonic solids) are the only three-dimensional shapes where every face is an identical regular polygon: the Cube, Tetrahedron, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron, and Octahedron.</note> And he confirms this opinion not with logical, light, doubtful, or old wives' tales—much less with foreign conjectures violently forced to fit his purpose—but with genuine, most appropriate reasoning drawn both from the Nature of things and from Geometry, which cannot be contradicted. The most powerful of these is the most elegant and sweet harmony and the resonant agreement of the Astronomical calculations (already produced from observations) with the distances of the five regular solids. For the astronomical calculations clearly indicate—as far as has been provided or could be provided by those whom no one focused on observation ignores are still lacking quite a few things—that the spaces between the planetary spheres are exactly as large as the intervals between the spheres that are circumscribed around and inscribed within the Cube (or Hexahedron), the Pyramid (or Tetrahedron), the Dodecahedron, the Icosahedron, and the Octahedron, respectively. <note>Kepler’s famous theory was that the distances between the six known planets could be explained by nesting the five Platonic solids inside each other.</note> Therefore, from this time forward, whoever wishes to inquire more fully into the motions of the heavens, and to repair and restore what is still lacking in Astronomy, now has an open door from the cause <term>a priori</term> through which to enter; he has a most upright rule by which, as if by a touchstone, <note>original: "Lydium lapidem," a stone used to test the purity of gold.</note> he may examine all his observations and his entire calculation. Rightly, therefore, I congratulate our century on this most ingenious discovery of the excellent mathematician Kepler, doubting not that through it we shall see all Astronomy restored in the very near future.

But if anyone is offended—as quite a few have been until now—by the "absurdity" of Copernicus’s hypotheses, which have been illegitimately condemned by many and defamed beyond reason; and because Kepler

<meta>catchword: Keplerus</meta>

# PREFACE.

->M 2<-

With this discovery of his, along with Copernicus, Kepler asserts the immobility of the Fixed Stars at the edge and of the Sun at the center of the World, and the circular mobility of the Earth outside the center. I ask that one first learn and examine the matter before passing judgment with a premature prejudice; let him read what *Copernicus writes in Book 1, Chapter 5 and the five following chapters*, likewise what our *Kepler writes in Chapter 1 of his Forerunner* <note>original: "Prodromi," referring to the *Mysterium Cosmographicum*</note>. Also read what *Rheticus* has in the following Narrative, where he lists the principal reasons why one should depart from the hypotheses of the ancient astronomers. And he will see: the question of the location and the perpetual rest of the Earth is by no means settled. To which I add this.

In the usual hypotheses—which hold sway more by tradition than by reason (it is therefore better and more advisable that they be proposed to the common people and that beginners be first trained in them, as they are widely known and for that reason easier to learn; likewise, it is usually expedient to retain them in other discussions unless one must enter the inner shrines of astronomy)—the Earth is placed motionless in the middle. This is based on the powerful argument taken from the properties of "gravity" and "levity" <note>The Aristotelian idea that "heavy" things naturally fall to the center and "light" things rise</note>, because heavy things are said to be carried downward toward the Center of the World, and light things upward from that same Center. But I ask, from where do we get this experience of light and heavy things? And how far does our knowledge of them extend, so that from them we can certainly conclude the Center of the entire World? Is not the Earth, and the Air around the earth, the entire seat and dwelling of all those things which are heavy or light to us? But what is the Earth, and what is the Air surrounding it, compared to the immense vastness of the whole World? They are a point, or tiny specks, or if anything smaller could be said, they have that proportion. Since this is so, do you not think a Philosopher would say that an argument built from a small part, or this tiny speck, to the whole World is weak? Therefore, we cannot be certain about the center of this most spacious world from those things that seek this tiny speck or flee from it. These heavy and light things of ours do indeed seek their own proper place, which according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> is the "perfection" of a thing, assigned to them by Nature. As *Copernicus in Book 1, Chapter 9* learnedly discusses, it is credible that this affection <note>the natural tendency to cohere</note> also exists in the Sun, Moon, and the other spheres of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, so that by its power they remain in that roundness in which they present themselves. If that place happens to be the center of the world anywhere, it happens only by accident. But Copernicus's astronomical reasons do not proceed from a part—and a very minute one at that—to the whole; but on the contrary, from the whole to the parts.

But from the very process of the usual hypotheses and those of Copernicus, it is easily recognized which deserves more trust. For Copernicus's hypotheses number, arrange, connect, and measure the order and magnitude of all the Orbs and Spheres in such a way that nothing in them can be changed or transposed without the confusion of the entire Universe; indeed, all doubt about their position and sequence remains excluded. On the contrary, in the usual hypotheses, the number of spheres is uncertain. For some count nine, others ten, others eleven spheres, and the number is not yet agreed upon. The order there is also doubtful: no definite distance, except for the Sun and Moon, can be given, let alone demonstrated. The dispute over Venus, Mercury, and the Sun has not yet been settled, nor will it ever be. *Regiomontanus, in Book 9, Chapter 1 of the Epitome of Ptolemy's Almagest*, confesses that which of them—Venus or Mercury—is situated above the other cannot be grasped with any certainty. And although *Proclus in Hypotheses of Astronomy* asserts that Mercury was seen passing under Venus, another much more serious question arises regarding the inexcusable "penetration" of the planetary spheres <note>The physical overlapping or crossing of the solid celestial spheres assumed in the old model</note>, which the proportion of their epicycles and eccentricities absolutely requires, as supported by calculation and observations. Neither *Albategnius in Chapter 5* nor *Alfraganus in Discussion 21*, nor other great mathematicians, however much they struggle, are able to defend this. For the invincible demonstrations of the Physicists do not admit such penetrations; however, the certainty of Geometry (which is the rule of truth in every <term>QUANTITY</term> <note>original: "QVANTO"</note>) contradicts the squeezing together of the spheres. To these I add that just as the distances of the spheres are doubtful, so too is no order certain. For except for the Sun and the Moon, in the rest it is the same—to use a <term>most paradoxical</term> <note>original: "παραδοξοτάτῳ" (paradoxotato)</note> example—whether you place Saturn above Mercury, or the latter above the former.

What shall I say of the most rapid and inestimable velocity of this so vast mass of the World, turning itself daily? Where first: the ineffable velocity surp— <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page; the catchword "perat" completes the word "superat," meaning "surpasses" or "exceeds."</note>

<meta>catchword: surpasses</meta>

<summary>Maestlin argues that the Copernican system is superior to the Ptolemaic model because it is mathematically unified, whereas the old system suffers from uncertain sphere counts and the physical impossibility of overlapping planetary paths. He also critiques the geocentric argument based on "gravity," noting that Earth's behavior is too small a sample to define the center of the entire universe.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Michael Maestlin's preface, moving from the philosophical justification for the Earth's motion to the mathematical and physical absurdities required by the old geocentric (Earth-centered) model.</meta>

# PREFACE.

Albategnius <note>al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> estimates the radius of the sphere of the fixed stars to be 19,000 Earth radii in Chapter 50 of his work. Alfraganus <note>al-Farghani, a 9th-century Persian astronomer</note> counts the same as 20,110 Earth radii in his 21st Distinction. Nor should anyone think that either Albategnius or Alfraganus estimated this distance from the Firmament to the Earth as being larger than is right; for a more accurate examination of the dimensions of the eccentrics and epicycles <term>eccentrics and epicycles|Geometrical circles used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex, non-circular movements of planets</term> through the spheres of all the planets demands a much greater gap from the Earth to the fixed stars. Erasmus Reinhold <note>A 16th-century German astronomer and mathematician</note>, following this examination (before he knew anything of Copernicus), is observed to have extended it to 25,000 Earth radii. Indeed, in the second part of his *Theories*, concerning the first type of "Passions," he attributes 2,298 Earth radii to the radius of the epicycle of Saturn. But in the units where the radius of Saturn's eccentric is 60 parts, Ptolemy demonstrates in Book 11, Chapters 5 and 6 of the *Almagest* <note>The definitive astronomical textbook of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> that its eccentricity is 3 parts and 25 minutes, and the radius of the epicycle is 6 parts and 30 minutes. Therefore, the maximum height of Saturn from the Earth is 96 parts and 55 minutes. If, therefore, the radius of the epicycle contains 2,298 Earth radii, it follows—by the rule of proportions—that Saturn, at its furthest distance from the Earth, is 24,718 Earth radii away. From this, no fewer than 25,000 Earth radii are granted to the sphere of the fixed stars, which is certainly higher than the highest point of Saturn. From this arises that speed of the star-bearing sphere, by which any star located in the middle of the circles between the poles of the World (that is, on the Equator) is snatched along more than fifteen hundred German miles <note>A German mile at this time was roughly 4.6 modern miles or 7.5 kilometers</note> in a single scruple <note>original: "scrupulo," a small unit of time equivalent to 1/3600th of an hour</note>, or the 3,600th part of an hour—a tiny space of time in which someone could hardly speak three or four words, even with a rushing tongue.

And to make this calculation even clearer: let us assume not this very great height of the Firmament, but at least that which is 20,110 Earth radii according to Alfraganus. Therefore, its total diameter has 40,220 Earth radii, which make up 34,589,200 German miles (counting 860 German miles for each radius, of which 15 make up one degree on the Earth). Then, according to the proportion of the diameter to the circle—which is 7 to 22 according to the demonstrations of Archimedes—the entire circumference of a great circle in the Firmament is calculated at 108,708,914 German miles. When these are divided by the 24 hours of the daily revolution, it follows that any star of the Firmament positioned on the Equator covers 4,529,538 miles every hour in its running; that is, more than forty-five hundred thousand German miles. In one minute of an hour, it covers 75,492 miles; that is, more than seventy-five thousand. And in one second <note>original: "scrup. secundo"</note>, it covers 1,258 miles; that is, more than twelve hundred German miles. Alternatively: since (as Cardanus <note>Gerolamo Cardano, a 16th-century polymath</note> says in Book 5 of *On Proportions*, propositions 58 and 218, to which the testimony of often-repeated and confirmed experience also agrees) four thousand beats of the arterial pulse in a person of temperate nature complete nearly one hour; therefore, if those 4,529,538 miles are divided by 4,000, it will be established that every star or point on the Equator of the Firmament must traverse a path of 1,132 miles—that is, more than eleven hundred German miles—in the time of a single pulse beat. (How small a pulse beat is, and how little it differs from the blink of an eye, is an observation everyone has at hand, or rather in their hand and their whole body). Furthermore, it is necessary for a much more rapid course to exist in the "highest heaven" or First Mobile <term>First Mobile|Primum Mobile; in the old system, the outermost sphere that moved all others</term>, a sphere far higher. But such an immense velocity for a natural body (for the heaven is a natural body, and therefore subject to the laws of Nature by the Creator) truly exceeds all belief.

Next, what is this "impotence of nature," that it could pour such an incomprehensible velocity into an immense celestial body, yet could not communicate any of this motion to a tiny point of the World—namely, the earthly body? How can it be that the entire system of the World is driven around—with no sphere of it excepted, not even the sphere of the element of fire (if there is one), nor the upper region of the air—and yet this one tiny point is not turned? Therefore, it is much more probable and more in agreement with reason that, this immense world having been freed from this daily rapidity, only this little globe [the Earth] moves with that motion. For it was easier for Nature to give this motion to the Earth, by which in one scruple (or the sixtieth part of an hour) a quarter of one degree passes in its great circle—that is, in 4 seconds of an hour, a quarter of one German mile passes. The flight of clouds often equals this speed, not infrequently exceeds it, and the fall of a lightning bolt incomprehensibly surpasses it. I pass over countless other points, of which not a few are recited by Copernicus, and by Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus, the only pupil of Copernicus</note> in his *Narrative*, and by our Kepler in his *Forerunner* <note>original: "Prodromo," referring to the *Mysterium Cosmographicum*</note>.

<summary>Maestlin uses mathematical calculations to show the physical absurdity of a stationary Earth, arguing that the stars would have to move at impossible speeds (over 1,100 miles per heartbeat) to circle the Earth daily. He concludes it is much more rational to believe the small Earth rotates on its axis than that the entire massive universe revolves around it.</summary>

<keywords>celestial speed, Earth's rotation, German miles, Albategnius, Alfraganus, Erasmus Reinhold, Saturn, Ptolemy, Archimedes, Cardano, geocentrism vs heliocentrism</keywords>

-># PREFACE.<-

->M 3<-

Some of the most excellent recent mathematicians have attempted to apply a certain remedy to these weaknesses of astronomy. Indeed, like the ancient theories, they place the Earth as the immobile center of the lunar and stellar spheres—and even the whole universe—but, following Copernicus, they declare that the Sun is the center of the other planets, though it remains mobile in both its annual and daily revolutions. <note>Maestlin is likely referring to the system proposed by Tycho Brahe, where the Sun orbits the Earth while the other planets orbit the Sun.</note> Certainly, those who establish this are great men and should not be deprived of their praise. However, with this correction of theories, they do nothing but **patch an old and worn-out cloak with new cloth**, the tear of which is usually made worse afterward. <note>original: "vetustam & attritam togulam nouo panno refarciunt" — an allusion to the Gospel of Matthew 9:16.</note> For by this position, the centers of motion and the driving forces are surely dissolved and pulled apart. The rest of the motions and spheres (or whatever it is that functions as spheres) are entangled in many more intricate difficulties; nothing is associated with anything else through reason or any proportion of size, motion, and order.

To these men, I oppose this single discovery of our Kepler. In this work, as proof of the opinion of the more recent Copernicus and the very ancient mathematician Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BCE) was the first known person to propose a heliocentric model of the solar system.</note>—to say nothing of others—the most elegant order of the parts of the World is most ingeniously demonstrated, as is the most beautiful and undeniable proportion of magnitudes and motions, in harmony with the **five regular solids**. <note>The Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron. Kepler’s "Mysterium Cosmographicum" argued that the distances between the six known planets were determined by these five shapes nested within each other.</note> These things can never be found or even hoped for in the ancient theories, nor in the "corrections" by recent authors. To whom, therefore, shall we think it safer to trust? To those who, wishing to avoid some apparent absurdities, plunge themselves into more serious ones, which they nevertheless prop up with wobbling supports and say nothing with reason? Or rather to him who asserts nothing without reason, confirms everything solidly, and solidly refutes what indeed seems absurd? **Plato is my friend, Socrates is my friend, but Truth is a greater friend.** <note>original: "Amicus ergo Plato, amicus Socrates, magis tamé amica Veritas."</note>

I have thought it necessary, kind Reader, to subjoin these things to Kepler’s learned *Precursor* <note>The "Prodromus," or "Forerunner," refers to Kepler’s "Mysterium Cosmographicum."</note>, which contains an exposition of the most hidden mysteries of Nature, discovered or noticed by no one until now. I am supported by an undoubting hope, as I said before, that on the occasion of this mystery (I have long since despaired of the other ancient and recent theories), we shall shortly have an astronomy so polished and so brilliant—if indeed any more polished or perfect cleansing and form of it can be hoped for and expected.

Because Master Kepler often refers in this *Precursor* to the *Narrative* of Georg Joachim Rheticus <note>Rheticus (1514–1574) was Copernicus’s only pupil and the first to publish an account of the heliocentric system.</note>, which he had written to Schöner <note>Johannes Schöner, a German polymath</note> in the year 1539 while living with Copernicus (before Copernicus had published his books on the *Revolutions*), and because that *Narrative* is not in everyone's hands, I judged it entirely necessary to add it to this *Precursor* of Master Kepler, together with the *Praise of Prussia* written by the same Rheticus—even if it was done without Kepler's knowledge and, because he was absent, without his consultation. I did this all the more because I saw that a great part of the *Precursor*, where the style has cut things short for the sake of brevity, would receive a great deal of light from these two writings. Furthermore, Rheticus here explains many of the more obscure passages in Copernicus's own books as a professional; hence, this *Narrative* and *Praise* can be considered a short commentary on Copernicus.

These are the reasons for adding this *Narrative* with Rheticus’s *Praise of Prussia*. However, so that our own effort might not be lacking in achieving these goals more easily, it seemed best to revise both the *Narrative* and the *Praise* with as much diligence as possible. I have added marginal notes and even the diagrams for the demonstrations which Rheticus had undoubtedly included, but which had been omitted in the printed copies by some thoughtlessness. If, however, there are things in these same writings that are somewhat foreign to our purpose, which we found in the edition published at Basel in the year 1541, we felt they should be faithfully rendered with the Title and Preface, even if they did not serve our main goal.

It was to be wished, however, that the second *Narrative*, which this author promises several times, had also been sent out; or if perhaps it was indeed written but lies hidden somewhere (I have not seen it published, nor have I understood from anyone that it has been seen), it would be better for it to be granted for public use than to be left to be gnawed away by moths in hiding. The same was to be wished regarding the commentaries of Erasmus Reinhold on those same books of Copernicus, had not the untimely death of that man cut short the work he had begun, as well as many other most useful labors for the **mathematical republic**. <note>original: "Reipub. mathematicæ" — the international community of mathematicians and astronomers.</note> You, best Reader, enjoy these things until our Kepler sends out his entire *Uranic* or *Cosmic* work, of which we have the *Precursor* here. Farewell.

Done at Tübingen, in our study, on the Calends of October <note>October 1st</note>, in the Year of Salvation 1596.
