<header>DEDICATORY [LETTER].</header>

<image-desc>A horizontal decorative woodcut band featuring symmetrical floral and arabesque patterns.</image-desc>

# TO THE MOST LEARNED MAN,

->MR. GEORG VOGELIN<-
->OF CONSTANCE, PHILOSOPHER AND<-
->Physician, a friend like a brother, Achilles<-
->P. Gassar of Lindau sends his<-
->greetings.<-

<image-desc>A square decorative woodcut initial letter 'E', showing a man in robes within a landscape featuring a tree and distant hills.</image-desc>

Behold, I send to you, most excellent sir, like the "Heraclitean stone" <note>original: "ὥσπερ φησὶν ἡ Ἡρακλεῖτις λίθος" — This refers to the magnet or lodestone, which Heraclitus and others noted for its power to attract; Gassar suggests this book is equally magnetic or compelling.</note> as the saying goes, this little book. It is not only new and unknown to our people, but also, unless I am entirely mistaken, marvelous to you and in every respect most paradoxical <note>original: "παραδοξώτατον" — meaning "contrary to received opinion."</note> even to the point of causing stupor. <term>Georg Joachim Rheticus</term> <note>A young mathematician who traveled to Poland to study under Copernicus and published the first account of his theories.</note>, Master of Liberal Arts and former Professor of Mathematics at Wittenberg, a citizen and my greatest friend, gave this to me from Danzig in recent days, together with a letter most full of these matters. Although this book may not correspond to the methods of teaching used until now, and might be considered contrary to the familiar theories of the Schools in more than one theme—and even "heretical" (as the Monks would say)—it nevertheless seems to offer a restoration, or rather the rebirth <note>original: "τὴν παλιγγενεσίαν"</note>, of a new and most true **Astronomy**. This is especially so since it boasts of most evident conclusions concerning those propositions about which you know there has long been controversy throughout the whole world—and not without much "sweat," as they say—among not only the most learned Mathematicians, but the greatest Philosophers. These concern the number of the **celestial spheres**, the **distance of the stars**, the **governance of the Sun**, the positions and circles of the **planets**, the fixed length of the year, the marked points of the **Equinoxes** and **Solstices**, and finally the place and motion of the **Earth** itself, along with other most difficult matters. 

Since this man brings forward the reasoning and decisions of all these things while faithfully demonstrating them with various proofs (apodixes) he has recently discovered, I do not see why that argument should be exploded, torn apart, or despised by the learned of our age. For it is well known, even among those only moderately imbued with mathematics and even the <term>ephemeris-makers</term> <note>original: "ephemeridistas" — people who calculated and published tables of daily celestial positions.</note> themselves, that astronomical affairs (which are believed to be the most certain of sciences because of the infallible rectitude of the compass and calculation) "limp" today in more than one area—both in the measurement of time and in the observation of motions. It is also clear that what **Geometry** specifically professes does not always square perfectly. 

Therefore, dearest Georg, since we feel ourselves being freed from many difficulties in the heavens, and moreover feel that most abstruse knots are being untied for us, I ask that you read this sent booklet diligently. Once read, judge it more sharply; and once judged, come, commend it uniquely to all cultivators of mathematics, especially your neighbors. Propose it to be studied frequently, so that in this way not only may a "Second Account" <note>original: "Altera Narratio"</note> be sent out more maturely, but this rare and nearly Divine work in its entirety (the arrival <note>original: "ἐποχὴν" — here meaning the definitive publication or fixed era.</note> of which these "Accounts" indicate like messengers) might be made better known, loved, and demanded with more frequent prayers from the Author himself. He is undoubtedly a man of incomparable learning and of Herculean, or rather Atlantean, labor. Through the instigation, effort, and diligent spur of my most esteemed friend's present writings, may the whole work be communicated to us at last. 

I especially wish for this through this dedication: that through you, who are most skilled in physical matters, an opportunity may be provided to followers of this most honorable discipline like yourself. Thus, with worthy gratitude, the means of growing may be given to the younger, and the handle for unearthing the truth against the examination of common eyes may be given to the elder, as liberally as it is abundantly. For you clearly perceive what that profession requires, and what magnificent things this summary promises. Therefore, apply your mind with integrity, as is your custom, so that you may proceed to receive and welcome this booklet. We must not later suffer with grief or complain more sadly that we have been deprived and utterly defrauded of the whole and most splendid banquet—of which we here take a most sumptuous taste—as if a most sweet morsel had been snatched from hungry jaws. Farewell, my friend, and in loving me, laugh at the judgment of the common crowd in this business; for there is no doubt that this novelty will one day be both pleasing and useful to all the learned, without any bitterness. 

At Feldkirch in Rhaetia, in the year 1540 from the birth of Christ our Savior.

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN,
## MR. JOHANN SCHÖNER, AS

->To his respected patron, G. Joachim Rhet-<-
->icus sends greetings.<- <note>original: "S. D." for "Salutem Dicit" — a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends health/greetings."</note>

<margin>
Of Nicolaus
Copernicus.
</margin>

On the day before the Ides of May <note>May 14, 1539</note>, I sent you a letter from Poznań, in which I informed you of my undertaken journey to Prussia. I promised that I would notify you as soon as possible whether the outcome responded to the fame [of the man] and my own expectations. However, although I have only been able to devote barely ten weeks to thoroughly learning the astronomical work of the learned Doctor to whom I have come—partly due to somewhat poor health, and partly because I was most honorably invited by the most reverend Lord <term>Tidemann Giese</term> <note>Bishop of Kulm and a close friend of Copernicus who encouraged the publication of his work.</note>, Bishop of Kulm, and set out with my Teacher for <term>Löbau</term> <note>Lubawa; the Bishop's residence.</note>, resting from my studies for several weeks—nevertheless, so that I might finally fulfill my promises and satisfy your wishes, I shall show, with what brevity and clarity I can, what my Teacher thinks about these matters I have learned.

<margin>
Regiomontanus
was extinguished
by poison in
Rome. In the
year 1476,
July 8, having
scarcely com-
pleted the
40th year of
his age.
</margin>

But first, most learned Mr. Schöner, I would wish you to be certain that this Man, whose work I now utilize, is in every kind of learning and in mastery of astronomy not inferior to <term>Regiomontanus</term> <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), the most influential astronomer of the 15th century.</note>. I prefer, however, to compare him with Ptolemy, not because I estimate Regiomontanus to be lesser than Ptolemy, but because my Teacher has this good fortune in common with Ptolemy: that, with the help of Divine mercy, he has completed the established restoration of astronomy, whereas Regiomontanus (alas, cruel Fates) departed from this life before he could set up his pillars <note>A metaphor for completing a monumental work.</note>.

<margin>
The Books
of the Re-
volutions of
Nicolaus
Copernicus.
</margin>

The learned Doctor, my Teacher, has written six Books, in which, in imitation of Ptolemy, he has embraced the whole of Astronomy by teaching and demonstrating individual points with mathematical and geometric method.

The First Book contains a general description of the world and the foundations by which he is to preserve the observations and appearances of all ages. To these he subjoins as much of the doctrine of sines and of plane and spherical triangles as he judged necessary for his work.

The Second is on the doctrine of the first motion <note>The apparent daily rotation of the heavens.</note>, and those things which he thought should be said in this place concerning the fixed stars.

The Third is on the motion of the Sun. And, because experience has taught him that the length of the year, numbered from the equinoxes, depends also upon the motion of the fixed stars, in the first part of this Book he shows, by true reason and indeed by divine skill, how to investigate the motions of the fixed stars and the changes of the solstitial and equinoctial points.

The Fourth Book is on the motion of the Moon and on Eclipses.

The Fifth is on the Motions of the remaining planets.

The Sixth is on Latitudes.

I have thoroughly learned the first three Books; I have conceived a general idea of the Fourth; and of the rest, I have already grasped the hypotheses in my mind. As far as the first two are concerned, I thought nothing need be written to you; and that partly for a peculiar... <note>The sentence is interrupted by the page break.</note>

<meta>This page continues Rheticus’s letter to Johann Schöner. Having introduced Copernicus as a "new Regiomontanus," Rheticus now begins to describe the technical specifics of Copernicus’s work, focusing on the movement of the fixed stars and the history of astronomical observations.</meta>

# ACCOUNT

...my own particular plan, partly because the doctrine of the first motion departs in no way from common and accepted reasoning, except that he has reconstructed from the ground up the tables of declinations, right ascensions, differences of ascensions, and the others pertaining to this part of the doctrine, so that they can be adapted to the observations of all ages through <term>proportional parts</term> <note>A mathematical method used to interpolate values between table entries, allowing for greater precision across different eras.</note>. Therefore, what he teaches in the Third Book, along with the hypotheses of all the remaining motions—so far as I can currently grasp them according to the thinness of my talent—I shall recite clearly to you, God willing.

When my Lord Doctor [Copernicus], at Bologna, was not so much a pupil as an assistant and witness to the observations of the most learned Man <term>Domenico Maria</term> <note>Domenico Maria Novara (1454–1504), an astronomer at the University of Bologna with whom Copernicus studied.</note>; and at Rome, around the year of our Lord 1500—being about twenty-seven years old, more or less—was a Professor of mathematics before a great crowd of students and a circle of great men and masters in this kind of learning; and then here in <term>Warmia</term> <note>A region in northern Poland (Ermland) where Copernicus served as a church canon.</note>, being at leisure for his own studies, had noted down observations with the greatest care, he chose from the observations of the fixed stars that which he had made concerning **Spica Virginis** in the year of our Lord 1525.

<insert>
*They report that Nicolaus Copernicus was born in the year 1473, on the 19th of February, at 4:48 p.m., on a Friday before the Chair of Peter. Francesco Giuntini therefore errs, writing that he was born on January 29, 1472. He died, however, in the year 1543, on the 19th of January <note>Historical records typically cite Copernicus's death as May 24, 1543; this insertion reflects a different tradition or error.</note>, at the age of 70, in which same year he had published those books of his Revolutions.*
</insert>

<margin>
On the motion of the fixed stars.
</margin>
He established that it [the star Spica] was distant from the autumnal point by nearly 17 degrees and 21 minutes, since he found its southern declination to be no less than 8 degrees and 40 minutes. Then, comparing all the observations of the Authors with his own, he found that the revolution of the **Anomaly** <note>In early astronomy, the "anomaly" referred to the irregularity or variation in the speed of a celestial body's movement.</note> or circle of diversity was complete, and that we in our age are in the second revolution since the time of <term>Timocharis</term> <note>An 3rd-century BCE Greek astronomer whose observations were crucial for identifying the precession of the equinoxes.</note>. Therefore, he geometrically established the mean motion of the fixed stars and the equations of the diverse motion.

<margin>
Ptolemy, Book 7, Chapter 3 of the Almagest.
</margin>
For because Timocharis’s observation of Spica, in the 36th year of the first period of Calippus, compared with the observation of the 48th year of the same period, teaches us that the stars in that age moved one degree in 72 years; and then from <term>Hipparchus</term> to <term>Menelaus</term> they always completed one degree in a hundred years, he established for himself that Timocharis’s observations fell in the last quadrant of the circle of diversity, in which the motion appeared average but diminished; whereas in the intermediate time between Hipparchus and Menelaus, the motion of diversity was in the slowest position.

<margin>
Albategnius, Chapter 51.
</margin>
Since indeed the observations of Menelaus compared with Ptolemy's show that the stars then moved through one degree in 86 years; therefore Ptolemy’s observations were made with the motion of the anomaly existing in the first quadrant, and the stars then moved with a slow motion added or increased. Furthermore, because from Ptolemy to <term>Albategnius</term> <note>The Latinized name of al-Battani (c. 858–929), a prominent Muslim astronomer whose data was vital to European astronomy.</note> 66 years correspond to one degree, and our observations compared with those of Albategnius show the stars completing one degree again in 70 years with the diverse motion—but compared to his other observations held in Italy—

<margin>
From the year 1515 to the year 1525.
</margin>
—the observation I mentioned above, when compared, shows the fixed stars again progressing through one degree in 100 years. It is also clearer than the sun that from the time of Ptolemy to Albategnius, the motion of diversity passed the first average limit, and the entire quadrant of the added average motion, and was in the place of greatest velocity around the times of Albategnius. But from Albategnius to us, the third quadrant of the diverse motion has been completed, and in the meantime the stars have progressed with a fast but diminished motion [toward] the other limit...

# THE FIRST ACCOUNT

...passed the limit of the mean motion, and in our age, it has again reached the fourth quadrant of the diminished <term>anomaly</term> <note>In astronomy, an 'anomaly' refers to the angular distance of a planet or point from its starting position in its orbit or cycle.</note> of the mean motion; therefore, the variable motion is once again seeking its slowest limit.

<margin>Copernicus, Book 3, Chapter 6.</margin>
However, so that my Teacher [Copernicus] might reduce these matters to a certain rule and show how they agree with all observations in order, he determined that the variable motion is completed in 1717 <term>Egyptian years</term> <note>A year consisting of exactly 365 days, favored by astronomers for its consistency compared to calendar years with leap days.</note>, and that the maximum <term>equation</term> <note>A mathematical correction applied to a mean or average motion to find the "true" position.</note> is approximately 70 minutes. 

<margin>Copernicus, Book 3, Chapter 6.</margin>
The mean motion of the stars, he found, is about 50 seconds in an Egyptian year, and a complete revolution of the mean motion would take 25,816 Egyptian years.

<margin>General consideration of the year from the equinox.</margin>
<margin>Ptolemy, Book 3, Chapter 2; Al-Battani, Chapters 27, 28; Copernicus, Book 3, Chapter 13.</margin>
This account of the motions of the fixed stars is also confirmed by the annual measurements observed from the <term>equinoctial points</term> <note>The points in the sky where the celestial equator intersects the ecliptic; these define the start of Spring and Autumn.</note>. It is established as a certainty why, from the time of **Hipparchus** to **Ptolemy**, a whole day (minus a twentieth part) was lost; then from Ptolemy to **Al-Battani**, nearly 7 days; and from Al-Battani to his own observations, which he conducted in the year of our Lord 1515, nearly 5 days. These discrepancies did not happen by some flaw in the instruments, as has been believed until now, but occur by a certain and internally consistent logic. Therefore, the uniformity of motion is by no means to be measured from the equinoxes, but from the fixed stars, as the observations of all ages—concerning the motions of the Sun, Moon, and the other planets—testify with a marvelous consensus. Because from **Timocharis** to Ptolemy the stars proceeded with a very slow motion, only a three-hundredth part of a day was lost beyond the quarter-day over 365 days; but from Ptolemy to Al-Battani, because the stars moved quickly, it is accepted that the year fell short of the quarter-day by a one-hundred-and-sixth part of a day. In our age, if observations are compared to those of Al-Battani, it is clear that the year is short of the quarter-day by a one-hundred-and-twenty-eighth part of a day.

<margin>The Tropical Year becomes longer if the Fixed Stars move more slowly; but shorter if they move more quickly.</margin>
Therefore, a greater length of the year (measured from the equinoxes) seems to correspond to a slow motion, and a smaller length to a fast one. An increase in the length of the year corresponds to a decreasing velocity, so much so that if the length of the year from the equinoxes is accurately examined in our age, it almost agrees with Ptolemy again. Consequently, it must be established that the equinoctial points move "backward" <note>This refers to the 'precession of the equinoxes,' where the equinox points move westward along the ecliptic over time.</note>, just as the <term>nodes</term> <note>The two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the Earth's orbital plane.</note> do in the case of the Moon, and that the stars do not move forward according to the sequence of the signs of the Zodiac at all. It was necessary to imagine, then, that there is a "mean equinox" that proceeds from the first star of the **Aries** constellation at a steady rate, leaving the fixed stars behind; and that on either side of this mean equinox, the true equinox itself moves by a regular but varying motion. The radius of this displacement does not much exceed 70 minutes. In this way, a certain logic for the length of the year from the equinoxes has existed for every age and can still be detected today; furthermore, this reasoning corresponds most exactly—nearly to the minute—to the observations of the fixed stars made by all skilled practitioners.

But so that I may provide you with some taste of this matter, most learned **Schöner**, look: I have computed for you the true precessions of the equinoxes for the times of certain observations.

Ptolemy’s <term>precession</term> <note>The slow movement of the stars relative to the equinoxes over time.</note>, when subtracted from the positions of the stars as recorded by Ptolemy, leaves the distance they stand from the first star of Aries. Then, the precession calculated by <term>Al-Battani</term> <note>original: "Albategnij"; a 9th-century Arab astronomer whose precise observations were vital to Copernicus.</note> is added to show the true location at the time of observation. This process is done similarly for all others. These calculations correspond exactly to the observations of all master astronomers, especially where individual minutes are noted, or where they are derived from recorded <term>declinations</term> <note>The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note>, or from the motion of the Moon reduced to greater precision, as our own observations compared with those of the ancients teach us. For, as you see, even if some minutes are neglected, they record at least a half, a third, or a quarter of a degree. However, these figures do not satisfy the motions of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in a planet's orbit where it is nearest to or farthest from the Sun.</note> of the planets; therefore, it was necessary to assign a specific motion to them, as will be clear from the Theory of the Sun.

<margin>
The sidereal year.
Chapter 27.
</margin>
Furthermore, since my Teacher [Copernicus] realized that the uniformity of motion must be taken from the fixed stars, he investigated the <term>sidereal year</term> <note>The time it takes for the Earth to orbit the Sun once relative to the fixed stars, rather than the seasons.</note> with the greatest care. He found it to be approximately 365 days, 15 minutes, and 24 seconds, and that it has remained constant from the time observations began. For although Al-Battani reports that the Babylonians reckoned three seconds more, and <term>Thabit</term> <note>original: "Thebit"; Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century astronomer known for his theory of "trepidation."</note> one second less, this can be attributed—without insulting their instruments and observations, which as you know can by no means be <note>original: "ἀνεξετάστῳ" (unexamined/without scrutiny).</note> beyond scrutiny—either to the variation in the Sun's motion, or even to the fact that the most ancient observers, lacking a certain calculation of eclipses, neglected the variations in the Sun’s appearance in their observations. However, this error across all the time from the Babylonians to us is not to be compared with the error of 22 seconds of a day between Ptolemy and Al-Battani. Moreover, that it was necessary for a day minus one-twentieth part to fall between Hipparchus and Ptolemy, and for nearly seven days to be missing between Ptolemy and Al-Battani, I have gathered for you with the greatest pleasure, most learned Master Schöner, from the aforementioned system of stellar motions and from my Teacher’s own treatise *On the Motion of the Sun*, as you will see shortly.

<margin>
On the change of the obliquity of the ecliptic.
Ptolemy, Book 1, Chapter 11 of the Almagest.
</margin>
My Teacher, the Doctor, discovered that the change in the maximum declination follows this pattern: while the cycle of the variation of the fixed stars is completed once, half of the change in the <term>obliquity</term> <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbital plane.</note> occurs. Therefore, he established that a full revolution of the change in obliquity takes place in 3,434 <term>Egyptian years</term>. It is well known that in the times of Timocharis, Aristarchus, and Ptolemy, the change in obliquity was in its slowest variation, so much so that they believed the maximum declination to be unchangeable, always <unclear>23 11/15</unclear> <note>This fraction equals 23 degrees and 44 minutes, the standard ancient value for the Earth's tilt.</note> parts of a circle.

Therefore, the pole of the equator (or the ecliptic) was near the middle of this Libration motion around the time of Al-Battani, but in this century it is near the other extreme where the motion is slowest—the point where one pole makes its closest approach to the other. 

But as we posited above, the motions of the fixed stars and the variation in the length of the year are saved by the motion of the equinoctial, and the vertices of the Earth are the poles of this motion, from which the elevations of the poles are measured. Thus, the proportional minutes were 58 in the time of Ptolemy, 24 in the time of Al-Battani, 15 in the time of Arzachel, and 1 in our own age. By making these proportional to the 24 minutes of difference, it is clear that a certain rule for the change in obliquity has been discovered.

...nor would he presume to defend the idea that a tongue performs all its actions through the same muscle and motive power. Therefore, my <term>Teacher</term> <note>original: "D. Præceptor"; referring to Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> assigned two motions to the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center; in the Copernican system, this relates to the Earth’s distance from the Sun.</note> of the Sun: a mean motion and a varying one, by which it moves under the sphere of the fixed stars. To these is added the fact that while the true <term>equinox</term> <note>The time when day and night are of equal length.</note> moves backward through the signs of the zodiac with a uniform but varying motion, the apogees of the Sun and the other planets—just like the fixed stars—are pushed forward. Therefore, so that the observations of all ages might correspond to one another in a consistent law, he was forced to distinguish these three motions from one another.

<margin>
*See below in the appendix for the Diagram of the Theory of the Sun.*
</margin>

To understand these things, you must assume the maximum <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> to be 417 parts and the minimum to be 321. The difference is 96 parts, which is the diameter of a small circle. The center of the eccentric orbit moves along the circumference of this small circle from east to west. Therefore, from the center of the world to the center of this small circle, there are 369 parts. All these parts, as just stated, are measured on a scale where the radius of the eccentric orbit is 10,000 parts. You now have the mechanism which he investigated from the three eccentricities mentioned above, in exactly the same way that his uniform motions are corrected from three lunar eclipses—truly a divine invention.

<margin>
*The motion of the center of the eccentric in the small circle.*
</margin>

Furthermore, he established that the center of the eccentric completes its revolution at the same speed with which the entire cycle of the change in <term>obliquity</term> <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis, which causes the seasons.</note> returns. This matter is worthy of the highest admiration, because it is completed with such great and wonderful harmony.

About 60 years before the birth of the Lord, the eccentricity was at its maximum, and at that same time, the Sun’s <term>declination</term> <note>The angle of the Sun above or below the celestial equator.</note> was also at its maximum. For the same reason, and in no other way, as the one decreased, the other also decreased. As I frequently experience in the varying fortunes of my own affairs, this and other such "jests of Nature" bring me relief and most sweetly soothe a troubled mind.

<margin>
*The Monarchies of the World change according to the motion of the center of the eccentric.*
</margin>

We see that all <term>Monarchies</term> <note>Referring to the "Four Kingdoms" of Daniel’s prophecy (Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome) which were believed to rule the world in succession.</note> began when the center of the eccentric was in some significant position on this small circle. Thus, when the Sun’s eccentricity was at its maximum, the Roman Empire declined toward a monarchy; and as that eccentricity decreased, the Empire also failed as if growing old, and finally vanished. When the center reached the quadrant—the middle point—the <term>Law of Muhammad</term> <note>original: "Lex Mahometica"; referring to the rise of the Islamic Caliphates.</note> was brought forth, and so another great Empire began and grew very rapidly according to the logic of the motion. Now, in 100 years, when the eccentricity will be at its minimum, this Empire too will complete its period; it is currently at its highest peak, from which, God willing, it will fall with a heavy crash just as quickly. When the center of the eccentric reaches the other middle point, we hope for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. For it was at this position around the creation of the world. Nor does this calculation differ much from the saying of <term>Elijah</term> <note>A Jewish tradition (The House of Elias) which predicted the world would last 6,000 years.</note>, who, by divine instinct, prophesied that the world would last only 6,000 years, during which time almost two revolutions are completed.

In this way, the greatest changes of the entire history of the world are seen as if inscribed upon this circle. Furthermore, what kind of Empires those must have been—whether established by fair laws or tyrannical ones—and how they grew from great...

Furthermore, as the center of the eccentric orbit descends toward the center of the universe, it is consistent that the center of the small circle proceeds in the order of the signs, advancing by approximately 25 seconds in each <term>Egyptian year</term> <note>A year of exactly 365 days, used by ancient astronomers for consistent calculations.</note>. Because the center of the eccentric moves from its highest distance in a backward direction, the <term>equation</term> <note>original: "æquatio"; a correction factor applied to a mean motion to find the true position.</note> corresponding to the motion of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its apogee.</note> for the time proposed is subtracted from the mean motion until a semicircle is completed; in the remaining part, however, it is added, so that the true motion of the apogee may be obtained. The maximum correction between the true and mean apogee, geometrically derived from the preceding facts as is appropriate, is 7 degrees and 24 minutes. The rest are established according to the ratio of the center of the eccentric in this small circle, as is customary. We have a certain "diverse motion" based on three given locations; however, there is some doubt regarding the "mean motion" because we do not have the true position of the Sun’s apogee under the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note> for those three locations. This is due to the error that occurred between <term>Albategnius</term> <note>The Arab astronomer al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD).</note> and <term>Arzachel</term> <note>The Arab astronomer al-Zarqali (1028–1087 AD).</note>, as our countryman <term>Regiomontanus</term> <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a central figure in European astronomy.</note> reports in Book 3, Proposition 13 of his *Epitome*.

<margin>An error is believed to have been committed among the observations of the solar apogee made by Albategnius and Arzachel.</margin>
Albategnius uses the mysteries of astronomy too freely, as can be seen in many places. If he also did this in establishing the position of the Sun’s apogee—even if we grant that he had the correct time of the <term>equinox</term>—it is still impossible to precisely establish the times of the <term>solstices</term> with instruments, as Ptolemy himself testifies. Indeed, a single minute of <term>declination</term> <note>The celestial equivalent of latitude.</note>, which certainly escapes the senses easily, can cheat us by nearly four degrees in this position—and to these four degrees correspond four days. How then could he establish the position of the Sun’s apogee? If he proceeded through the intermediate locations of the ecliptic, as Regiomontanus discusses in Proposition 14 of that same third book, he used an argument that was hardly more certain. Therefore, let him blame himself for his error, for he chose eclipses that did not occur near the apogee, but rather near the mean longitudes of the Sun’s eccentric; in those positions, even if the Sun’s apogee were placed six degrees away from its true location, it could induce no notable error in the eclipses.

<margin>In the year 1515, the Sun’s apogee was found at 6 degrees 40 minutes of Cancer.</margin>
<margin>Motion of the Sun’s mean apogee.</margin>
<margin>The true motion of the same.</margin>
<margin>The <term>Alfonsine</term> calculation <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables, the standard astronomical tables of the late Middle Ages.</note></margin>
Arzachel, according to Regiomontanus, boasted of having 402 observations and of having established the location of the apogee from them. We grant that through such diligence he might have found the true <term>eccentricity</term>, but since it is not clear that he consulted lunar eclipses near the <term>absides</term> <note>The two points—apogee and perigee—where a body is farthest from or closest to its center of motion.</note> of the Sun, his supporters have no more evidence for his establishment of the highest apsis than they do for Albategnius. Here you see with how much labor my <term>Teacher</term> <note>Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> had to strive to establish the mean motion of the apogee. For nearly forty years, in Italy and here in <term>Varmia</term> <note>The region in northern Poland (Warmia/Ermland) where Copernicus lived and observed the stars.</note>, he observed eclipses and the motion of the Sun. He chose this specific observation, by which he established that in the year of our Lord 1515, the Sun’s apogee occupied 6 degrees and two-thirds <note>i.e., 6 degrees and 40 minutes.</note> of Cancer. Then, examining all the eclipses in Ptolemy and comparing them to his own—which he observed most diligently—he established that the annual mean motion of the apogee is approximately 25 seconds relative to the fixed stars, and approximately 1 minute 15 seconds relative to the mean equinox. By this reasoning, using both the mean and diverse motion and applying the true <term>precession</term> of the equinoxes, it is gathered that the true location of the apogee from the true equinox was: in the time of <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>Ancient Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BC).</note> at 63 degrees; in the time of <term>Ptolemy</term> at 64 and a half degrees; in the time of Albategnius at 76 and a half degrees; in the time of Arzachel at 82; and in our own age, everything agrees with experience. These progressions match better than those of the Alfonsine Tables, according to which the Sun's apogee [is placed] at 13 [degrees]...

<meta>This page continues Rheticus’s explanation of the Sun’s motion, comparing the observations of his teacher, Nicolaus Copernicus, with those of ancient and medieval astronomers. It argues for the superiority of Copernicus's "perpetual" tables over the temporary ones of the past.</meta>

-># FIRST ACCOUNT<-

<margin>
He errs too much in placing the Sun's <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Sun's apparent orbit where it is farthest from the Earth.</note>.
</margin>
It is established that the apogee was at 2 and a half degrees [of Gemini] in Ptolemy's time; in our own, it is at the beginning of Cancer. According to the opinion of <term>Arzachel</term> <note>original: "Arzahelis"; an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer.</note>, we come two degrees closer to the mark. The calculation of the apogee's location by <term>al-Battani</term> <note>original: "Albategnij"; a 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> exceeds theirs by 1 degree, while we, not without cause, fall short of his by 6 degrees. For my Master, the Doctor [Copernicus], can by no means depart from Ptolemy and his own observations—partly because he has seen and detected these things with his own eyes, and partly because he recognizes that Ptolemy examined the movements of the Sun and Moon with extreme diligence through eclipses, and established them as accurately as possible. However, the fact that we are forced to differ from him by nearly one degree is because the motion of the apogee, which Ptolemy himself thought was fixed, has taught us otherwise; for this reason, my Master has also applied care in examining the lesser motions in this place.

<margin>
Table of the Sun’s motion.
</margin>
You have here my Master’s opinion regarding the motion of the Sun. He has therefore composed tables by which, for any given time, he may gather the true position of the Sun’s apogee, the true <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The amount by which the Earth's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, the true <term>equations</term> <note>Correction factors used to find the true position from the mean position.</note>, and the equal motions of the Sun relative to the fixed stars and the mean equinoxes. From these, he collects the true position of the Sun corresponding to the observations of all ages. From this it is manifest that the tables of Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Theon, al-Battani, <margin>The tables of others are temporary; Copernicus’s tables are perpetual.</margin> Arzachel, and the <term>Alfonsine Tables</term> <note>The standard astronomical tables of the late Middle Ages.</note> (partially compiled from these) are only temporary and can last at most 200 years, until a notable difference in the length of the year, eccentricity, or equation occurs. This same thing happens by a certain similar reason in the motions and appearances of the remaining planets. Not without merit, therefore, could my Master’s astronomy be called "perpetual," as the observations of all ages testify, and the observations of posterity will undoubtedly confirm. Furthermore, he calculates his motions and positions from a fixed point at the first star of Aries, since there is a consistency of motions relative to the fixed stars. Then, by adding the true <term>precession</term> <note>The slow, wobbling shift of the Earth's axis that changes the position of the equinoxes over time.</note>, <margin>The starting point of Copernicus’s calculation is fixed; namely, from the fixed stars.</margin> he collects and establishes how far the true positions of the planets were from the true equinox in individual ages.

<margin>
Pico della Mirandola.
</margin>
If such a doctrine of celestial matters had existed shortly before our time, <term>Pico</term> <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), who wrote a famous critique of astrology and highlighted the inaccuracies of current astronomy.</note> would have had no occasion in his eighth and ninth books to attack not only astrology, but even astronomy itself. For we see daily how notably the common calculations deviate from the truth.

<margin>
Special consideration of the length of the year from the equinoxes. It is strange that many still do this today.
</margin>
In the correction of the Calendar, most people list the various lengths of the year established by different authors, but they do so confusedly; they determine nothing, which is certainly strange for such great mathematicians.

<margin>
Four causes of the unequal motion of the Sun and the revolving year.
</margin>
You see, however, most learned Master <term>Schöner</term> <note>The Nuremberg mathematician to whom Rheticus is writing this letter.</note>, four causes from the aforesaid for the unequal motion of the Sun relative to the equinoxes: the inequality of the precession of the equinoxes; the inequality of the Sun's motion in the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The Sun's apparent path across the sky.</note>; the decrease in eccentricity; and finally, the progression of the apogee for a twofold reason. For these same reasons, the year measured from the equinoxes can by no means be of equal length. Ptolemy can indeed be easily forgiven for positing that equality should be taken from the equinoxes, since he established that the fixed stars move equally in the order of the signs and that the position of the apogee was fixed, nor could he detect that the Sun’s eccentricity was decreasing. But how others wish to excuse themselves, I do not see. For even if we were to grant them that the stars and the Sun’s apogee are carried by the same motion in the order of the signs, and that therefore nothing changes in reality regarding the time from the true equinox, but rather because of a failure of the [instruments]...

<meta>This page continues Rheticus’s discussion of solar motion, specifically addressing the variations in the length of the tropical year and reconciling the observations of the ancient astronomers Hipparchus and Ptolemy through the Copernican model.</meta>

-># FIRST ACCOUNT<-

...it would be most absurd in our own age to say that every variation <note>original: "defectum omne... diuersitatem"</note> occurs for this reason, since the progression of the Sun’s <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Sun's orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> changes the length of the year very little. Nevertheless, it does not follow that the Sun regularly returns to the true equinox in an always equal period of time—just as we say the Moon is regularly moved away from the <term>mean apogee</term> of its <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain retrograde motion.</note> and returns to it in an equal time, as the most learned Marcus Beneventanus reports according to the opinion of the <term>Alphonsine Tables</term> <note>A set of astronomical tables used in the Middle Ages, named after King Alfonso X of Castile.</note>. For since we certainly cannot deny that the Sun’s <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The degree to which the Sun's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> changes, they themselves must see how they can affirm that the length of the year observed from the equinox does not change, given the change in the angle of variation <note>original: "anguli diuersitatis"; also known as the prosthaphaeresis or the correction applied to mean motion.</note> relative to the mean motion. I truly congratulate the state and all students whom the labor of my Teacher, the Doctor [Copernicus], will benefit, because we now possess a certain calculation for the variation of the year.

<margin>Reconciliation of the annual variation between Hipparchus and Ptolemy.</margin>
But so that you may more easily perceive all these things in your mind, most learned Master Schöner, behold, I set the same thing before your eyes in numbers, so that I may finally respond to those things I promised above. Let the Sun be at the point of the mean vernal equinox at the time of the observation of the autumnal equinox made by Hipparchus, in the year 147 before the birth of the Lord; at that time, it preceded the first star of Aries by 3 degrees and 29 minutes. Let the Sun proceed from that same point of the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> so that in a <term>sidereal year</term> <note>The time it takes the Sun to return to the same position relative to the stars; roughly 365.256 days.</note>—namely, 365 days, 15 minutes, and approximately 24 seconds <note>These are sexagesimal fractions of a day: 15 minutes = 1/4 of a day or 6 hours.</note>—it returns to that same point. <margin>Magnitude of the sidereal year.</margin> Because the mean equinox moves to meet the Sun by nearly 50 seconds during a sidereal year, it happens that the Sun reaches the mean vernal point sooner than it reaches the place from which it departed—where, namely, the Sun and the mean equinox were joined at the same point of the ecliptic. <margin>Magnitude of the equal tropical year.</margin> Therefore, the year measured from the mean equinox is shorter than the sidereal year; from our hypotheses, it is calculated to be approximately 365 days, 14 minutes, and 34 seconds. But if we inquire how many days and parts of a day, with respect to the mean equinox, accumulate in the 285 years between Hipparchus and Ptolemy, we find it to be approximately 69 days and 9 minutes. Thus, 2 days and 6 minutes would be lacking if we assumed an increase of a quarter of a day for each individual year. Let us therefore consider the remaining causes until we find only one day, minus a twentieth part of a day, to be missing. At the time of Hipparchus's observation, the true equinox preceded the mean equinox according to the order of the signs by approximately 21 minutes of the starry ecliptic, at which point the Sun then was; but in Ptolemy's time, the true equinox followed the mean by approximately 47 minutes. Therefore, when the Sun in Ptolemy's time had reached the 21st minute before the point of the mean equinox—where it had left the true equinox in Hipparchus's time—it was not yet the true equinox, nor was it when it reached the mean equinox; but after it surpassed that by forty-seven minutes, it fell "into the center of the earth," as Pliny says, namely, into the place of the true equinox. <margin>Book 2, chapter 19.</margin> Therefore, the Sun had to ascend 1 degree and 8 minutes, an arc which it completed in 1 day and 8 minutes of true motion. I keep this to one side and consider how much the angle of variation decreased in this place, and I find that approximately one minute of a day corresponds to it. It is clear, therefore, counting the days from the mean equinox, that a time of 1 day and 9 minutes is added; wherefore Ptolemy rightly reported that between his observation and that of Hipparchus, from true equinox to true equinox, there were 285 years, 70 days, and 18 minutes: and accordingly 57 [sixtieths] of a day...

<meta>This page continues Rheticus’s detailed mathematical reconciliation of historical astronomical observations. -># THE ACCOUNT<-

...minutes of the day are lacking, which is also clear from the subtraction of 1 day and 9 minutes from the 2 days and 6 minutes previously required in respect to the <term>mean equinox</term> <note>The theoretical position of the equinox if the Earth's precession were perfectly uniform.</note>.

<margin>Annual variation between Ptolemy and Al-Battani.</margin>
But let us speak of the discrepancy of 7 days between Ptolemy and Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategnium"; Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD) was a significant Arab astronomer whose observations corrected many of Ptolemy's errors.</note>, which is particularly notable because it covers a larger interval of time—namely 743 years—making all the underlying causes more visible. In Ptolemy's time, the mean equinox preceded the first star of Aries by approximately 7 degrees and 28 minutes in the <term>order of the signs</term> <note>original: "in signorum antecedentiam"; referring to the backward motion of precession.</note>. However, as the mean equinox moved steadily to meet the Sun (as has been stated), it happened that in the years between Ptolemy and Al-Battani, an excess of roughly 180 days and 14 minutes accumulated through additions relative to the mean equinox. Therefore, 5 days and 31 minutes will be lacking if we compare the time to the mean equinox with the result produced when one day is collected every four years <note>The standard leap year calculation.</note>. Furthermore, in Ptolemy’s time, the Sun had left the <term>true equinox</term> <note>The actual observed position of the equinox, which varies due to "libration" or oscillation.</note> at 47 minutes after the mean equinox in the order of the signs; but in the age of Al-Battani, the true equinox was 22 minutes before the mean equinox. Therefore, the Sun reached the true equinox earlier than the mean, or earlier than where it had left the true equinox, which is the opposite of the previous example. 

Thus, as much time as corresponds to 1 degree and 9 minutes will be deducted from the days relative to the mean equinox; this is added to the remainder, namely 5 days and 31 minutes. Because we must proceed in the same way with the difference in the <term>angle of variation</term> <note>original: "anguli diuersitatis"; the correction for the Sun's non-uniform motion.</note> due to the decrease in <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much the Earth's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> (to which 30 minutes of a day correspond), one day and 30 minutes will be deducted from the average time due to the change in the angle of variation and the unequal motion of precession, with the other two causes of the Sun’s unequal motion being mixed in. The true addition from the time of Ptolemy to the time of Al-Battani’s observation will emerge as 178 days and 44 minutes. But this same decrease, when joined to the 5 days and 31 minutes, shows that 7 days and 1 minute have fallen away—which is what was to be shown.

### DIAGRAM OF THE ANOMALY OF THE PRECESSION 
Of the Equinoxes, and the unequal magnitude of the Tropical year.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram titled "SCHEMA ANOMALIÆ PRÆCESSIONIS". DE is the diameter of the circle of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The variation or irregularity in motion.</note> of the equinoxes, through which the true equinoctial moves back and forth in a <term>libration</term> <note>An oscillating motion, like a swinging pendulum.</note>. F is the location of the true equinox, or the intersection of the true equinoctial and the ecliptic, in the time of Hipparchus; G, however, is the location in the time of Ptolemy, and H in the time of Al-Battani. CF is 21 minutes. CG is 47 minutes. CH is 22 minutes. FG is 68 minutes, and GH is 69 minutes, of which CE or CD is 70 minutes. Reinhold <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), a leading astronomer and mathematician who used Copernican data to create the Prutenic Tables.</note> in the Prutenic Tables reckons CE or CD to be 1 degree, 11 minutes, 22 seconds, and 30 thirds.

Therefore, may God grant a kingdom in Astronomy without end to my most learned Teacher <note>Referring to Nicolaus Copernicus.</note>, and may the Lord deign to govern, protect, and increase it for the restoration of astronomical truth, Amen.

-># FIRST ACCOUNT<-

<margin>He promises he will speak of the theories of the remaining planets in another narrative.</margin>
I had decided, most learned Mr. Schöner, to briefly write for you a complete treatment of the motion of the Moon and the rest of the planets, as well as the fixed stars and the Sun, so that you might understand what benefits are to flow to students of mathematics and to all posterity from the books of my Teacher, as if from a most fertile spring. But when I saw that the work was growing too large for the present, I thought a special Account should be instituted for this matter. Therefore, what I consider necessary to run ahead of these things and prepare the way, I will explain in this place; and I will sprinkle in certain general things about the hypotheses of the motion of the Moon and the other planets, so that you may conceive greater hope for this whole work and perceive what necessity compelled him to assume other hypotheses, or theories.

<margin>Much labor lay upon Ptolemy; a much greater labor lay upon Copernicus.</margin>
Since at the beginning of our Account I stated that my Teacher <note>Copernicus.</note> arranged his work in imitation of Ptolemy, I see that nothing more is left for me to say to you about his method of correcting motion. For no one to whom <term>Urania</term> <note>The Muse of astronomy.</note> is favorable can sufficiently admire and praise Ptolemy’s indefatigable diligence in calculation, his certainty of observations (which was almost beyond human strength), his truly divine method of investigating and executing all motions and appearances, and finally his method of teaching and demonstrating, which was everywhere so consistent with itself. In this, however, a greater labor lies upon my Teacher than upon Ptolemy, because he is forced to collect into a certain and mutually consistent ratio, or harmony, the series and order of all motions and appearances which the observations of 2,000 years—like the most excellent guides in the widest field of astronomy—unfold. In contrast, Ptolemy had the observations of the Ancients for barely a fourth part of such a time <note>Ptolemy worked roughly 500 years after the earliest systematic Greek observations, whereas Copernicus had to reconcile data spanning from ancient Babylon to his own time in the 1500s.</note> to which he could safely commit himself. And since by <gloss>time</gloss> <note>original: "$\tau\tilde{\omega} \ \chi\rho\acute{\omicron}\nu\omega$"</note>, the true God and Teacher of the laws of the celestial state, the errors of astronomy are opened to us—since an imperceptible or even neglected error at the beginning of the constitution of hypotheses, rules, and astronomical tables reveals itself as time proceeds, or even propagates immensely—astronomy is not so much to be restored by my Teacher, the Doctor, as to be built up anew from the foundation. Ptolemy could quite elegantly accommodate most of the hypotheses of the Ancients, such as those of Timocharis, Hipparchus, and others, to the series of every diversity of motion known to him from such a small elapsed time of observations. Therefore, rightly and prudently—because it was also more plausible—he chose those hypotheses which seemed more consistent with reason and our senses, and which the greatest craftsmen before him had used.

<margin>Other hypotheses had to be assumed by Copernicus because he saw that the usual ones did not satisfy the permanence of motions.</margin>
However, since the observations of all craftsmen, and heaven itself, and mathematical reasoning convince us that the Ptolemaic and common hypotheses are by no means sufficient for demonstrating a perpetual and mutually consistent connection and harmony of celestial things, and for collecting them into tables and rules, it was necessary for my Teacher to devise new hypotheses. Namely, by assuming these, he could deduce by good consequence, geometrically and arithmetically, such accounts of motions as the Ancients and Ptolemy once perceived when raised on high with the <gloss>divine eye of the soul</gloss> <note>original: "$\tau\tilde{\omega} \ \theta\epsilon\acute{\iota}\omega \ \psi\upsilon\chi\tilde{\eta}\varsigma \ \stackrel{\prime}{\omicron}\mu\mu\alpha\tau\iota$"</note>, and such as diligent observations today teach those following in the footsteps of the Ancients to be in the heavens. Thus indeed, in the future, students will see what Ptolemy and the other ancient au-

...minutes of the day are missing, which is also clear from the subtraction of 1 day and 9 minutes from 2 days and 6 minutes, as previously required with respect to the mean equinox. <note>The "mean equinox" is a theoretical point that moves at a constant speed, used by astronomers to average out irregularities in the Earth's motion.</note>

<margin>*The annual difference between Ptolemy and Al-Battani.*</margin>
Indeed, let us speak of the discrepancy of 7 days between **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, 2nd-century Alexandrian astronomer.</note> and **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Albategnium"; a 9th-century Arab prince and astronomer.</note>, which is remarkable because it involves a larger interval of time—namely, 743 years—whereby all the causes [of the discrepancy] will be more conspicuous. Consequently, as much time as corresponds to 1 degree and 9 minutes will be subtracted from the days with respect to the mean equinox, and added to the remainder (namely, 5 days and 31 minutes). # ACCOUNT

...minutes of a day are lacking, which is also evident from the subtraction of 1 day and 9 minutes from the 2 days and 6 minutes previously required with respect to the mean equinox.

<margin>Annual variation between Ptolemy and Albategnius.</margin>
Indeed, let us speak of the discrepancy of 7 days between **Ptolemy** and **Albategnius** <note>Also known as al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a prominent Arab astronomer whose observations corrected many of Ptolemy's earlier findings.</note>, which is particularly striking because it involves a larger interval of time—namely 743 years—and therefore all the underlying causes will be more visible. In Ptolemy’s time, the mean <term>equinox</term> <note>The moment the Sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night of equal length.</note> preceded the first star of **Aries** by about 7 degrees and 28 minutes in the direction <term>against the order of the signs</term> <note>original: "in signorum antecedentiam." This describes the movement of precession, where the equinoxes appear to move backward through the zodiac over long periods.</note>. Since the mean equinox subsequently moved to meet the Sun (as has been stated), it happened that in the years between Ptolemy and Albategnius, approximately 180 days and 14 minutes were added relative to the mean equinox. Therefore, 5 days and 31 minutes will be missing if we compare the time of the mean equinox to the result obtained when one day is collected every four years <note>This refers to the standard leap year calculation in the Julian calendar.</note>.

Furthermore, in Ptolemy’s time, the Sun had left the true equinox at 47 minutes after the mean equinox in the <term>order of the signs</term> <note>original: "in signorum consequentiam," referring to the Sun's standard eastward motion through the zodiac.</note>. However, in the age of Albategnius, the true equinox was 22 minutes before the mean equinox in the direction against the signs. Therefore, the Sun reached the true equinox earlier than it reached the mean equinox (or earlier than where it had left the true equinoctial point), which is the opposite of the previous example. Consequently, however much time corresponds to 1 degree and 9 minutes will be subtracted from the days relative to the mean equinox. When added to the remainder—namely 5 days and 31 minutes—and because we must proceed in the same way with the difference in the angle of diversity due to the decrease in <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle; Copernicus noted that the Earth's orbit was becoming less "stretched" over time.</note> (to which 30 minutes of a day correspond), then 1 day and 30 minutes will be subtracted from the average time. This subtraction is due to the change in the angle of diversity and the unequal motion of precession, mixed with the other two causes of the Sun’s unequal motion. This results in a true addition of 178 days and 44 minutes from the time of Ptolemy to the time of Albategnius’s observation. But that same decrease, when added to the 5 days and 31 minutes, shows that 7 days and 1 minute have been lost—which is what needed to be demonstrated.

### DIAGRAM OF THE ANOMALY OF PRECESSION
#### Of the Equinoxes, and the unequal magnitude of the Tropical Year.

<image-desc>An astronomical diagram showing a large circle with a vertical line AB representing the Ecliptic. Point A marks the first star of Aries. A central point C represents the mean equinox. A diagonal line DE shows the path of the "libration" or oscillation of the equinoxes. Points F, G, and H on the circle represent the positions of the true equinox during the lives of Hipparchus, Ptolemy, and Albategnius, showing how the point has shifted non-linearly over centuries.</image-desc>

*AB is the Ecliptic. A is the first star of Aries. C is the mean equinox, or the intersection of the mean equinoctial and the ecliptic. Its precession from A is uniform. DE is the diameter of the circle of the anomaly of the equinoxes, through which the true equinoctial moves back and forth by libration. F is the position of the true equinox (the intersection of the true equinoctial and the ecliptic) in the time of **Hipparchus**; G is the position in the time of Ptolemy; and H is the position in the time of Albategnius. CF is 21 minutes; CG is 47 minutes; CH is 22 minutes. FG is 68 minutes, but GH is 69 minutes, of which CE or CD is 70 minutes. **Reinhold** <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), a leading astronomer who later calculated the "Prussian Tables" based on Copernicus's work.</note> in the Prussian Tables reckons CE or CD as 1 degree, 11 minutes, 22 seconds, and 30 thirds.*

# NARRATIO

[au]thors might have use of them, so that they may recall them—who have been excluded from the schools until now—and restore them to their former honor, as if returned by <term>right of postliminy</term> <note>original: "postliminio." A legal term for the restoration of rights to a person returning from exile or captivity; here, Rheticus means restoring the ancients to their rightful place.</note>. The poet says, *There is no desire for the unknown* <note>original: "Ignoti nulla cupido," a quote from Ovid's *Ars Amatoria*.</note>. Therefore it is no wonder that **Ptolemy**, along with all of Antiquity, has lain neglected in darkness until now—just as you, most excellent Master **Schöner**, along with other good and learned men, have no doubt often lamented.

The calculation of **Eclipses** alone seems to defend the honor of **Astronomy** among the unlearned common people. Yet we see daily how much the current calculations differ from the observations, both in their timing and in the predicted magnitude of the eclipse. Truly, we should by no means reject the most accurate observations of **Ptolemy** and other excellent authors as false and worthless—as we see some people doing when establishing astronomical tables—unless we find that some manifest error has crept in, proven by the passage of time. For what is more human than to be sometimes mistaken and deceived, even under the appearance of truth, especially in these most difficult and obscure matters, which are by no means obvious?

Book four.
General considerations regarding the motion of the Moon, with its new hypotheses.

In demonstrating the motion of the **Moon**, my **Preceptor** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> adopts theories and explanations of movement which show that the excellent ancient Philosophers were by no means blind in their observations. Therefore, just as we showed above that the increase and decrease of the year taken from the equinoxes is regular, so too from a diligent examination of the motions of the **Sun** and **Moon** can it be deduced what the true distances of the Sun, Moon, and **Earth** from each other were in every age, and what values for the diameters of the Sun, Moon, and shadow were found at various times; this is done so that a certain calculation of the <term>parallaxes</term> <note>original: "diuersitatis aspectuum." The apparent shift in position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth.</note> of the Sun and Moon might also be maintained. Our **Regiomontanus** <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), the influential German astronomer whose *Epitome of the Almagest* was a standard textbook.</note> says in Book 5, Proposition 22 of the *Epitome*: *But it is strange that the Moon, when it is in the perigee of its epicycle at quadrature, does not appear so large; for if it were fully illuminated, it ought to appear four times larger than it does at opposition when it is in the apogee of its epicycle.* **Timochares** and **Menelaus** <note>Ancient Greek astronomers whose observations Rheticus cites to show that even the ancients noticed the Moon's size didn't fluctuate as much as Ptolemaic theory predicted.</note> felt the same, as they always used the same lunar diameter in their observations of the stars. But experience also taught my Preceptor that the parallaxes and the sizes of the Moon's body at every distance from the Sun differ little or not at all from those occurring at conjunction and opposition. Thus, it is clear that an <term>eccentric</term> <note>An orbital path whose center is not the center of the Earth.</note> cannot be attributed to the Moon in the way commonly accepted. Therefore, he posits that the orbit of the Moon encompasses the Earth with its adjacent elements, and the center of its <term>deferent</term> <note>The main circle carrying the smaller epicycles.</note> is the center of the Earth, upon

</margin>
which the center of the Moon's epicycle is carried uniformly by the deferent. That is to say, on the first epicycle—which appears at the middle time between conjunctions or oppositions and <term>quadratures</term> <note>The points where the Moon is 90 degrees away from the Sun (first and last quarter).</note>—he attaches another small epicycle carrying the body of the Moon. # FIRST [NARRATION]

...the center of the small and second **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note>, being carried along in the upper part toward the preceding signs <note>original: "in antecedentia," referring to westward motion against the stars.</note> and in the lower part toward the following signs <note>original: "in consequentia," referring to eastward motion.</note>, revolves. He posits that this motion—measured from the true **apogee** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note>, which is shown in the upper part of the first epicycle by a line drawn from the center of the Earth through the center of that same epicycle to the circumference—is equal and regular. 

The **Moon** also moves regularly and uniformly on the circumference of the small and second epicycle, departing from the true apogee of the small epicycle, which is indicated by a line originating from the center of the first epicycle and passing through the center of the second to its circumference. And this is the rule of this motion: that the Moon itself revolves twice in this smaller epicycle during one period of the **deferent** <note>The large circular path that carries the epicycle.</note>, so that in every conjunction and opposition <note>New moons and full moons.</note> the Moon is found in the **perigee** <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> of the small epicycle, but in the **quadratures** <note>The quarter moons.</note> it is found in its apogee. This is the mechanism, or hypothesis, by which my Master **Preceptor** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> excludes all the aforementioned inconsistencies; he demonstrates to the eyes that this hypothesis satisfies all appearances, as can also be gathered from his tables.

<margin>Book five.</margin>
Furthermore, most learned Master **Schöner**, just as you see us here freed from the **equant** <note>original: "æquante." A mathematical device used by Ptolemy to account for planetary speed variations, which Copernicus rejected because it violated uniform circular motion.</note> in the case of the Moon, and having adopted a theory that corresponds to experience and all observations: so too does he remove equants in the remaining planets. He assigns to each of the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.</note> only one epicycle and an **eccentric** <note>An orbital circle whose center is offset from the Earth/Sun.</note>, both of which move uniformly about their own centers, and the planet completes revolutions in the epicycle equal to those of the eccentric. For **Venus** and **Mercury**, however, he uses an eccentric of an eccentric. 

He teaches, nevertheless, that their motions can similarly be presented through an eccentric of an eccentric, and their revolutions through **eccentrepicycles** <note>A combined model of eccentrics and epicycles.</note>. For the fact that planets are seen every year as direct, stationary, retrograde, near to, or far from the Earth, etc., he demonstrates can be caused by a regular motion of the terrestrial globe, in addition to what is established above. This motion is: that the **Sun** occupies the center of the universe, while the Earth is carried around in the place of the Sun on an eccentric, which he chose to call the **Great Circle** <note>original: "Orbem Magnum." Copernicus’s term for Earth's annual orbit around the Sun.</note>. And truly, it is a thing of divine nature that a certain and fixed reckoning of celestial matters should depend upon the regular and uniform motions of a single terrestrial globe.

# NARRATION

...diligence <note>The text completes the word *diligentia* from the previous page.</note>, and the relationship of **Jupiter** to us in its morning and evening rising; this same fact may also be easily gathered from this. However, it is in the variation of the risings of **Mars** that it is most especially and greatly noticed. Because the star of Mars has a very dull light, it does not deceive the eye in the same way as **Venus** or Jupiter; rather, it reflects a change in magnitude according to the proportion of its distance from the Earth. Consequently, since Mars in its evening rising <note>When a planet rises at sunset, it is in "opposition" and closest to Earth.</note> appears to equal the star of Jupiter in size, so that it is distinguished only by its fiery glow, yet in its appearance and hiding <note>Referring to when it is near the Sun.</note> it can hardly be distinguished from stars of the second magnitude, it follows that it approaches very close to the Earth in its evening rising, but conversely is as far away as possible in its morning rising. This certainly cannot happen by means of the **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one in the old Ptolemaic system.</note> in any way. It is therefore clear that another place must be assigned to the Earth to restore the movements of Mars and the other planets.

<margin>4.</margin> Fourth, my Master the **Preceptor** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> saw that by this single reasoning it could conveniently be brought about that—as is most proper to circular motion—all the revolutions of the circles in the world would move equally and regularly about their own centers and not about foreign ones. <note>This refers to Copernicus's rejection of the "equant," a point used by Ptolemy to maintain the appearance of regular motion while violating the principle of uniform circular motion.</note>

<margin>5.</margin> Fifth, since it must be established no less for mathematicians than for physicians—as **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher (c. 129–216 AD).</note> emphasizes everywhere—that: *Nature does nothing in vain* <note>original Greek: "Μηδὲν εἰκῇ τὴν Φύσιν ἐργάζεσθαι"</note>; and:
<margin>These words are in Book 10 of *On the Use of Parts*.</margin> 
*Our Creator is so wise that not just one use was given to each of the things created by Him, but two, three, and often more* <note>original Greek: "οὕτως εἶναι τὸν δημιουργὸν ἡμῶν σοφὸν, ὡς μὴ μίαν ἕκαστον τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτῆς γεγονότων ἔχειν τὴν χρείαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ δύο, καὶ τρεῖς, καὶ πλείους πολλάκις"</note>; why, then, when we see that an infinite number of appearances are satisfied by this unique motion of the Earth, should we not attribute to God, the founder of nature, that same industry which we see common clockmakers possess? For they take the utmost care not to insert any little wheel into an instrument that is either superfluous or whose function could be more conveniently supplied by another part with its position slightly changed. And what would move my Master the Preceptor, as a mathematician, not to assume a suitable system for the motion of the terrestrial globe? Especially when he saw that by assuming such a **hypothesis** <note>In this context, a foundational mathematical model.</note> for establishing a certain doctrine of heavenly things, a single **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> suffices for us, and that one immovable; with the Sun immovable in the center of the universe; while in the motions of the remaining planets, **eccentrepicycles** <note>A combination of an eccentric circle and an epicycle.</note> or **eccentrecentrics** or epicycles suffice.

To this is added that the motion of the Earth in its own orbit provides the **arguments** <term>The "argument" or anomaly refers to the specific part of a planet's motion that makes it appear to slow down or move backward (retrograde).</term> of all the planets except the Moon. This single motion alone seems to be the cause of every diversity of movement—specifically that which appears in the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> relative to the Sun, and in Venus and Mercury around the Sun. Finally, this motion ensures that each of the planets is content with only a single deviation in the latitude of its carrying circle; thus, the principal motions of the planets also demand such hypotheses.

<margin>6.</margin> Sixth and lastly, this especially moved my Master the Doctor and Preceptor: he saw that the chief cause of all uncertainty in **Astronomy** was that the practitioners of this science (I say this with the permission of the divine **Ptolemy**, the father of Astronomy) recalled their theories and the reasons for correcting the motions of the heavenly bodies too loosely to that rule which warns that the order and motions of the heavenly spheres consist of a most absolute system. For even if we grant them their honor most amply (as is right), nonetheless was it not to be wished that, in establishing the harmony of motions, they had imitated musicians? For when a single string is either tightened or loosened, musicians with the greatest care and diligence [adjust] the sounds of all the others...

# FIRST BOOK

O 3 <note>This is a signature mark used by printers to keep the pages of a book in the correct order.</note>

...diligence <note>The text completes the word *diligentia* from the previous page.</note> applied, they form and adjust the parts until they all together return the desired harmony, nor is any dissonance noted in anything. If **Albategnius** <note>Also known as al-Battani, a famous 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note>, to mention him for a moment, had followed this in his work, we would undoubtedly have a more certain calculation of all movements today. It is likely that the **Alfonsine** <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables, the standard astronomical tables of the late Middle Ages, sponsored by King Alfonso X of Castile.</note> astronomers took much from him, and because this one thing was neglected, sometimes (if one is willing to admit the truth) the ruin of the entire science of **Astronomy** was to be feared. In the common principles of Astronomy, it was possible to see that all celestial appearances direct themselves toward the mean motion of the **Sun**, and the entire harmony of celestial movements is established and preserved according to its guidance. Hence, the Sun was called by the Ancients the *leader of the chorus* <gloss>leader of the chorus</gloss> <note>original Greek: chorēgos</note>, governor of nature, and King. But how he carries out this administration—whether in the same way **God** governs this whole universe, as **Aristotle** beautifully depicts him as the *ever-leader* <gloss>ever-leader</gloss> <note>original Greek: aei hēgemōn</note>, or whether he himself, by traveling through the whole sky so many times and resting in no place, acts as God's administrator in nature—this does not yet seem entirely explained or perfected. Whether of these is rather to be assumed, I leave to the Geometers and Philosophers (those at least who are steeped in mathematics) to determine. For in evaluating and judging controversies of this kind, the sentence must be passed not based on plausible opinions, but on mathematical laws (in whose court this case is argued). The former mode of governance <note>Remote governance like a king from a throne.</note> was rejected, and the latter <note>The Sun physically traveling the sky.</note> was accepted. But my Master the **Preceptor** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> decided that the rejected method of the Sun's governance in nature must be recalled, yet in such a way that a place is still left for the accepted and approved one. For he sees that even in human affairs, it is not necessary for an Emperor to run through every single city himself to perform the duty imposed on him by God; nor does the heart migrate into the head, or the feet, or other parts of the body for the sake of preserving the living creature, but presides over its duty through other *organs* <gloss>organs</gloss> <note>original Greek: organa</note> destined for this by God.

Then, when he established that the mean motion of the Sun ought to be a motion that does not consist merely of imagination (as it does in the other planets), but has a cause in itself—since it appeared most truly to be the *leadership* <gloss>leadership</gloss> <note>original Greek: chorēgian</note>—it followed that he proved his opinion to be firm and not far from the truth. For he felt that through his **hypotheses**, the efficient cause of the equal motion of the Sun could be geometrically deduced and demonstrated, showing why this mean motion of the Sun was necessarily found in all the movements and appearances of the remaining planets according to a certain rule, as it appears in each one. And from there, once the motion of the Earth in an **eccentric** <note>A circle whose center is slightly off-set from the center of the universe.</note> was established, a certain doctrine of celestial things was at hand, in which nothing need be changed; rather, the whole system was restored anew into its proper ratios, as was consistent. We could not even suspect such a governance of the Sun in nature with our common theories, and we used to neglect many of the Ancients' *praises* <gloss>praises</gloss> <note>original Greek: enkōmia</note> of the Sun as if they were merely poetic. You see, therefore, what kind of hypotheses my Master the Preceptor had to assume to save the movements, once these things were so established.
