# THE FIRST ACCOUNT

...is the reason why those things are true. Thus, when my learned Teacher <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543).</note> determined that he must adopt such hypotheses as would contain the causes for the observations of past centuries—confirming them as true—and, as was to be hoped, would also be the causes by which all future astronomical predictions of the phenomena <note>original Greek: τῶν φαινομένων</note> might be found true: in the beginning, having overcome no small labors, he established through hypothesis that the stellar sphere (which we commonly call the eighth) was created by God for this purpose: to be that dwelling which, by its embrace, contains the entire nature of things. For this reason, He created it as the place of the universe, fixed and immobile. And because motion is not perceived except by comparison to something fixed—just as those sailing on the sea, for whom no more lands appear, see the sky on all sides and the sea on all sides, and feel no motion of the ship when the sea is calm of winds, even if they are carried with such speed that in an hour they might traverse several great miles—therefore God marked that entire sphere with stellar globes, specifically for our sake, so that by them (being indeed fixed in place) we might observe the positions and motions of the other contained spheres and planets.

<margin>
The order of the spheres of the World.
</margin>
<margin>
The highest stellar sphere, fixed and immobile.
</margin>
<margin>
Why the Creator wished the eighth sphere to be marked with so many stars.
</margin>

<margin>
The Sun, immobile in the middle of the World.
</margin>
<margin>
Pontanus, in the book *Urania*.
</margin>
Next, which is indeed consistent with these things, God placed the Sun in the middle of this theater as His administrator in nature and the King of the entire universe, conspicuous in His Divine majesty,
> According to whose rhythms both the Gods move, and the world
> Receives its laws, and keeps its prescribed covenants. <note>These lines are from Giovanni Pontano’s (1426–1503) didactic poem *Urania*, which sought to reconcile Christian thought with astronomy.</note>

<margin>
Below the stellar sphere: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars.
</margin>
<margin>
Around the Sun: Mercury, Venus.
</margin>
<margin>
Between Mars and Venus, the Great Orb containing the Earth with the elements and the sphere of the Moon.
</margin>
The remaining spheres are distributed in this manner: the first place below the firmament, or stellar sphere, fell to the sphere of Saturn; within which that of Jupiter is contained, and then that of Mars. The Sun, however, is surrounded by the sphere of Mercury, and then the sphere of Venus, so that the centers of the spheres of the five planets are found around the Sun. But within the concave surface of the sphere of Mars and the convex surface of Venus—since a sufficiently large space is left there—the globe of the Earth with the adjacent elements, surrounded by the lunar sphere, is carried around by a certain Great Orb <note>term: Orbis Magnus; the annual orbital path of the Earth around the Sun.</note> which contains within itself the spheres of Mercury and Venus, as well as the Sun. Thus, the Earth has its motions not otherwise than one of the stars among the planets.

---

-> A D D I T I O N <-

That this order and arrangement of the spheres of the world was not first thought of by Copernicus, but was handed down by the ancient philosophers, is witnessed by Archimedes in his book *The Sand Reckoner*, in which he writes thus about Aristarchus: *Refuting those things which were written by astrologers (concerning the common hypotheses in which the Earth is placed as the center of the world), Aristarchus of Samos published certain positions from which it follows that the World is many times larger than the one just mentioned. For he posits that the fixed stars and the Sun remain immobile; but the Earth is carried around the Sun according to the circumference of a circle which is situated in the middle of its course. He posits that the sphere of the fixed stars, located around the same center as the Sun, is of such great magnitude that the circle in which he posits the Earth is carried around has the same proportion to the distance of the fixed stars as the center of a sphere has to its surface (that is, a proportion which is in no way perceptible),* etc. Moreover, it is clear from Ptolemy, Book 3, Chapter 2, that Aristarchus flourished around the 44th year after the death of Alexander the Great—that is, around the year 280 before the birth of Christ, and 1,876 years before our own age.

Reflecting more carefully on this distribution of the whole universe according to the opinion of my Teacher <note>Nicolaus Copernicus.</note>, I understand that Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman natural philosopher.</note> felt both brilliantly and correctly when he said: > To investigate what lies outside the World, or the heavens, by whose curvature all things are covered, is neither of concern to men, nor can the human mind grasp such a conjecture. Indeed, we shall proceed only as far as He has willed, nor

<margin>The world is immense and similar to the infinite.</margin>
shall we attempt to cross the limits established by Him. Furthermore, that the world is immense and truly like the infinite—even regarding its internal space—is indeed admitted from the fact that we see all the stars twinkling, with the exception of the planets; even Saturn, which is the closest of them to the [starry] heaven, is carried in the greatest circle. # FIRST ACCOUNT

...horizon divides the orb of the stars into equal parts, so that the great circle of the universe intersects it, and the orbs of their revolutions are proved to have equality from the fixed stars: it is clear enough that the orb of the stars is most similar to the infinite, since indeed the great orb <note>The "Great Orb" refers to the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun.</note> vanishes when compared to it, and all the <term>phenomena</term> <note>original: τὰ φαινόμενα (ta phainomena) — the observable appearances of the heavens.</note> are observed no differently than if the Earth had settled in the middle of the universe.

### ADDITION.

Copernicus, at the end of Book 1, Chapter 10, also adds this reasoning:
> There ought to be the greatest difference between the moved and the unmoved. Here, I think this should not be passed over:

I believe one should by no means listen to Tycho Brahe—otherwise a most excellent Mathematician and a second Ptolemy—when he sharply attacks this so vast distance of the Orb of the Fixed Stars from the center of the World (at which the Great Orb of the Earth vanishes, and is therefore like the infinite), for the sake of preserving his own ancient and customary hypotheses regarding the Earth’s position in the middle of the World.

Specifically, where in the <term>Progymnasmata</term> <note>Tycho Brahe's "Introduction to the Restored Astronomy," a foundational but anti-Copernican text.</note> on page 403, he asserts it to be absurd if it is established with Copernicus that a vastness still void of stars lies between Saturn and the Fixed Stars. And on page 481: "If one were pleased to agree with the Copernican speculation regarding the annual motion of the Earth, an immense vastness would still remain between Saturn and the eighth sphere <note>The 'Eighth Sphere' was the traditional term for the outermost shell of the universe containing the stars.</note>, before the Earth's annual motion, in respect to this sphere, would vanish completely as it ought: So much so that the interval from the center of the Universe to the highest point of Saturn would be contained more than seven hundred times within this gap and the Fixed Stars; and that space would be entirely empty of stars, and destined for no use that falls within the senses—which is absurd to believe."

Likewise, although on the same page he does not deny that it is uncertain whether all stars are equally distant from the center of the World, and it is more likely that some are placed higher and some lower; and even on page 470 he advises that the Fixed Stars are not necessarily all removed by an equal distance from the Earth, for some of them could be higher than others by a great interval—from which it is not clear how wide that vastness of the heavens is which these fixed stars occupy, and thus they are undoubtedly removed unequally.

However, on page 483 he gives his opinion: "In my judgment," he says, "one ought not to admit too great a vastness here for the limits of the Eighth Sphere. For it cannot be so wide that the smallest stars, which are considered of the Sixth Magnitude, are elongated from the Earth by such a gap that they are made equal to those which are of the first and principal brightness. For this interval would turn out to be beyond measure vast; such that it would contain more than 155,000 Earth radii. And thus they would have to be raised eleven times higher than the height we have assumed." <insert>Tycho, however, assumed the sphere of the stars to be no less than 13,000, yet no more than 14,000 Earth radii distant from the center of the Universe.</insert> "And thus that space assigned to the Eighth Orb would also encompass eleven times that gap which exists from the Earth to its own presupposed borders. Which surely exceeds all measure and belief."

I respond: Whoever favors Copernicus’s opinion as set forth in this *First Account* by Rheticus, will not unwillingly grant some of the things reviewed. 

1. They themselves confess that it is uncertain whether the fixed stars in the Firmament are distant from the center of the Universe by an equal interval: And, that it is more likely that some of them are higher, some lower: However, they have nothing certain to establish about that, because that inquiry leads to absolutely nothing regarding the principal goal of Astronomy—namely, the demonstrations of the <term>phenomena</term> of celestial motions. 

2. None of them fall into such madness as to think all Fixed Stars are equal in size, and appear larger or smaller only because of a lesser or greater distance from us: since it is more than well-known to all that even those stars we call "Wandering" <note>The planets.</note> differ from one another by a notable difference in size. Why then should the stars not also differ? 

3. Furthermore, they do not disagree that perhaps not too great a vastness should be admitted for the limits of the Eighth Sphere; although they confess that the admission of that vastness—however great it may be between its inner and outer surfaces—is not in their power, but placed in the hand of the Almighty Creator. 

4. Hence they are not so curious as to search out how wide that Starry Sphere’s gap is: nor whether the highest stars are two or three times, or eleven or twenty times higher than the lowest; but for discerning the phenomena it suffices for them to assume them as if they all cling fixed in one and the same concave surface of that orb. For they do not presume to know too deeply <note>A common theological warning against intellectual pride.</note>, nor to transcend beyond or outside that concave surface of the Starry Orb, except as much as the Holy...

# ACCOUNT

Holy Scripture wished them to know about these things. But they religiously and with grateful hearts admire, contemplate, and—as far as is granted by divine grace—scrutinize the rest of Nature enclosed within the starry Heaven. 5. I add this also: Just as the supporters of **Aristarchus** <note>Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BCE) was an ancient Greek astronomer who first proposed a heliocentric model, long before Copernicus.</note> and **Copernicus** are not worried about that vastness of the Starry Sphere from its concave to its convex surface, but commit that care to the Omnipotent 
<margin>
*Isaiah 40:12*
</margin>
Divine Majesty, who "measures the Heavens with a span," so they would by no means argue with those who deny that the distance of those same Fixed Stars from the center of the Universe is so great that it encompasses the highest altitude of **Saturn** from the same center seven hundred times or more. (According to **Tycho's** numbers, who on page 480 computes the most remote revolution of Saturn at a distance of 12,900 <term>earth radii</term> <note>original: semidiametri terrae — the distance from the center of the Earth to its surface, used as a standard astronomical unit of the time.</note>, although the star of Saturn itself is not removed further than 12,300 earth radii, it would contain more than ninety hundred earth radii.) For no necessity demands that this likeness of Infinity be enlarged until the "Great Orb" of the Earth <note>The Earth's annual orbit around the Sun.</note> entirely vanishes compared to the Starry Orb, as **Tycho** thinks (even though in the Great Orb, even according to **Tycho’s** numbers, it would entirely vanish if indeed it produced a <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions.</note> in the fixed stars of no more than two-fifths, that is, almost to half of one <term>arcminute</term> <note>original: scrupuli primi — a 60th of a degree.</note>). Because even a much more restricted altitude is immense—that is, unsearchable and not investigable by any instruments or any skill—it therefore deservedly earns the right to be called "similar to the infinite." For even if it were smaller, it can nonetheless satisfy all phenomena to be observed and demonstrated, just as the laws of Astronomy require. For Parallaxes, if the Great Orb of the Earth induces any upon the fixed stars, happen most only to those stars which rise and set around midnight; however, whatever stars are elevated above the horizon, or ascend or descend at other hours, the parallaxes among them are already smaller, and therefore they vanish all the more from the eyes and become unobservable. Therefore, even if those horizontal parallaxes were of one, or two, or even three arcminutes—of the kind that occur in the Sun according to the opinion of **Ptolemy** and **Copernicus**, as well as **Tycho**—they would nevertheless be observable by no instruments, partly because of their smallness, and partly (and indeed chiefly) because of the <term>refractions</term> of the rays of sight around the horizon, which absorb all observation of parallaxes. Therefore, no one can be convicted of absurdity who does not hesitate to assert that the proportion of the distance of the Fixed Stars from the center of the World is at least equal to the proportion of the distance of the Sun from the Earth (that is, to the semi-diameter of the Great Orb), and for that reason, the Orb of the Fixed Stars can even thus be said to be similar to the infinite. Hence **Copernicus** nowhere says that the Great Orb entirely vanishes compared to the Orb of the Fixed Stars; rather, in Book 1, Chapter 5, he says it is "not comparable"—evidently to the senses, as he speaks in Chapter 6—and in Chapter 10, that it, or its image, vanishes from the eyes because of the immense height of those stars. So in Chapter 11, he says the distance of the Sun and Earth exceeds our sight in the Sphere of the Fixed Stars. Likewise in Book 3, Chapter 15, that it cannot be estimated in relation to this, etc. Therefore, it is beyond doubt that **Copernicus** was looking to the judgment of the eyes, not to the universal exclusion of all parallax, since that remoteness of the starry Orb suffices for the demonstrations of motions, because of which, and at which, the quantity of the Great Orb cannot be perceived by the eyes. It is entirely very likely that such a remoteness, indicated in the said manner and weighed according to all circumstances, even if it does not exceed the highest altitude of Saturn seven hundred times, it nevertheless equals it a hundred or two hundred times.

But although in those things which have been recounted concerning such an immense height of the Firmament, every discrepancy between **Copernicus** and **Tycho** could be removed without difficulty, it is nevertheless quite harsh (not to say injurious toward the Omnipotence and unsearchable Wisdom of God the Creator, and for that reason **Tycho** is not to be listened to in this) when it is contended that the height of the Starry Orb from the center neither is, nor can be, so great that the Great Orb of the Earth vanishes compared to it; likewise, when certain limits are prescribed to the same Starry Orb between its innermost and outermost surfaces. For it was not enough to have said: "In my judgment, one ought not to admit a too great vastness to the limits of the <term>Eighth Sphere</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars in the traditional geocentric model.</note>, nor could it be so vast, etc."; but it is added further: "that to believe these things is absurd, and exceeds all measure and faith." It is of the same weight where it is similarly pronounced absurd to believe that so great an interval remains between Saturn and the Fixed Stars, as was indicated above. The reason given: because that space would be entirely empty of stars, and destined for no use that falls within the senses. What is this, I ask, other 
<margin>
*Job 37:18*
*Isaiah 40:13*
</margin>
than to accuse the Omnipotence of the Creator of impotence, and to prescribe laws to All-Wisdom? "Has mortal man helped the Spirit of the Lord, and been His Counselor, that he might enter into counsel with Him?" 
<margin>
*Isaiah 40:26*
*Psalm 147:4*
</margin>
As if, indeed, He whose omnipotent hand could raise the highest distance of the revolution of the single star of Saturn from the center of the Natural World to 12,900 earth radii (and most certain demonstrations deduced from observations prove it is not less), that same hand could not also raise the Firmament of so many illustrious Stars, gloriously shining with flashing splendor, the number of which is known only to God, who [calls] them all [by name]...

<margin>Luke 1:37. John 1:3. Psalm 33:6. Psalm 145:3. 147:5.</margin>
...He calls them by name, they are known to Him. Could He not have raised up the beauty of the creation three or four times, or ten or eleven, or even a hundred or a thousand times further? Nothing from within hindered Him, because He can do all that He wills; for with Him, "no word is impossible." Likewise, nothing from without could stand in His way, because He Himself is infinite, and His power is infinite. He who created this entire **Theater of the Universe** <note>original: "Theatrum" — a common Renaissance metaphor for the world as a display of God's glory.</note> from nothing through the **Word**, could have created a thousand other worlds through that same word, had He so willed. Why, then, does the "emptiness" in such a vast space from **Saturn** to the **Fixed Stars** offend **Tycho**, as if it were destined for no use perceived by the senses? Does he think it is given to man to bind the unsearchable Wisdom of God to human senses? "Great is our Lord," says the Psalmist, "and greatly to be praised, and of His power there is great strength. Of His greatness there is no end (or, no searching out) and of His wisdom there is no number." Therefore, there are innumerable other things created by the most Wise Creator which neither fall under human senses nor can be investigated by the sharpest human wit. And why is this not also criticized by **Tycho**: that the Creator, in such a spacious amplitude of the World—stretching from the center to the highest altitude of **Saturn**—placed only seven Stars <note>The "seven stars" refers to the traditional planets: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> and the **Earth** with the remaining Elements, leaving the entire rest of the region, through every circuit and in every direction, empty and void of any body that can be perceived by the senses?

But while **Tycho** strives to remove what seem to him to be absurdities, he entangles his own opinion in equally heavy absurdities. One of them (to say nothing of others here) is the inestimable and beyond-all-belief perpetual velocity of the **Starry Sphere** in its daily motion. This speed is hardly less than that which (as said above) accompanies the measurement of the celestial orbits according to **Alfraganus** <note>Alfraganus (al-Farghani) was a 9th-century Persian astronomer whose works on the size and distance of planets were standard for centuries.</note>. **Tycho** determined that the Starry Sphere is no less than 13,000 <term>earth radii</term> distant from the center. In this matter, those who embrace the opinion of **Copernicus** gladly agree with him. Yet **Tycho** himself contends that this same sphere is no higher than 14,000 earth radii. But come, for the purpose of examining this, let us take the middle number between these two, which is 13,500. The total diameter then becomes 27,000 earth radii, which are (counting 860 <term>German miles</term> <note>A German mile in this period was approximately 7.5 kilometers, significantly longer than a modern English mile.</note> for each) twenty-three million, two hundred and twenty thousand (23,220,000) miles. Accordingly, following the proportion of the diameter to the circle (which is 7 to 22), the entire circumference at the **Equator** will be numbered at 72,977,143 miles; that is, beyond seventy-two million, nine hundred and seventy-seven thousand German miles. A twenty-fourth part of these <note>The distance covered in one hour of the 24-hour daily rotation.</note> contains 3,040,714—that is, beyond thirty hundred thousand and forty thousand miles. And such a journey must be completed by every Star or point on the equatorial circle within the space of a single hour. And a four-thousandth part of this <note>The distance covered in the time of a single pulse beat.</note> holds 760 German miles, which is the path each of those stars must finish within the stroke of a single **pulse of an artery** (as was said above in the Preface before this Account, citing **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath who wrote extensively on mathematics and medicine.</note>), for a man of temperate nature. But it is absurd to believe this. So that this absurdity may appear more evidently, the same **Cardano**, as a Physician, writes in Book 5, Proposition 118 *On Proportions*: "In one stroke of a temperate arterial pulse, there are contained nearly five strokes of the pulse of an infant suffering from a very sharp fever." Truly, in this most imperceptible time, that celestial motion would complete one hundred and fifty miles. Or: Suppose it is granted—even in superabundance—that someone, within one stroke of a temperate arterial pulse, could blink their eyes six or seven times by quickly closing and opening them again (a time which everyone feels to be entirely and truly imperceptible, and no different from a single moment), in such a tiny time—that is, in every single moment—every Star in the **Firmament** would have to cover more than one hundred full German miles. Whether this is to be believed of a natural celestial body, and not accepted as an absurdity and simply impossible, anyone—provided they enjoy some use of reason—will judge. These and similar absurdities are all far exiled from the hypotheses of **Copernicus**. Which, then, will you give greater credit to: these things which are connected in a most fit order of arrangement and motion, or those which neither agree harmoniously, nor presuppose a motion consistent with themselves or with Nature?

Just as in demonstrations, these most sweet things are usually imprinted on our minds not so much by words as by perfect and absolute ideas. Nevertheless, even in a general contemplation of the hypotheses, one can see how an ineffable convenience and a consensus of all things offers itself. For besides the fact that in the common hypotheses there appeared to be no purpose for the fashioning of the spheres,

120 NARRATIO

<margin>
The matters which are most heavily litigated: these are most correctly settled in the work of **Copernicus**.
</margin>
...it appeared that the spheres, whose immensity could be perceived by neither sense nor reason, were being driven by the slowest and fastest motions. Some experts established that all lower spheres were swept along by the daily motion of the **Supreme Mover** <note>original: "supremo mobili" — in the geocentric system, an outermost sphere that was thought to drag all other planets around the Earth once every 24 hours.</note>, even though they have not yet been able to settle the great crowd of disputes stirred up on this matter regarding how a superior sphere can have authority over an inferior one. Others, such as **Eudoxus** <note>A Greek astronomer who proposed a system of concentric spheres.</note> and those who followed him, assigned to each planet its own sphere, by whose motion it would be carried around the Earth once in a natural day. Furthermore, immortal Gods! What a "gladiatorial combat" and how great a dispute there has been up until now regarding the positions of the spheres of **Venus** and **Mercury**, and how they ought to be arranged in relation to the **Sun**. Truly, this dispute is still "before the judge" <note>original: "sub iudice" — a legal metaphor meaning the case is still undecided.</note>, and who does not see that it is extremely difficult, and even impossible, for it ever to be settled if those common hypotheses are maintained?

What, likewise, would prevent someone from placing **Saturn** below the **Sun**, or **Venus** and **Mercury** above **Saturn**, provided the ratio of the spheres and the **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one, used to explain planetary loops.</term> to each other were preserved? For in those same old hypotheses, the common dimension of the planetary spheres relative to one another has not yet been demonstrated, by which any sphere could be geometrically circumscribed in its own place. Indeed, let me pass over in silence here what great "tragedies" the detractors of this most beautiful and sweet part of philosophy have stirred up on account of the size of the epicycle of **Venus**, and because, by assuming **equants** <term>equant: a mathematical point used by Ptolemy to explain why planets seem to speed up or slow down, though it violated the principle of perfectly uniform circular motion.</term>, the movements of the celestial spheres were assumed to be unequal around their own centers. In the hypotheses of my **Master Teacher** <note>original: "D. Præceptoris" — referring to Nicolaus Copernicus.</note>, however, with the **Starry Sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> established as the boundary as has been said, each planetary sphere proceeds uniformly with the motion attributed to it by nature, completes its own period, and suffers no force from a superior sphere to be dragged in a different direction. Add to this that the spheres with larger circuits complete their revolutions more slowly, and those closer to the **Sun**—which one might call the principle of motion and light—complete theirs more quickly, as is fitting. Therefore, **Saturn**, taking up its free path under the **Ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun through the stars.</note>, completes its revolution in 30 years; **Jupiter** in 12; **Mars** in two. The center of the **Earth** determines the length of the year relative to the **Fixed Stars**. **Venus** traverses the **Zodiac** in seven and a half months. **Mercury**, however, surrounding the **Sun** in the smallest sphere, surveys the world in 88 days.

<margin>
Only six moving spheres. The **Great Orbit** is the measure of the other spheres.
</margin>
And thus there are only six moving spheres surrounding the **Sun**, the center of the universe, of which the **Great Orbit** <term>Great Orbit: the path of the Earth around the Sun.</term> carrying the Earth is the common measure; just as it is for the spheres of the **Moon**, and likewise the distance of the **Sun** from the **Moon**, etc., and those things which proceed from the center of the terrestrial globe.

<margin>
Regarding this group of six spheres, you will find a more evident and specific reason above on page 84.
</margin>
And indeed, who could choose another number more convenient or more worthy than the number **six**? And by what other number could one more easily persuade mortals that this entire universe was divided into its spheres by **God the Founder** and the **Architect of the world**? For that number is most highly celebrated both in the sacred oracles of God and by the **Pythagoreans** and other philosophers. What, moreover, is more fitting for this Artificer of God than that this first and most perfect Work should be enclosed by the first and most perfect number <note>The number 6 was considered "perfect" by ancient mathematicians because its factors (1, 2, and 3) add up to itself.</note>? Furthermore, that the **Celestial Harmony** should be perfected by the aforementioned six moving spheres, where all the spheres follow one another in such a way that no immense gap is left from one to the next; and each is so protected by geometry and maintains its place in this manner, that if you should try to move any one of them from its place, you would simultaneously dissolve the entire system.

FIRST ACCOUNT.

But having first tasted these general matters, let us now approach the enumeration of the circular motions which belong to each of the spheres and to the bodies adhering to and resting upon them. First, however, we shall speak of the hypotheses of the motions of the terrestrial globe, upon which we dwell. Since my Master <note>Nicolaus Copernicus</note>, following Plato and the Pythagoreans—the greatest mathematicians of that divine age—judged that circular motions should be assigned to the spherical body of the Earth to explain the causes of the phenomena <note>original Greek: τῶν φαινόμενων (tōn phainomenōn) — the appearances of the heavens</note>, and since he saw (as Aristotle also testifies) that by attributing one motion to the Earth, other motions likewise belong to it in imitation of the stars, he judged it must be assumed that the Earth is moved by three principal motions. 

<margin>Which motions belong to the Great Orb and the things adhering to it.</margin>
<margin>Three motions of the Earth. 1. Daily.</margin>
For first, having assumed the universal distribution of the world as was just said, he established the Earth within the orbit of the Moon, enclosed by its own poles like a small sphere on a lathe. By the ordering of the divine power, the motion of this globe from west to east produces day and night, and presents one face of the heaven after another to mortals, according as the Earth turns itself toward the Sun. 

<margin>2. Annual.</margin>
In the second place, the center of the Earth, along with the elements resting upon it and the lunar sphere, is carried uniformly around the Great Orb <note>the Earth's orbital path around the Sun</note>—of which we have already made mention more than once—in the plane of the ecliptic, following the sequence of the signs of the Zodiac. 

<margin>3. Of Declination.</margin>
Third, the equator and the axis of the Earth have an inclination that changes relative to the plane of the ecliptic, and this is reflected back against the motion of the center. Thus, wherever the center of the Earth may be, the equator and the poles of the Earth—on account of this inclination of the Earth’s axis and the immensity of the starry sphere—always look toward almost the same parts of the universe. This happens because, as much as the center of the Earth is moved forward along the Great Orb, the ends of the Earth's axis (the poles) are understood to proceed nearly the same amount backward each day, describing small circles around the axis and poles that are equidistant from the axis and poles of the Great Orb or the ecliptic. 

<margin>4. A motion is added which is completed by two librations of the poles.</margin>
When we have added to these motions—according to my Master's opinion—the two librations <note>slow oscillations or "wobbles"</note> of the Earth's poles, and likewise the two motions by which the center of the Great Orb moves under the ecliptic with both uniform and varying motion, we shall have (most learned Mr. Schöner), along with what was said above regarding the motions of the Moon around the Earth's center, the true system of hypotheses. From this, the entire doctrine—which the Moderns call the "First Motion" <note>the apparent daily rotation of the entire sky</note> and which we possess concerning every kind of motion of the starry sphere—can be derived, and the causes can be assigned to those things which have been observed to occur regarding the motions and eclipses <note>original: "passiones"</note> of the Sun and Moon through the diligent observations of craftsmen over the past two thousand years. This is to say nothing of what shall be spoken of more fully later: that the motion of the Great Orb creates the appearances seen in the remaining five planets. So much learning is contained within so few principles, and as if within a single sphere. 

<margin>The hypotheses of Copernicus agree with common ones in the doctrine of the First Motion.</margin>
In the doctrine of the First Motion, nothing needs to be changed. For the properties of those things which are related to one another at the maximum declination will be investigated by the same logic for the other parts: the declinations of the ecliptic, right ascensions, the ratio of shadows and gnomons <note>the vertical rods of sundials</note> throughout the whole world, the lengths of days, oblique ascensions, the rising and setting of stars, and so on. 

<margin>Besides the Ecliptic, the remaining circles of the First Motion.</margin>
However, there is this difference between these hypotheses and those of the Ancients: in these, contrary to what was prescribed by the Ancients, no circle besides the ecliptic is actually described by the imagination within the starry sphere. The others—such as the equator, the two tropics, the arctic circles...

# ACCOUNT

<margin>These circles are properly described on the earth and secondarily in the heaven.</margin> ...and the Antarctic circles, horizons, meridians, and all other circles pertaining to the doctrine of the first motion—verticals, altitude circles, parallels, colures, etc.—are properly designated on the globe of the Earth, and are referred into the heavens through a certain relationship. Among those things that appear around the Sun (besides the appearance of the daily revolution around the earth, which it has in common with all the stars and remaining planets, and which Ptolemy and the Moderns attributed to the Sun's own motions), there occur to it also those things which are found to happen concerning the changes of the solstitial and equinoctial points, and the distances of the stars from them, as well as the variations of the apogee from the fixed stars. All these things offer themselves to our eyes exactly as if the Sun and the sphere of the stars were moved; for as they are commonly believed to emerge or rise in the east and gradually be raised above the horizon until they reach the meridian, from which they descend in like manner and then pass through the lower hemisphere, completing their daily revolutions day by day, sufficiently evident causes are found from the first motion, which my Master <note>Nicolaus Copernicus</note> attributed to the earth according to Plato.

<margin>By the second motion of the earth, the Sun appears to move through the zodiac.</margin> Moreover, that the Sun appears to us to progress according to the sequence of the signs, and that we persuade ourselves it describes the ecliptic <note>the path the Sun appears to take across the sky</note> with such a motion and establishes the annual time, can happen through the second motion which my Master attributed to the earth. For the Earth, carried by the Great Orb <note>the Earth's orbit around the Sun</note> and staying between the stars of Libra and the Sun, we—who indeed think the earth is at rest—will judge the Sun to occupy the starry Aries; for a line projected from the center of the earth through the Sun into the sphere of the stars will fall into the constellation of Aries. Then, as the earth progresses to Scorpio, the Sun will be seen to seek Taurus, and in this manner permeate the Zodiac, although while the Sun itself is at rest, we establish that this motion belongs to the Earth. And the sidereal year will be the time in which the center of the Earth (or the Sun in appearance) revolves once from the same star back to the same star.

<margin>The third motion of the earth is the cause of the changes of the parts of the year on earth. The Equinoctial is oblique to the Ecliptic. Hence the other circles are inscribed on the earth. Tropics: Equinoxes. The remaining parallels of the days. Arctic and Antarctic.</margin> The third motion of the earth produces certain and ordered successions of the seasons in the whole world; for through this it happens that the Sun and the rest of the planets appear to be carried in a circle oblique to the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note>, and there is the same relationship of the Sun to individual regions of the earth as would have been if the earth occupied the center of the universe by hypothesis and the planets moved in an oblique circle. For since the plane of the equinoctial—on account of the motion of its poles, as was said—is reflected and declines from the plane of the ecliptic in comparison to the Sun, or as the Greeks say <term>it is slanted <note>original Greek: λοξοῦται (loxsoutai)</note></term> and <term>inclines <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐγκλίνει (kai enklinei)</note></term>, the same declination of the equinoctial from the ecliptic returns under nearly the same places of the ecliptic, and the poles of the daily revolution themselves are always turned under almost the same position of the sphere of the stars. Then, at the maximum declinations of the equinoctial from the plane of the ecliptic toward the Sun, a line going out from the center of the Sun to the center of the earth cuts the globe of the earth (which is turned around by daily revolution) in a conical section and describes the tropics. Furthermore, when the plane of the equinoctial is most reflected from the plane of the ecliptic toward the Sun, the equinox occurs in the whole earth, for indeed the globe of the earth is cut into two hemispheres at the equinoctial by the aforementioned line. But the remaining parallels of the days are marked on the earth according as the reflection and declination (or, to use the words of Ptolemy, the <term>slanting <note>original Greek: λόξωσις (loxōsis)</note></term> and <term>inclination <note>original Greek: καὶ ἔγκλισις (kai enklisis)</note></term>) of the equinoctial toward the Sun mix together. But the Arctic and Antarctic circles are described by the points touching the horizons. But the polar [circles]... <note>The text continues on the next page; the Latin catchword is "ceptori", likely completing "Præceptori" or "Master".</note>

<meta>This page continues the detailed technical explanation of how the Earth’s various motions—rotation, revolution, and the "third motion" of its axis—recreate the celestial phenomena traditionally attributed to the moving Sun and spheres. # FIRST ACCOUNT

<margin>Polar circles.</margin>
<margin>Colures.</margin>
...equidistant to the poles of my Master’s <note>Nicolaus Copernicus</note> ecliptic, describe circles around the poles of the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note>. On the globe of the Earth, however, a great circle passing through the equinoctial poles and the aforementioned poles equidistant to the ecliptic will be the colure of the solstices; another circle, intersecting this one at right spherical angles at the equinoctial poles, will take the place of the colure of the equinoxes. In this manner, one understands that the proper circles of any given place, or any number of other circles, are easily inscribed upon the Earth and are then projected from there to the overarching heaven.

<margin>By what reasoning Copernicus demonstrates the apparent motion of the Sun.</margin>
Furthermore, since the command of observations has dictated that the globe of the Earth has flown out into the circumference of the eccentric <note>An off-center circular path</note>, and the Sun has settled in the middle of the universe, a reversal occurs. In the common hypotheses <note>The Ptolemaic system</note>, the center of the eccentric was located between the center of the entire universe (which was the same as the Earth’s center) and the stars of Gemini in our age. Conversely, in my Master’s hypotheses, the center of the "great circle" <note>The Earth's orbit around the Sun</note>—which we referred to at the beginning of our Account as the center of the eccentric—is found between the Sun (the center of the universe for my Master) and the stars of Sagittarius. The diameter of this great circle falling upon the center of the Earth represents the line of the Sun’s mean motion. Since the line projected from the center of the Earth through the center of the Sun into the ecliptic determines the Sun’s true position, it is not obscure how the Sun is thought to move unequally under the ecliptic according to the tradition of Ptolemy and the Moderns, and how the angle of diversity from the mean motion is investigated geometrically. While the Earth exists at the highest point <term>apsis<gloss>the point in an orbit farthest from or nearest to the center</gloss></term> of the great circle, the Sun is believed to occupy the position of the apogee in the eccentric; conversely, while the Earth lingers at the lowest point, the Sun is seen in the perigee.

<margin>Apparent motion in the fixed stars, and the variation of the obliquity of the ecliptic.</margin>
But truly, the reason why the fixed stars seem to move away from the equinoctial and solstitial points, and why the maximum obliquity <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis</note> of the Sun varies, etc.—which I deduced at the start of this Account from Book III of my Master's work—my Master has concluded that these depend on the motion of declination (which we proposed generally) and upon two mutually occurring <term>librations<gloss>swinging or oscillating motions like a pendulum</gloss></term>. From the poles of the ecliptic—which, as was said not long ago, are equidistant—let 23 degrees and 40 minutes of a great circle be counted out on both sides. There, let two points be noted which represent the poles of the mean equinoctial, and as is fitting, let two colures be designated distinguishing the mean solstices and equinoxes.

<margin>The third motion of the earth, or rather the fourth.</margin>
These things should certainly be conceived for the sake of learning, and let them be sketched on the small sphere containing the globe of the Earth, by whose uniform motion the third motion (which is indeed attributed to the Earth) happens. With the center of the Earth lingering between the Sun and the stars of Virgo, let the mean equinoctial be reflected or tilted toward the Sun, and let the line of the Sun’s true position pass through the common section of the plane of the ecliptic, the mean equinoctial, and the colure distinguishing the mean equinoxes. This is done so that it is the mean vernal equinox and simultaneously the true vernal equinox, where the logic of the motions will demand it so, as will clearly be established from what follows. From this place, as the center of the Earth proceeds by a uniform motion relative to the fixed stars each day by 59 minutes, 8 seconds, and 11 thirds, the mean vernal point completes the same amount in precedence over the center of the Earth, and moving with a slightly faster pace, describes a larger angle by nearly 8 thirds. And this is the cause why we said earlier that the motion of declination was nearly equal to the uniform motion of the Earth’s center toward the fixed stars. But as the angle increases thereafter—which is designated from the vernal point of the mean equinoctial over the center of the Earth (according to the rule already set down)—before the center of the Earth [returns] to the place of the ecliptic from which it departed,

# N A R R A T I O N

<margin>These are properly described on the Earth and secondarily in the heavens.</margin>
The Arctic circles, horizons, meridians, and all other circles belonging to the doctrine of the first motion <note>The daily rotation of the celestial sphere</note>—vertical circles, circles of altitude, parallels, colures, and so on—are properly designated on the globe of the Earth and are referred to the heavens through a certain relationship. However, among those things which appear to happen concerning the Sun (besides the daily appearance of its revolution around the Earth, which it has in common with all the stars and the remaining planets, and which Ptolemy and more recent astronomers attributed to the Sun’s own motions), there also occur to it those things which are found to happen concerning the changes of the solstitial and equinoctial points, the distances of the stars from these points, and the variations of the apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center</note> from the fixed stars. All these things present themselves to our eyes exactly as if the Sun and the sphere of the stars were moving; for the reasons why they are commonly believed to emerge or rise in the east and gradually be elevated above the horizon until they reach the meridian—from which they descend in like manner, then pass through the lower hemisphere, and complete their daily revolutions day by day—are found to have sufficiently evident causes from the first motion, which my Master <note>Nicolaus Copernicus</note> attributes to the Earth following Plato.

<margin>By the second motion of the Earth, the Sun appears to move through the zodiac.</margin>
Furthermore, the fact that the Sun appears to us to progress according to the sequence of the signs <note>The order of the Zodiac signs</note>, and that we persuade ourselves it describes the ecliptic with such a motion and establishes the annual time, can happen through the second motion which my Master attributes to the Earth. For while the Earth is carried in its "great circle" and stays between the stars of Libra and the Sun, we—who indeed think the Earth stands still—will believe that the Sun occupies the constellation of Aries; for a line drawn from the center of the Earth through the Sun into the sphere of the stars will fall upon the constellation of Aries. Then, as the Earth progresses toward Scorpio, the Sun will be seen to seek Taurus, and in this manner to pass through the Zodiac, even though we establish that this motion belongs to it while the Sun itself is at rest. And the sidereal year will be the time in which the center of the Earth (or the Sun in appearance) revolves once from the same star back to the same star.

<margin>The third motion of the Earth is the cause of the changes in the parts of the year on Earth.</margin>
<margin>The equinoctial is oblique to the ecliptic. From this, the other circles are inscribed on the Earth.</margin>
The third motion of the Earth produces certain and ordered successions of the seasons throughout the whole world; for through this motion it happens that the Sun and the remaining planets appear to be carried in a circle oblique to the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note>, and the relationship of the Sun to each tract of the Earth is the same as it would have been if the Earth occupied the center of the universe by hypothesis and the planets moved in an oblique circle. For since the plane of the equinoctial, because of the motion of its poles (as has been said), is reflected and declines from the plane of the ecliptic in comparison to the Sun—or, as the Greeks say, <term>is tilted</term> <note>original: λοξόεται</note> or <term>inclined</term> <note>original: ἢ ἐγκλίνει</note>—under almost the same places of the ecliptic, the same declination of the equinoctial returns from the ecliptic, and the poles of the daily revolution themselves always remain under nearly the same position of the sphere of the stars. Next, at the maximum declinations of the equinoctial from the plane of the ecliptic toward the Sun, a line going out from the center of the Sun to the center of the Earth dissects the globe of the Earth (which is turned about by its daily revolution) in a conic section and describes the tropics. <margin>Tropics:</margin> <margin>Equinoxes.</margin> Furthermore, when the plane of the equinoctial is most reflected from the plane of the ecliptic toward the Sun, the equinox occurs throughout the entire Earth, since the globe of the Earth is cut into two hemispheres at the equinoctial by the aforementioned line. <margin>Remaining parallels of the days.</margin> But the remaining parallels of the days on Earth are marked as the reflection and declination (or, to use Ptolemy's words, <term>inclination or slanting</term> <note>original: λοξωσις ἢ ἐγκλισις</note>) of the equinoctial toward the Sun mingle together. <margin>Arctic and Antarctic circles.</margin> The Arctic and Antarctic circles, truly, are described by the points touching the horizons. But the polar circles to my Master <note>Nicolaus Copernicus</note>...

# T H E  F I R S T <note>original: "PRIMA", referring to the *Narratio Prima* or First Account</note>

<margin>Polar circles.</margin>
<margin>Colures.</margin>
The polar circles are described around the poles of the equator, equidistant from the poles of the ecliptic <note>The ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun; the poles of the equator and ecliptic are tilted relative to each other</note>. On the globe of the Earth, the great circle passing through the poles of the equator and the aforementioned poles equidistant from the ecliptic will be the **colure of the solstices** <term>colure: one of two principal meridians of the celestial sphere</term>; another circle, intersecting this one at right angles at the poles of the equator, will take the place of the **colure of the equinoxes**. In this manner, one understands that the specific circles of any given location—or as many others as one likes—can easily be inscribed upon the Earth, and from there, projected back toward the sky extended above.

<margin>How Copernicus demonstrates the apparent motion of the Sun.</margin>
Furthermore, because the globe of the Earth has moved out into the circumference of the eccentric <note>An "eccentric" is an orbital circle whose center is not the Sun itself, used to explain why seasons have different lengths</note> due to the command of observations, the Sun has taken its seat in the center of the universe. In the common <note>Ptolemaic/Geocentric</note> hypotheses, the center of the eccentric was located between the center of the entire universe (which in those systems was the same as the Earth) and the stars of **Gemini** in our age. Conversely, in my Master’s <note>Copernicus's</note> hypotheses, the center of the **Great Circle** <term>Great Circle: the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun</term>—which at the beginning of our *Narration* we understood to be the center of the eccentric—is found between the Sun (the center of the universe for my Master) and the stars of **Sagittarius**. Since the diameter of the Great Circle passing through the center of the Earth corresponds to the line of the Sun’s mean motion, and the line drawn from the center of the Earth through the center of the Sun into the ecliptic determines the Sun’s true position, it is not obscure how the Sun is estimated to move unequally beneath the ecliptic according to the tradition of Ptolemy and the more recent astronomers, and how the angle of diversity from the mean motion is investigated geometrically. When the Earth is at the highest aphelion <note>original: "abside," the highest point of the orbit</note> of the Great Circle, the Sun is believed to occupy the position of the **apogee** in the eccentric; conversely, when the Earth lingers at the lowest point, the Sun itself is seen in the **perigee**.

<margin>Apparent motion in the fixed stars, and the variation of the obliquity of the ecliptic.</margin>
<margin>Third motion of the Earth, or rather the fourth.</margin>
But indeed, by what reason the fixed stars appear to move away from the equinoctial and solstitial points, and why the maximum obliquity <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis</note> of the Sun varies, etc.—which I deduced at the start of this *Narration* from my Master's Book III—my Master has concluded that these depend on the **motion of declination** (which we proposed generally) and on two **librations** <term>libration: a slow swinging or oscillating motion</term> that run counter to each other. From the poles, which are equidistant from the poles of the ecliptic (as was said not long ago), let 23 degrees and 40 minutes of a great circle be counted on both sides; let two points be noted there to represent the poles of the **mean equator**, and as is fitting, let two colures be designated to distinguish the mean solstices and equinoxes. These things are certainly conceived and sketched for the sake of learning on a small sphere containing the globe of the Earth, through whose uniform motion the **third motion**—which is indeed attributed to the Earth—occurs. While the center of the Earth stays between the Sun and the stars of **Virgo**, the mean equator is reflected or tilted toward the Sun, and the line of the true position of the Sun passes through the common intersection of the plane of the ecliptic, the mean equator, and the colure distinguishing the mean equinoxes. This occurs so that it is the mean vernal equinox and simultaneously the true vernal equinox, where the logic of the motions will require it, as will be clearly established from what follows. From this position, as the center of the Earth proceeds with a uniform motion relative to the fixed stars at a rate of 59 minutes, 8 seconds, and 11 thirds <note>Standard Babylonian-style sexagesimal units of time/arc</note> each day, the mean vernal point completes the same amount in the preceding direction upon the center of the Earth, and moving with a slightly faster pace, describes a larger angle by about 8 thirds. And this is the reason why we said before that the motion of declination is nearly equal to the uniform motion of the center of the Earth relative to the fixed stars. But as the angle designated from the vernal point of the mean equator over the center of the Earth (according to the rule already set down) increases continuously, before the center of the Earth returns to the place in the ecliptic from which it departed...

...if it [the Earth] returns again, the line of the Sun’s true position will fall upon the mean equinox; and the stars will appear to us to move forward in order by some mean or uniform motion, according to the rate of anticipation. This anticipation, as I said at the start, is approximately 50 seconds in an Egyptian year <note>A year of exactly 365 days, used by ancient and early modern astronomers for ease of calculation</note>, and in 25,816 Egyptian years it grows into a complete revolution. It is clear, therefore, what the mean equinox is, what uniform precession is, and how these things can be presented to the eyes as if by a mechanical model.

<margin>
How
Librations
are made.
Copernicus, Book 3,
Chapter 4.
</margin>
On librations <note>An oscillatory motion where a point moves back and forth along a straight line</note>. Let there be a determined straight line AB—for example, 24 minutes—and let this be divided into two equal parts at point C. Then, with one foot of a compass placed at C, let a circle DE be described with a radius CD toward A of 6 minutes (that is, a fourth part of the whole line). Let two small circles of the same size be made of other material (if I may speak thus for now) and arranged so that one is applied to the circumference of the other, each being able to move around its own center. Let the one that carries the other on its circumference be called the "first" circle, and let it be fixed to the center of line AB at point C. Let the center of the second small circle be marked F, and let a point G be marked anywhere on its circumference as desired. 

Now, if point G of the second small circle is applied to A (the end of the assumed line) and its mark D, and in an equal time G describes an angle in one direction about the center F that is double the angle described by F about C in the opposite direction; it is clear that in one revolution of the first small circle, point G has traversed the line AB twice, and the second small circle has revolved twice. Because by such a description of a straight line through two combined circular motions <note>This mechanism is known today as a "Tusi couple"</note>, point G moves slowest near the ends A and B, but more rapidly in the middle around C, it pleased the Master <note>original: "D. præceptori," referring to Copernicus</note> to call such a motion of point G along the line AB a "Libration."

<margin>
Libration.
Book 3, Chapter
3. Motion along
the diameter.
</margin>
This motion is a motion along a diameter: for by imagining a circle whose diameter is AB with center C, from the theory of chords <note>An early form of trigonometry</note>, whatever position point G is in along the same diameter AB by the combined motion I described, the line GC is established as the half-chord of twice the arc HA, cutting the diameter AB at G. 

<margin>
Book 3,
Chapter 4.
</margin>
From this, the table of <term>prosthaphaereses; the corrections added or subtracted to a "mean" or average position to find the "true" position</term> is constructed according to the length AG. The Master calls the motion of the first small circle about C the <term>Anomaly; the angular distance of a planet from its starting point in its orbit</term>, for it is by that motion that the correction is determined. 

Indeed, let center F of the second small circle, moving to the left from point D on the circumference of the first circle, describe an angle (the angle DCF) of, for example, 30 degrees. There, in the circumference of circle AB, a line CFH projected from center C will contain an arc AH of the same number of degrees, similar to arc DF of the first small circle.

### FIRST. 125

...which from the center is 1000, specifically as far as G is from A on the diameter AB. If, however, 60 is presupposed from B, then GA will be 4 of such units and GB 56. <margin>The first libration, by which the variation of the obliquity of the Ecliptic is demonstrated.</margin>
Having understood these things in a broad and general way <note>original: "παχυτέρᾳ sane Μέση" (more roughly or generally)</note>, it will be easy to understand how the maximum <term>obliquity: the angle between the Earth's equator and the plane of its orbit</term> of the equator varies from the plane of the ecliptic, and how the true precession of the equinoxes becomes unequal. At the start (since shorter arcs do not differ perceptibly from straight lines), let it be understood that the pole of the mean equator AB is applied as is appropriate: but let the line AB be an arc of the <term>colure: a great circle on the celestial sphere passing through the poles and the solstices or equinoxes</term> distinguishing the mean solstices, between the northern pole of the mean equator and the adjacent pole of those circles which are equidistant from the poles of the ecliptic. Therefore, B is the limit of the minimum distance of the pole of diurnal revolution (or the Earth's pole) from the pole of the ecliptic, as stated; A, however, is between the same northern pole of the mean equator and the plane of the ecliptic, whence it is the point of the maximum distance of the Earth's pole from the pole of the ecliptic. Furthermore, describe 24 minutes with the line AB by means of two small circles, using a similar mechanism with the southern pole moved, the law of opposition being preserved, as if the world were hanging and changing its maximum declination.

<margin>In the first libration, the Earth's poles on the colure of the mean solstices ascend and descend 24 minutes; thus the inclination of the equator to the ecliptic varies by 24 minutes.</margin>
And let it be assumed that the first small circle completes its revolution in 3434 Egyptian years, and the point from which the beginning of the motion of <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet or the Earth's axis from its starting point in a cycle</term> starts is point A on the circumference of the circle whose diameter is described by the first libration. It will immediately be clear to anyone that if the Earth's poles had no other libration besides this one, and the Earth's poles did not depart from the colure distinguishing the mean solstices, then by such a motion of the Earth's poles only the angle of inclination of the plane of the true equator to the plane of the ecliptic would decrease from A toward C to B because of the progress of its poles; conversely, by completing the other half-cycle from B to C toward A, it would increase. Because of this, no inequality in the precession of the equinoxes would appear.

<margin>The second libration, by which the unequal precession of the equinoctial points is demonstrated.</margin>
Furthermore, since it is established for certain by observations that the true equinoctial points are separated from the mean equinoctial points on either side by 70 minutes at the maximum <term>prosthaphaeresis: the correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the true motion</term>, and that the change in obliquity has a twofold ratio to this: the Master <note>referring to Nicolaus Copernicus, whom the author Rheticus often calls "the Master" or "the Preceptor"</note> set his mind to establishing and introducing a second libration upon that first one. By this libration, the Earth's poles would run out to the "sides of the world" from the colure distinguishing the mean solstices, and they would do so in such a way that the arc ACB of this second libration (or the straight line) constitutes four right angles with the colure distinguishing the mean solstices. But in the north, A occupies the right side of the world and B the left; in the south, however, A occupies the left and B the right; and let the C of this second libration describe those 24-minute lines through the known marks G of the first libration on both sides of AC and B. Finally, let the poles of the Earth be truly fixed to these G marks. And by this second

<margin>...deviating towards the sides of the world, the intersection of the true <term>equinoctial: the celestial equator, representing the projection of Earth’s equator into space</term> with the ecliptic varies by 70 minutes on either side from the mean. Book 3, chapter 7.</margin>
...to be taken, the Master <note>original: "D. Præceptor," a title Rheticus uses for Copernicus</note> established the second <term>libration: a slow, swinging oscillation like a balance</term> as if it reached the mean through the true vernal point; he made it depend on that, especially since in this way the investigation of the <term>prosthaphaeresis: a mathematical correction used to find a true position from a mean or average position</term> is easier. Therefore, line AB will be 140 minutes, and so arranged that *a c* corresponds to the northern line of the second libration; let *c* be placed at the mean vernal point, and let the true vernal point occupy the mark *c*, and let the distance from the center of either of the small circles be 35 minutes. Furthermore, the starting point from which the motion begins is the mean vernal point, from which the true vernal point runs out to the right toward A. The <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet or point from its starting position in its orbit</term> is counted from the highest point of the circle whose diameter the true vernal point describes, which is determined on the circumference of that same circle to the north of the mean <term>colure: one of two great circles that intersect at the celestial poles</term> of the equinoxes.

<margin>Simple anomaly and double anomaly.</margin>
And since in one restoration of the <term>obliquity: the angle between the Earth's equator and its orbital plane</term>, the inequality of the precession is completed twice, the anomaly of this second libration will be completed in 1,717 Egyptian years. For this reason, the anomaly of the obliquity taken from the tables, when doubled, yields the anomaly of the precession; and the former is called the "simple anomaly," while the latter is called the "doubled anomaly."

If only this second libration had to be posited, the angle of inclination between the true equinoctial plane and the ecliptic—which would certainly be worthy of notice—would not vary, as is clear; indeed, all the diversity of appearances occurring would then be detected in the inequality of the precession of the equinox was alone.

<margin>From these two librations, twisted garlands are traced.</margin>
However, with both librations coinciding, the poles of the Earth—meeting each other with motions around the poles of the mean equinoctial as has been said—will trace the shapes of **twisted garlands** <note>original: "corollarum intortarum," a famous metaphor for the complex path the Earth's axis traces in the sky</note>.

<margin>By this other libration, the true length of the solar year is made sometimes shorter, sometimes longer.</margin>
And when the poles of the Earth fall upon the colure distinguishing the mean solstices, the true colure will lie in the same plane as the mean; and the true vernal point will be joined with the mean. Nevertheless, unless the poles of both equinoctials are joined, the planes of the equinoctials and of the colures distinguishing the solstices and equinoxes (both mean and true) will not entirely coincide. When the northern pole stays in the part from C of the second libration toward the right limit A, with the southern pole established at the opposite point, the true equinox follows the mean, and the Sun falls into the mean equinoctial before the true. But when the poles of the Earth switch sides—namely, so that the northern pole holds the left side of the colure of the mean solstices and the southern holds the right side—the true equinox precedes the mean, and the Sun meets with the true equinoctial sooner than with the mean. Furthermore, as the poles of the Earth move forward from A toward B, because the true equinox proceeds as if to meet the Sun, the year measured by the equinoxes decreases for this reason; but from B toward A, as it essentially flees from the Sun, the year measured by the equinoxes increases. And while the poles of the Earth linger around C, a notable increase or decrease of the year is perceived in a shorter space of years.

<margin>The motion of the fixed stars also appears faster or slower from this.</margin>
And since the apparent progression of the fixed stars is gathered from the annual quantity relative to the equinoxes, by that same reasoning, the elongation of the points of the solstices and equinoxes from the fixed stars is observed to be faster or slower in the direction of the preceding signs.

## ADDITION.

### DIAGRAM OF BOTH LIBRATIONS, FOR DEMONSTRATING
### the change in obliquity and of the true intersection
### of the equinoctial with the ecliptic.

<image-desc>A complex astronomical diagram depicting the celestial sphere (ABCD) with the ecliptic and various intersecting circles representing librations. Points are labeled with letters (A-Z, α, β). Lines H-E-I and O-E-P represent two different librations intersecting at a central pole E. Various arcs and circles illustrate the shifts in the equinoctial points and the change in obliquity. Lettered annotations like 'MXFRK' and 'LTGZN' are placed on the circular paths.</image-desc>

Let **A** be the pole of the **Ecliptic** <note>The "ecliptic" is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year.</note>, and **B C D** be the semicircle of the Ecliptic in the middle **Colure** <note>A "colure" is one of the two principal great circles of the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles; here, it refers to the one passing through the solstices.</note> of the solstices. Let **E** be the pole of the **equinoctial** <note>The "equinoctial" is the celestial equator.</note>, **F C G β** be the mean <note>In astronomy, "mean" refers to an idealized, average position, as opposed to the "true" or actual observed position.</note> positions, with the mean equinox at **C**, and the mean **obliquity** <note>Obliquity refers to the angle of the Earth's tilt relative to its orbit.</note> at **B F**, or **A E**, which is 23 degrees and 40 minutes. Of the first **libration** <note>A "libration" is a slow, swinging oscillation, similar to the movement of a balance scale.</note>, by which the pole of the true equinoctial recedes from the mean **E**, let the arc or straight line be **H E I**, an arc of the colure of the solstices, and its quantity be 24 minutes. By this, therefore, the true obliquity is changed. For when the true pole is at **H**, the true equinoctial is **K C L**; but with the same pole at **I**, the equinoctial is **M C N**, whose obliquity there is 23 degrees 52 minutes, and here 23 degrees 28 minutes. Furthermore, let the line (or quasi-line) of the second libration be **O E P**, an arc of the colure of the equinoxes, and its quantity be 56 minutes. By this, the true intersection of the true equinoctial and the ecliptic—and the true beginning of the Zodiac, from which the series of signs and the motions of the stars are numbered—is varied. For when the true pole is at **P**, the true intersection of the equinoxes is at **S**, but when it is at **O**, it is at **T**; this arc **S T**, according to Copernicus, is 2 degrees 20 minutes, for that amount corresponds to the line **O P** in obliquity. Furthermore, these librations combine these diversities among themselves under this condition:

1. When the true pole is at **E**, placed in the middle of both librations, the true equinoctial coincides with the mean at **F C G**.
2. From **E**, the true pole tends toward both **H** and **P**, though with an unequal pace; for the libration of the equinoxes along **O P** is double the libration of the obliquity along **I H**, because the former is asserted by Copernicus to be completed in 1,717 years, and the latter in 3,434 years. Therefore, when the true pole reaches **P**, the other libration will cause it to stand between **E** and **H**. Wherefore, by the combined motion, the true pole is carried away to **Q**, and it twists the true equinoctial into **R S T**, whose obliquity is not yet at its maximum, but the intersection with the ecliptic is furthest from the mean, namely at **S**.
3. As the true pole returns from **Q** (as if from **P**) toward **E**, and simultaneously ascends further into **E H**, it is carried to **H** by the guidance of both librations and the combined motion. From this, the true equinoctial **K C L** is owed to it, which, having the maximum obliquity near **B K**, again intersects the ecliptic at the mean equinox **C**.
4. In like manner, the same true pole returns from **H** to **E**, and exiting from **E** toward **O**, is restored again to **E**. For just as it had arrived at **H** from **Q**, so now it departs into **β**. In which place the true equinoctial is **X Y Z**, corresponding from the opposite side to the equinoctial **R S T**.
5. Both librations afterward restore the same pole to **E**, and the true equinoctial to **F C G**. At this time, therefore, the entire variation of the equinoxes is completed, but only half of the change in obliquity, because the true pole has gone out from **E** to both its boundaries **P** and **O**, but only to one of the other's boundaries, **H**, and has returned to **E**. Whence the true equinoctial point, having been translated from **C** into **S** and **T**, has returned to **C**, and the true obliquity, having been led down from **F** into **K**, is united with **F** again. And the path of the true pole from the combined motion was the half-crown **E Q H β E**. A very similar ratio of variations is produced as the pole proceeds through the other half of the crown, **E α I V E**. For from **α** the true equinoctial is restored in **X S Z**; from **I**, in **M C N**; from **V** in **X Y Z**, until, this period also being completed, it returns to **E**. And at this time all the variation of the equinoxes **E S C T C** is completed, and the other half of the obliquity **F M F**. From these things it can be seen that the obliquity decreases from **K** to **M**, and increases from **M** to **K**. Next, that when the true equinoctial point goes from **S** to **T** (if the precession of the mean equinox **C** is understood to occur toward **B** and then **D**), the true precession is retarded; for which reason the motion of the fixed stars appears slower, and the magnitude of the Solar Year is prolonged. On the contrary, when the same point tends from **T** to **S**, the true precession becomes swift, and the motion of the fixed stars appears more rapid, and the turning Solar Year is notably shortened.

The progress of the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> itself under the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note> depends on the movement of the center of the small circle and the center of the <term>Great Orb</term><note>original: "Orbis magni"; in the Copernican system, this refers to the Earth's orbital path around the Sun.</note> in a uniform motion along the circumference of the small circle. The diameter of the Great Orb, or the ecliptic, passing through the centers of the Sun and the small circle, is the line of the mean <term>apsides</term><note>The points of greatest or least distance in an orbit.</note> of the Sun; but the diameter through the centers of the Sun and the Great Orb is the line of the true apsides. Just as the center of the Great Orb is found between the Sun and the place in the ecliptic where the Sun is believed to hold its perigee, so similarly the center of the small circle is established between the position of the mean perigee and the Sun. In the time of Ptolemy, the line of true apsides was terminated on both sides by the first star of Aries at 57 degrees and 50 minutes at the place of the apparent apogee, and at 237 degrees and 50 minutes for the perigee; however, the mean apsides were at 60 degrees and 16 minutes and the opposite point at 240 degrees and 16 minutes. For the center of the Great Orb had moved from the highest point of the small circle, at a distance of nearly 21 and one-third degrees from the center of the Sun, in <term>precedence</term><note>Moving "in precedence" or "in antecedentia" means moving westward, opposite the usual order of the zodiac signs.</note>; indeed, it moved by the same amount in that time as the simple <term>anomaly</term><note>The angular distance of a planet from its apogee.</note>, which is also that of the obliquity. But as the center of the small circle proceeds uniformly over the center of the Sun, and the center of the Great Orb proceeds on the circumference of the small circle, the highest <term>apsis</term> of the Sun was seen, at the time of the observation made by the <term>Master</term><note>original: "D. Præceptor"; a respectful reference to Nicolaus Copernicus.</note>, to hold 69 degrees and 25 minutes from the first star of Aries. Furthermore, the <term>eccentricity</term><note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> of the Great Orb—or of the Sun's eccentric, if one prefers to speak that way—which for Ptolemy was one-twenty-fourth part of its distance from the center of the Great Orb, in our age reaches nearly one-thirty-first part, as the observations in <margin>Copernicus, Book 3, Chapter 16.</margin> show; and once the Master's hypotheses are established, this is easily deduced by applying mathematical demonstration.

The change in the eccentricity of the Sun, or the Great Orb, also varies the eccentricities of the other planets.

How the eccentricities of the five planets are varied because of the motion of the center of the Great Orb in the small circle, as we proposed in the causes for renewing the hypotheses, can be understood without great effort. <margin>
In Saturn, this variation is not noticeable because of the magnitude of its orbit.
</margin>
In Saturn, since even the entire diameter of the small circle has no very perceptible relation to the distance from the center of its deferent (because Saturn is carried first beneath the starry orb), observations will not be able to suggest any variation in Saturn's eccentricity.

Next, because Jupiter's apogee stands nearly a quadrant away from the Sun's apogee, today, because of the progression of the center of the Great Orb, no sensible change in its eccentricity is detected, even though there would be a notable and perceptible ratio of the small circle's diameter to the distance from the center of its own orb. And this is the reason why in Mercury, too, no change of eccentricity is felt, since it similarly encloses the side of the Sun's apogee with its own apogee.

<meta>This page continues Rheticus’s defense of the Copernican system.
