<margin>
How he was accustomed to proceed in these astronomical matters.
</margin>
...to proceed to his own conclusions, and to weigh by what reasoning all things agree among themselves. Furthermore, those sound consequences which he gathered there, led by Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy</note>, he referred back to the <term>hypotheses</term><note>In this context, a "hypothesis" is a fundamental mathematical model used to explain celestial movements.</note> of Ptolemy and the Ancients. And after he found that those same models—weighing them with the greatest care—had to be set aside because of astronomical necessity <note>original: "anagke," meaning a compelling force or logical requirement</note> (and indeed not without Divine inspiration and the will of the Gods), he assumed new hypotheses. Then, applying Mathematics, he established geometrically what could be deduced from such sound consequences. Finally, he reconciled both the observations of the Ancients and his own to these assumed hypotheses: And thus, after all those labors were exhausted, he finally wrote down the laws of Astronomy.

<margin>
Another Comparison.
</margin>
In this way, I think Plato should be understood: that the Mathematician investigating the motions of the stars is most rightly compared to a blind man, who, with only his staff as a guide, must complete a great, infinite, slippery journey entangled in infinite detours. What will happen? Walking for a while with anxiety, searching for the way with his staff, and sometimes leaning upon it in despair, he will call upon heaven, earth, and all the Gods to come to his wretched aid. God will permit this man to test his own strength for some years, so that he may finally understand that he cannot be freed from instant danger by his staff alone. Furthermore, when he is just about to lose heart, God takes pity on him and stretches out a hand, leading him by the hand to the desired goal. The "staff" of the Astronomer is Mathematics itself, or Geometry, by which he first dares to test and set foot upon the path. For what are the strengths of human intellect compared to investigating these divine things so far removed from us? What are our clouded eyes? Therefore, unless God out of his kindness has instilled "Heroic impulses" in him, and led him by the hand (as it were) through a journey otherwise incomprehensible to human reason, I would hardly believe the Astronomer to be any better or more fortunate than that blind man—except that, sometimes trusting in his own wit and showing divine honors to that staff of his, he will congratulate himself that Urania herself has been called back from the Underworld. But when he rightly considers the matter with himself along the way, he will feel he is no more blessed than Orpheus, who indeed in his mind saw his Eurydice following him as he ascended from the Underworld full of joy; but afterward, when he reached the mouth of Avernus <note>A crater in Italy believed to be the entrance to the Underworld</note>, just when he most hoped he had her, she slipped from his sight back to the depths and vanished.

<margin>
Anticipating an Objection.
</margin>
Let us consider then, as we began, the hypotheses of my Master and Teacher <note>Nicolaus Copernicus</note> regarding the remaining planets, to see whether, with a constant spirit and with God leading the way, he has brought Urania back to the world above and restored her to her dignity. Someone might perhaps try to evade those things said about the motion of the Earth regarding the apparent motions of the Sun and Moon, although I do not see how he could transfer the logic of the <term>precession</term><note>The slow "wobbling" of the Earth's axis that changes the positions of stars over centuries.</note> to the sphere of the Fixed Stars. Indeed, if anyone wishes to look at the apparent motions of the remaining planets—either for the principal goal of Astronomy and the logic and harmony of the system of spheres, or for the ease and elegance found everywhere when the causes of appearances are brought to light—he could demonstrate them no more conveniently or correctly than by these assumed hypotheses. So much so that all these things appear to be most beautifully linked together like a "golden chain"; and each of the planets, in its own position and its own order and in every diversity of its motion, bears witness that the Earth moves, while we—because of the various positions of the terrestrial globe to which we cling—believe that they wander in various ways
<margin>
Ecclesiastes 3.
</margin>
by their own motions. And indeed, if it is true anywhere else...

### THE FIRST ACCOUNT.

...to see how God has left the world to our debates, which is certainly most conspicuous in this place. Nor do I think anyone can be moved by the fact that God allows Ptolemy and other outstanding heroes <note>By "heroes," Rheticus refers to the great astronomers of antiquity.</note> to disagree in this part, since this is not the kind of opinion that Socrates calls "destructive to men" in the *Gorgias* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue *Gorgias*, where Socrates discusses the danger of false beliefs regarding the soul and justice; Rheticus argues that astronomical errors are not morally ruinous.</note>. Neither the art itself [astronomy] nor that divining power flowing from it will suffer ruin because of this.

<margin>*How and on what occasion the hypotheses of the Ancients arose.*</margin> The Ancients attributed all the diversity of motion, which they found the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> to have in relation to the Sun, to their own epicycles <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent).</note>. Then, when they saw that the remaining apparent inequality in these same planets could by no means be caused by the calculation of the eccentric alone, and the calculation in the computation of those motions—following the pattern of the hypotheses of Venus—agreed with experience and observations, they thought that such a reason for the second apparent inequality should also be assumed, just as they concluded Venus had from demonstrations. Namely, just as in Venus, so the center of each planet's epicycle would move equidistant from the center of the eccentric, but would obtain equality of motion with respect to the **equant center** <term>equant</term><note>A mathematical point used by Ptolemy to account for the observed speed changes of planets; it was controversial because it violated the principle of perfectly uniform circular motion.</note>, toward which point the planet itself also had a relation by its own motion in the epicycle, departing equally from the mean apogee. However, just as Venus completed its revolutions by its own peculiar motion in the epicycle, but proceeded by the mean motion of the Sun by reason of the eccentric, they conversely looked to the Sun in the epicycle, but were carried by peculiar motions in the eccentric. The observations themselves, as they established them, required this while they strove to keep the Earth in the middle of the universe. But besides those things they judged appropriate for saving the appearances of Venus, they thought the theory of Mercury required another place for the equant, and that the center itself, from which the epicycle was equidistant, should be revolved in a small circle.

<margin>*Defects of the ancient hypotheses in the motion of longitude.*</margin> These things were discovered quite sharply, as are almost all the inventions of the Ancients, and they are consistent enough with the motions and appearances—if we admit that the celestial spheres have inequality [speed variation] over their own centers (which nature, however, abhors) and if we attribute to the planets as their own the first and most notable diversity of apparent motion of the five planets, when it is established that it appears in them through an accidental cause <note>Rheticus argues that the "backward" motion of planets is an illusion (an accident) caused by the Earth's own motion, rather than a physical movement of the planet itself.</note>. 

In the latitudes of the planets, the Ancients also seem to neglect that <margin>*Defects of the same in the motion of latitude.*</margin> **axiom** <term>axiom</term><note>original: "ἀξίωμα" (axioma). The fundamental principle that celestial motions must be perfectly circular or composed of circles.</note> that all motions of celestial bodies are either circular or composed of circles—unless perhaps someone wants it to be understood that the reflections and declinations of Venus and Mercury occur (as was said a little while ago about the motion of the Earth's declination) and the declinations of the epicycles in the three superior planets, and the deviations in the inferior planets, happen through the motion of **librations** <term>librations</term><note>A back-and-forth oscillation or swaying motion, used here to describe the tilting of planetary orbits.</note>. Even if this is granted in the reflections and declinations of Venus and Mercury, since the angles of their inclinations, the eccentric planes, and the epicycles remain the same everywhere, common calculation nonetheless refutes that the declinations of the epicycles in the three superior planets and the deviations of Venus and Mercury occur through librations. To speak only of the deviations, they researched and established the "proportional minutes" by which we reason out the deviations for the locations of the epicycle center outside the nodes and apsides, by the same reasoning as in the doctrine of the first motion of the parts of the ecliptic's declination-

### ACCOUNT

<margin>
Book 3, proposition 21 of the *Epitome* of Ptolemy’s *Almagest*. <note>The *Epitome* was a standard textbook by Peuerbach and Regiomontanus that summarized Ptolemy's work.</note>
</margin>
...they are investigated by inclination: it happens that at the sixtieth degree from any of the apsides <term>apsides: the points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center</term> of the eccentric, with the center of the epicycle of Venus being present, we find a deviation of 5 minutes. For Mercury, however, it is 22 and a half minutes. But if the carrying circle <term>deferent: the large circular path that carries a smaller epicycle</term> were set to deviate by librations <term>libration: a slow rocking or oscillatory motion</term>, in such a position of Venus's epicycle, a true calculation would require no more than a 2 and a half minute deviation, and for Mercury, 11 and a quarter minutes. For in that position of the center of the epicycle, the angle of inclination of the plane of the eccentric to the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the Sun's apparent path across the sky</term> would be found to be no greater than 5 minutes for the former, and 22 and a half for the latter, according to the specific nature of the motion of the librations. Yet perhaps Johannes Regiomontanus <note>A famous 15th-century astronomer whose work was essential to both Columbus and Copernicus.</note> thought scholars should be warned that the calculation in latitudes is only approximately true.

<margin>
What would Rheticus have done if he had noticed that Geometry of God regarding the 5 regular bodies, about which Master Kepler discusses? <note>This marginal note is anachronistic; Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) published his work on the five regular solids long after Rheticus wrote this in 1540. It likely comes from a later editor or reader.</note>
</margin>
Finally, since men by their nature desire to know—as Aristotle shows in several places—it is not a burden to the fates that the causes of the "phenomena" <note>original Greek: *τῶν Φαινομένων*, referring to the observed appearances of the stars</note> are never quite so hidden and wrapped in Cimmerian darkness <note>A classical metaphor for total, eternal darkness</note> as Ptolemy himself testifies along with us. Meanwhile, I will not bring forward more about the hypotheses of the Ancients regarding the five planets than perhaps either the enumeration of the "new" (as I may call them) hypotheses or the comparison to the Ancients requires. Indeed, I love Ptolemy and those who follow him as much as I love my Teacher <note>Rheticus’s respectful title for Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> from my heart; since I always keep in view and memory that holy precept of Aristotle: "It is necessary to love both, but to be persuaded by the truer ones" <note>original Greek: *Φιλειν μὲν ἀμφοτέρους, πείθεσθαι δὲ τοῖς ἀληθεστέροις δεῖ*</note>. Although I know not how, I feel myself more inclined toward the hypotheses of my Teacher. This happens perhaps partly because I am finally bringing myself to understand more correctly that most sweet saying attributed to Plato for its gravity and truth: "God always geometrizes" <note>original Greek: *Τὸν Θεὸν ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖν*</note>; and partly because, in my Teacher's restoration of astronomy, with the mist dispersed and the sky now open and seen with "both eyes" (as the saying goes), I behold the force of that most wise saying of Socrates in the *Phaedrus*: "If I think anyone else is able to see things that are by nature one and many, I follow behind him in his footsteps, as if he were a God" <note>original Greek: *ἐάν τέ τινα ἄλλον ἡγήσωμαι δυνατὸν εἰς ἓν καὶ ἐπὶ πολλὰ πεφυκότα ὁρᾷν, τοῦτον διώκω κατόπισθε μετ' ἴχνιον, ὥστε Θεοῖο*</note>.

<margin>
Through one Great Orb, the appearances of the 5 planets which they have in relation to the Sun are demonstrated. The rest are proper to themselves. Hypotheses of the motions of the five planets according to longitude.
</margin>
Thus, having confirmed these things which my Teacher has said so far concerning the motion of the Earth, it follows (just as we reported in the reasons for renewing the hypotheses) that all the diversity of the apparent motion of the planets, which seems to happen in them "because of their configurations relative to the Sun" <note>original Greek: *παρὰ τὰς πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον σχηματισμὸς*</note>, occurs because of the annual motion of the Earth in the Great Orb <term>Great Orb: *Orbis Magnus*, Copernicus's term for the Earth's orbit around the Sun</term>; and so the planets in truth still proceed only with that other inequality which is observed according to the parts of the zodiac. For this reason, only those hypotheses by which two diversities of motion can be demonstrated are suitable for them. Just as my Teacher preferred to use an epicycle upon an epicycle for the Moon, so for the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, to demonstrate more conveniently the order and proportion of the motions, he chose eccentric-epicycles; but for Venus and Mercury, he chose eccentric-eccentrics.

->NB. These triple hypotheses—namely, of two epicycles, of eccentric-epicycles, and of the eccentric of centers—are consistent; therefore, one may freely use one or the other of them at will in demonstrating the motions of all the planets.<-

<margin>
The reason why Copernicus refers the centers of the other planets and their motions not to the Sun, the center of the world, but to the center of the Great Orb.
</margin>
However, since we look up at the motions of the three superior planets as if from the center of the Earth, but look upon the revolutions of the inferior planets <note>Venus and Mercury</note> as if they were below us, it was consistent that the centers of the planetary orbits be referred to the center of the Great Orb, from which we then most correctly transfer all motions and appearances to the center of the Earth itself. Therefore, even in the five planets, that eccentric must be understood whose center is outside the center of the Great Orb.

<meta>This page continues Rheticus’s detailed explanation of Nicolaus Copernicus’s new astronomical system. After discussing the difficulties of calculating planetary latitudes in the previous section, Rheticus now outlines the specific geometric models—the "hypotheses"—for the movements of the planets in longitude (along the zodiac), specifically focusing on how Copernicus replaces the Ptolemaic equant with a system of circles to maintain uniform motion.</meta>

<header>FIRST [ACCOUNT].</header>

<margin>
The orbs and motions of the three superior planets. See below in the Appendix.
</margin>
But so that the reasoning for establishing the new hypotheses <term>hypothesis: here, a geometric model used to explain and predict planetary positions</term> may be more correctly understood, and so that everything may finally become more and more clear and open, let us first assume that the planes of the eccentrics <term>eccentric: a circular orbit whose center is offset from the center of the system</term> of the five planets are in the plane of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the Sun’s apparent annual path, or the plane of the Earth's orbit</term>. Let us also assume the centers of the carrying circles <term>deferent: the large circle that carries a smaller epicycle</term> and the equants are located around the center of the Great Orb <term>Great Orb: the Earth’s annual orbit around the Sun in the Copernican system</term>, just as they were around the center of the Earth among the Ancients. Then, let the spaces between the center of the Great Orb and the points—or centers of the equants—be divided into four equal parts. Furthermore, for each of the three superior planets <note>The "superior" planets are those further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, the center of the eccentric should be raised toward the apogee <term>apogee: the point furthest from the center of motion</term> to the third section from the center of the Great Orb. Then, using the length of the remaining fourth section as a radius, let an epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle</term> be described on the circumference of the eccentric; thus the mechanism for the proper motion of each planet in longitude will appear. If, therefore, according to the opinion of my teacher <note>Rheticus always refers to Copernicus as "my teacher" or "the Preceptor."</note>, the planet proceeds in the upper part of this revolving epicycle in the order of the signs <term>in consequentia: moving eastward through the zodiac</term>, and in the lower part against the order of the signs <term>in antecedentia: moving westward</term>, so that when the center of the epicycle is at the apogee of the eccentric, the planet itself is found at the perigee <term>perigee: the point closest to the center of motion</term> of its own epicycle; and conversely, when the center of the epicycle lingers at the perigee of the eccentric, the planet occupies the apogee of the epicycle; and if, by this similarity of motions, the planet on the epicycle completes its revolutions in the same time as the center of the epicycle on the eccentric; it is then clear that once the equants of the superior planets are removed, the variation of motion with respect to the center of the Great Orb is regular and composed of uniform parts. For an epicycle adopted in such a way takes over the function of the equant <note>Copernicus considered the "equant"—a point where motion appears uniform but is not centered on the circle's center—to be a violation of physical principles; he used small epicycles to achieve the same mathematical result through purely uniform circular motion.</note>, and the eccentric around its own center, and the planet on the epicycle around the center of the epicycle to which it is attached, describe equal angles in equal times.

<margin>
The orbs and motions of Venus.
</margin>
The motion of Venus, however, will be established as follows: having rejected the carrying circle (the role of which the Great Orb fulfills), let a small circle be described around the third section, using the length of the remaining fourth section. Then, let the center of the epicycle of Venus—which will here be called the "eccentric of the eccentric," the "second eccentric," and the "movable eccentric"—be moved on the circumference of said circle by this rule: that whenever the center of the Earth falls on the line of the apsides <term>apsides: the line connecting the closest and furthest points of an orbit</term>, the center of the eccentric itself exists at the point of the small circle nearest to the center of the Great Orb. However, when the mean Earth is in its orb between either of the apsides, the center of the eccentric of Venus itself stays at the point of the small circle furthest from the center of the Great Orb, and it moves toward the same parts in the order of the signs just as the Earth moves—completing, however, two revolutions in one circuit of the Earth, as follows from these points.

<margin>
The orbs and motions of Mercury.
</margin>
But the reasoning for the motions of Mercury agrees in general with the theory of Venus, with the addition of an epicycle upon which the planet itself describes a diameter through libration <term>libration: a back-and-forth oscillation along a line</term>, because of the remaining variation. Furthermore, so that it may accommodate itself to the motion of the Earth, it receives a quantity for the radius of the movable carrying circle of 3,573 units. For the eccentricity of the first carrying circle, it has 736 units; the quantity for the radius of the small circle containing the movable center of the carrying circle is 212 units; and the diameter of the said epicycle is 380 units—where the radius from the center of the Great Orb to the center of the Earth is 10,000 units. In its motion, it follows such a law that the center of the movable eccentric is most distant from the center of the Great Orb (contrary to what happened with Venus) when the Earth is on the line of the planet's apsides; and it reaches its maximum proximity when the Earth is a quadrant away from the planet's apsides. It will have, as is evident, a fixed epicycle, whose diameter faces the center...

<meta>This page continues Rheticus’s explanation of the geometric models (hypotheses) used in Copernicus’s system to explain the movements of the planets. On the previous page, he began describing how the motion of a planet on a small secondary circle (epicycle) can be used to simulate a straight-line back-and-forth motion (libration), avoiding the need for the "equant" used by Ptolemy.</meta>

<header>ACCOUNT</header>

...of the immobile carrying circle <note>original: "deferentis inobilis"</note>, the planet itself, by a creeping motion of oscillation <term>libration: a back-and-forth motion along a straight line produced by the combination of two circular motions</term>, describes a straight line, with this rule being observed: that when the center of the movable eccentric <term>eccentric: a circular orbit whose center is not the center of the system</term> is at its greatest distance from the center of the Great Orb <term>Great Orb: the Earth’s annual orbit around the Sun in the Copernican system</term>, the planet holds the perigee <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the center of motion</term> of its epicycle, which is the lower limit of the diameter it describes. Conversely, it reaches the other limit, which could be called the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion</term>, when the same center of the movable eccentric is nearest to the center of the Great Orb.

The motion of the planets' apsides <term>apsides: the two points in an orbit, such as apogee and perigee, where the planet is at its maximum or minimum distance</term>, as well as certain other matters, are reserved for another Account.

<margin>
How the true motions are demonstrated relative to the center of the earth. See below in the Appendix.
</margin>
This is almost the entire reasoning of the hypotheses for explaining every proper variation of the planets' motion in longitude <term>longitude: the position of a planet along the zodiac or ecliptic</term>. Therefore, if our eye were located at the center of the Great Orb <note>In the Copernican system, the center of the Earth's orbit is near the Sun.</note>, the visual rays from it passing through the planets—acting like lines of true motion projected onto the sphere of the stars—would be carried around the ecliptic by the planets in no other way than the ratios of the said circles and motions require, so as to show their proper variations of motion in the Zodiac. But because we inhabitants of the Earth contemplate the apparent motions of the heavens from it, we refer all motions and appearances to its center as if to a base and the intimate home of our dwelling. We do this by drawing lines from Earth's center through the planets, just as if an eye were moved from the center of the Great Orb to the center of the Earth. It is clear that from this perspective, the variations of all the phenomena <note>original Greek: "τῶν φαινομένων"</note>—as they appear to us—must be calculated. However, if one intended to gather the true and proper variations of the planets' motion, this would have to be achieved through lines coming out from the center of the Great Orb, as has been said.

<margin>
The motions of the planets are first computed relative to the center of the Great Orb, then to the center of the earth. Just as in the ancient hypotheses, first to the center of the epicycles, then to the planets themselves.
</margin>
Nevertheless, so that we may more quickly explain from those things that remain to be listed among the phenomena <note>original Greek: "ἐν τοῖς φαινομένοις"</note> of the planets, and so the entire treatment may be easier and more pleasant, let us conceive in our minds not only the lines of the true apparent motions proceeding from the center of the earth through the planets into the ecliptic, but also from the center of the Great Orb—these are called the lines of the motion's "proper variation." 

Thus, as the Earth moves in the motion of the Great Orb, when it arrives at the point where it is placed in the same straight line between the Sun and one of the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, the planet will be seen to rise at sunset. And because the Earth is then at its closest to the planet, the Ancients assumed the planet itself was at its closest point to Earth because it was at the perigee of its own epicycle. But as the Sun approaches the line of the planet's true and apparent position—which happens when the Earth reaches the opposite side of the aforementioned place—the planet begins to disappear at sunset and becomes most distant from the Earth, until the line of the planet's true position also passes through the center of the Sun. Then, with the Sun intervening between the planet and the Earth, the planet is hidden. Following this occultation, because of the perpetual motion of the Earth, the line of the Sun’s true position moves away from the line of the planet's true position. The planet is then seen to rise again in the morning, once it has reached a sufficient distance from the Sun as required by the arc of vision.

<margin>
Description of the mean and true apogee in the epicycle of the ancients, and in the Great Orb of these hypotheses.
</margin>
Furthermore, since in the hypotheses of these three planets the Great Orb performs the office of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one; in the old system, this explained why planets seem to stop and go backward</term> attributed to each planet by the Ancients: on the diameter of the Great Orb, continued as far as the planet, the true apogee and perigee of the planet with respect to the Great Orb will be found. However, the mean apogee and perigee are found on the diameter of the Great Orb which moves parallel to the line drawn from the center of the eccentric to the center of the epicycle...

<meta>This page continues the technical description of how the Earth’s motion in the "Great Orb" (its annual orbit around the Sun) creates the illusion of planetary movements, specifically focusing on why planets seem to move backward at times.</meta>

-> FIRST <-

R 2

<meta>catchword: fourth</meta>

...is moved, and when the Earth is in the half-circle facing the planet, it approaches that planet; in the remaining and opposite half, it moves away. In the former case, the ends of the diameters of the Great Orb <term>Great Orb: the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun in the Copernican system</term> represent the perigees <term>perigee: the point in an orbit where a body is closest to the Earth</term>, while in the latter they represent the apogees <term>apogee: the point in an orbit where a body is farthest from the Earth</term>, since that first half-circle takes the place of the lower part of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term>, and the second half takes the place of the upper part.

<margin>The Point of Direction, Station, and Retrogradation of the Planets.</margin>

<margin>Regarding all of these, see Chapter 1 of the *Precursor* <note>original: "Prodromi," likely referring to a preliminary work or introduction</note>, above on page 15, and the tables on page 18; also below in the appendix.</margin>

<margin>Note regarding Mars: When it is brought closest to the Earth, it allows for parallax <term>parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions</term>, for it becomes closer to the Earth than the Sun itself.</margin>

Suppose that not far from the conjunction <term>conjunction: when two celestial bodies appear close together in the sky</term> of the Sun and a planet, the center of the Earth is in the true position of the planet's apogee relative to the Great Orb, and the line of its proper diversity <note>the line representing the planet's actual eccentricity</note> coincides with the line of the planet's apparent position. As the Earth moves forward from this location, the line of proper diversity and the line of the planet's true position will begin to intersect within the body of the planet. One line will proceed according to its regular, diverse motion in the order of the zodiac signs <note>original: "in signorum consequentiam"</note>, while the other, reflecting away from it, will make it appear to us that the planet is traveling faster along the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the path of the Sun across the sky</term> than it is actually proceeding by its own motion.

However, when the Earth reaches the portion of the Great Orb closer to the planet, the planet immediately appears to turn backward <note>original: "in antecedentia," meaning against the order of the zodiac signs</note>, so that the apparent progress of the planet subsequently seems slower to us. Furthermore, because the Earth "ascends" toward the planet, the line of the Sun's true motion will be advanced by the planet; and the planet will be perceived to approach us, as if descending from a higher region. The planet will continue to appear "direct" <note>moving forward</note> until the center of the Earth reaches a position on the Great Orb where the daily angle of reflection—the line of the planet's true place moving backward—is equal to the daily angle of its proper diversity moving forward. At that point, because the two motions cancel each other out, the planet will appear to stand still for several days (the "first station"). The duration of this depends on the ratio of the Great Orb to the planet's own eccentric circle, the planet's position in its own orbit, and the speed of its motion.

Furthermore, once the Earth has moved even closer to the planet from this point, we are led to believe the planet is regressing and moving backward. This occurs because the reflection significantly exceeds the planet's own motion until the Earth reaches the planet’s true perigee relative to the Great Orb. At this point, the planet is in the middle of its backward journey and stands nearest to the opposition of the Sun and Earth. When Mars is found in this position, in addition to the common reflection (or "parallax of the Great Orb"), it also admits another parallax due to its perceptible proximity—the distance from the Earth's center to the planet—as diligent observation will testify.

## ADDITION.

To confirm this view—which follows from the hypotheses of Copernicus and is extremely contrary to the commonly held theories—it is pleasing to add what the most excellent and noble mathematician, Tycho Brahe, a Dane, observed through his experiments. As observations made by such a highly skilled artist, their reliability certainly cannot be doubted. In a letter given to Dr. Peucer in the year 1588, he writes as follows: *I decided to make a trial of which of those astronomical systems discovered so far (namely the Ptolemaic or common ones, those handed down by Copernicus, or those of the men who devised the fiction of homocentric circles) might approach closer to the truth. At last, with great diligence and no small expense, having acquired various astronomical instruments by which the motions of the stars could be measured centrally—not merely to the minute of a degree, but even to its half or...*

*...as these things could be explored with certainty by a fourth part <note>original: "quarta parte," likely referring to a quadrant or a specific division of an astronomical instrument</note>, I did not fear to undertake this subtle consideration. Having then obtained several accurate observations regarding its rising, its setting, and its transit across the meridian <term>meridian: the imaginary line running north-south through the sky used to measure the highest point of a celestial body's path</term>, I discovered that Mars caused a larger parallax <term>parallax: the apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations; a larger parallax indicates the object is closer</term> than the Sun itself. Therefore, Mars becomes closer to the Earth when it is at its opposite point to the Sun. This occurred because its distance from Earth was smaller, which made its motion appear a little more intense. Since I held this to be sufficiently explored in Mars, and since I had observed the same thing in Venus several times during the day (even at the meridian itself) and confirmed it by comparison at sunset—and indeed by another peculiar method around February 24, 1587, when I saw it within a day or two both in the evening and the morning (which is otherwise very rare)—I proved this by comparing the apparent motion with the effects of parallax. Thus, because all these things did not fit the Ptolemaic hypotheses <note>the Earth-centered system of Claudius Ptolemy</note> at all, I was driven to subsequently attribute more and more faith to the Copernican discovery.*

### A LATER ADDITION.

*I was greatly congratulating myself when I saw this opinion of Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus, Copernicus's only pupil</note> confirmed by the testimony of Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the preeminent observational astronomer of the late 16th century</note>. But later, I read in the book **On the Motion of Mars** (Chapter 11) by Johannes Kepler, the most excellent Imperial Mathematician, that this very observation from the year 1582 was found to be both doubtful and false after it began to be suspected. For after examining all the observations from Tycho's own book—that is, his original manuscript—Kepler saw that Tycho's assistants, whose labor he used for observations and calculations, had deceived both themselves and Tycho through some unknown prejudice. For the calculation of the assistants, when dissected to the quick (as it ought to be), did not provide what it had promised. Instead, it corresponded to Kepler’s own opinion: that the Sun is much further away from the Earth than has been believed until now. From this, it follows that if the star of Mars ever admits any parallaxes, they are neither observable nor sensible. Kepler proves this same point from his own observations, which he adds in that same place. Therefore, my own self-congratulation has collapsed, and this opinion regarding the parallaxes of Mars must be revoked. In the meantime, however, nothing is taken away from the truth itself and the primary question—namely, that Mars sometimes becomes closer to the Earth than the Sun. You, honest reader, should read that 11th chapter and examine it for yourself.*

Finally, when the Earth is moved forward from this central conjunction <term>conjunction: here, the alignment of Earth and the planet</term> with the planet, that reflection <note>the apparent backward motion</note> toward the preceding signs will decrease in the same proportion as it had previously increased. This continues until, once the motions are balanced again, the planet becomes stationary at its "second station." Afterward, as the planet’s own motion overcomes the reflection, it is directed forward, with the Earth preceding it. Eventually, the planet appears in the middle of its "direction" <note>forward-moving phase</note>, and the Earth again reaches the true apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the center</term> of the planet from which we first tracked it. Thus, all the appearances we have mentioned are introduced to us in order for each of the planets.

What the ancients called the "Argument" of a planet, the Copernicans call "Commutation."
</margin>
And this is the first utility of the Great Orb <note>the Earth's orbit around the Sun</note> in the contemplation of the motions of the planets: it frees us from the three large epicycles in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. Furthermore, what the ancients called the "Argument of the Planet," my Teacher <note>likely referring to Copernicus or Rheticus</note> calls the "Motion of Commutation" <term>commutation: the component of a planet's apparent motion caused by the Earth's own movement</term> of the planet. We use this to calculate the appearances occurring by reason of the Earth's motion in the Great Orb. These are nothing other than the parallaxes of the Moon, given the relationship between the center of the Earth and its orbits.

The motion of the center of any planet's epicycle, subtracted from the uniform motion of the Earth (which is also the mean motion of the Sun), leaves the equal motion of commutation. It is numbered from the mean apogee, from which the Earth is also equally distant; from this, the true and apparent motion of any planet is readily available.

# FIRST #

...called <note>original: "ἐγκλίσεις" (enkliseis)</note> **inclinations**, let [this motion] be mixed with these. Whereas others demonstrated this same motion through the center of the <term>deferent: the large circular path that carries a planet or its epicycle</term> of the epicycle of Venus (which has now been removed), my Master <note>The "Master" or "Preceptor" refers to Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> judged that another method, more consistent with observations, should be undertaken. To help us follow this method of the Doctor, my Master, for explaining the **deviation**—and to do so as easily as the other things proposed so far—let us establish that the plane we just mentioned is the **mean plane**, and is therefore fixed. From this fixed plane, the **true plane** wanders now here, now there, according to a certain rule. 

But because all motions are perceived with less labor and effort in respect to the poles, we must first understand that one of the poles of the mean plane is raised toward the north from the plane of the ecliptic <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> by the amount of the angle of inclination, while the other pole is depressed by the same amount toward the south on the opposite side. What we are about to show concerning the northern pole, or things happening around it, should be understood by a similar reasoning regarding the southern pole, naturally accounting for their opposite positions. 

Therefore, let us assume there is a **mobile circle** around the northern pole of the mean plane. The distance from the center of this circle corresponds to the maximum slants of the mean plane away from the true plane. The northern pole of the true plane itself describes the diameter of this circle through a motion of <term>libration: a slow swinging or oscillation, like the movement of a balance scale</term>. 

Furthermore, let this mobile circle follow the planet's motion, so that as Venus proceeds in its own path, it leaves behind either of the two subsequent intersections. It does this by a law such that, after exactly one year, it finally returns to the intersection it left. 

When a <term>great circle: a circle that represents the shortest distance between two points on a sphere</term> is drawn through the poles of both planes, the <term>nodes: the two points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term> or intersections are determined by counting 90 degrees on both sides from where this circle crosses the true plane, at the point where the poles of the true and mean planes differ.

Meanwhile, while Venus completes its period toward either of the nodes, the diameter of the said mobile circle is traversed twice by the pole of the true plane through its oscillating motion. These things occur in such a way that the planet appears to have entered into a **pact** with the center of the Earth: whenever the Earth is at the <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a body is furthest from or closest to its center</term> of the deferent, Venus—wherever it may be in its true deferent—deviates most to the north from the mean plane; that is, it stands furthest outside the mean path. 

Furthermore, when the Earth is a quarter-turn (a quadrant) away from the apsides of the deferent, the planet itself, along with its entire true plane, lies exactly in the plane of the mean deferent. But as the Earth traverses the remaining intermediate places, the planet also holds its course in intermediate deviations. To ensure this "pact" between the Earth and the planet remains perpetual, God ordained that the first small circle of libration (as I may call it) should revolve once in the same time that Venus makes one return to either of the mobile nodes. 

To make these things clearer by an example: if at the beginning of the motion of deviation, the northern pole of the true plane were at its furthest point south from the pole of the adjacent mean plane; and if Venus were at its maximum northern limit of deviation while the Earth’s center stayed at one of the apsides of Venus—then in a quarter of a year, the Earth’s annual motion will bring it to the place halfway between the apsides. At that same time, the planet will reach its intersection or **mobile node**. 

And because the motion of oscillation is synchronized with the motion of the planet toward its nodes, the first small circle of libration will also complete a quarter-turn. Through the other small circle (which is twice as fast as the first), the pole of the true plane will be positioned directly under the pole of the mean plane, whereby both planes will be joined together. But as the planet recedes from this node, the Earth proceeds toward the other apsis of the first eccentric, and the pole of the true plane [continues] through...

It describes a "pact" between Earth's motion and Venus's orbit, where the planet's tilt relative to the ecliptic is perfectly synchronized with Earth's annual position.</summary>

# NARRATIVE #

the <term>libration: a slow back-and-forth oscillation, like the swinging of a pendulum</term> will be moved from the pole of the mean plane toward the north. Thus it will happen that even if Venus is in the south, as in our example, the southern latitude is nevertheless diminished; if she is in the north, it increases. Moreover, at the place where it arrives, the pole of the true plane will reach its maximum northern limit by the motion of the libration, and the planet, by its annual motion toward the <term>nodes: the two points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term>, will again have its maximum northern deviation midway between each intersection. 

It appears, therefore, that the purpose of this assumed circular motion is so that the revolution of Venus toward the nodes occurs within a year. Thus, whenever the Earth is positioned on the line of the <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a planet is closest to or farthest from the sun</term>, the planet will have its maximum deviation from the mean plane, regardless of where it is in its true plane; and when the Earth is positioned midway between the two apsides, it is at the nodes. Furthermore, by the motion of the libration, when Venus is in one of the nodes, both planes are joined; and that part of the true plane which she enters always moves northward from the mean plane. Thus, as is fitting, this latitude remains perpetually northern.

<margin>
Reasons and methods for the latitude of Mercury.
</margin>
Just as the plane of Venus, which we have chosen to call the "mean plane," is intersected by the ecliptic on the line of the first eccentric's apsides—and one half of that plane projects northward from the highest apsis, while the other half turns southward according to the law of opposition—so too in Mercury, by a similar reasoning, there is a mean plane. This plane, as is appropriate, is inclined on both sides from the plane of the ecliptic along the line of its own apsides, so that, conversely, the half of the mean plane extending from the highest apsis is northern in the preceding direction. 

<margin>
Latitudes of declinations and reflections in Mercury.
</margin>
Therefore, in the annual revolution of the center of the Earth, the <term>declinations: the northward or southward distance from the celestial equator</term> and **reflections** in Mercury will be found to be swapped relative to those of Venus. But so that these variations might be even more conspicuous, God arranged the **deviation** of the true plane of Mercury from the mean plane so that the half which the planet enters always moves southward from the mean plane. When the Earth stays at the apsides themselves, the planet lies with its true plane within the mean plane. 

<margin>
Latitude of the same deviation.
</margin>
The result is that, regarding latitude, it has no differences from Venus except for those already mentioned, and the fact that this deviation is greater in Mercury than in Venus, just as it also has a greater angle of inclination. Otherwise, the remaining variations of Mercury’s latitudes are easily gathered in the same way as those of Venus.

> *Part of the labor begun remains, part is exhausted:*
> *Here let the cast anchor hold our ships:*
<note>original: "Pars superat cœpti, pars est exhausta laboris: / Hic teneat nostras ancora iacta rates:" — a quote from Ovid's *Ars Amatoria*</note>

...to finish this first Narrative of ours with the words of the Poet.

As for the second part of my promise, I shall begin to compile it as soon as I have unrolled the entire Work of my Master with the required study. I hope that both will be all the more pleasing to you because you will see how clearly my Master's hypotheses agree with the <note>original: "τοῖς φαινομένοις" (tois phainomenois)</note> **phenomena** <note>the observed facts or appearances of the stars</note> as proposed by the observations of craftsmen—so much so that they can even be converted into one another, like a good definition with the thing defined.

<margin>
Epilogue.
</margin>
Most distinguished and learned Master Schöner, whom I must always honor as a father: it now remains for you to look kindly upon this effort of mine, such as it is. For although I am not unaware of what my shoulders can bear and what they might refuse to carry, nevertheless your singular and (if I may say so) fatherly love for me has ensured that I did not fear to go under this "heaven" and, as far as was possible, to report everything to you. I pray that God, the Best and Greatest, may deign to turn this to good, and breathe favor upon me, so that...

# FIRST #
## NARRATIVE ##

<sig>S 2</sig>

<margin>Copernicus is excused because he departed from the opinion of the ancients not at all out of a desire for novelty or an ostentation of talent (of which he is accused by some without merit), but because the requirements of the facts demanded it.</margin>
...that I may lead the work I have begun by a right path to its proposed end. If, however, anything was said with a certain youthful heat (with which we are always endowed, as the saying goes, with a spirit more great than useful), or if anything slipped out through imprudence that might seem to be said too freely against venerable and holy Antiquity—more than perhaps the magnitude and gravity of these matters required—you will certainly (and of this I have no doubt) take it in the best part. You will look rather at my intention toward you than at what I have actually achieved.

Furthermore, I would wish you to decide this about that most learned man, the Master Doctor <note>Referring to Nicolaus Copernicus</note>, my teacher, and to be most fully persuaded that for him nothing is more primary or more hallowed than to follow in the footsteps of <term>Ptolemy: the 2nd-century Alexandrian astronomer whose geocentric (Earth-centered) model dominated science for 1,400 years</term>. Indeed, he has followed the Ancients and those much older than himself, just as Ptolemy himself did. But while he understood that the <note>original Greek: τὰ φαινόμενα</note> **observations** which guide the astronomer and the mathematical logic were forcing him, he also accepted certain things even against his own will. Meanwhile, he thought it sufficient if he directed his arrows at the same target as Ptolemy with the same art, even if he assumed a bow and arrows made of a far different material than Ptolemy used. In this place, one should seize upon that saying: <note>original Greek: δεῖ δ' ἐλεύθερον εἶναι τῇ γνώμῃ τὸν μέλλοντα φιλοσοφεῖν</note> **"He who intends to philosophize must be free in his judgment."** 

Moreover, as it is alien to the character of any good man, and especially to a philosophical nature, my Master Teacher is so far from such behavior that he would never think of rashly departing from the opinions of the ancient philosophers out of some desire for novelty, unless for great reasons and because the facts themselves demanded it. His age is different, his gravity of character and excellence of learning are different, and finally, the loftiness of his talent and greatness of soul are too great for such a fault to fall upon him. Such things belong instead to youthful age, or to <note>original Greek: τῶν μεγαφρονώντων ἐπὶ θεωρίᾳ μικρᾷ</note> **"those who think great things on the basis of a small observation,"** to use the words of Aristotle; or they belong to fiery talents moved and ruled by any wind and their own passions, so that, as if the pilot were cast out, they seize upon whatever comes their way and defend it most fiercely. 

But let truth prevail, let virtue prevail, let the arts be held in perpetual honor, and let every good Craftsman of his art bring forth into the light what is useful, defending it in such a way that he may be seen to have sought the truth. Nor indeed will my Master Teacher ever shrink from the judgments of good and learned men, which he undergoes voluntarily...

# PRAISE OF PRUSSIA #

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a personification of Fame (Fama) blowing two trumpets, surrounded by scrolls and leafy ornamentation.</image-desc>

Pindar, in that Ode which is said to have been consecrated in golden letters in the temple of Minerva <note>Pindar’s Olympian Ode 7, celebrating the boxer Diagoras of Rhodes</note>, celebrating the Rhodian boxer Diagoras, a victor in the Olympics, says that his homeland was the daughter of Venus and the most beloved wife of the Sun. He adds that Jupiter rained much gold there because the people worshipped his daughter Minerva; for this reason, they were made famous by her in the name of Wisdom and the <term>encyclopedic education: the "circle of learning" or well-rounded education (original Greek: ἐγκυκλοπαιδίας)</term> which they cultivated with great devotion. Whether anyone could more aptly apply this magnificent <term>encomium: a formal expression of high praise (original Greek: ἐγκώμιον)</term> of the Rhodians to any other region in this age of ours than to Prussia (about which I intend to say a few words, as you also happened to wish to hear), I certainly do not see. For as Pindar says:

> The ancient stories of men say
> That when Zeus and the immortals
> Were dividing the earth,
> Rhodes was not yet visible in the open sea,
> But the island lay hidden in the salty depths.
> While the Sun was absent, no one

> And so they left the holy God
> Without an allotment of land.
> When he reminded them, Zeus was about to 
> Cast the lots again, but the Sun 
> Did not allow it, for he said 
> He himself could see a land rising 
> From the floor of the gray sea, 
> A land nourishing for many men, 
> And kindly to cattle.

<margin>Amber in Prussia.</margin>
In the same way, the sea undoubtedly held Prussia in ancient times. And what more certain or immediate sign could one find than the fact that <term>amber: a fossilized resin used in jewelry and medicine (original Latin: succinum)</term> is found today on the mainland, very far from the shore? Therefore, by the same law and as a gift of the gods, having been born from the sea, the land fell to Apollo <note>The Greek god of the Sun, often identified with Helios</note>, whom he now loves as his wife, just as he once loved Rhodes. Can the Sun not reach Prussia with direct rays in the same way as Rhodes? I admit it; but he compensates for this in many other ways. What he provides in Rhodes through the directness of his rays, he achieves in Prussia by his long stay above the horizon. Furthermore, I think no one will deny that amber is a special gift from God, with which He wished to adorn this region in particular. Indeed, if one considers the nobility of amber and the use it has in medicines, one will rightly judge it sacred to Apollo and a remarkable gift of his, with which he presents his wife, Prussia, in great abundance as if with a most precious ornament. And since Apollo, besides the art of medicine and <term>prophecy: the art of foretelling the future (original Greek: μαντικὴν)</term>, which he first discovered and cultivated, also with zeal...

<sig>$ 3</sig>

...since he is also possessed by a love of hunting, it seems that he chose this region above all others. And since he foresaw long ago that the monstrous Turks would devastate his own Rhodes, it does not seem unlikely that he transferred his seat to these parts and migrated here with his sister Diana. For into whatever parts you turn your eyes—if you consider the forests—you would say they were stocked with <margin>game preserves <note>original Greek: ζωάγρια (zoagria)</note></margin> game preserves and apiaries planted by Apollo himself. If you look at the groves and fields, and their rabbit warrens and aviaries; if you look at the lakes, ponds, and springs, you would call them sacred to Diana and the private pools of the Gods. And so it appears that he chose Prussia above other regions as, I say, a paradise of wealth. Besides the stags, fallow deer, bears, wild boars, and other commonly known wild beasts, he brought in the aurochs <note>The aurochs (Latin: urus) was a large, extinct species of wild cattle once common in the European forests.</note>, elks, and bisons, which can scarcely be found in other places. Meanwhile, I shall pass over in silence the many and truly rare kinds of birds, as well as the types of fish.

Furthermore, the "offspring" which Apollo has produced from his "spouse" Prussia are: **Königsberg** <note>Latin: Regius mons; literally "King's Mountain."</note>, the seat of the most illustrious Prince, the Lord Albert, Duke of Prussia, Margrave of Brandenburg, and the patron of all learned and famous men in our age. **Thorn** <note>Latin: Torunna.</note>, <margin>Nicolaus Copernicus</margin> once a great trading center, but now famous enough because of its "nursling," my Lord Teacher <note>Rheticus refers to Copernicus here. Though Copernicus lived in Warmia, he was born in Thorn.</note>. **Danzig** <note>Latin: Gedanum.</note>, the metropolis of Prussia, conspicuous for its wisdom, the majesty of its Senate, its riches, and the glory of the rebirth of literature. **Warmia** <note>Latin: Varmia.</note>, a college of many learned and pious men, famous for the most reverend Lord Johannes Dantiscus, a most eloquent and wise prelate. **Marienburg**, the treasury of the most serene King of Poland. **Elbing**, an ancient residence of Prussia which also takes up the holy care of letters. **Kulm**, famous for literature and the place from which the "Kulm Law" <note>A set of legal rights used in many towns in the State of the Teutonic Order and later Poland.</note> took its origin. Indeed, you would call the buildings and fortifications the royal palaces and houses of Apollo. The gardens, fields, and the whole region you would call the delights of Venus, <margin>A Plain <note>original Greek: Πεδίον (Pedion)</note></margin> so that it might not undeservedly be called "The Plain."

Furthermore, it is not hidden that Prussia is a daughter of Venus, if one considers either the fertility of the earth or the charm and pleasantness of the whole region. Venus is said to have been born from the sea; so too is this Prussia of hers a daughter of the sea. Therefore, it does not only provide such fertility that Holland and Zeeland are nourished by its harvest, but it is also, as it were, a granary for neighboring kingdoms, as well as for England and Portugal. Besides these things, it supplies in abundance to others all the best kinds of fish and other precious things in which it itself overflows. Moreover, Venus, being anxious for those things which pertain to cultivation, splendor, and living well and humanely—and as the nature of the soil did not refuse them—brought it about that these things could be grown and held in these parts; finally, with the help of the sea, she ensured they could be conveniently imported into Prussia from elsewhere. But since these things are better known to you, most learned Master Schöner, than that they should be related by me at greater length, and since they are treated by others in entire books published on the subject, I shall refrain from a more copious praise.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I will add only this: as the Prussian people are numerous by the blessing of the presiding Divinity, so they are also endowed with singular humanity. Moreover, they cultivate Minerva <note>Goddess of wisdom and the arts.</note> with every kind of art, and for this reason, they feel the kindness of Jupiter. For, not to speak of the lower arts attributed to Minerva, such as architecture and its relatives: first the most illustrious Prince, then all the prelates and nobles of Prussia who hold the highest power, and the governors of the Republics, embrace (as becomes heroes) with the greatest zeal the literature that is being reborn everywhere in the world. Thus, both individually and by common counsel, they strive to nourish and propagate it. Wherefore Jupiter...

...a tawny cloud having gathered, it rained much gold. This is how I interpret it: because Jupiter is said to preside over Empires and Republics, when Great Men take up the care of the studies of wisdom and the Muses, then God gathers the minds of subjects, as well as neighboring Kings, Princes, and Peoples, as if into a golden cloud. From this he distills peace and all the benefits of peace, like golden drops: minds that love tranquility and public peace, cities established with good laws, wise men, the honorable and holy education of children, and finally the pious and pure propagation of religion, and so forth. The shipwreck of Aristippus <note>Aristippus (c. 435–356 BCE) was a follower of Socrates. The story of his shipwreck on Rhodes is a classic anecdote about how education is the only wealth one can carry through a disaster.</note> is often cited, which they say he suffered at the island of Rhodes; when he was cast ashore and saw certain geometric figures on the beach, he ordered his companions to be of good cheer, crying out that he saw the "traces of men." Nor did his opinion deceive him, for by the learning in which he excelled, he easily obtained the necessities for sustaining life from men who were both learned and lovers of virtue. So, as the Gods may love me, most learned Master Schöner <note>Johannes Schöner (1477–1547) was a famous German polymath and the recipient of this "First Account."</note>, since the Prussians are most hospitable, it has not yet happened to me in these parts that I entered the house of any great man without either immediately seeing geometric figures upon the very threshold, or discovering Geometry sitting within their minds. For this reason, nearly all of them, being good men, favor students of these arts with whatever zeal and service they can; for true wisdom and learning are never separated from goodness and beneficence.

He undertook to compose Astronomical Tables with new rules <note>Latin: *canones*; in astronomy, these are the mathematical rules or tables used for calculation.</note>, and promised that if he could be of any use, he would not defraud his own people.

But since he had perceived long ago that observations, by their own right as it were, demand such hypotheses as would not so much overturn the order of motions and spheres correctly accepted and commonly believed up to now—once they had been discussed and examined—as they would appear to conflict with our physical senses. In this way, it would happen that he would stir up no strife among the Philosophers; common Mathematicians would have a corrected calculation of the motions; but the True Artists, whom Jupiter has looked upon with more favorable eyes, would easily arrive at the principles and sources from which everything was derived by using the numbers provided. ...still had to be elaborated upon by the learned, regarding the true hypothesis of the motion of the starry sphere based on the Alfonsine teaching) <note>The Alfonsine Tables were the standard planetary data sets of the late Middle Ages, which were becoming increasingly inaccurate by Copernicus's time.</note> so that everything would be clearly evident to the learned. <margin>Tidemannus Giese. He persuaded Copernicus, with excellent arguments, that he should imitate the candor of Ptolemy, moving beyond the [limit] or envy of the Alfonsines. 1. The work itself would be incomplete, which is clear from the example of the inconveniences of the Alfonsine Tables.</margin>
Thereupon, the Most Reverend [Giese] showed that this gift to the Commonwealth <note>The "Commonwealth of Letters" or the collective world of scholars.</note> would be incomplete unless he also proposed the causes of his Tables, and following the example of Ptolemy, added the design, the reason, the foundations, and the demonstrations by which he sought the mean motions and <term>prosthaphæreses</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæreses." These are "equations of the center," or corrections applied to a planet's mean motion to find its true position.</note>, and confirmed the <term>roots</term> <note>original: "radices." In astronomy, these are "epochs"—the precise positions of celestial bodies at a specific starting date.</note> for the beginnings of time. To this he added how much inconvenience and how many errors this matter had brought into the Alfonsine Tables, since we were forced to assume and approve their findings, not otherwise than they were accustomed to say, **"he himself said it,"** <note>original Greek: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (autós épha). This refers to a blind appeal to authority (the "Ipse dixit") rather than proof.</note> which has no place at all in Mathematics.

<margin>2. Scarcely any craftsmen will find the true foundations of those tables: or if found, they will bring them forth, or dare to bring them forth.</margin>
Furthermore, since these principles and hypotheses are diametrically opposed to the hypotheses of the Ancients, there would scarcely be any craftsman in the future who would see the principles of the Tables and bring them into the public light after the Tables had acquired strength by agreeing with the truth. The situation here is not like what often happens in Empires, councils, and public business, where plans are hidden for a while until the subjects, having perceived the benefit, provide a sure hope that they will approve the plans themselves.

<margin>3. The learned and philosophers will inquire into physical principles all the more diligently on this occasion. Book 2, last chapter of *On the Heavens*. Whether it is certainly demonstrated that the Earth is in the middle of the World. Whether parts of the earth seek the center of the Earth insofar as it is Earth: or insofar as it is the center of the world? Whether circular motions attributed to the earth are to be considered "violent"? Whether straight and circular motion can be separated in actuality.</margin>
As for the Philosophers, the more prudent and learned will more diligently examine the series of Aristotelian disputation, and weigh how Aristotle, after believing he had demonstrated the immobility of the earth with several arguments, finally took refuge in that argument: **"The evidence of the mathematicians about astronomy also bears this out; for the phenomena occur, as the arrangements defining the order of the stars change, as though the earth were situated at the center."** <note>original Greek: "Μαρτυρεῖ δ’ τούτοις καὶ τὰ παρὰ τῶν Μαθηματικῶν λεγόμενα..." Rheticus is quoting Aristotle’s *De Caelo* (On the Heavens), noting that Aristotle relied on the astronomers of his day to "prove" his physics.</note> Furthermore, they will determine for themselves that if this conclusion cannot be supported by the preceding arguments, lest we lose our oil and labor spent, a true account of Astronomy must rather be adopted. Then the fitting solutions of the remaining disputes must be sought, and by returning to principles, it must be examined with greater diligence and equal zeal whether it has been demonstrated that the center of the earth is also the center of the universe; and if the earth were lifted to the orbit of the Moon, whether the torn-off parts of the earth would seek the center of their own globe, or the center of the universe—especially since all falling bodies fall at right angles to the surface of the earth's globe. Moreover, since we see the magnet has a natural motion toward the north of the daily revolution, [one must ask] whether the circular motions attributed to the earth are necessarily **"violent"** <note>In Aristotelian physics, "natural" motion is an object's inherent tendency (like fire rising), while "violent" motion is forced or contrary to nature.</note>. Further, whether three motions—away from the center, toward the center, and around the center—can be separated in actuality: and other things by which Aristotle, as if they were foundations, refuted the findings of Timaeus and the Pythagoreans. And they will weigh these and similar things with themselves, if they wish to look to the principal end of Astronomy, and to the power and industry of God and Nature.

<margin>4. The learned, who [cling] more stubbornly to the ancient opinions they have conceived...</margin>
But if the learned everywhere intend and decide to insist more sharply and stubbornly on their own principles, my Teacher <note>Referring to Nicolaus Copernicus.</note> warned that he ought not to expect a better fortune than that of Ptolemy...

Through these and many other arguments, as I have learned from friends who share in all his affairs, the most learned Prelate <note>Tiedemann Giese, the Bishop of Chełmno (Culm).</note> finally won over my Teacher <note>Referring to Nicolaus Copernicus.</note>, obtaining a promise that he would permit the learned and posterity to pass judgment on his labors. Since this most munificent Prelate loves these studies exceedingly and cultivates them diligently, he even possesses a bronze armillary sphere <note>term: armillary sphere; a model of objects in the sky, consisting of a spherical framework of rings centered on Earth or the Sun.</note> for observing the equinoxes, similar to the two (though somewhat larger) that Ptolemy mentions having been in Alexandria, which learned men from all over Greece once flocked to see. The other of my patrons is the distinguished and energetic Lord Johannes von Werden, Burgrave of Nowe, etc., and Consul of the illustrious city of Danzig. When he heard from certain friends about my studies, he did not disdain to greet me, through his representatives, and to ask that I meet him before I departed from Prussia. When I mentioned this to my Teacher, it pleased him on my behalf, and he described the man to me in such a way that I understood I was being called by someone like Homer's Achilles. For besides the fact that he excels in the arts of war and peace, he also cultivates Music with the favor of the Muses, using its most sweet harmony to refresh and stir his spirit to undertake and endure the burdens of the State. He is worthy of being made a "Shepherd of the People" <note>original: Ποιμένα λαῶν</note> by God Almighty; and blessed is the State over which God has placed such administrators. In the *Phaedo*, Socrates condemns the opinion of those who said the soul was a harmony—and rightly so, if they understood nothing beyond the mixture of elements in the body. But if they defined the soul as a harmony because the human mind alone, along with the gods, understands harmony—just as it alone counts and calculates (for which reason some have not feared to call the soul a Number)—and because they saw that the gravest diseases of the soul are sometimes cured by musical melodies, then this opinion (that the soul of a man, especially a heroic one, is called a harmony) will seem to hold no disadvantage. Therefore, one might most rightly call those States blessed whose governors possess "harmonic souls," which is to say, philosophical natures. Certainly, that famous Scythian did not possess such a soul, for he preferred to hear the neighing of a horse rather than an excellent musician whom others listened to with amazement. # ON THE DIMENSIONS
# OF THE CELESTIAL ORBS AND SPHERES
# according to the Prussian Tables, following the opinion of Nicolaus Copernicus.

## APPENDIX BY MASTER MICHAEL MAESTLIN
## *Professor of Mathematics at the University of Tübingen.*

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a figure and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

So that nothing should be lacking from the most learned and ingenious *Forerunner* <note>Referring to Kepler's book, the *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, which this text was appended to.</note> of the most skilled mathematician Master Johannes Kepler, and the eloquent *Narrative* of Rheticus, I thought it worthwhile to add to them, by way of an Appendix, the dimensions of the sizes—or rather, the heights—of the celestial spheres by which the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> are moved, according to the hypotheses of Copernicus. Although these could have been excerpted and written down without much labor from Copernicus himself, and partly from Ptolemy, I preferred to take them from Erasmus Reinhold. For he himself, as he declares in the preface to the *Prussian Tables* <note>The *Tabulae Prutenicae* (1551), astronomical tables used to calculate the positions of planets, based on Copernicus's work.</note>, and as the numbers of those tables attest, discussed the observations and demonstrations proposed by Copernicus much more exactly and accurately than Copernicus himself. Therefore, I think that the numbers with which Reinhold measured the spheres of the world, and from which he constructed those tables of his called "Prussian," should be followed as perfections. 

It would be desirable if Reinhold's *Commentary* on Copernicus's books—or rather on his own *Prussian Tables*, which he promised several times—were available; from it we could not only describe these dimensions, but also astronomy itself would undoubtedly be greatly aided by many supports for more easily restoring the defects from which it still suffers. But because both this and other most useful works were interrupted by the man's unexpected and untimely death, the other remaining path must be attempted, by which one returns from the end to the beginning through a "retrograde method" <note>Working backward from the results to find the initial principles.</note>. Therefore, the numbers written in his tables must be resolved, and from them must be extracted those values which Reinhold found through a diligent examination of observations and demonstrations for the sake of establishing those very tables. I hope that these things will be of no small use to this admirable discovery of Master Kepler's, presented in this book.

->A P P E N D I X<-

### THEORY OF THE SUN, OR RATHER THE GREAT ORB
### of the Earth, and its dimension.

<image-desc>An astronomical diagram showing several overlapping circles and arcs. A central point 'A' is surrounded by a large outer circle labeled 'B-C-D' (the Zodiac). Inside this are smaller circles and points labeled 'E', 'F', 'G', 'H', 'I', 'K', 'L', 'M', 'N', 'O', 'P', 'Q', 'R', and 'S', illustrating the varying eccentricity of the solar orbit or Earth's orbit according to the Copernican system. Two small circular paths for centers of eccentricity are shown.</image-desc>

In this diagram, **A** is the center of the world, in which, according to Copernicus, the **Sun** resides. **B C D** represents the **Zodiac** in the sphere of the fixed stars. **E F G** is the **eccentric** <note>An 'eccentric' is a circular orbit where the central body—the Sun—is not at the exact geometric center.</note>, or the annual orb of the earth, whose eccentricity is assumed to be mobile; for its center **H** revolves around **I** in a small circle **H K L**. When this center is at **H**, the highest point from **A**, the eccentric is, as stated, **E F G**, and **A H** is the maximum possible eccentricity. But when the same center is brought down to **L**, the lowest point from **A**, the eccentric is transposed from position **E F G** to **M N O** by its change in placement, and **AL** becomes the minimum eccentricity of all, according to Proposition 8 of the third book of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid's *Elements* of Geometry.</note>. However, we must understand here an **eccentric of the eccentric**, or an **eccentreccentric orb**, in whose embrace these eccentrics **E F G** and **M N O** are contained, and which carries the center around **H K L** about its own center **I**, just as is conceived in the ancient theories of **Ptolemy**, or the common hypotheses, regarding the theory of Mercury.

Astronomers <note>original: "Artifices" (Artificers), meaning practitioners of the mathematical arts.</note> understood this kind of approach of the true center of the eccentric toward **A**, and its recession from the same, by the variation of the <term>prosthaphæreses</term> <note>Also known as the 'equation of center,' this is the difference between the mean position and the true observed position of a celestial body.</note>. For in the age of **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**, they were found to be much larger, and thereafter smaller. This approach of the centers is entirely consistent with those observations. For if straight lines **H F** and **L N** are drawn parallel outside the line of the apogee, and likewise **A F** and **A N**, the former [H F and L N] designate the **mean motion**, and the latter [A F and A N] the **true motion** of the Sun or the earth in the same arc of the eccentric (since **E F** and **M N** are equal by Proposition 26 of the third book). But it is manifest that angle **H F A** is greater than **L N A**, for the reason that, with **F H A** and **N L A** being equal by Proposition 29 of the first book, **F A H** is seen to be smaller than **N A L**, as if it were a part of it.

Copernicus reasons that the same center of the eccentric descended from **H** toward **L** in a circular line based on the unequal motion of the Sun’s **apogee** <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>. For that which Ptolemy believed to be entirely immobile from the time of Hipparchus to his own, due to its excessive slowness, Copernicus discovered to proceed more quickly. To this corresponds the motion of center **I**, in the small circle **I P Q**, which is uniform about **A**, by which the line of the mean apogee **A I B** proceeds uniformly through the Zodiac according to the order of the signs; but at **H** the center of the true eccentric moves against that order, and about **L** it moves according to that order. There, therefore, around **H**, at the maximum eccentricity, the line of the true apogee—drawn from center **A** through the center of the true eccentric—meets the line of the mean apogee at almost equal paces; but here around **L**, both tend toward the same point. Moreover, the greatest distance between the true and mean apogee is marked by a straight line from **A** tangent to the small circle, such as **A K R** is here, indicating the center of the eccentric described from **K** (only the arc is depicted here, with the apogee at **S**).

The motion of the eccentric is annual. The motion of the anomaly from the mean apogee...
