->A P P E N D I X. 151<-

It is also nearly a year. The revolution of the true eccentric center <note>The 'eccentric center' is the point around which the Earth orbits, which is slightly offset from the Sun in this model.</note> in the small circle **H K L** is, according to Copernicus (Book 3, Chapter 20), 3,434 years; this is equal to the anomaly of the obliquity of the ecliptic <note>The 'obliquity of the ecliptic' refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbital plane, which astronomers then believed changed over very long periods.</note>. To the circle **I P Q**, Copernicus attributes an annual motion (Book 3, Chapter 22) of 24 seconds, 20 thirds, 14 fourths <note>These are sub-divisions of a degree: a second is 1/60th of a minute, a third is 1/60th of a second, and a fourth is 1/60th of a third.</note> beneath the sphere of the fixed stars. Therefore, its period rises to 54,000 years. Reinhold <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), a leading astronomer who calculated the Prutenic Tables based on Copernican theory.</note>, following his own calculations, makes its annual motion 25 seconds, 33 thirds, 12 fourths; for there is that much difference between the simple motion of the Sun and its annual anomaly. Thus, the revolution is completed in a little more than 50,000 years. However, under the Zodiac, it completes its circuit in 17,000 years.

Reinhold himself provided the dimension of these Orbs in his table of the Sun's eccentricity, on leaf 98. For in such parts where the radius of the eccentric is 1,000,000, he assumed the maximum eccentricity **A H** to be 41,700 parts (Copernicus, in Book 3, Chapter 21, set it at 417 where the radius of the eccentric is 10,000), but he makes the minimum **A L** 32,190. Therefore, **H L** is 9,510.

### LUNAR THEORY AND ITS DIMENSION.

Copernicus, having rejected the eccentric-epicycle <note>A mathematical model used in older Ptolemaic astronomy where a body moves on a small circle (epicycle) which itself moves on an off-center circle (eccentric).</note> of the common hypotheses from lunar theory—since it satisfied neither the apparent size of the Moon's body (as noted above on page 109) nor the lunar parallaxes <note>Parallax is the change in the apparent position of the Moon when viewed from different points on Earth; older models made the Moon appear much larger or closer than it actually was at certain times.</note>—explains the motion of the lunar course through a concentric circle with two epicycles.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the Copernican lunar theory. It features a central point A (Earth) at the bottom of the diagram, with a vertical line extending through points L, H, C, N, E, to P. A larger circle centered at C represents the first epicycle (EFGH), and a smaller epicycle (IKLM) is attached to it. Various lines and points (P, E, N, M, I, L, Q) demonstrate the positions of the Moon at different phases relative to the Earth and the Sun, illustrating the change in the apparent size of the epicycle during the lunar cycle.</image-desc>

In this diagram, **A** is the center of the Earth; **B C D** is a portion of the concentric circle or lunar orb; **E F G H** is the first, larger epicycle, whose apogee <note>The point furthest from the Earth.</note> is **E** and perigee <note>The point closest to the Earth.</note> is **G**. At **F** and **H**, the smaller or second epicycle **I K L M** is positioned. The larger epicycle carries the first along the orb **A B C** in a monthly motion through the Zodiac according to the sequence of the signs; however, the larger epicycle carries the smaller one above it against the same orb, also in a nearly monthly motion, according to **E F G H**. But the smaller epicycle moves the Moon, which is attached to it, in a half-month cycle according to **I K L M**. Copernicus assigned to the concentric circle the role of the eccentric in the common hypotheses of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, whose 2nd-century Geocentric system was being replaced by the Copernican model.</note>. To the smaller epicycle, he assigned the role of the eccentricity of those same hypotheses, by this law of motion: that the Moon is found in conjunction <note>Symbolized by ☌; when the Moon and Sun are on the same side of Earth (New Moon).</note> and opposition <note>Symbolized by ☍; when the Moon and Sun are on opposite sides of Earth (Full Moon).</note> with the Sun at point **I**, the point nearest to center **C** of the larger epicycle; but in every quadrature <note>Symbolized by ☐; the quarter-moons.</note>, it is found at point **L**, the point furthest from that same center **C**. From this, it follows that for the New and Full Moons, the epicycle of apparent motion is **N I O**, but for the half-moons it is **P L Q**. Of these, the former is the smallest and has the smallest <term>prosthaphaereses</term> <note>original: 'prosthaphaereses'. These are mathematical corrections (equations of the center) added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the true position.</note> according to **C A I**; the latter is the largest and has the largest corrections according to **C A L**. This is not because the first epicycle itself becomes closer or further from the Earth due to some eccentric, but because the apparent epicycle, being composed of two as it were, grows and shrinks in size. Next, this second...

<meta>This page continues the technical mathematical appendix. While the previous page focused on the long-term cycles of the Sun and the Earth's orbit (the "Great Orb"), this page shifts to the Lunar theory, comparing the geometric models of Ptolemy (the ancient standard) and Copernicus (the modern revision), specifically focusing on how they account for irregularities in the Moon's motion.</meta>

->A P P E N D I X.<-

the <note>original: "epicyclus"</note> <term>epicycle</term> <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in pre-modern astronomy to explain variations in speed and distance.</note> of the first [motion] resolves the irregularity. For the arc which Ptolemy (Book 5, Chapter 5) believed to intervene between the mean and true <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> of the epicycle, the smaller epicycle provides by the arc **I K** or **I M**, by which the arc **E F** or the angle **E C F** is increased or decreased by the angle **F C K** or **F C M**.

It is indeed a remarkable thing that Ptolemy, truly blind here (if I may use the same simile as Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus (1514–1574), the sole pupil of Copernicus who helped publish his master's work.</note>), guided only by his staff, aimed so excellently at the mark in demonstrating the motion of longitude. 1. He posits an **eccentric** <note>A circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth.</note> that moves uniformly not around its own center, but around the center of the Earth: in its place, Copernicus substituted a **concentric orb**. Therefore, the regularity of its motion around the center of the Earth is not granted to it by mere assumption, as it was there, but is its rightful due. 2. The **epicycle** in both models appears to increase and decrease: in Ptolemy's model, this is because of its approach to and recession from the Earth, but in Copernicus's, it is due to the combined motion of two epicycles. 3. The motion of the **Moon** in the epicycle is unequal in both: in the former, because of a certain manufactured "mean apogee," and in the latter, because of the size of the second epicycle; except that this <term>equation</term> <note>original: "æquatio"; a mathematical correction used to find the true position of a planet from its mean/average position.</note> increases at the beginning of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its apogee.</note> in the former, and at the end in the latter. 4. And although in particular numbers these equations differ greatly between Ptolemy (or in the *Alphonsine Tables* <note>13th-century astronomical tables produced in Spain.</note>) and Copernicus (or in the *Prutenic Tables* <note>16th-century tables calculated by Erasmus Reinhold based on Copernicus.</note>)—such as the fact that the maximum equation of this anomaly is quite different in both location and quantity. For in Ptolemy, at 114 degrees, 3 minutes, 53 seconds of the anomaly, it grows as large as 13 degrees, 8 minutes, 7 seconds, as Petrus Nonnius <note>Pedro Nunes (1502–1578), a Portuguese mathematician and cosmographer.</note> most learnedly demonstrates in his 4th, 5th, and 6th Annotations on the *Theories of Purbach* <note>Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), whose "New Theories of the Planets" was the standard textbook before Copernicus.</note>. Yet according to the *Prutenic Tables*, that <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>Another term for the "equation" or correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to get the true motion.</note> rises to 12 degrees, 26 minutes, 58 seconds, while the anomaly is 77 degrees, 33 minutes, 2 seconds. Nevertheless, at that location—namely, a quadrant <note>90 degrees.</note> from the beginning of this anomaly—where Ptolemy (Book 5, Chapter 5) took the opportunity to separate the true apogee from the mean, they agree wonderfully.

Reinhold did not express the numbers for the dimensions of the particular orbs here as clearly as he did for the Sun, but they can be derived from the Tables of Equations in this way. The equation of the first epicycle at 1 Sexagesimal [60] and 38 degrees [total 98 degrees] is 4 degrees, 55 minutes, 54 seconds, with an excess of 2 degrees, 44 minutes, 6 seconds, which makes 7 degrees, 40 minutes: the maximum equation of the "divided moon." This is surely the angle **C A L**, where **A L** touches the epicycle **P L C**. Ptolemy (Book 5, Chapter 3) demonstrates such a value from observations; Copernicus (Book 4, Chapter 8), although confirming it with no new observation, resumes it. There is no doubt, therefore, that Reinhold also intended this to be the foundation of his calculation. Therefore, in the triangle **C A L**, because the angle of contact is a right angle, the angle at **A** is 7 degrees, 40 minutes; wherefore, in such parts where **A C** is 1,000,000, from the Table of Sines, **C L** (or **C P**, or **C Q**) is given as 133,410.

Next, according to the degree of anomaly at 1 Sexagesimal [60] and 30 degrees [total 90 degrees], the equation of the second epicycle is noted as 12 degrees, 9 minutes, 56 seconds. -># A P P E N D I X.<-

...one forty-fourth part of the Earth. The Sun, indeed, in its magnitude, exceeds more than 7,300 Moons.

For the sake of delight, I am pleased to add this as well. Since Astronomy, with the help of her sister mathematical arts—namely Geometry and Arithmetic—has flown all the way to the Sun and Moon and measured both their heights and magnitudes: come, let the circle of Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy.</note> herself explain these things to us. Though the Sun and Moon appear to us from Earth as flat circles, she shall reveal the circumferences, diameters, and surface areas of these circles in <term>German miles</term> <note>A historical unit of distance; in the 16th century, one German mile was approximately 7.5 kilometers.</note>, as this is a more commonly known measure.

Having found the proportion of the diameters of the Sun and Moon compared to the Earth (which is: for the Sun ☉, 5 parts 30 minutes 30 seconds; for the Earth, 1 part; and for the Moon ☽, 0 parts 17 minutes 0 seconds), and knowing also that the circumference of the Earth's <term>Great Circle</term> <note>The Equator.</note> is 5,400 German miles, the other values sought will not remain hidden.

1. Since the proportion of the circumferences of a circle is the same as the proportion of the diameters: it will be known from this that the circumference of the Sun’s circle contains a little less than thirty thousand (30,000) miles, while that of the Moon contains over one thousand five hundred (1,500) miles.

2. Archimedes demonstrates that the ratio of the circumference to the diameter is roughly triple and one-seventh (just as 22 is to 7). From this, the diameter of the Sun ☉ is calculated to be a little less than nine thousand five hundred (nearly 9,500), and the diameter of the Moon ☽ nearly five hundred (nearly 490) German miles. These diameters appear to us to be two feet, or rather one foot, in size, divisible into 12 <term>digits</term> <note>A traditional astronomical unit where the disk of a celestial body is divided into 12 equal parts to measure the magnitude of an eclipse or apparent size.</note>.

3. The half-diameter <note>The radius.</note> multiplied by the half-circumference measures the area of the circle; as Archimedes demonstrates regarding the circle, this is equal to a right-angled triangle bounded by the radius and the circumference of the circle. Therefore, the area or plane of the Solar circle exceeds the number of seventy million (70,000,000) square German miles. The plane of the Lunar circle, however, exceeds one hundred eighty-six thousand (186,000) square German miles. Thus much regarding the Lights of heaven, which God created so that they might divide the day and the night, and distinguish the months and the years.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary motion models. -># A P P E N D I X.<-

...in the lower [circle], by this law: that when the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one.</note> is at point B, the planet resides in its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note> G; and conversely, when the epicycle is at D, the planet is at H. By this equality of motions, it happens that while the center of the epicycle moves outside B and D—such as at C—the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> and perigee also shift. In this case, at position C, the angles B A C and K C L (where K is the same as G or I in the previous diagram, and L is the planet) are equal. From this, it follows that the line N L—assuming A N is equal to the radius of the epicycle—must be parallel to A C, and the angle B N L must be equal to angle B A C. Therefore, just as the center of the epicycle moves around A, so the Planet has an equal motion around N. The path of the Planet, however, is the line distorted from G through L to H, which circles roughly around point M (at a distance of one-third $\frac{1}{3}$ of the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance the center of an orbit is offset from the center of the world.</note> E from A). However, **Copernicus** demonstrates in Book 5, Chapter 4, that this path is not perfectly circular. From this arise two points: 1. That **Ptolemy** believed this path G L H of the planet to be truly circular, and therefore placed the planet's eccentric orbit around M. 2. That he established this eccentric G L H should revolve uniformly not around its own center M, but around a different center N, which is therefore called the **Center of the Equant**, and it possesses double the eccentricity of M. <note>original: "Ecce vtroq; oculo cæcus, quam nihil, solius Astronomici baculi aut virgulæ ductu, a via aberrauit?"</note> Behold, though blind in both eyes, how little he strayed from the path while following only the lead of his astronomical staff or rod!

But if we prefer to demonstrate the motion of these planets through the "eccentric of an eccentric," everything returns to the same result. Here, the circle B C D, with center A, represents the motion that drives the center of the true eccentric along the circumference N M—moving toward N in the order of the signs, and toward M against the order of the signs. This follows the rule: whenever the planet is at the apogee or perigee of the eccentric, the center of the true eccentric is at M, and the position of the eccentric itself is along G C H. But when the same planet is a quadrant’s distance away, at C or rather L, the center of the true eccentric rises to N and shows the position of the eccentric according to F C I, where F L is a quadrant. Thus, the path of the planet is again the curved line G L H, not unlike a circle. And N is the point of equality, around which the Planet itself proceeds regularly; for when it is placed at G or H, a straight line is drawn from the center of the true eccentric to the planet through N, because they are on the same line. When it moves to L, that center is united entirely with N. Elsewhere, whenever the center of the true eccentric stays outside M and N, the straight line from it to the planet always passes through N. Necessarily, therefore, just as the motion of the planet is uniform around the (nevertheless mobile) center of the true eccentric, it is likewise made equal around N. This is the **First Anomaly** of the planet relative to E, the center of the World.

After this, the circle O P Q R around E represents the **Great Orbit** of the Earth. In this orbit, the **Second Anomaly** of the Planet (which it has in relation to the Earth) is demonstrated, because looking at the planet from different parts of this orbit produces various angles of apparent motion. For example: if the Planet is at G, its motion relative to E (the center of the World) is the same as its apparent motion only if the Earth is at Q or O. For from the half-circle Q R O, the planet appears further ahead (in <term>consequence</term> <note>Moving forward in the order of the zodiac signs.</note>), but from O P Q it appears further back (in <term>antecedence</term> <note>Moving backward against the order of the zodiac signs; retrograde motion.</note>) from the line E G. Likewise, the motion of the Earth from P (or slightly before) through Q to R (or slightly after) causes the planet to appear to move faster in consequence than the line E G requires; but as the Earth passes through O, whatever speed was gained is here taken back. Thus, the planet not only becomes slow, but appears to move backward in antecedence. **Ptolemy** thought these things were caused by a specific epicycle unique to each planet; but here, this one **Great Orbit** is sufficient.

### DIMENSIONS OF THE SPHERE OF SATURN ♄.

In the Prutenic Tables, for an <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its apogee (farthest point).</note> of 1 <term>sexagesimal</term> <note>In the astronomical system of the time, a "sexagesimal" represents a unit of 60 degrees.</note> and 30 degrees, the <term>prosthaphairesis</term> <note>A correction or "equation" added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the true position.</note> of the eccentric is recorded as 6 degrees, 29 minutes, and 53 seconds. In the diagram, that anomaly is B C, or F L, a quadrant from the eccentric's apogee, and the prosthaphairesis is the angle N L E, due to the eccentricity of the orbit F L from E; or, it is the angle R E T from the mean apogee of the <term>commutation</term> <note>The relative position of the planet and the Sun.</note> (with line R E P being parallel to line N L or A C) to T, its true apogee. However, in a system where the radius of the sphere of Saturn A C (or N L) is 100,000 (this value of the <term>total sine</term> <note>The standard radius used in trigonometric tables of the era.</note> is sufficient here, and it is likely that Reinhold used no larger number), the second table of tangents shows N E to be 11,390, and its half M E to be 5,695. From these, the distance of Saturn at apogee E G from the center of the world is known to be 105,695, and at <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center.</note> E H to be 94,305, where the radius of the sphere itself is 100,000. **Copernicus**, in Book 5, Chapter 9, has 10,569 and 9,431, where A B is 10,000; for in chapters 5 and 6, he measured E N as 1,139, E A as 854, and B G (or A N) as 285.

Next, for the same anomaly of 1 sexagesimal and 30 degrees, the prosthaphairesis of the orbit's <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent displacement of the planet as seen from Earth due to the Earth's own motion.</note> is noted as 1 degree, 53 minutes, and 40 seconds, with an Excess of 0 degrees, 42 minutes, and 19 seconds to be added, so that the other prosthaphairesis is 6 degrees, 35 minutes, 59 seconds. The first of these is the angle E G F, and the other is E H F, corresponding to a quadrant of the <term>Great Circle</term> <note>In the Copernican system, the "Great Circle" (Orbis Magnus) refers to the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> O P or Q P—the former when Saturn is at apogee G, and the latter when it is at perigee H. Therefore, in the right-angled triangles G E P and H E P, using the given angles at G and H, the remaining angles at the right angles, G P E and H P E, also become known. Thus, where the radius of the Great Circle E P is 100,000 (it is helpful to make the radius of the Great Circle the "total sine" both here and in what follows, so it becomes a common measure for all the spheres), E G is calculated from the second Table as 968,600, and E H as 864,312 or 864,300. (One may assume this number instead of the other without any sensible difference; for it is neither necessary nor useful to investigate everything with excessive and minute precision, which it could be proven in many instances that Reinhold also did.) From this, the total G E H is 1,832,900, and its half is 916,450. Where the radius of the Great Circle is 1 part, Saturn's maximum altitude from the center of the world E G results in 9 parts, 41 minutes, 10 seconds; and the minimum E H in 8 parts, 38 minutes, 35 seconds. The mean distance, which is the radius of the sphere of Saturn, is 9 parts, 9 minutes, 52 seconds. Furthermore, the straight line E P, the radius of the Great Circle, contains 1,160 radii of the Earth, as we computed above.

Where and how large this maximum parallax prosthaphairesis might be when Saturn is moving in its <term>apsides</term> <note>The points of greatest or least distance in an orbit.</note> is easily found; for the lines G V and H X, tangent to the Great Circle, contain them along with the now-known E G and H. Therefore, from E G and E H, the Table of hypotenuses or <term>secants</term> <note>Trigonometric ratios used to find distances from angles.</note> offers the angle E G V at apogee as 5 degrees, 55 minutes, 33 seconds, and E H X at perigee as 6 degrees, 38 minutes, 39 seconds. The complements of these angles to a right angle are the angles G E V and H E X, or the arcs O V and Q X, indicating the distance of the Earth from the apogee of the commutation, which there is 1 sexagesimal, 35 degrees, 55 minutes, 33 seconds; and here 1 sexagesimal, 36 degrees, 38 minutes, 39 seconds.

## DIMENSIONS OF THE SPHERE OF MARS ♂.

The calculation for the dimension of the Martial sphere is a little more intricate, because **Reinhold** <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), an astronomer who calculated the Prutenic Tables based on Copernican theory.</note> computed all the prosthaphaireses of Mars according to its diminished <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>. For after the center of the Great Orbit (which we have hitherto accepted as the center of the world for the reasons stated above) notably approached the true Sun—the center of the world—and thus also the center of the orbit of Mars, he also changed its eccentricity E A or E M so that it became perceptible in the prosthaphaireses; see **Copernicus**, Book 5, chapter 4, folio 143a, and chapter 16, folio 158a; likewise above on page 131.

For an <term>anomaly</term>, in the tables of Mars ♂, of 1 <term>sexagesimal</term> <note>A unit of 60 degrees.</note> and 30 degrees, the prosthaphairesis of the eccentric is found to be 11 degrees, 3 minutes, 3 seconds, which is angle L N E; because of this, the second table reckons E N as 19,530 in parts of the radius of the sphere itself N L, which is 100,000.

Then, at the same anomaly of 1 sexagesimal and 30 degrees, the apogeal prosthaphairesis of the parallax of the orbit is set as angle E G P, 30 degrees, 59 minutes, 4 seconds; and with the excess of 5 degrees, 1 minute, 58 seconds added, the perigeal parallax, angle E H P, is 36 degrees, 1 minute, 2 seconds. Therefore, of which units E P is 100,000, of such units E G must be 166,530 and E H 137,550, and the whole diameter G H 304,080; its half indeed, H M or A B, is 152,040, and E M is 14,490. But where the radius A B of the sphere of Mars ♂ was previously 100,000, E M comes out as 9,530, of which units E N was also 19,530. Therefore, the remainder M N is 10,000. However, E M and M N ought to have been equal unless the eccentricity had been diminished; Reinhold assumes it to be 470 parts smaller. **Copernicus**, in Book 5, chapter 15, teaches that E N was demonstrated by **Ptolemy** to be 2,000 parts and E A to be 1,500; but he says in chapter 16 that he himself found E A to be 1,460, of which units A B is 10,000.

But of which units E P is one part, in this minimum eccentricity, E G is 1 part, 39 minutes, 55 seconds, and E H is 1 part, 22 minutes, 32 seconds, and the radius A B of the sphere of Mars ♂ is 1 part, 13 minutes, 13 seconds.

### THEORY OF THE SPHERE OF VENUS ♀, AND ITS DIMENSION.

The logic of the motion of Venus ♀ is very similar to that in the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which orbit further from the Sun than Earth.</note>; for its theory can be explained equally through an eccentric of an eccentric, or through an eccentric-epicycle, or, if one prefers, through a concentric with two epicycles, just as was done in the preceding sections. The difference is that Venus is closer to the center of the world, inside the Great Orbit <note>The *Orbis Magnus*, or Earth's orbit around the Sun in the Copernican system.</note>; and while the epicycles or eccentric-eccentrics of the three superior planets are commensurable with their own proper eccentric, those in Venus do not follow their own eccentric, but rather the Great Orbit. Thus it happens that those superior planets strictly maintain a single path for their motion—namely, the circle (or quasi-circle) G L H; but Venus, not remaining confined by these constraints, wanders into all the angles of the region enclosed between the circles marked with dots, as is clear from the nearby figure.

The outer orbit Q L K, around E, is the Great Orbit of the Earth; the sphere of Venus is visible within it. The motions of its orbits are bound by these laws: Whenever the Earth is at the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center.</note> Q, or the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the center.</note> R of Venus, the center of Venus’s eccentric at M approaches the center of the world E as closely as possible, and Venus herself is found in the circle G C M. However, when the Earth is placed in <term>quadrature</term> <note>A 90-degree angle relative to the Sun.</note>, as around L, that center recedes to point N, the furthest point from the center of the world, and Venus is then seen in the eccentric F C I, wherever she may be within it, etc.

In this theory, the decrease in the eccentricity of the Great Orbit—as its center E approaches the center of Venus's orbit A—is perceptible, just as it is in Mars; for its sake, the prosthaphaireses are found to be diminished. **Reinhold** <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), the German astronomer who calculated the Prutenic Tables based on Copernicus's work.</note> also calculated them here according to this diminished eccentricity.

### THE THEORY OF MERCURY (☿), AND ITS MEASUREMENT.

The theory of this planet consists of many complications, just as the labor of its measurement is constant, because of the <term>prosthaphæreses</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæreses"; these are correction angles used to calculate a planet's true position from its average motion</note> of several orbits being mixed together much differently than in the preceding examples. Its theory according to Copernicus is as follows: With the Center of the World at **A** (which here, as in the preceding ones, is the center of the Great Orbit <note>The "Great Orbit" refers to the Earth's orbit around the Sun in the Copernican system.</note>), the Great Orbit is **BCD**. **E** is the center around which the center of the eccentric’s eccentric <note>Copernicus used nested circles to explain the complex variations in planetary speed and distance.</note> carries the center of the <term>eccentrepycycle</term> <note>a secondary circle whose center is itself on an off-center path</note> around in a small circle **FG**, though by different laws. For whenever the Earth is in the line of the apogee **B**, or the perigee **D**, the center of the eccentrepycycle ascends to **F**, the peak of the small circle most remote from **A**; therefore the position of the eccentric itself is **HI**. Mercury himself is found at the lowest peak of the epicycle, **K** or **L**, closest to the center of the eccentric; thus in that position, the circle of Mercury's path is **KML**, the narrowest it can possibly be. (The epicycle **NIO** in the theory of the Moon on page 164 corresponds to this.) But if the Earth is in a position midway between the <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit closest to or farthest from the center</note>, such as at **C**, the center of the eccentric descends to **G**, the point closest to the center of the world **A** (these things happen in an entirely opposite manner from the superior planets) and restores the eccentric to **NO**. Mercury himself, however, ascends to the highest peak of the epicycle **P** or **Q**, and describes the widest orbit of his path along **PRQ** (the epicycle **PLQ** in the Moon's theory corresponds to this). Furthermore, Copernicus established that Mercury does not move through the circumference, but ascends and descends through the diameter of this epicycle, the sort of <term>librations</term> <note>oscillatory or back-and-forth linear motions</note> that can occur according to the method explained on page 125. By these motions, it happens that when the Earth is at **B**, the <term>prosthaphæreses</term> of Mercury's parallax are the smallest of all; for Mercury's orbit is both at its smallest, according to **KML**, and it appears smallest because the Earth is at its most remote distance from it. But at the perigee **D**, the orbit is again indeed at its smallest, but it appears larger because it is closer. In the quadrature <note>a 90-degree angle relative to the Sun</note> at **C**, the orbit is indeed at its largest, but because it is further from the Earth, it appears no larger. But around **S**, at a third of a circle from **B**, or a sixth from **D**, Ptolemy and Copernicus establish that it appears largest, and therefore requires the greatest corrections <note>prosthaphæreses</note>, by which it may depart furthest from its mean place or from the Sun, since in that place, this effect is produced by a mutual compensation of the distance and the true magnitude.

It is easily evident from what has been said that the measurement of Mercury's orbits must be investigated differently from the tables of corrections, because even if the parallaxes are smallest at the apogee, the excess placed nearby is not of the perigee, but of another place, distant by a sixth [of a circle] from there, where the orbit has another magnitude and the center has another position. Nor can the proportional minutes <note>fractions of a degree used for fine adjustments</note> be sufficiently trusted here. Therefore, the procedure must be as follows.
